recipes.name: "Normal" Medium Gloop
recipes.description: "Normal" Gloop. This is a demonstration of "gloop" at a more normal glaze chemistry with a fixed flux ratio of 0.25:0.75, boron level of 0.15, and Silica:Alumina ratio of 8.0. These tests were created using a line blend, moving from low to high Silica and Alumina. At the low end, the blends are proper glazes, while at the high end the blends act more like self-glazing clays. The middle blends can be classified as "gloops". This is the second test of the line blend, with the second highest level of Alumina and Silica. It is a "hard" gloop. Other tests from this blend: "Normal" Hard Gloop "Normal" Soft Gloop Note: I added Veegum T so that the gloop is more plastic and more easily molded in the wet stage. You could substitute Veegum with Bentonite, or you could just leave it out completely. I added some Mason Stain for color, you could also leave it out for a white gloop. Preparation: Tests were prepared by adding 40% water by weight, blending at high speed, then drying into a paste on plaster. The test samples were then rolled into balls and placed on top of test tiles. Compare to a similar result with B2O3 0.3: https://glazy.org/recipes/59365

recipes.description: "Normal" Gloop. This is a demonstration of "gloop" at a more normal glaze chemistry with a fixed flux ratio of 0.25:0.75, boron level of 0.15, and Silica:Alumina ratio of 8.0. At the low end, the blends are proper glazes, while at the high end the blends act more like self-glazing clays. The middle blends can be classified as "gloops". recipes.name: 20ish x5 Pink
recipes.description: This is the first color glaze I've attempted to make. I've been thinking about it for over a year—but after a couple failed attempts in other's kilns—I waited until I got my own to try any glaze development. It took a bit of research and tweaking to get it to even work, but it's just about exactly what I was hoping for. The pink is variegated all over, but it's darker when thick and very blush when thinner. The first pics here are of a piece that was poured, which resulted in some really lovely variation. The second piece was double dipped and it's a bit too pink. But it's interesting how it shows the range of variation in one glaze. The third piece has dark specs from the clay and a fade from surfacing slowly from a full dip. Something to pursue for sure. ## Tin:Chrome Pink The pink is a reaction between Tin Oxide (often used to opacify a clear glaze) and Chrome Oxide (green in color and a common way to make a green glaze). I originally read about it in the comments of a Facebook group post (https://bit.ly/2XCbn7b) over a year ago. They said that an 80:1 ratio of Tin to Chrome would create a pink reaction: "Those are actually speckles of chrome oxide that have been flashed with tin oxide. If you have too much chrome, the tin flashing goes dull and green. But if you just have a little chrome in ratio to tin, the tin flashes the chrome pink." My first attempt added 14% Tin and 0.18% Chrome (80:1) to my existing base glaze. It came out a pretty disgusting green. 14% is a lot of Tin, especially considering how expensive that shit is. But I now know the ratio was good. At the time I got some feedback from some knowledgeable folks in another FB group which led me to try a few things: lowering the Tin to 5% and scaling the Chrome down in proportion; switching the Silica from 200 to 350 mesh; switching the Frit from 3134 to 3124. This second test came out clear—the reaction wasn't working. More recently I found a recipe by David Tsabar on Glazy (https://glazy.org/recipes/7871). His recipe used a Tin:Chrome ratio of 250:1—an even smaller amount. But I think the more important change was to the base glaze. ## Base Glaze I read in a Ceramic Arts Network article by John Britt that "The calcium content of the glaze should be high (10–15% or 0.7–0.9 moles). It is also important to have no zinc in the recipe or the glaze will turn brown. Alumina is also best if kept low. Some recommend no magnesium oxide (talc, dolomite, or magnesium carbonate) in the base recipe while others use small amount of MgO to achieve interesting red/burgundy colors" David started from the same base glaze I use (Tony Hansen's 20x5), but made some alterations: He lowered the Feldspar to 15%, which contributes a fair amount of Al₂O₃ (Aluminum Oxide) and increased the Wollastonite to 25%, which provides most of the CaO (Calcium Oxide). Perhaps there were other variables—I've moved countries since the initial tests so all the materials come from different mines—but I believe the change to the base glaze facilitated the reaction. ## Line Blend After successfully getting a very pale pink with 0.02% Chrome, I wanted to see how pink I could get it. I'd saw a red glaze in the same Ceramic Arts Network article that had 0.20% Chrome in 5% Tin. So I hypothesized that doing a line blend from 0.02%–0.20% Chrome would result in a pale pink to red spectrum. The result was a really nice range of pinks between 0.02% and 0.06%. By 0.10% the color starts shifting toward puce instead of red, as the green of the chrome starts showing. An interesting color but clearly not red. In the test tiles, the pink also looked much better on a pure white clay body. My theory here is that even though 5% Tin should be enough to opacify a clear glaze, the Tin is sort of 'used up' by the Chrome. These pics have a bit of Zircopax (another opacifier) added which appears to lighten it. I was meticulous with my calculations and measurements for these tests—I'd worked out how much base glaze to add to the combined tests to dilute it down to 0.04% and not have any waste. But I absentmindedly added Chrome after having a couple beers at the pub so I had to yolo-eyeball it. ## Further Tests - Tin is $120 a kilogram, so it'd be good to use less of it. A pale pink might be achievable keeping the ratio on the higher end (80:1) but dropping the volume of both. E.g. 2.5% Tin and 0.03% Chrome. - I added some Zircopax to opacify the base glaze to provide a better backdrop for the pink on less than pure-white clay bodies. There's about 4% in here due to my yolo-eyeballing and that actually seems really quite nice. But might do another line blend or just start the next batch should start with 4 or 5%. - John Britt mentioned in the Ceramic Arts article that adding a small amount of MgO could result in red/burgundy colors which could be interesting to pursue. It'd be amazing to tweak the base glaze enough to maintain pink but get red instead of puce with higher amounts of Chrome.

recipes.name: AC Purple Spot and color variations
recipes.description: This recipe is evolved from experiments trying to make John Britt's Purple Spot glaze. The base is Randy's Red or Randy's Blue, depending on what is added as a colorant. A magnesium purple spotted glaze which I could not replicate with my materials. John gave me a lot of help and recipes to try with my frits. His recipe called for Minspar. The Forshammer feldspar I use is too low in natron. After a lot of failed tests, I changed the feldspar to nepheline syenite, adjusted the recipe on the calculator and have this result. The glazes has to be applied very thickly. Fired fast to cone 6 ox. with no hold. Holds will change the crystal formation, so different colors and crystal sizes are possible. Recently I saw a test made with an equal sub. of GB for Ulexite and fired to cone 7. It looked very similar.

recipes.name: Al's Shino
recipes.description: From Steve Davis Website: http://kazegamas.com/ Shinos 1: http://kazegamas.com/shinos1.htm There are 72 shinos shown on 4 web pages. They are organized from left to right with 3 tiles of the same glaze shown on 3 different clay bodies. They are Aardvark Clay's Nara Porcelain, Long Beach, and Black Mountain. Every shino was glazed with a doulble dip, waxed with a simple "S" pattern, and left to dry for 2 weeks to grow sulfates on the surface. The "S" pattern has no sulfate build up. A medium reduction was started at cone 012 through cone 2. From there the kiln was fired in neutral to cone 10.

recipes.description: The original recipe can be found here: https://digitalfire.com/4sight/recipes/albertasliprutilebluecone631.html The article above suggests calcining part of the Alberta Slip, I have found that to be unnecessary. The color comes out just as strong without the extra step. The glaze looks beautiful on white or dark clay.

recipes.name: Alberta Slip Rutile plus Cobalt Carb
recipes.description: This is a good option if you are having trouble getting blue from Tony Hansen's GA6-C recipe which usually requires a slow cool. I added 2% cobalt carbonate to this recipe to guarantee the blue without a slow cool. You can experiment with smaller amounts of cobalt too. 0.5-1% has worked well for some other potters who have tried this. I do not roast/calcine any of the Alberta Slip as Tony recommends - I find the glaze is fine without it and will only crack on drying if applied thickly - and even then, the cracks smooth out beautifully in my firings. I keep it at 1.45 SG and do a 2 second dip on Plainsman m390 and m350 clay. The glaze does settle quickly so make sure to stir it every few minutes. I'm now able to get blue without cobalt so I'm using Tony's original recipe now, but adding cobalt was an excellent helper for me when I first started. This is a perfect replacement for Amaco Blue Rutile. - Stiina From the Alberta Slip Rutile description: "The original recipe can be found here: https://digitalfire.com/4sight/recipes/albertasliprutilebluecone631.html The article above suggests calcining part of the Alberta Slip, I have found that to be unnecessary. The color comes out just as strong without the extra step. The glaze looks beautiful on white or dark clay."

recipes.name: Alisa Butter Base
recipes.description: Author: Alisa Liskin Clausen Comments: Glaze made because I mixed WoDo 40/10 wrong and could remember my mistake. The initial mistake glaze looked semi mat which is a base I have been trying to get. After some changes to get the Silica higher, I made this base. Overall a smooth surface, butter sheen, fattens up with additions of Rutile and Titanium. Can get glossier with some oxide mix addtions. Copper gives some oil spot effects, dark and browns. Good color results with Cobalt and Opacifiers. Must look at edges, and closely overall, as there are many color nunances and changes. Some high fire looks as well.

recipes.name: Alkaline Lee Rexrode
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Alkaline for chartreuse: 0.5% chrome oxide From Margaret Bohls: fired cone 9 electric Gorgeous satin, slightly sugary surface. Slightly translucent. I use the Base White as a complementary glaze to a shiny white or clear glaze over porcelain, for a "white on white" effect. The chartreuse, although equally gorgeous, fumes like mad and may affect glazes next to it on the same pot or in the same area in the kiln, either by turning them green or by making them wrinkle or bubble. Some glazes are unaffected. I isolate this glaze in the kiln.

recipes.name: Amber Assault +F38 Frit + Li 04
recipes.description: From Linda Arbuckle: Under 45x magnification, slight crazing. > "I put this together for a friend of mine who was using a lowfire barium amber. I was looking at Sr ambers and olive green transparent lowfire glazes. At some point I’d like to add just a touch more lithium to the Higher Power and Amber Assault + Li and Sr tests to get rid of very mild crazing I see under magnification. Other goals were to have a lowfire glaze that had enough clay to apply well. I find the very high frit lowfire glazes have to go on so very thin that they’re a challenge to dip-glaze well. They always look too thin to me, and if they’re thick, they trap bubbled and get crater-y." Firing Notes: All tiles fired upright. 03 sitter cone to give an junior cone 04 bending visual. Average coating of glaze on the left, thicker on the right. On terracotta clay with slips (white, black, green, pink, yellow). I’d like to test bumping the lithium up just a tad on the Higher Power to get rid of the slight crazing. Doesn’t show crazing unless viewing under magnification, so it’s slight.

I began by testing many recipes and noting both likes and dislikes of each glaze test. Noticing patterns, it became obvious to me that I really enjoyed a shino that included the ingredient Spodumene. BINGO! I also enjoy simple recipes with few ingredients the most, so the recipe came quite easily after the testing. Enjoy! Notes: This is a cone 10 glaze that likes a hot firing. What I love about it: it fires from creamy white to dark orange, thick to thin; it pinholes beautifully where you trim; it has a wonderful feel; it doesn’t crawl. recipes.name: Anderson Blue
recipes.description: Matt glaze almost black where thin, army green where thick. Nice colonial (bluish slate) over white slip Well I finally got around to typing this thing up...^9-10 Blues Thank you one and all for all the donated recipes. I only tested 31 out of almost 100 I received. I'll continue testing and reporting as the winter DRAGS on. All the glazes were tested on #900 Miller clay which is a toasty ^10 stoneware. One side of the test tile was brushed with a thick coating of Cynthia Bringle's wet/dry white slip. Each glaze was dipped in three thicknesses on a heavily textured tile. All tiles were fired to a (hard)^9 (10 tipping)reduction firing. 1 hr. Body reduction at ^08 and 1 hr. glaze reduction at ^9 then a quick reox. before shutdown. Any time potash or Custer spar is called for, I used G-200. All ball clay is OM-4 . Many glazes I substituted 75% of the amount of Barium with Strontium. All kaolin is EPK. Remember... glazes don't travel well. Your results will probably be TOTALLY different. Please test before use. Tracy Wilson Saltbox Pottery

recipes.name: Andie's Golden Fake Ash
recipes.description: Found on the Clayart mailing list in a message by Bob Johnson. Bob writes: > A while back Bill Schran and Jackie Miller asked me to share the recipes for Hannah's fake ash and Andie's fake ash. Sorry for the delay, but I am happy to do so: I believe that these glazes are available on the internet, so I believe I am not violating any confidences. Hannah's Golden Fake Ash (cone 6 oxidation or reduction) Strontium Carbonate 9.90 Whiting 28.43 RedArt 56.96 Ferro 3195 4.71 Add: Bentonite 1.00 Red Iron Oxide 3.24 Yellow Iron Oxide 2.75 > Note: Various versions of this can be found on the internet. This one, I believe, was originally a cone 10 recipe that may have been modified by Steven Hill for cone 6 electric. It was originally developed by Hannah Brehmer of Ashland, Oregon. Hannah's Blue Ash is essentially the same recipe, but with 1.27% cobalt oxide instead of the iron oxides. (If using cobalt carbonate instead of the oxide, you must make the conversion.) Steven Hill also has a fake ash, made with copper carb, that gives a greenish hue. You can find it also on the internet at http://www.carolclarksonpottery.com/blog/2016/05/25/Copper-Ash-Glaze-Recipe-Steven-Hill.aspx > Andie's Golden Fake Ash (cone 6 oxidation or reduction) Strontium Carb 12 Lithium Carb 2 Gerstley Borate 10 Bone Ash 5 Dolomite 24 RedArt 27 Kentucky Old Mine #4 20 > Note: This is very well-behaved, for an ash-type glaze. I like to use it in combination with Val Cushing's G4 ash glaze, with 3% RIO + 2% Yellow iron oxide + 5% rutile. Put the Val Cushing near the top of the pot, because it will run. You can see this combination on a covered jar shown on my Flickr page at https://www.flickr.com/photos/psychoceramics/ > The Val Cushing G4 ash glaze recipe is in the ClayArt archives. See: https://lists.clayartworld.com/pipermail/clayart/2014-November/003974.html > Anyone else have a favorite ash (or fake ash) glaze you are willing to share? > Bob Johnson in Wilbur, Oregon

recipes.name: Anita’s Green Crackle /Yellow Matte
recipes.atmosphere: Reduction, Salt & Soda, Wood, Oxidation, Neutral
recipes.description: Simple 3 ingredient glaze developed from a Triaxial under the direction of John Britt. Applied very thick will pool in recesses to a Green Crackle Celadon on B-mix and where thin on iron-bearing stoneware (like studio pug that has some brown clay but mostly light stoneware) will give a light yellow matte that lets the speckles in the clay shine through. Poured will give lots of variation due to thick/thin application areas and gives a wood fired look to the surface. Designed to run so leave room at the bottom, will crackle if thick and green, won’t crackle if thin and yellow matte. No colorants needed as the iron in Alberta Slip is sufficient. If you use or make any changes to this glaze please give me credit (Anita Ries) by keeping the original name and add the word “modified.” TIPS Add 2% bentonite if making large batches as the high neph sy content will cause this glaze to hardpan Use less water to get the green crackle effect and thin the mixture down using teaspoon or so of Darvan 7 or Sodium Silicate. If you add too much water, this will give you a thin application no matter how many times you dip, resulting in a more yellow/tan matte surface. Play w/ the application to create visual interest in your piece and get green crackle and yellow/tan matte areas. This glaze does well substituting Redart or local clay high in iron. Leave room at the bottom in case it runs Do not apply too thick a coat on the inside of functional vessels, the glaze will be green and pool nicely but may allow liquids to slowly leak at the bottom. For functional items that will hold liquids, it’s better to be judicious with the application. Thank you to the following artists for their feedback by testing the glaze and/or submitting images of their results: Paula Weiss Ginger Lukas Robyn Irene Vicki Chamberlain

recipes.name: Ash Glaze Rhodes revised
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Ash use mixed hardwood ash + CMC Last year, with a lot of help from Tom Buck and some of the other Clayart gurus, I adjusted one of the old Daniel Rhodes ash glazes. Original recipe (Cone 9-10): Mixed hard wood ash 35 Oxford spar 35 China clay 15 Talc 15 I fire in an electric kiln. I would never describe it as a foolproof glaze, but if applied with care, it's so beautiful that it just knocks out all the reliable competition. I bisque at ^06 and am now firing at ^6. I have gone to ^9, but that seems to present more problems with pinholing and crazing. Also, I wash the ash. I have also used the same recipe with unwashed ash. The difference is that I would describe the unwashed ash glaze as stony matt and the washed ash glaze as opaque satin matt. Haven't tried this recipe at a lower temperature. You might want to give it a try. marjory r. kline

Once I screen the content I took some of the larger particles and included it in the clay. The largest particles left over, and there most likely will be some, was put in the urns and sealed. So the finished product contained bone ash in the clay, in the glaze and in the end after final firing the cremains left over were sealed in each container and returned to the family. some of the small calcined (from cremation) fragments acted like iron bleeding in spots through the clay and glaze. It didn't run and I did add some colorants to this glaze. The results were nice!

recipes.name: Ash McWhinnie Base
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Ash For a Cone 6 glaze, Nepheline Syenite can be substituted for the Custer Feldspar. Kevin O'Hara asked about a reliable base formula for an ash glaze. We have been using the glaze base provided by Harold McWhinnie in his November 1986 'Ceramics Monthly' article (A Multipurpose Glaze, p. 75). We repeat it below. If you have any questions about this glaze, we believe that Harold is now monitoring the Clayart list regularly. We have experimented with various types of wood ash. We now use pecan hull ash. Fortunately, we have many pecan trees in the area along with cracking plants that kindly supply us with the hulls. There is a lot of oil in pecan hulls (including many nuts) so they burn hot with very little but fine ash. We do not wash this ash; however, we have found that we must wash other wood ash. We experimented with Victoria's Secret ash (burned their ceasely catalogs) but found it full of trash and required cleaning. John and Judy McCain Palo Pinto Pottery

recipes.name: ash Zakin's GK
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Ash > ClayArt Listserv recipe < If you find this glaze useful, please consider submitting it to the GlazeBase project with full documentation. Use one of the GlazeBase submission formats available on the CeramicsWeb web page. comments: Use unwashed fireplace ash. Doesn't add to 100 because of the strontium/barium substitution, the bentonite, and the ash. This may be closer to cone 5 than cone 6 but seems to work over a range of a couple cones. This is Zakin's GK base with 15% unwashed, mixed fireplace ashes, with strontium substituted for barium and superpax for opax. By itself over porcelain, the glaze is not particularly interesting. But other glazes on top of it run and drip and blend together nicely. I've found that if I glaze the lower 2/3 or 3/4 of a pot with a well-behaved glossy glaze, brush a coat of this ZGK ash glaze on the top 1/3 or so and then brush or dip some third glaze on top of the ash glaze, I get a nice pattern of runs that don't go off the bottom of the pot onto the kiln shelf (usually). Different glazes give different kinds of runs and bands of different glazes are interesting too. The few times I tried a matte glaze on the bottom, the pots cracked. Could have been coincidence. But I've been sticking with glossy glazes on the bottom since then. submitted by: Janet Price e-mail:

recipes.name: Ashes to Ashes
recipes.description: I love this glaze. A pale green glaze with speckles -- it just looks elegant. The wood ashes were taken from my neighbor's fire pit, and he burns a variety of wood (probably a lot of cottonwood branches). The pale green is due to the wood ash, while the speckles (I'm pretty sure) are due to iron oxide particles from a rusting fire grate. This source will be difficult to replicate exactly. The horsetail ash was collected by me, and has an accurate corresponding laboratory analysis, so this could be adapted easily to other materials. The source of wood ash will be variable, as will any iron oxide inclusions, which adds to the charm. The glaze has stable ratios, but of course this will vary with the wood ash. I add 0.7% CMC gum to make it brushable, and brush 3 coats.

I think things would run less at cone 6 without sacrificing the crystals (since we know they work already in this base at that temp). I fired these without a hold, but in a big oval kiln (takes a day to naturally cool). Also regarding running: I do loooooongggg dips. 10 seconds. because I am mostly using these glazes like paint on flat tiles (with cmc) and they go on THICK as is my painting style. no running happens on flat work. 0. control 1. + 1 tin 2. + 1 tin, 3 rutile 3. + 3 rutile 4. + 3 rutile, 1 cobalt carb 5. + 3 rutile, 1 copper carb 6. + 2 cobalt carb 7. + 2 copper carb 8. + 2 manganese carb 9. + 2 manganese carb, 2 rutile 10. + 2 RIO 11. + 2 RIO, 1 chrome ox, 1 cobalt ox 12. + 2 RIO, 1 chrome ox 13. + 2 RIO, 1 cobalt carb 14. + .5 chrome 15. + 2 nickel carb 16. +5 purple inclusion stain

I think I'll continue to test glazes that contain phosphorous, zinc, and boron with samarium in order to get stronger responses.

Mi abuela debe haber estado a punto de mandarlo al diablo, más de una vez. Tenmoku https://glazy.org/recipes/34904, con materiales locales (Argentina). Buen rendimiento desde cono 5/6 hasta 9/10, tanto a leña como gas. En eléctrico es tan sólo un marrón oscuro del montón. - Hermoso color berenjena acetinado, con algo de reflejo metálico, en reducción fuerte (horno de gas), cono 5½/6. - Marrón acetinado oscuro en ox, cono 6 - Negro/amarronado, brillante/acetinado, quebrando en marrón rojizo en quema a leña (conos 6 al 10) Tenmoku https://glazy.org/recipes/34904, using local materials (Argentina). Good performance from cone 5/6 until 9/10, gas or wood fired. In electric kiln, only one more dark brown. - Beautiful brown/aubergine, satin, strong reduction, some metallic look, (gas kiln), cone 5½/6. - Dark brown in ox, cone 6 - Brown, almost black, breaks redish/brown, showing texture in wood firing (cones 6 until 10)

recipes.name: Baby Blue Crystalline
recipes.description: High fire crystalline based on the late Peter Ilsley's 'Dusty Rose'. This crystalline glaze is best applied in three different thickness, starting with the bottom 3rd at 0.5mm thick, middle 3rd at 1mm thick and the top 3rd at 1.5mm thick. Like most crystallines it requires the piece be placed on a catcher with a layer of kiln wash (70% Alumina Hydrate 15% Kaolin 15% Calcined Kaolin) applied to the foot of the piece and the raised section of the catcher that the piece is to sit on then join the piece and catcher with water. Fire to maturity, then crash cool to 1080ºC (‪1976º‬F‬) to aid nucleation and raise to 1100ºc (‪2012º‬F) with in 10 minutes and hold at 1100ºc (‪2012º‬F) for 1 hour. Further holds include, 1080ºC (‪1976º‬F‬) 1 hour, 1100ºc (‪2012º‬F) for 1/2 hour, 1080ºC (‪1976º‬F‬) for 10 minutes, and 1050ºC (‪1922º‬F‬)for 1/2 hour. Then clamp up kiln and end firing! You may choose to do a Post Reduction from 815ºC (‪1499º‬F‬) to 700ºC (‪1292‬º‬F).

recipes.name: Bald bug
recipes.description: This glaze is the result of me ‘improving’ on one of the glazes I had previously tested. I recently reread “Mastering Cone 6 Glazes” about making stable and functional glazes. After rereading how to make a stable glaze I finally understood that all the numbers they were referring to in the book was talking about the UMF and wanted to go back on some glazes that I believed could be improved from some tweaking in the chemistry. That glaze in question was Charle’s Titanium with copper carbonate (3%) and rutile (2%). I noticed some flaws with that test. It crazes, there wasn’t enough silica and alumina which made it way too fluid, and the R2O:RO flux ratio didn’t meet an ideal ratio of 3:7. After going through the recipe I readjusted the ingredients. I met the minimum amount of silica and alumina that is required for a “stable glaze” in Ron Roy and John Hesselberth’s book ,MC6, while also lowering the thermal expansion at the same time which makes the glaze less likely to craze. Then finally I took in account for the colorants which also influence the flux ratio in the extended UMF, so I added 2% zinc which helped me meet the ideal ratio for a stable glaze. I strongly recommend the book to those interested in making durable and functional cone 6 glazes. Substitution for wollastonite by using whiting. https://glazy.org/recipes/101138

recipes.name: Barium Boron Ash
recipes.description: Needs to be corrected for fit and pinholes but every clay body is a different can of worms. The barium/boron eutectic makes it hard to say what cone this fires to - the longer it is in kiln or the greater the thermal mass of the kiln the more it will flux. Formulated originally without the ash or slip clay it was semi-satin, semi- gloss somewhere around cone 2. Boron subdues the copper coloration. I'm not taking responsibility for anyone using these glazes, etc. Something is probably toxic. They are examples of my research and they work out in formulation. Which is what they are examples of. So go formulate your own non-toxic glazes, if that is possible. It's probably bad for the environment too. Email me with questions as to household performance, as that may be indicative of other problems. The badly crazed surfaces are not considered to be a continous-non porous sanitary surfaces. Eric Hansen, Lawrence, Kansas

It pooled very glassy with a crystallized yellowish surface. There is a red spot in the middle of the test tile. I have tested this glaze twice, both on white and on brown stoneware. Both times, the glaze showed a well melted, multi coloured gloss. The glaze was an more overall yellowish brown on the brown stoneware. Smooth and slightly more of a semi gloss. I glazed the insides of several pots with this glaze. The glaze literally popped off the slides of the pot in big chunks and splinters. This is the first time I have witnessed a glaze shiver so severely minutes after the pots were unloaded. They continued to shiver in small splinters a day after. Now I have thrown them away, carefully, but they could still be pinging and popping. The test tiles are from very recently and from over a year ago. They have not shivered.

recipes.name: Base Bill Aycock's
recipes.description: The base glaze is shiny, almost clear, that is a little fluid at ^6+ . My glazes that get the effect are all at ^6, and usually contain Boron- whether from Gerstley Borate, a frit, or Colemanite. I use a dark Rutile, and some zinc- which is a little contradictory, because of the effect of zinc on Iron colorant. Rutile has a secondary effect when blue is from Cobalt-- the color effect from Cobalt is somewhat transparent, and the opacifier effect of rutile gives the Cobalt blue something to show up against A nice 'hint' of blue can be the effect of a small amount of Cobalt in a transparent glaze with a fair amount of Rutile. and Iron wash under it can also cause interesting variations. This gives a good white with 5% rutile, with opalescent tones and, with luck and a good clay to work on, some blues. Try adding a small amount of Cobalt. This glaze seems to have a lot of ingredients, but I had to change spars, and readjust the recipe using a line blend to zero in on what I wanted. Note that there is no clay-- you may need to use a suspender, or add a little Bentonite. The Strontium I substituted for Barium is a little coarse and can settle. If you try it- please let me know the results. submitted by: Bill Aycock e-mail:

recipes.name: Base Charlie Cummings Color
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Mid-fire Chrome does well at less than 1%. Cobalt 1%. Black iron oxide works better than red iron. Copper looks beautiful but causes the glaze to bubble and shiver. Rutile can be unpredictable. I use titanium dioxide instead. Mason stains give great colors. Add 5% 6-tile if you want to use encapsulated cadmium stains. Charlie Cummings This is the base for most of my glazes. It is somewhat shiny. I like it that way and I don't care what anyone else thinks! I mix them to close to 46 on the hydrometer. The metal oxides effect the thickness and each variation is adjusted within a range of 45-48. I always layer my glazes. I like the way they break when layered. I dip for at least 3 full seconds for each coat. Thin pots need longer. The glaze goes on thick. I've found that fritted glazes tend to thin as they fire. Three layers of glaze is generally a bad idea. The rule in my studio is, “if you insist on using 3 layers, the third layer must be applied only on the top 1/3 of the pot." See this glaze in action at: http://www.claylink.com/Dinner2004/cummings.html Or http://www.claylink.com/Earthenware2005/Cummings2.html See what my studio members have done with it at: http://www.claylink.com/cccs2006.html (Actually all of our glazes and clays are represented in this show.) I use a black glaze under this glaze on most of my pots. I have to keep some secrets.

It would be worth getting a copy of the article because there are many color variations suggested, many of which we've tested and had beautiful results. If you have trouble finding a copy, e-mail me directly with your address and I'll mail you one. With 5% tin it is a beautiful, fat white semi-mat glaze. The clay body you use makes a huge difference. When I have used the glaze over the GWU clay body (which fires from cones 6-10), the glaze is yucky and transparent. When used over a cone 6 temp clay made with Redart, it is beautiful. Good luck. recipes.description: I use a cone 3-5, even cone 6 white versatile majolica (electric firings) for a major client and this glaze shows off its drips quite well. In fact, it is contributing to some unwanted seconds. The glaze is a great white, but the application is crutial and I am wondering about the glaze poise, or the set of the glaze on the ware. I think the glaze is adequately flocculated with a solution of bentonite and Flocs, and runs at an SG of about 1.6. We have experimented with various dipping strategies, to no avail.There are still streak marks, thick and thin marks, from dipping. The pots are mugs, all the same, and all glazed the same. Usign tongs with sharpened points, the mugs are dipped in an arc motion to glaze both the inside and the outside and as they are raised from the glaze bucket, on an angle, the interior glaze slowly decants out. There are still streaks and uneven parts on the ourside surface, but only on the side that the glaze runs off. The opposite side is perfect. submitted by: Jonathan Kaplan e-mail:

recipes.name: Base Kaplan's Revised 3-5
recipes.description: (The following is in response to a glazeing problem that J. Kaplan was haveing with the original base.) It sounds like the problem is one of glaze formulation rather than of application. I would guess that the glaze has too high a surface tension because of the (relatively) high amount of zinc. Looking at it chemically it looks like a higher fire glaze that has been brought down in temperature by the addition of zinc, so the zinc can't just be left out. I guess the easiest solution is to substitute an oxide with a lower surface tension for the zinc. That would point to lead, barium and strontium. I assume that lead and barium are out of the question, so I did a quick substitution using strontium carbonate. The additions of bentonite and floccs would definitly help this glaze for dipping. submitted by: Pete Pinnell e-mail:

recipes.name: Base_Hanny TP Brillante Cn5.5 (COL_G2926B)
recipes.description: Este esmalte fue desarrollado a partir de una base transparente brillante para Cn6 de: https://digitalfire.com/recipe/g2926b. Se cambiaron los materiales para incluir materiales disponibles en Colombia a partir de la misma fórmula de Seger y se ajustó el ratio Si/Al. Agregar agua al 85% del peso seco, y a continuación ajustar su gravedad específica a 1.44 g/ml adicionando agua a necesidad. Luego de ajustar la densidad, necesita adicionar solución saturada de Sales de Epsom Compatible con pastas blanca ceniza 1180°C, amarilla, negra JP para Conos 5 (1186°C), 5.5. (1203°C), 6 (1222, 1243°C) //// This glaze was developed based on: Cone 6 Whiteware/Porcelain Transparent Base Glaze from https://digitalfire.com/recipe/g2926b. The materials were changed to include locally available materials in Colombia while using the same UMF, and the Si/Al ratio was adjusted to 8. Add water to 85% of the dry weight, then adjust its specific gravity to 1.44 g/ml by adding water as needed. After adjusting the density, you need to add a saturated solution of Epsom salts. Compatible with white ash clay bodies at 1180°C, yellow, and black Colombian provider at Cones 5 (1186°C), 5.5. (1203°C), 6 (1222, 1243°C).

recipes.name: Basic Aerni Ash (Modified)
recipes.description: An ash glaze from John Britt's Cone 10 glaze book, page 162, Ash section. The modification was derived from a teapot's description on page 163. I really like that photo and one day I'll figure out how to apply this glaze so that rivulets from, perhaps with a spray gun. Interesting note: The type of ash you use will alter what this glaze ends up looking like. I used nutrient poor mesquite and pecan ash from wood firings, Bill Kitt used Red Oak and Ash tree ash, from Virginia. I've been very impressed with apple tree ash and would love to see a trial with that!

recipes.name: Basic Black
recipes.description: Reliable black iron glaze. In direct sunlight, small clusters of yellowish crystals are visible in the glaze. I mix this to a specific gravity of about 1.45, and flocculate with Epsom salts. It applies well, and doesn't tend to crawl, despite the high clay content. Produces good mottling when layered under Opaque White #1, Blanco R4.2 and PSM 2. Crazes on the earthenware I use, but this can be eliminated by adding 5% Silica.

recipes.name: Basic Celadon
recipes.description: Receta básica 25x4 (feldespato/carbonato de calcio/arcilla/cuarzo) encontrada en el libro de Britt. Atenti: la ausencia de boro sugiere que se trata de una receta para cono 10 y podría estar infracocida a cono 6, comprometiendo su durabilidad. Bajar la cantidad de ox de hierro para obtener el clásico celadón claro mantecoso. Es la misma receta básica que Blue Les's para cono 10 https://glazy.org/recipes/156 y Basic Clear https://glazy.org/recipes/10161 para conos 5/7 Basic recipe 25x4 (feldspar/whiting/clay/silica), from Midfire Britt's book. Attention: boron absence suggest that this is a recipe for cone 10 and could be underfired at cone 6. Lower the Rio % for more light/buttery celadon type. Same recipe as Blue Les's listed for cone 10 https://glazy.org/recipes/156 and Basic Clear https://glazy.org/recipes/10161 for cones 5/7 Tinkar Z: local Ball Clay

Chemical Analysis Na2O 0.07 Al2O3 0.12 SiO2 1.12 K2O 0.05 B2O3 0.09 TiO2 0.00 MgO 0.67 Fe2O3 0.00 CaO 0.21 Alumina:Silica ratio is 1.00 : 9.09 Neutral:Acid ratio is 1.00 : 5.19 Alkali:Neutral:Acid ratio is 1.00 : 0.22 : 1.12 Expansion coefficient: 67.2 x 10e-7 per degree C Oxides causing abnormal expansion effects: B2O3 Here's some recipes for a couple of crawling glazes. The high magnesium content of the glazes is what encourages the crawling action. The first one crawls into rounded bumps. Someone on the list sent it to me. The only problem that I have with this glaze (and I use the word glaze loosely in this case) is that after you dip your pieces into the glaze it tends to flake off before and sometimes during the firing. I usually brush Amaco Velvet Underglazes on the pots first and then dip them in glaze. The glaze application should be thick to encourage the crawling... happy testing, John Post Sterling Heights, Michigan

recipes.name: Bernd Pfannkuche's Rutile Pink (Modified)
recipes.description: A glaze recipe from Bernd Pfannkuche. The result may vary depending on your source of Rutile. Rutile is mostly Titanium dioxide but it also contains other impurities including a very small amount of chrome. Therefore, Tin Oxide, Silica, and Calcium form sphene to trap chrome and produce the light pink color. In essence, this is another Chrome Tin Pink recipe without the explicit addition of chrome. Originally this recipe was 40% Neph. Sye. and 40% Silica but looking at the Stull Map this would be more like Cone 7/8 so I made a slight modification to bring the firing temperature down to Cone 5/6.

recipes.name: Berry Rust (new)
recipes.description: Unity (from Insight calculation) CaO 0.49 8.55% MgO 0.36 4.51% K2O0.02 0.46% Na2O 0.14 2.79% Fe2O3 0.17 8.32% TiO2 0.00 0.06% P2O50.09 3.92% B2O3 0.20 4.37% Al2O3 0.32 10.12% SiO2 3.01 56.90% Cost/kg 0.79 Si:Al 9.54 SiB:Al 10.17 Expan 6.43 I just had a look at the Berry Rust glaze tests, the original formula, and the recalculated fritted formula. They were fired to cone 10 Ox. buy my wife, Linda Owen, in her trusty Skutt Kiln. Thanx Linda! The two glazes are nearly identical. I didn't expect that, but ya never know. The original formula with gerstley borate has more calcium-borate-iron crystals floating in the matrix but you really can't see this without a hand lens. A customer who has purchased pots with the original formula would be hard pressed to tell the difference. I feel like I've just taken the Pepsi Challenge!! The tests were fired on porcelain. Four tiles were made of each glaze, eight in all and the separate formulas were fired side by side in the top, middle, and bottom of the kiln. No significant differences were seen. I might also mention that I used English Bone Ash, and not Tri-Calcium Phos. All the tiles were inspected with a hand lens and no crazing was evident in either formula. A separate set has been fired to cone 10 R but won't be available until tomorrow. That's about it for now, e-mail me or post to clayart if I've forgotten to mention anythin, and I probably have...it's my hobby! The formulas and receipes are posted below. Happy testing,.....Craig Martell-Oregon

In addition, in reference to an earlier note about the changing reds over time, I think this red becomes somewhat brighter (and more red) the older the glaze is. I don't yet use a lot of it so it sits for quite a while (3-5 months). submitted by: Bob Kavanagh e-mail: Notes: John Post: works best if applied thin, turns greenish where thick. Seems to yield redder fired results as the glaze ages in the bucket. Notes: Wendy Moore: on porcelain at cone 10 in reduction, a beautiful brown/burgundy/gold, almost a hares fur looking glaze. recipes.name: Best RIO wash/stain u (you) will ever have
recipes.description: I do a lot of sgraffito carving on my pots because my sensibility tends to be very graphic/sign driven in all forms that it takes.. this means I need a good iron wash to sit in the crannies and make everything pop. This is that iron wash. It never lets me down. Does not flux! Does not settle! Does not even need to be sieved to be perfect! Just give it a stir or shake the jar and off you go. Works under every clear I've ever tried. Solves the problem of getting the RIO to take to the water - the gerstley gives it something to cling to! I don't even really measure, I take a heaping spoonful of RIO and a heaping spoonful of GB and I add water until it's the consistency I love, which is like thin syrup. Perfect for marking glaze tiles as well. All temperatures. Never leave home without it. I am pretty sure I inherited the gerstley trick from Adelaide Paul when I was at MICA, but can't be sure. I'm sure it works for all oxides.

recipes.name: Better Satin 7
recipes.description: I think this is the one. I have fired so far, with clear, black mason stain, and green mason stain, with great results. I have tested with the sharpie marker/ acetone test with the best results so far, leaving no marks. I still need to test cutlery marking and a leech test. Starting with Simple Satin 1, and experimenting all the way to this version; Better Satin 7. I had issues along the way, problems would be solved, but others would arise. This is where I have landed. The price is a little higher because of the Frit, but I think it will be successful in the long run. I mix this glaze to 1.4 SG, and flocculate with epsom salt. Firing Schedule (drop and soak plus slow cool to 1400): 108/hr to 250, 60 minute hold 250/hr to 2000 108/hr to 2100, 15 minute hold 108/hr to 2200, 15 minute hold 9999/hr to 2100, 15 minute hold 150/hr to 1400, off It takes my kiln (18x20) around 17 1/2 hours to fire.

recipes.name: Black H38-40 Sondahl Gloss
recipes.description: So here's a black glaze I've just developed, and I hereby throw to the sharks It's probably unnecessarily complicated because it's a hybrid of two other glazes. I think I'd rather have more RIO than Cobalt, due to cost, but it's hard to knock success, and it breaks to a nice blue when white is over it. -- Also, it wouldn't surprise me a bit if the bone ash is superfluous The recent posts on foodsafe black have prompted me to state my own opinion on black glazes. I think black glazes need not be avoided totally for foodware, but common sense argues that some blacks are better than others. If the base glaze doesn't leach harmful chemicals, then one must concentrate on combinations of oxides to produce the color with the least toxicity. Though I've never seen an authoritative ordered list of nasty chemicals, Red Iron Oxide, Cobalt Carb, and Copper Carb seem safer to me than Manganese Dioxide, Nickel, Cadmium, and Chrome. From an old Laurel's Kitchen cookbook, I read that Iron, Copper, Zinc, Manganese, Cobalt, Chromium, Nickel, Tin, and even Vanadium are all trace minerals essential for animals. I assert that most glazes release traces at best of these minerals. However, we are caught in a world which can measure in Parts per Billion, and all kinds of things look significant at that level. I sometimes wonder how long the ozone holes at the poles existed before we had the means to ascertain their existence. Brad Sondahl http://www.camasnet.com/asondahl Contributing to the potluck of the WWW

recipes.name: Black Matte
recipes.description: I want to plug Ceramic Material Workshop (https://www.ceramicmaterialsworkshop.com/). This was the first glaze I made by working backwards from the UMF. I knew what I wanted, a true black matte that would be well melted at cone 6. After my first CMW course I knew what the UMF for a black matte looked like and how to translate UMF into a glaze. This black matte is a true matte. It has an R2O : RO ratio of 0.22 : 0.77. Not ideal but ok. Ca is the primary flux (0.42). The Si and Al levels are good with 2.32 Si and 0.49 Al. The Si:Al ratio is 4.75 making this a true matte. This is also reflected in the position of the glaze on Stull's map. Because it is a cone 6 glaze I wanted to be sure it has 0.15 boron for ideal melt and durability at cone 6, so it has 0.15 boron. Additionally, we have a Bristol reaction with the Zn and Ca. We know the glaze will be fully melted at cone 6. The glaze is well behaved, it does not run for me at all. The glaze is outside the crazed region of Stull and this has not crazed for me yet. I use a slow cool firing cycle, E4 in John Britt's Mid-Range book. But I don't expect this glaze to be impacted by firing cycle. This glaze does appear to have some phase separation going on. It looks like there is a mixture of more matte glass streaking through it. Very hard to photograph and I am just my phone :)

recipes.name: Black Small Crawl
recipes.description: Shout out to Ceramic Materials Workshop. A Cu-Zn black crawl glaze. This will produce very small metallic black beads of glaze. This needs to be mixed with more water than normal. I used 150:100 water to dry ingredients for the batch pictured. It's not a fun glaze to mix. Even with the extra water it's thick. The application is key for this one. I have found that if it is too thick I don't get the nice beads, instead I get rectangles that tend to have upward pointing edges. Not a pleasant texture. Too thin an application and the glaze becomes more green than black. The picture posted was a 5 second dip. If you try this glaze just know what too thick and too thin looks like, then adjust your water content accordingly. I do not recommend using Darvan or anything else to alter the glaze even though it is difficult to mix. Dispersants will alter the behavior of the glaze. I use this regularly (love the texture on handles), I have had no studio issues with the glaze. I have never had problems with Zn based crawls flaking or becoming powdery. In my experience, Zn based crawl glazes are well behaved. This one is no exception. Because I am using Cu as the AM flux, the areas of clay the glaze leaves exposed has a green tint. I find it pleasant. Your mileage may vary. I have not tested this in reduction. I also have no reason to believe that it would misbehave in reduction.

recipes.description: from Ellen Baker Rich glossy deep blue. no crazing (although it's hard to tell with such a deep blue) Well I finally got around to typing this thing up...^9-10 Blues Thank you one and all for all the donated recipes. I only tested 31 out of almost 100 I received. I'll continue testing and reporting as the winter DRAGS on. All the glazes were tested on #900 Miller clay which is a toasty ^10 stoneware. One side of the test tile was brushed with a thick coating of Cynthia Bringle's wet/dry white slip. Each glaze was dipped in three thicknesses on a heavily textured tile. All tiles were fired to a (hard)^9 (10 tipping)reduction firing. 1 hr. Body reduction at ^08 and 1 hr. glaze reduction at ^9 then a quick reox. before shutdown. Any time potash or Custer spar is called for, I used G-200. All ball clay is OM-4 . Many glazes I substituted 75% of the amount of Barium with Strontium. All kaolin is EPK. Remember... glazes don't travel well. Your results will probably be TOTALLY different. Please test before use. Tracy Wilson Saltbox Pottery 4 Shaw Rd. recipes.name: Bleeding Blue
recipes.description: A rutile blue on top of a copper red. When applied thickly, you get a dark, intense blue with spots of red that "bleed" through. I've also considered naming this recipe "I-Can't-Believe-it's-not-Cobalt Blue". This glaze's color is pretty dependent on the firing pattern, and will probably look different if you try it. As a rule of thumb, decreasing the amount of barium used will turn this glaze into a pale rutile blue with no "bleeding" effect, and increasing the barium will turn it into a dark reddish-blue and eventually a dark copper red. Chromatically, there's a lot going on in this glaze. On the surface, there's a floating rutile blue, and underneath you have a copper red that makes this glaze darker and occasionally bleeds through. The tin in this glaze is not an opacifier, and is there to develop the copper red underneath--if you take out the copper but leave the tin, the whole thing turns an opaque white. As mentioned before, tweaking the barium is the easiest way to control the color. HCP's Erie Blue uses Strontium, and while this has the advantage of being safer to work with, Strontium seems to be runnier than Barium and doesn't create as intense blues with my school's firing schedule as Barium. And this variant looks closer to HCP's original pictures than when I tried using the original recipe? Revision of HCP's Erie Blue, using 6g Barium instead of the original's 6.6g Strontium.

recipes.name: Bleu Ginette
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Ash Ash washed 5 times and 200-mesh sieved. Ginette is my wife, among all the glazes that she has seen over the years it is the one she likes most. It is deep blue and has a lot of light mottling (nearly white in nature). Applied thin it is a kind of a light buff, but applied very thick it becomes deep blue with a lot of very light mottling. If applied thick it will crack, just put the raw glaze in place by rubbing with your fingers and it will work nicely. What do you like most about this glaze? The beautiful light mottling. Is this glaze reliable? Yes Does this glaze tend to craze/crawl/pinhole/etc.? It cracks at the moment of application but there are no surface flaws once it is fired. What consistency should the glaze be for pouring/dipping? Thick How thickly should the glaze be applied to the pot? Thick How does this glaze interact with other glazes? Not tested How do you typically fire? Typical oxidation until cone 04, ended by a short period of soaking of 30 minutes Do you experience problems with the raw glaze? No GlazeBase recipe Submitted by: Edouard Bastarache

recipes.name: Blue Barium True Matte
recipes.description: This recipe was inspired by a cone 10 recipe shared with me by V. Chin, though has been extensively revised. Yields a lovely pastel blue matte, with green highlights (the green is a mystery to me, since cobalt is the only colorant). Exercise caution with the barium carbonate when mixing, avoid breathing the dust, and definitely don't eat it, as it is converted to poisonous barium chloride by stomach acid. Considering that this appears to be a well-balanced glaze, barium leaching is likely minimal, but I would not consider it food-safe until formal leach testing has been completed (I'm looking into this). Use a liner glaze as appropriate. I added 80% water by weight. For brushing, add 0.7% CMC gum (mix dry powder into dry glaze ingredients before adding water).

recipes.name: Blue Celadon - Choy Blue
recipes.description: Spanish red iron oxide is prefered. I have found that my blue celadon glaze, which is very similar to others given to you, likes all the reduction I can give it. I fire blue celadon pieces in the same firings I go for carbon trapping with my shinos. The extra reduction along with a good thick application of the blue celadon glaze, I think, encourages the bubbles trapped in the glaze which gives it a nice softness to the glossy glaze. I introduce a heavy reduction at cone 010 through to cone 06 then lighten up a bit for the rest of the firing. Also, drips melt out and do not show. Despite the only average amount of clay in the glaze, but high amount of feldspar and flint, the glaze does not run at all at cone 10 EPK helps and use Spanish Red Iron oxide and do not get any speckling. I feel the blue celadon glaze is much nicer on porcelain. You may need to add a suspender, I don't though. I have substituted Strontium Carbonate for half of the Barium and all of the Barium at 1 part Barium to 3/4 parts Strontium and received just as nice results. I have the understanding from talking with other colleagues that the glaze should be safe from Barium poisoning because it is a glossy glaze where enough silica molecules have combined with the Barium molecules to make it stable. But, I have never had it tested. Does anyone know if this is true or not? Please reply. Enjoy, Cone 10 down, submitted by: Steve Loucks e-mail:

recipes.name: Blue Green Sugar Maples
recipes.description: "I have introduced a cooling cycle to the firing. The cycle is as follows and the firing is accompanied by a Cone 6 witness cone. After 12 consecutive firings, the witness cones are identical from firing to firing." The firing cycle: Rate Temp Hold Time rA1= 360 F1 = 900 0 rA2= 300 F2 = 1800 0 rA3 =200 F3 = 2016 0 rA4 = 108 F4 = 2197 0.3 rA5 = Full F5 =1800 0 rA6 =150 F6 = 1300 0 rA7 = 0000 To summarize, I fire at a rate of 360/hr to 900 degrees F, then at 300 degrees/ hr to 1800 degrees F, 200 degrees/hr until 2016 degrees F is reached, then 108 degrees/hour to 2197 at which time I hold it at that temperature for 30 minutes. The kiln is shut off until a temperature of 1800 degrees F is reached and then turned on to slow the rate of cooling to 150 degrees/hr until 1300 degrees F is reached. At this point the kiln is turned off and cools naturally. Western Pennsylvania Potters Community http://wpapotters.blogspot.com/2012/04/links-to-cone-6-oxidation-glaze-tests.html http://www.wpapotters.blogspot.com/2011/10/cone-6-oxidation-results-group-7.html

recipes.name: Blue on green crystalline
recipes.description: Note: Crystalline glazes are very runny, in order to make sure these glazes don't ruin your kiln shelving, catchers must be made. Here is a great video addressing how this can be handled: https://youtu.be/J0uj--a6g Grows blue crystals on a blue-green background. This is my second most reliable glaze for crystalline and works well at cone 6. I feel the melt should be lowered slightly more but I have not tested it yet. it should be a simple matter of raising the lithium in a line blend and seeing how things turn out The firing schedule is just a fast fire to cone 6 (use witness cones) and then naturally cooled down to 1820º F and held for 4 hours, then risen to 1850º F and held for another hour. Generally, at a lower temperature, your crystals will grow slowly, but they will be more round, full, and smoother. The higher you hold them, the faster they grow, but with the tradeoff of being more needle-like and they may have a rougher texture depending on additives.

recipes.name: Blue Val Cushing Smooth Satin Matte (+1 Cobalt)
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Cushing Handbook 1994 Smooth Satin/Mat Base Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 800C hold 1 hour Significant Flaw: crazing Notes: Alisa Clausen: glossy, transparent base, crazed badly on white midrange stoneware, oxides did not move under glaze. With 10 zirconia, glossy, white glaze, crazed on white midrange stoneware, oxides did not move under base. With 2 cobalt carbonate, glossy, dark blue glaze, no visible crazing. With 1 cobalt carbonate plus 2 chrome oxide, semigloss, dark green glaze, no visible crazing. With 1 copper carbonate, very glossy, transparent glaze, light green, crazed. With 10 ochre, slightly less glossy, ochre brown glaze, slight crazing. With 10 red iron oxide, slightly less glossy, dark brown glaze, no visible crazing. Notes: Steve Slatin: some of the Cushing glazes are formulated for the far edge of what works. My favourite, Rusty Bronze done as green runs at cone 6, and if you have a cool at all slow it gets very matte, but if you turn off your kiln at cone 5Â½ and do a fast cool, you get a fabulous mix of glossy where thick and microcrystalline with a nice texture shift where thin. And one percent of bentonite in the glaze bucket just changes it entirely.

recipes.name: Bone Ash Ivory
recipes.description: This is one of my favorite matte white glazes for cone 10. It uses bone ash, giving the glaze a pleasant "tooth" (please excuse the pun), and an beautiful crazing pattern. It was a modified glaze recipe from John Britt's Cone 10 glaze book, "Bone Ash White". Using G200 instead of NC-4, results in a more earthy white. The goblet pictured in this recipe has had its craze-marks stained with dark red wine, and a layer of red iron oxide was painted underneath the layer of glaze. It is a bit runny. It can be fired on green ware. Others may disagree with me, but I consider this glaze to be food safe since its recipe contains only "vitamins" such as phosphorous, potassium, sodium, magnesium, calcium, and if they were to leach, they would not be harmful if ingested. Just don't paint anything toxic underneath the glaze, or use it on a non-dinnerware safe clay, such as black mountain clay, which contains manganese, and don't use this glaze in a casserole dish or storage container.

recipes.name: Boyd Eutectic Transparent
recipes.description: From Steve Davis Website: http://kazegamas.com/ Shinos 1: http://kazegamas.com/shinos1.htm There are 72 shinos shown on 4 web pages. They are organized from left to right with 3 tiles of the same glaze shown on 3 different clay bodies. They are Aardvark Clay's Nara Porcelain, Long Beach, and Black Mountain. Every shino was glazed with a doulble dip, waxed with a simple "S" pattern, and left to dry for 2 weeks to grow sulfates on the surface. The "S" pattern has no sulfate build up. A medium reduction was started at cone 012 through cone 2. From there the kiln was fired in neutral to cone 10.

recipes.name: Brain Coral Crawl / Lichen Crawl
recipes.description: A slight variation of this crawl glaze from Alfred Ceramics: https://glazy.org/recipes/23816 I added some whiting to soften the crusty edges. Application thickness is important to getting the right amount of crawl, so try a few different application thicknesses out when testing. The thickness comparisons (with 5% Deep Orchid Stain) were my first tests of this glaze. I think my first tests must have had less water than the color tests. I did color tests at 1.35 SG but 1.45-1.5 SG maybe better. All the color tests were mixed to a specific gravity of 1.35 and dipped in the glaze once for 10 seconds.

recipes.name: Brilliant Matte Purple
recipes.description: Semimatt dark blue breaking to turquoise. ok From Brian Kemp, via Rose Downs on ClayArt listserv. CLAY COLOR/TYPE: Buff Stoneware Fired at 100 degrees per hour to 600 degrees, then free for all to cone 6-7. Kiln Size, Cromarty 25 cu ft. Manufactured in the UK. CONTRIBUTOR: Brian Kemp, Nanyang Technological University, Block B, Room 216, 469 Bukut Timah Rd., Singapore, 1025 TEST SITE: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore Whoever was looking for a Turquoise Glaze. I have 2 recipes for glazes a pottery teacher gave me. We call them Brilliant Matt Purple and Brilliant Matt Turquoise. They are volatile so be very careful with your kiln shelves. There is Barium Carbonate in the recipes, so they are poisonous whilst in the raw state. Please wear masks and gloves and if possible work at an extractor fan. I just put a normal fan pointing out the window and work behind it. I hear from production potters that Barium can leach thru your skin. Be careful and practise Good Safety Habits. As you can see they both use the same ingredients, but in different proportions. I have a friend / customer (they usually become friends) who is a production potter (with a 200 cubic foot parafin fired kiln), who uses the BMT and is delighted with it. He fires to cone 6 (1200/1220 C)You have to watch your application thickness to get the result you want. We have fired the BMP from 950 C to almost 1300 C with different results but always pleasantly surprised. Do not expect consistancy with these glazes. submitted by: Ralph Loewenthal e-mail:

recipes.name: Bristol SiC Celadon
recipes.description: For an upcoming Red Lodge Clay Center group exhibition, I wanted to try to make my "Painted" series of high-fire reduction celadon work in mid-fire oxidation. This locally-reduced Silicon Carbide (SiC) Bristol Celadon glaze isn't perfect. Some have slight areas of carbon trapping on the interiors, and I didn't have time to resolve the bubbles. But I'm happy to have gotten some work out in time for the show. Again, special thanks to David Tsabar, Ben Ho and William Chau for the groundwork in SiC reduction. One of the best results from a biaxial testing the effect of Silicon Carbide and Zinc Oxide on oxidation celadons. This is not a "fake" celadon, the color comes from the reduction of iron. Nice color and glossy finish but still too many bubbles. I was in a rush to make some work for a show. This could be further refined. Having no clay, this recipe definitely needs suspension with bentonite or maybe even Veegum-T. The 0.5% Veegum I added to this recipe doesn't actually help that much, you should probably try bentonite instead. I've had good luck controlling suspension by flocculating. By adding a solution of epsom salts or vinegar, you can prevent the glaze from settling as quickly. This glaze looks a lot different on darker or "dirtier" porcelain bodies. I am using my cone 6 porcelain body here: https://glazy.org/recipes/54919

recipes.description: Glaze Type: Metallic (fire to cone 7 in sitter) I use Redart and EPK. Note: A thick coat yields best results. rafael molina-rodriguez re: blistering of this type of glazes - I've had the same problem when firing this type of glaze on the bottom of an ancient Paragon High-fire kiln ( square, top-loading ). This kiln has approximately one cone differential from top to bottom. I solved the problem of already fired pieces by refiring them in a hotter zone of the kiln. The blisters disappearred. Now I place all bronze glazed pieces at or near the top.

recipes.name: Buckner Orange Carbon Trap
recipes.description: From Steve Davis Website: http://kazegamas.com/ Shinos 1: http://kazegamas.com/shinos1.htm NC-4 substituted for F-4 There are 72 shinos shown on 4 web pages. They are organized from left to right with 3 tiles of the same glaze shown on 3 different clay bodies. They are Aardvark Clay's Nara Porcelain, Long Beach, and Black Mountain. Every shino was glazed with a doulble dip, waxed with a simple "S" pattern, and left to dry for 2 weeks to grow sulfates on the surface. The "S" pattern has no sulfate build up. A medium reduction was started at cone 012 through cone 2. From there the kiln was fired in neutral to cone 10.

recipes.name: Burke's Strong Celadon
recipes.description: I've seen this glaze recipe posted various places and attributed to Rebecca Grant. Great for texture, and it works great over underglazes. Sensitive to uneven glazing. Looks patchy if not evenly applied. A classic celadon look. Color gets a bit greener on stoneware and bit more minty on porcelain or whiter clay bodies.

recipes.name: Bush Fake Ash
recipes.description: A wood-fired surface is another story. I'm not sure it's possible to simulate the wood ash texture in oxidation. The best results I've achieved are from the following: These are nice sufaces, but if you want Richard Aerni-like wood ash texture again I'm not sure it's possible. Good luck! Two years ago I took a part-time job teaching ceramics at Navarro College in Corsicana, Texas. The college has only one kiln. It' an ancient Paragon High Fire. The design is square and toploading with very small cu. ft. It's been a real challenge to develop an attractive palette of clays and glazes for oxidation firing. I do majolica, colored clays, and cone 6 oxidation ( cone 7 in the sitter). Rafael Molina

recipes.name: Butter Base
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: similar oxides to Clear Satin Matte and Moore White Matte Notes: Alisa Clausen: used Frit 623 for Frit 3124. With 5 rutile plus 3 tin dioxide, smooth, rutile yellow/beige gloss. On test with clay that has iron flecks, flecks were very visible under glaze. Where the glaze is thinner, it is overall slightly more beige than yellow. Where thickets, it becomes a lighter, brighter yellow. Where thick and thin meet, there are smooth streaks of yellow. Very well melted. With 10 titanium dioxide plus 5 rutile, same as with tin, but slightly less streaking, slightly less white in outer edges of streaks. With 20 titanium dioxide plus 10 rutile, glaze is stiffer. No streaking.

recipes.name: Butter New - Tig Duprey
recipes.description: A beautiful buttery, satin light yellow. Need to check for stability, surface durability, and over all utility on vertical surfaces. Does very well over light texture. Check over carvings and slip trailing. From Dupre, Marcy M IV LTC RET From ClayArt: Dear Mudbuds, A while back, a dear friend gave me a copy of Mimi Obstler's "Out of the Earth, Into the Fire." One of the materials Mimi and her crew experimented with is rotten stone. I did some test tiles of the experiments in the book, and wanted to work on making a more yellow glaze. After many tests, I came up with a glaze I call "New Butter," recipe included below. You can find rotten stone at your hardware store. Comes in pint containers, and is used for furniture finishing. It's a gray powder, very fine, fairly inexpensive. Rotten stone, sometimes spelled as rottenstone, also known as tripoli, is fine powdered porous rock used as a polishing abrasive in woodworking. It is usually weathered limestone mixed with diatomaceous, amorphous, or crystalline silica. Your results may vary with your water supply and location on the planet, but I find the glaze to be a beautiful "touch-me" satin butter-yellow. I wouldn't use it on plates, though, because of utensil marks. As always, test, test, TEST! Tig DuprePort Orchard, WA --------------------------------------- Cone Six - 456 New Butter-------------------------- Range: 5-7Firing type: OxidationGlaze type: FeldspathicColor: Pastel yellowSurface: Satin mattTransparency: Opaque Recipe: Nepheline syenite 15.00 300.0 Kona F-4 feldspar 15.00 300.0 Dolomite 15.00 300.0 Gillespie borate 15.00 300.0 Spodumene 13.00 260.0 Silica 27.00 540.0 -------- ----- 100.00 2000.0 Rotten stone 15.00 300.0 Notes: Got the basic idea from Mimi Obstler's "Out of the Earth, Into the Fire." Tried the neph sy 85/rottenstone 15 recipe in the book, formulated a different recipe to make it a more stable glaze. AUG 2003: A beautiful buttery, satin light yellow. Need to check for stability, surface durability, and over all utility on vertical surfaces. Does well over light texture, obscures details. Check over deep carvings and slip trailing. Source: DupreDate: 08/07/2003

recipes.name: Buttermilk
recipes.description: I have a problem with the following glaze that I hope some of the glaze chemistry Guru's out there might be able to help me with. I have used this glaze for years now with good success but it requires cone 10 flat and 11 tipping to mature. I would like to lower the temp. to a 9 flat and cone 10 tipping but don't really know where to begin. I fire a 35 cubic ft. Minnesota Flat Top with natural gas. If anyone can get me started, I would be grateful. Also, I have been trying to paint with stains over this glaze. I use them mixed with water and gerstly borate but can't get a smooth flow going. I was wondering how mixing the stains right in with some of the Buttermilk would work. Does anyone have suggestions??? Many thanks for your time. I love this group and have learned so much from reading your shares. Gloria Davidson My Turn Pottery

recipes.name: Buttermilk revised
recipes.description: can also use Custer feldspar instead of G-200 spar. I may have lowered the temperature too much - so - mix this one (500 grams) and test it in a cool part of your kiln (with large cones beside it. Then mix equal parts (by volume) with your original. This will give you the recipe between the two. If it is better than either the new one I am sending add each ingrediant together (fome my new one and your old one) to get the recipe for the middle one. Gerstley borate 10.5 + 13.0 = 23.5 divided by 2 =11.75 for instance. By the way both glazes are seriously short of Alumina and Silica and oversupplied with Magnesium so don't consider this a durable glaze. There is not a toxicity problem because there are no problematic oxides in the glaze - just be careful what you mix with and put under or over this glaze in areas that will come in contact with food. Ron Roy Toronto, Canada

recipes.name: BUTTERSCOTCH GLOSSY
recipes.description: (An orangey tinted clear glaze - I like it for stone ginger bottles and other old-timey things) Here are a couple of standards from the Richmond Potters Club, and a few of my own formulation that have worked well in ^6 oxidation. They aren't revolutionary (my exciting ones have things like barium in them, or are less predictable for a classroom situation) but they have been reliable, and allow for some play. They all calculate out to well within the INSIGHT limit formulas for maturity at ^6. If anyone tests these and comes up with problems, new ideas, good variations etc. could they let me know? I'll look forward to a larger list being posted to clayart. Veronica Shelford

recipes.description: part of a series I did to produce a saturated calcia matte glaze using wollastonite instead of whiting. Note you need to split the kaolin with calcined kaolin. Remember to use 12% less calcined because of the LOI. I also tried high alumina low silica and sure enough, that gives a matte too, just like the textbooks say. recipes.name: Candace Black
recipes.description: From John Britt's mid range book. I stopped using this glaze on functional ware. The bowl pictured started fading after being put in the dishwasher. I suspect the lack of boron to be the reason the glaze isn't durable. I fire with the E4 schedule in Britt's mid-range book. A quick hold at peak temp, 10 or 15 minutes, a crash cool of 100 degrees F, then a very long slow cool to 1400 F. Worth noting; when I have tried this glaze with a crystal firing schedule I get no oil spots at all.

recipes.name: Carmen's Turquoise
recipes.description: "I have introduced a cooling cycle to the firing. The cycle is as follows and the firing is accompanied by a Cone 6 witness cone. After 12 consecutive firings, the witness cones are identical from firing to firing." The firing cycle: Rate Temp Hold Time rA1= 360 F1 = 900 0 rA2= 300 F2 = 1800 0 rA3 =200 F3 = 2016 0 rA4 = 108 F4 = 2197 0.3 rA5 = Full F5 =1800 0 rA6 =150 F6 = 1300 0 rA7 = 0000 To summarize, I fire at a rate of 360/hr to 900 degrees F, then at 300 degrees/ hr to 1800 degrees F, 200 degrees/hr until 2016 degrees F is reached, then 108 degrees/hour to 2197 at which time I hold it at that temperature for 30 minutes. The kiln is shut off until a temperature of 1800 degrees F is reached and then turned on to slow the rate of cooling to 150 degrees/hr until 1300 degrees F is reached. At this point the kiln is turned off and cools naturally. Western Pennsylvania Potters Community http://wpapotters.blogspot.com/2012/04/links-to-cone-6-oxidation-glaze-tests.html http://www.wpapotters.blogspot.com/2011/10/cone-6-oxidation-results-group-8.html

The clay body used was Frost ^6 and Laguna #15 Porcelains. Some of the tiles crazed, some additives created a satin glaze, while others are a transparent gloss. recipes.name: Celadon Blue Green V&O
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Celadon also from Alfred Looks like a pretty typical celedon to me.. glossy with no crazing Well I finally got around to typing this thing up...^9-10 Blues Thank you one and all for all the donated recipes. I only tested 31 out of almost 100 I received. I'll continue testing and reporting as the winter DRAGS on. All the glazes were tested on #900 Miller clay which is a toasty ^10 stoneware. One side of the test tile was brushed with a thick coating of Cynthia Bringle's wet/dry white slip. Each glaze was dipped in three thicknesses on a heavily textured tile. All tiles were fired to a (hard)^9 (10 tipping)reduction firing. 1 hr. Body reduction at ^08 and 1 hr. glaze reduction at ^9 then a quick reox. before shutdown. Any time potash or Custer spar is called for, I used G-200. All ball clay is OM-4 . Many glazes I substituted 75% of the amount of Barium with Strontium. All kaolin is EPK. Remember... glazes don't travel well. Your results will probably be TOTALLY different. Please test before use. tracy wilson Tracy Wilson Saltbox Pottery 4 Shaw Rd. Woolwich, ME 04579 phone: 207-443-5586 fax: 207-442-8922 email: web: http://www.ime.net/dwilson/

recipes.name: Celadon Clear
recipes.description: This glaze is the result of testing done in the Summer of 2018. I identified two types of Orton Cone 6 clears- a "celadon-like" clear with a fine matrix of small bubbles, and a "super-clear" with almost no bubbles and a water-like appearance. This glaze is the best result I found for a "celadon-like" clear at cone 6. It is derived from an Si:Al biaxial test with R2O fixed at 0.2 and B2O3 fixed at 0.18: http://www.derekau.net/2018/07/15/orton-cone-6-r2o-0-2-b2o3-0-18-regions/ This test was inspired by Sue's Clear: https://glazy.org/recipes/10997 This glaze has fairly low expansion and seems to have a good fit for the clay bodies I tested. It takes colorants quite well. A very small addition of stain, cobalt, and/or copper can yield results very similar to a high-fire reduction celadon glaze.

recipes.description: Glaze Type: Mid-fire I've been using a Cone 6-9 oxidation Faux Celadon glaze on porcelain (Standard Ceramics). It looks quite a bit like a real celadon except a bit darker. It was fine until about a year ago when I started getting pinholes AND there would be a slight crawling in some places on the pot. The pot needed to be refired each time, then the crawling healed. I tried applying the glaze more thinly, but that didn't matter, I still got the strange bald spots. Thinking it might be oil or dirt on the surface, I went over each surface with a dry Scrubbie, then wiped them down with a damp sponge. I still had bald spots. Pinholes appeared on the bottom of the pots. (My pots have carved feet which raise the bottoms of the pots and the bottoms get glazed.) For a while I thought it was just me, but a colleague of mine used the same batch of glaze and had the same problem. submitted by: Sandy e-mail: Recipe calls for an addition of Black Stain 0.2

I use 5% of a native Oregon clay that is very high in Iron. You could maybe get the same color with 5% or so of Alberta slip, or Albany. 1 to 2% additions of red or black iron will give celedons. It is often said that black iron oxide gives bluer celedons, so you might want to try that. It is important to keep a glaze's content of titanium at a near zero level to develop blue celedons as well. Titanium will encourage green. I ran your Neph Sy celedon through Insight and you could reduce the crazing and maybe eliminate it by the direct substitution of potash feldspar for the Neph Sy. You might want to try both Custer and G-200. Custer is higher in silica and would be the most effective one to lower the glazes expansion. G-200 will give a bit better melt I think..........Craig craig martell

recipes.name: Ceramics Bible Blue-Green Celadon
recipes.description: I got this out of a book called "The Ceramics Bible" Our kilns are very good at reducing. The color is very deep, the surface glossy with small indents on the surface. There is a fair amount of large bubbles in the glaze melt but no crazing on Coleman Porcelain (crazed on stoneware oxidation firing) with great response to texture/lots of depth. I will get a stoneware test in redux asap. The oxidation test lacks the indents on the surface but has very fine foggy bubbles. It is a pale yellow in oxidation.

recipes.name: Cerberus Oil Spot
recipes.description: A black oil spot glaze with metallic highlights. Based on Jake's cone 6 versions of TC's oil spot tests, but made more fluid at cone 5.5. A possible origin of the name Cerberus (the multi-headed dog of the Greek god Hades) is the Proto-Indo-European word k̑érberos, meaning "spotted". Hades' dog might have literally been named "Spot". Yes, I got the idea for the name from The Punisher. I thought the Netflix series was great.

recipes.name: Cerulean Blue Heaven
recipes.atmosphere: Oxidation, Neutral, Reduction, Salt & Soda, Wood
recipes.description: I personally have never seen this flash red. I've gotten bloody purple, which was heavy heavy reduction the entire firing. I don't bother with mixing it thick, either. I mix to normal SG and add epsom instead of bentonite to gel it and it sticks fine, fires gorgeous blue. This glaze should be everywhere. It's not even expensive. The tin, maybe. Doesn't run when applied right Doesn't settle out for us at all, but i throw a tsp - tbsp of epsom right into the dry mix without thinking about it. From Richard Gralnik via the facebook group. Blue celadon in Ox, gorgeous bloody blue/reds in R "settles badly if not properly deflocculated. 148 sg is too thin." https://glazestuff.wordpress.com/2012/05/23/cerulean-heaven-aka-dalys-2-red-but-it-comes-out-blue-cone-10-reduction-d-j-brewer/?fbclid=IwAR1gDWe2kwTuc05uNvufBd1S45anO5-rSUNaPDbTTZHXqJ2ok4vCVf2oAuE
