recipes.name: Chappell Floating Blue, Blue Hare
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: James Chappell The Potters Complete Book of Clay and Glazes Source/Alternate names: same oxides as Slate Blue With Green Specks, similar to Blue Jean Blue and Cobbled Floating Blue Notes: Candice Roeder: a deep blue-brown background of great depth with lighter mottled blues that seem to float on the surface of the background glaze. with more of the lighter mottled blues where the application is thickest. Watch thickness near the bottom of the pot. It fires best on the light side of cone 6 (standard cone just bending), seems to get greener and more fluid the higher you go. Cone 5 works well, too. The book says to weigh the ingredients very carefully, use distilled water or water that is known to have a low mineral content. Mix then add the CMC solution. The book warns that the glaze is fickle, and recommends against firing this glaze in the same kiln with glazes that contain copper, chrome, nickel or manganese. Mineral content of the water is an important factor. I have noticed an adverse effect as the author noted, and now fire an entire kiln load of this glaze. Notes: Martha Muzychka: not what I expected, mostly green with a few spots of blue. On black stoneware clay, it gives an unusual cloudy effect. Notes: Ivy Glasgow: a popular and beautiful (when done right) glaze. The original Floating Blue pigments have been tested and found to be food safe. When floating blue works, it is lovely. Key seems to be firing to no more than Cone 5-1/2 and cooling quickly. Notes: James Chappell: the colours seem to float on a surface of a darker background of great depth, reminiscent of a deep pool of water. Its colour and opacity vary greatly with thickness so it highlights irregularities in the surface. Phase separation in the translucent matrix makes the colour swirl as small rivulets of more fluid glass flow around more viscous phases. Titanium crystals in the matrix make it sparkle. Calcium-borate boron-blue crystals grow on the surface. Bubbles of escaping gases create pools of lighter coloured glass surrounded by darker rings. Small black speckles are produced by unground particles of iron. Use distilled or low mineral water, force all material through an 80 mesh screen, stir thoroughly before and during use to prevent settling out of the iron content, apply the thickness of a dime, fire to cone 6 oxidation exactly, and cool normally. Do not substitute any other chemicals for those given, it is a fickle glaze. It depends on the Gerstley borate to suspend it. Notes: I substitute Cobalt Carb 2.0. What caught my eye, was the description of it as slate blue, which doesn't fit my results. So, I picked up the original recipe, and it differs from the one Sharon posted. You might try this version in your tests. It is called Floating Blue...from James Chappell's book, Clay and Glazes. This glaze produces a deep blue-brown background of great depth with lighter mottled blues that seem to float on the surface of the background glaze. The glaze has more of the lighter mottled blues where the application is thickest. Watch thickness near the bottom of the pot. The C.M.C. measurement refers to a premixed CMC and water solution. For the Silica, I use 325 mesh Flint. The rutile, is just powdered rutile from the ceramics supply. It fires best on the light side of cone 6 (standard cone just bending), seems to get greener and more fluid the higher you go. Cone 5 works well, too. I do not find a need for bentonite. The book says to weigh the ingredients very carefully, use distilled water or water that is known to have a low mineral content. Mix then add the CMC solution. Sieve two or three times through a 60 to 80 mesh sieve to thoroughly disperse the cobalt, iron, and rutile. The book warns that the glaze is fickle, and recommends against firing this glaze in the same kiln with glazes that contain copper, chrome, nickel or manganese. Mineral content of the water is an important factor. I have noticed an adverse effect as the author noted, and now fire an entire kiln load of this glaze. The glaze should be stirred occasionally during application because the iron has a tendency to settle. Chappell's Suggested variations: Stipple on additional glaze with brush or apply with sponge for an even more mottled effect. Or: lightly sponge a thin wash of 3 grams of chrome oxide to 100 grams of water plus a tablespoon of CMC over the top to produce a floating blue glaze with subtle green tints. Or: Over the glaze, sponge lightly with a rutile wash consisting of 2 grams rutile per 100g of water for a floating blue glaze with slightly tan crystalline tints on the surface. submitted by: Candice Roeder source for original recipe: James Chappell

recipes.name: Charcoal
recipes.description: For my black I added these colorants, rather than those above: Chrome.......1.14 Cobalt Carb 4.55 Red Iron Ox..3.41 I am having a problem with a glaze. It is a cone 6 oxidation glaze, charcoal variation of Pinnell Strontium Matt Glaze. I am trying to achieve a (cobalt)bla variation, rather than the greenish black that the Charcoal version produces. I took colorants from a favorite black glaze recipe and used those percentages i Strontium Matt base. The results were black, but very dry and underfired lookin fire this glaze to cone 7, BTW) Could the colorants I added have a refractory effect, and if so, how do I correc problem? Any ideas? I'd appreciate help on this one. Thanks. Candice Roeder living in the sticks in Michigan

recipes.description: High fire crystalline based on the late Peter Ilsley's 'Dusty Rose'. This crystalline glaze is best applied in three different thickness, starting with the bottom 3rd at 0.5mm thick, middle 3rd at 1mm thick and the top 3rd at 1.5mm thick. Like most crystallines it requires the piece be placed on a catcher with a layer of kiln wash (70% Alumina Hydrate 15% Kaolin 15% Calcined Kaolin) applied to the foot of the piece and the raised section of the catcher that the piece is to sit on then join the piece and catcher with water. Fire to maturity, then crash cool to 1080ºC (‪1976º‬F‬) to aid nucleation and raise to 1100ºc (‪2012º‬F) with in 10 minutes and hold at 1100ºc (‪2012º‬F) for 1 hour. Further holds include, 1080ºC (‪1976º‬F‬) 1 hour, 1100ºc (‪2012º‬F) for 1/2 hour, 1080ºC (‪1976º‬F‬) for 10 minutes, and 1050ºC (‪1922º‬F‬)for 1/2 hour. Then clamp up kiln and end firing! You may choose to do a Post Reduction from 815ºC (‪1499º‬F‬) to 700ºC (‪1292‬º‬F).

recipes.name: Chrome tin Pink
recipes.description: I started from on of my base glazes 'Patricias mooie' (https://glazy.org/recipes/19531) I made with my students some nice grids. We tried to find pink with chrome and tin. On the 'X-axis' we added each time 1,5% Tin starting from the base glaze. On the 'Y-axis' we added each time 0,2 % Chrome. So in the lower left corner you find the base glaze and in the upper right corner you find the base glaze with 9% Tin and 0,8% Chrome.. So for example you find a nice pink at 6% tin and 0,2% Chrome.

Moving up in Al2O3, the glazes become more opaque and change color from red to pink. This test was just meant as a starting point for developing Chrome Tine Pink-Red glazes. One could further explore varying Boron & Tin levels or test the effect of additives like Iron & Titania. Note: Lately I've seen multiple people adding too much Chrome to recipes. Many Chrome pink/reds have very small amounts of Chrome, for example this recipe has 0.08% That's NOT 8%, it's not even 0.8%! Please use the batch calculator and make sure you are adding the correct amount. Al2O3 0.25 (This recipe.) Al2O3 0.30 Al2O3 0.35

recipes.name: Clausen Dark Blue Gloss
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Alisa Clausen Notes: Alisa Clausen: Stable, blue gloss, a very nice medium to dark blue, bright in hue.

recipes.name: Clausen Ebony
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Alisa Clausen Notes: Alisa Clausen: exciting to use only 2 ingredients, used local Oldenwalder clay for the original Barnard. Resulted in a highly glossy brown and black glaze that moved, but did not drip. In center of test bowl, is a pool of deeply rich cognac coloured brownish red. Pinholing where thickest. A lot of movement in the glaze surface over the lip of the test bowl. Varied greatly depending on thickness of application from streaked brown gloss where thin, to deep, pinholed cognac colour where thickest.

recipes.name: Clausen Glittering Brown
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Alisa Clausen Notes: Alisa Clausen: a very glittery brown glaze that looks like fools gold in natural light. I have not often seen such a sparkle in a glaze surface. It has a dark background surface with a copper sparkle. Looks like a Disney version of Tenmoku.

recipes.name: Clausen Glittering Brown / cono 4
recipes.description: Receta de Clara Giorello, modificada para llevarla a cono 4. Tiene el aspecto de una venturina. No contiene alúmina, en vertical tiende a escurrir. Aplicarlo en capa no muy gruesa. Se usó la frita 174 de Crecer, que corresponde a la 3134 de Ferro. Receta de C. Giorello, derivada de una original de Alisa Clausen: https://glazy.org/recipes/17887

recipes.name: Clausen Glittering Brown frit/3134
recipes.description: Usé la frita 174 de Crecer, equivalente a la 3134 de Ferro. Ofrece una hermosa variación de colores, con negro, marrón, rojo, naranja, ocre, amarillo y reflejos dorados en superficie. Se mantiene bien en paredes verticales pero puede escurrir y mostrar cabezas de alfiler si la aplicación es muy gruesa. I used Ff 3134 frit. Nice color variegation, with black, brown, red, orange, ochre, yellow and gold. Well behaved, but tendency to run and pinholing when too thick. Source/Alternate names: Alisa Clausen Notes: Alisa Clausen: a very glittery brown glaze that looks like fools gold in natural light. I have not often seen such a sparkle in a glaze surface. It has a dark background surface with a copper sparkle. Looks like a Disney version of Tenmoku.

recipes.name: Clausen Light Gray Semimatte
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Alisa Clausen Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 800C hold 1 hour Notes: Alisa Clausen: covering, semi mat glaze that is well melted. Smooth surface. Where thickest, the glaze is a dark gray, where thinner, the colour has blue cast and is not as covering.

recipes.name: Clausen Opal Blue
recipes.description: Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 800C hold 1 hour Notes: Alisa Clausen: used Johnson Matthey J frit instead of 3134, 1.5 cobalt carbonate instead of 1 oxide. A glossy opalescent green glaze, with opaque patches and rivulets of periwinkle blue where thickest. This glaze did not run, and has surface with many nuances. Please note that Ron Roy suspects that this glaze could break down in the dishwasher, due to its low alumina.

recipes.name: Clausen Semimatte Base
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Alisa Clausen Source/Alternate names: similar oxides to Lewis Semimatte Base Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 800C hold 1 hour Notes: Alisa Clausen: A semi mat glaze that is cream in colour with a yellow cast. It also has crystals on the surface, giving the surface a slight sparkle. Where it pools, it is glassy. With 2 cobalt carbonate, a semi mat, dark gray glaze that is covering and smooth. With 5 rutile plus 2 cobalt carbonate, a semi mat glaze that is a bluer gray than the original. The surface has crystals, giving the surface a slight sparkle. With 5 rutile, a gloss glaze under a cream, streaked shell. Blue opalescent areas where thickest. Breaks clear.

recipes.name: Clausen Semimetallic Base
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Alisa Clausen Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 800C hold 1 hour Notes: Alisa Clausen: A gloss, covering dark black brown. Breaks transparent over high areas on test tile. With 2 cobalt carbonate, a well covering, semi gloss, metallic, even black glaze Needs to be thick. With 5 rutile, a gloss, covering dark brown mustard colour glaze. Breaks transparent over high areas on test tile. With 5 rutile plus 2 cobalt carbonate, very similar to version with just cobalt, but overall surface has a slight sparkle. Colour is not as even and on very close examination, can see dark blue speckles.

recipes.name: Clausen Shino
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: modified Malcolm Davis Shino Significant Flaw: crazing, excessive soluble material (soda ash) Notes: Alisa Clausen: all white, thick, covering shino glaze. Crazed.

recipes.name: Clausen Simple Blue

recipes.name: Clausen Snowflake
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Chris Clarke Snowflake, revised Notes: Alisa Clausen: Streaking and movement in a gloss surface. Pools to attractive medium, bright blue. Stayed where glazed.

recipes.name: Clausen ToDo Base
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Alisa Clausen revision Tony Martens Dolomite white Source/Alternate names: same oxides as ToDo Base 1, similar to ToDo Base Notes: Alisa Clausen: With 10 black stain, a smooth, black matt, greenish where very thin. Medium grey stain gave a smooth, dark grey matt. With 10 red iron oxide, really smooth, clinging iron brown with some darker and lighter areas depending on application. Very traditional looking iron semi matt. Good feel to surface. Adding 4 rutile made little difference. With 10 ochre, one shade lighter than Clausen ToDo Base Brown, same smooth, matt surface with a good feel.

recipes.name: Clear -Coile Hooven
recipes.description: I've been using Coile Hooven's recipe for clear glaze for porcelain with good results. It doesn't crackle/craze (eye of the beholder thing) and can run the gamut from non-milky matte at lower temp to a nice high gloss at c.10-11. (The recipe lists it as Cone 10 Clear) (use a mortar & pestle to grind Cornwall stone before mixing) I use this over a porcelain throwing body from Val Cushing's notebook (published and distributed during Summer Class 1993): GROLLEG 55 (1 full bag) KONA 4 SPAR 20 FLINT 12 PYRAX 13 MACALOID 2 (or Bentonite: let sit with water in mixer overnight. Add dry mix next day) As with any porcelain, the longer it ages, the better. I make mine ideally 6 months in advance, wrapped a la the Alfred Roll in 35# batches. Hope this helps. Tricia

recipes.description: For 2 years I struggled with this concept & finally gave up. The fuel savings (?) were not worth the effort. The results don't compare to ^10. I agree with Peter Pinnell- sell another mug to pay for the difference in firing costs. add- 10% iron for temmoku or- 2% tin oxide & 1% copper carb. for red Due to the lower sintering point of ^6 glazes- you have to start reduction fairly early- at least by stoneware standards. Try ^010 as a starting point & go from there. I also used a clay body that had a higher iron content than my present ^10 body- it seemed to make a difference. submitted by: Tom Gray e-mail:

recipes.name: Clear bob's base
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Mid-fire Variations: berry rust: 10% red iron oxide deep river red: 20% RIO midnight blue: 5% cobalt carb., 2% RIO, 1% copper carb. silver yellow: 6% vanadium oxide, touch of rutile majolica: 7% tin oxide By itself without colorants, this glaze is fairly clear, not perfectly transparent at cone 6-7 but becoming glass like at 8-9. It is smooth to the touch, pleasing to feel. Very tolerant and forgiving. It is somewhat uninteresting by itself although it is as stable as you can imagine. Add colorants for the real action! How long have you been using this glaze? 8-10 years Where is it used? Bob Kavanagh's studio. Where did this recipe come from? I developed it over a few years. What do you like most about this glaze? It is stable, adaptable, accepts diverse colors well, applies easily, is virtually fault free - a good friend. Does this glaze tend to craze/crawl/pinhole/etc.? With the majolica, it may crawl if the glaze is applied VERY thickly. How do different firing temperatures/atmospheres affect the glaze? It may be used in reduction as well as in oxidation, although I now use it only in oxidation. I developed it while I was working in a reducing atmosphere. The differences between oxidation and reduction lie in the clarity of the glaze (much clearer in oxidation) and of course the impact of reduction on iron bearing oxides. How does the glaze behave on different clay bodies? Very adaptable to stoneware, porcelain, rough, smooth, etc. What consistency should the glaze be for pouring/dipping? Dip hand into bucket; can hardly see skin under glaze on hand: thick cream. How thickly should the glaze be applied to the pot? Varies with oxide addition. Likes to be moderately thick for richest results. How does this glaze interact with other glazes? I had not been happy with combining it with others, so I stopped. It can be layered with itself with different colorants in each layer. What is your kiln type and size? 10 cubic foot, Tucker's Cone Art, electric How do you typically fire? 0 to 212 in two hours: hold 10 minutes. 212 to 1040 at about 300 degrees an hour. very slowly from 1040 to 1070. as quickly as possible from 1070 to 2100. about 150 degrees an hour until cone 7-8. Do you experience problems with the raw glaze? no problems GlazeBase recipe Submitted by: bob kavanagh -------------------------------------------------------------------- ----

recipes.name: Clear Donna's
recipes.description: Glaze Type: High-fire I am having a problem with my clear liner. On all our cone 10+ firings, in ox or red., we have a great clear. In salt fire, however, if the vapor hits the inside of, say a bowl, or if the clear is on the outside of the pot, then it crazes horribly. If we prevent the vapor from hitting the surface of the clear, it does well. (or if it is very thin on the outside of the pot). This glaze does very well in our wood fire kiln-no crazing at all. It will be matt if it doesn't get a good cone 10 if that helps any. Pat Chesney Waco, Texas

recipes.name: Clear durable
recipes.description: Glaze Type: High-fire This is an excellent transparent/clear glaze that is very hard and durable. I have used it over colored slip, with sgraffito into the slip and with oxides and stains brushed over it and the decorations don't move. This glaze can be brought to the VERY edge of the foot without moving. I use it inside of all my functional work and when decorating with colored slips I use it over the whole surface of the pot. It is an excellent glaze that will always perform well especially when you are in a hurry to get things fired. No surprises. Food-safe. Variations: Can add 1/4 % Copper Carbonate for Light Green in Oxidation ^9-10 firing. How long have you been using this glaze? Almost 20 years Where is it used? In my studio Where did this recipe come from? I got this recipe from Kieth Campbell from Ontario, Canada but believe that it is an Alfred Univ. glaze originally What do you like most about this glaze? There are no surprises and I can count on it every time. Its food safe. Is this glaze reliable? Very Does this glaze tend to craze/crawl/pinhole/etc.? Crazes if applied TOO THICK. How do different firing temperatures/atmospheres affect the glaze? Electric/Oxidation or Gas fired/Reduction or neutral fire are all equally as good. How does the glaze behave on different clay bodies? On porcelain and white stoneware it is clear white. On buff and or red bodies it goes somewhat grey because of the iron in the clays. Very pleasent on all clays. I have tested and used on all the above clays. What consistency should the glaze be for pouring/dipping? The consistancy of my glazes is like homo milk. The normal consistancy. I dip to the count of 5 - 10. How thickly should the glaze be applied to the pot? Normal. I spray this glaze as well to 1/16th of an inch or better. How does this glaze interact with other glazes? I like it the way it is for my work. Test your glazes and see what happens. I have sprayed other glazes on rims etc. and all worked fine. What is your kiln type and size? 30 cu.ft. downdraft gas kiln. How do you typically fire? Heating...pilots (4) on over night or at least a 9 hour period. Burners (4) on low over night or till cone 07 is down. Turn up the burners to 1/2 way mid. reduce kiln for 30 to 45 mins. depending on the weather. Cut the reduction (open dampers to almost open and a light reduction till cone 10 falls. Clear kiln, shut off and seal. Slow 36 hour cool before cracking the door and work comes out in about 48 hours. Do you experience problems with the raw glaze? NO....this glaze can be stirred easily even after 8 weeks of non use and stays stirred for long periods of time while glazing. I make a large green garbage pail of my well used glazes and they last me for a yr. or more. No smells etc. What is your water pH? City water. Any other comments? Try this glaze...it will be a main stay in your studio. ;>}}} GlazeBase recipe Submitted by: Peggy Heer / Heer Pottery Ice Cream Flavor: Chocolate -------------------------------------------------------------------- ----

recipes.name: Clear Glaze 5-6
recipes.description: A fabulous clear glaze! I tested about 15 clears last year and only came up with 2 that I would consider using. This glaze is incredibly forgiving - doesn't show drips, overdips, differences in thickness, is glassy clear w/o yellow, and doesn't craze. I am absolutely thrilled with this glaze. It only has 4 ingredients, too. I use this over slips and underglazes and it's fine. I also use lusters over it with great results. What can I say? This is THE PERFECT clear glaze. Have fun. Laura in Oregon

recipes.description: From Linda Arbuckle: Under 45x magnification, slight crazing. > "I put this together for a friend of mine who was using a lowfire barium amber. I was looking at Sr ambers and olive green transparent lowfire glazes. At some point I’d like to add just a touch more lithium to the Higher Power and Amber Assault + Li and Sr tests to get rid of very mild crazing I see under magnification. Other goals were to have a lowfire glaze that had enough clay to apply well. I find the very high frit lowfire glazes have to go on so very thin that they’re a challenge to dip-glaze well. They always look too thin to me, and if they’re thick, they trap bubbled and get crater-y." Firing Notes: All tiles fired upright. 03 sitter cone to give an junior cone 04 bending visual. Average coating of glaze on the left, thicker on the right. On terracotta clay with slips (white, black, green, pink, yellow). I’d like to test bumping the lithium up just a tad on the Higher Power to get rid of the slight crazing. Doesn’t show crazing unless viewing under magnification, so it’s slight.

recipes.name: Clear Meloy revised
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Stoneware Revised by adding more flint to make a slightly lower thermal expansion and stop crazing. This was the best clear I found in testing about 9 or 10 clear recipes. Many were good clears but had a slight celadon tinge. This one is stable, clear and light grey over white stoneware with no appreciable greenish hue. No crazing over the shop clay bodies (commercially available west coast stoneware clays). RB SDSU 1994 How long have you been using this glaze? two years Where is it used? San Diego State University Where did this recipe come from? originally Meloy Clear (origin unknown, maybe Pete Meloy?) Looks to be a variation on the classic 4-3-2-1 Leach clear. What do you like most about this glaze? very clear, applies well, few glaze faults, cheap to make, non-toxic. Is this glaze reliable? yes Does this glaze tend to craze/crawl/pinhole/etc.? no How do different firing temperatures/atmospheres affect the glaze? may work as low as cone 6 but with reduced clarity. How does the glaze behave on different clay bodies? no problems What consistency should the glaze be for pouring/dipping? average consistency. How thickly should the glaze be applied to the pot? thin to medium thickness for best clarity, thinner on porcelain. How does this glaze interact with other glazes? works well with most other stoneware glazes. What is your kiln type and size? Alpine 30 cu. ft. updraft gas kiln How do you typically fire? 12-16 hour heating, reduction from cone 06 to cone 8, more neutral atmosphere after that. no soak. 24-36 hour cooling. Do you experience problems with the raw glaze? no Any other comments? Unity Formula for MELOY CLEAR revised- 0.188 K2O 0.485 Al2O3 4.725 SiO2 0.083 Na2O 0.004 TiO2 0.729 CaO 9.7:1 Si:Al Ratio Percentage Analysis- 71.44 % SiO2 12.43 % Al2O3 4.46 % K2O 1.28 % Na2O 10.30 % CaO 0.08 % TiO2 GlazeBase recipe Submitted by: Richard Burkett Ice Cream Flavor: Ben & Jerry's Cranberry Orange sorbet -------------------------------------------------------------------- ----

recipes.name: Clear/Transparent
recipes.description: Glaze Type: High-fire This is an excellent transparent/clear glaze that is very hard and durable. I have used it over colored slip, with sgraffito into the slip and with oxides and stains brushed over it and the decorations don't move. This glaze can be brought to the VERY edge of the foot without moving. I use it inside of all my functional work and when decorating with colored slips I use it over the whole surface of the pot. It is an excellent glaze that will always perform well especially when you are in a hurry to get things fired. No surprises. Food-safe. Variations: Can add 1/4 % Copper Carbonate for Light Green in Oxidation ^9-10 firing. How long have you been using this glaze? Almost 20 years Where is it used? In my studio Where did this recipe come from? I got this recipe from Kieth Campbell from Ontario, Canada but believe that it is an Alfred Univ. glaze originally What do you like most about this glaze? There are no surprises and I can count on it every time. Its food safe. Is this glaze reliable? Very Does this glaze tend to craze/crawl/pinhole/etc.? Crazes if applied TOO THICK. How do different firing temperatures/atmospheres affect the glaze? Electric/Oxidation or Gas fired/Reduction or neutral fire are all equally as good. How does the glaze behave on different clay bodies? On porcelain and white stoneware it is clear white. On buff and or red bodies it goes somewhat grey because of the iron in the clays. Very pleasent on all clays. I have tested and used on all the above clays. What consistency should the glaze be for pouring/dipping? The consistancy of my glazes is like homo milk. The normal consistancy. I dip to the count of 5 - 10. How thickly should the glaze be applied to the pot? Normal. I spray this glaze as well to 1/16th of an inch or better. How does this glaze interact with other glazes? I like it the way it is for my work. Test your glazes and see what happens. I have sprayed other glazes on rims etc. and all worked fine. What is your kiln type and size? 30 cu.ft. downdraft gas kiln. How do you typically fire? Heating...pilots (4) on over night or at least a 9 hour period. Burners (4) on low over night or till cone 07 is down. Turn up the burners to 1/2 way mid. reduce kiln for 30 to 45 mins. depending on the weather. Cut the reduction (open dampers to almost open and a light reduction till cone 10 falls. Clear kiln, shut off and seal. Slow 36 hour cool before cracking the door and work comes out in about 48 hours. Do you experience problems with the raw glaze? NO....this glaze can be stirred easily even after 8 weeks of non use and stays stirred for long periods of time while glazing. I make a large green garbage pail of my well used glazes and they last me for a yr. or more. No smells etc. What is your water pH? City water. Any other comments? Try this glaze...it will be a main stay in your studio. ;>}}} GlazeBase recipe Submitted by: Peggy Heer / Heer Pottery Ice Cream Flavor: Chocolate -------------------------------------------------------------------- ----

recipes.name: Cobalt Blue (June Perry Red variant)
recipes.description: Cobalt Blue is a dependable Cone 5-6 oxidation glaze with a deep blue glossy finish breaking to lighter blue highlights. Turn kiln off! Although I don’t think anything below 1050oC did much in the growing phase you will be pleased with the outcome.

recipes.name: Conrad Engobe (Judy Nelson-Moore version)
recipes.description: published in Ceramic Arts Network, 2014, attributed to Judy Nelson-Moore: Can fire from cone 04-7 or even wider range. "I use this engobe in several ways: 1) as a white-out over something I don't like. Refire at bisque temperature and then put another surface over the top. 2) As a texturizing layer... works best put over a low-fire shiny glaze, then refire to temperature above original glossy surface so that glaze bubbles underneath. Makes a wrinkled skin on top...very interesting texture." "Picture (in magazine) shows Conrad Engobe over cone 7 engobe/stains which was then re-bisqued and fired in a tin-foil saggar. The engobe picked up the fuming well." "This recipe comes from Lana Wilson's article "Lichenlike Surfaces" in the February 1990 Ceramics Monthly. Can add stains (10%). Wilson says add black stain and use under lichen surface. She says reduce neph sye if too shiny, which I don't understand because it is VERY dry matt. Slightly different recipes in different sources. Apply by spray or brush. 1-3 coats depending on use desired. Sticks well to refired surface. Ball clay makes it look gray/brown but fires a nice dead white."" "Test #1: "white" engobe version tested as-is using the base recipe only. A very dry matte translucent warm white. Would add 5-8% zircopax to increase opacity if desired. fired to ^6" "Test #1: "black" version: added 10% "Best Black" mason stain #6600. A lovely dry matte warm black surface - very opaque. fired to ^6"

recipes.name: Conrad G375 Moonlight Blue
recipes.description: (Mile Hi in Denver has Ilmenite). Likes a fast cooling to develop that electric blue. One dip gives you brown, two dips a deep blue. Tends to break on ridges. Where real heavy you get white. Flows quite a bit, especially combined with other glazes. Watch your bottom feet,try to give it a good foot or a strong ridge to stop flow. Tapering the bottom edge with a straight edge helps too. Otherwise your shelf will be a beautiful shade of blue. If thick, tends to pinhole, likes to dry and be rubbed out before firing. Tempermental glaze---can crawl just enough to make you crazy generally under rims and on the inside of rims....probably is thicker there and shrinks when drying. To Mix, we've found it best to dissolve the Cornwall first and let set a bit, then add everything else. Screen through a 40 once and an 80mesh twice for finest crystalization. This is a compilation of several background messages re: the Conrad Moonlight. We use Conrads Moonlight (which was discussed about 6 months ago here) with about 1/2%cobalt Carb. added. It's a cone 10 glaze. I first started using it in electric firing, and a year ago switched to gas. At first in the gas, it was muddier and tended toward rutile blue-green. Then, experimenting, we cooled the kiln faster to match the curve of the electrics. Voila, nice sharp crystals and blue. It also seems to be quite sensitive to temperature, over fire it and it grabs iron from anywhere and goes blue green or brownish. I also might note that it is quite sensitive to application. It must go on thick to develop a good blue. (even sometimes giving almost purple). Thick in the bucket, double dip as soon as the sheen leaves, dry completely, then rub lightly everywhere and especially on compund curves. This is a Cornwall recipe and tends to crawl if not thorughly bonded to the clay surface. The thickness required doesn't help. Don't know what it might do at c6 but if you can get it there, the above notes might help. One note, I mentioned that it's sensitive to temp. It's happiest between 9-1/2 and 10-1/2. Also we use it on a white stoneware. On iron body clays, it tends toward blue green or brown-green...not too pretty. Joyce brought up a good pointThe rutile blue Moonlight from Conrad (G375) is r understand, most rutile blues are. The way we work around this is to provide a ridge at the foot and, when Betsy applies the glaze, she takes a stainless rib and carves a taper into the ridge. Sounds time consuming, and is, but it goes pretty fast after you've done (not had) a few. The main time we lose pieces from running now is where there's an overlap with another glaze, especially Temmoku. But by keeping it high on the pot, it can be controlled. Good Luck. It can be a fantastic rutile blue, best I've seen. I'll be off the list for a week, at Rosen, but will pull digests during the week. Tom Wirt Clay Coyote Pottery Hutchinson, MN

recipes.name: Copper Blue
recipes.description: from H.S. days at Gould Academy I'd had this glaze mixed up for years and retried it. Very dry matt deep turquoise blue/green going to teal where thick. Beige where thin. Didn't react well to CB slip Well I finally got around to typing this thing up...^9-10 Blues Thank you one and all for all the donated recipes. I only tested 31 out of almost 100 I received. I'll continue testing and reporting as the winter DRAGS on. All the glazes were tested on #900 Miller clay which is a toasty ^10 stoneware. One side of the test tile was brushed with a thick coating of Cynthia Bringle's wet/dry white slip. Each glaze was dipped in three thicknesses on a heavily textured tile. All tiles were fired to a (hard)^9 (10 tipping)reduction firing. 1 hr. Body reduction at ^08 and 1 hr. glaze reduction at ^9 then a quick reox. before shutdown. Any time potash or Custer spar is called for, I used G-200. All ball clay is OM-4 . Many glazes I substituted 75% of the amount of Barium with Strontium. All kaolin is EPK. Remember... glazes don't travel well. Your results will probably be TOTALLY different. Please test before use. Tracy Wilson Saltbox Pottery

recipes.description: In use RLC. Note: 1/2 cup Epsom Salts / 10000gm. eliminates settling. Frit 3195 may be substituted for 3110. Good reduction yields blood red. Oxidation is celadon-like green. Apply medium / thin won't be red / thick it crawls. If overlapped on another glaze - may crawl. Here is a formula that has recently been used here at Richland College, Dallas, Tx. recipes.name: Copper Red (U. Houston)
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Copper red (Oxblood) This glaze is a very wonderful red, but like all reds, it's very temperamental. A heavy reduction at the end is recommended. Firing time should be between 12 and 20 hours. Not enough reduction during the firing will cause the glaze to be clear. How long have you been using this glaze? I've used this glaze off and on for 2 years. Where is it used? University of Houston Where did this recipe come from? This could be a Carlton Ball glaze, but I'm not sure. Is this glaze reliable? The firing process is what's difficult about this glaze. You should start reducing around cone 5 and do a heavy reduction at the end. Does this glaze tend to craze/crawl/pinhole/etc.? You should make sure the surface of the pot is clean of dust. How do different firing temperatures/atmospheres affect the glaze? Too muddy of a reduction will cause the copper to burn out. Too little will cause the glaze to run clear. How does the glaze behave on different clay bodies? White or light bodies are best, but it does work on red clay bodies. What consistency should the glaze be for pouring/dipping? Once you have mixed the glaze with water, you need to use it that day. A thick application is best. Dipped if possible. Once mixed the elements settle out and will not work if remixed. How thickly should the glaze be applied to the pot? The thicker the better, but the glaze will run. How does this glaze interact with other glazes? It works great with rutile glazes. What is your kiln type and size? I used an updraft reduction kiln about 9 cubic feet. How do you typically fire? I build temperature up to a cone 6 then reduce there for an hour, then go the rest of the way up reducing all the way. With a heavy reduction at the end. Then let it cool completely with all holes plugged and dampers shut tight. Do you experience problems with the raw glaze? Keep materials dry until you are ready to use. It will not stay mixed and the chemicals alter if left wet for more than 48 hours. GlazeBase recipe Submitted by: Suzanne -------------------------------------------------------------------- ----

recipes.name: Copper Red Dependable
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Copper red Oxblood needs to be thick mp. Begin reduction at cone 012 fairly heavy and then go into moderate reduction after cone 05 drops. Continue moderate to light reduction until cone 10 then a brief oxidation period of about 10 minutes. If you over-reduce it will be liver brown and under reduced will be celadon. One solution to a problem (uneven, spotty reduction and under reduced)we had was to turn down the gas and air. To slow it down and reduce at the above schedule. We were firing in an Alpine updraft with blowers and just running the same schedule as the people who fired before us. 4 pounds pressure (natural gas) with the blowers at 70. Something like that. But we reduced the gas and the air and the firing was 100% better. No more spotty reduction or unreduced pots. (I kind of miss those unwanted interesting results though.) submitted by: John Britt e-mail:

Variation 2 is a 5050 blend of the other versions, so is easy to add to your tests. recipes.name: Cream-breaking Red
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: a Readers Digest craft book Notes: Candice Roeder: a nice fat cream to beige glaze, glossy but not garish. Breaks to reddish brown where thin. If your clay body has much iron in it, the reddish breaking is quite pronounced, with speckles. I use it on white stoneware up to cone 7, and sometimes on porcelain, though on porcelain it is less earthy looking. It is a nice neutral earth tone. Stores well, coats well. Well behaved and forgiving. Dark slips used underneath will show through. In reduction it comes out brown. Notes: Ron Roy: when I calculate this glaze and compare it to all three sets of limit formulas I use - with B2O3 in and out of unity - the answer is always the same - this is a low fire glaze (08 at best.) At cone 6 it has less then half the alumina and silica needed for a stable glaze at that temperature. One of the reasons unbalanced glazes like this are so attractive is: when there is more flux than needed for melting the silica and alumina in the glaze, the flux starts looking for something to melt - that something is the clay (mostly the silica part of clay) it is on. Most of us like that effect (breaking on edges etc.) - which comes more naturally in hi fire reduction.

recipes.name: Crude Oil
recipes.description: This glaze only makes sense looking at the extended UMF calculations. This glaze is intended to mimic Jian ware using Matt Fiske's "Faux Eosin" glazes as a jumping off point. I had seen some manganese saturate glazes but none had the iridescence in oxidation that I was looking for. I was tipped off that the secret to iridescence lays in the usage of multiple alkaline earth fluxes. This particular glaze uses a ratio of 1:4 calcium to manganese. This test came from a line blend between two glazes with the same base and chemistry one with manganese and one with calcium. Tests in the range of of 1:9 to 4:6 all produced some form of iridescence. The tests below 1:4 had a rougher surface which may have been an error in application. A line blend using zinc and manganese with the same base was also done. Zinc results had a interesting texture in the same range as the calcium blend but produced no iridescence. One direction for further research will be a finer grained line blend in the 1:9 to 2:7 ratio with calcium and manganese. A second direction will be trying to change the dark brown color of the underlying glass matrix using opacifiers. A third and final direction will be additional testing with other fluxes particularly iron.

recipes.name: Crushed Strawberry Copper Red Glaze
recipes.description: From "My Work, My Way: Fifty Years in the Studio" by Harlan House, 2019. https://www.harlanhouse.com/ https://www.harlanhouse.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/2019%20HHBK-FINAL.pdf For far too many years, getting a good copper red glaze was a must. It took decades of trying tests in each kiln load, but finally I got something that worked. I did not want anything liver-like; this has what I wanted. These glazes are not easy, and vary from load to load. Even different locations in a kiln affect them. Keep trying… And yes, you will be wondering. Why is the batch in pounds, and the copper in grams? It turns out that my old scales are good at larger loads, but not at small ones. The amount of copper is so small, that I had to use my gram scales for the batch. So there. Soda feldspar 52.63 pounds 400m or 40 micron silica 26.3 pounds Whiting 10.5 pounds Dolomite 5.3 pounds Zinc oxide 3.2 pounds Tin oxide 1.3 pounds Bentonite 0.8 pounds Iron oxide 0.5 pounds Copper carbonate 150 grams This glaze is best thickly applied…really thick. This means that if it is too hot, it will run, so put a silica dusted cookie under your pot. The iron in the glaze gives it better color, but also if any atmospheric oxygen is in the kiln, the red will turn into a good crackle celadon. Sometimes you get both on the same piece. Bonus.

recipes.name: Crystalline Glaze Hewitt
recipes.description: Note that this glaze did not have a cone specified, but it appears to be a cone 9 glaze. I do not have experience with crystalline glazes but I do know of an excellent article that appeared in Ceramic Review No.137 (Sept/Oct 1992) by Derek Clarkson. His recipes are all based on the previous approximate percentages. The china clay was listed as China Clay/Alumina Colouring Oxides - cobalt, copper and manganese most often used, followed by iron and nickel. The article gives ten specific recipes around the above with colour illustrations to show the very dramatic crystal effects. For each of these examples the article also gives the firing details of the times of crystal growing periods and the diameter of the largest crystal. There is also a mass of detail on the application of the glazes with copious illustrations. Derek Clarkson says that Porcelain bodies are the most suitable. White stoneware bodies can also be used but the crystals are smaller. If you are unable to get sight of a copy of this article please contact me by e-mail if you want further information. submitted by: David Hewitt e-mail:

recipes.name: Daly/MC44
recipes.description: Mg/Ca dry glaze, sourced from Greg Daly, in "Dry Glazes" by Jeremy Jernegan, p. 92. I subbed O.M. 4 Ball Clay for EPK. Without Cu2O3, it's like white cake frosting, with large crackle; matte. With Cu2O3, it's a metallic black with a light haze over it, still matte. If really thin, some green. In the book, it's shown as ∆9 reduction with the recipe. Another image is on page 83, a bowl by Greg Daly, fired to ∆8 oxidation. That image is a beautiful smooth satin, the glaze seeming to break. Obviously, for non-functional work. Feb. 2023. Tested with EPK, as in original glaze. Matte black, no haze, shivers on Laguna ∆6 porcelain, #15 WC 616. I prefer the O.M.4 look. Changed name to reflect Greg Daly, not placement in book.

recipes.name: Dan Turnidge Base I
recipes.description: From the Clayart Mailing list at http://www.potters.org/subject37353.htm Jocelyn McAuley on tue 23 jan 01 Hello all, After much information gathering and anticipation I've finally started testing some of my gathered macro crystalline glazes... and have come up against a couple walls! I could really use some help and advice. My first problem was in seiving my glazes. I really don't want to ballmill my tests, but even after attacking my calcined zinc with a mortar and pestle, I can't get all of it through an 80s. I ended up using a tea strainer (which appeared to have worked ok). Is this normal with zinc oxide, or is it something that comes with a really old batch of it? My next problem came with programming the Skutt at school. Even following their suggested crystalline program, I came up against err 2, which I believe is "the program is in hold and the temperature is 50 degrees or more above the hold temperature". I tried running miniature fires going up to 150 degrees to test the "9999" I used for the ramp. They didn't seem to indicate much... Here is the crystalline firing program I tried: 1 200 degrees/hr to 1652, 0 hold 2 400 degrees/hr to 2300, 0 hold 3 9999 to 2000, 1:30 4 9999 to 1950, 1:30 5 9999 to 1930, 1:30 6 9999 to 1900, 0:10 Was I expecting too much out of my kiln? I really didn't want to have to resort to physical intervention with the kiln (cracking the lid, etc). Next firing, this weekend, I am going to babysit the firing the entire way. Some way or another I am going to force it to stick with my holds! Here are the glaze recipes I am testing this week Cone 9 Dan Turnidge Base II Ferro frit 3110 49.1% Zinc Oxide 22.6% Silica 22.6% Titanium Dioxide 5.7% Bentonite 2.0% Cone 9 Dan Turnidge Base I Ferro frit 3110 50.0% Zinc Oxide 24.7% Silica 19.6% Kaolin 0.5% Titanium Dioxide 5.2% Bentonite 2.0%

recipes.name: Dan Turnidge Crystalline Base
recipes.description: ☆Receta, muestras y fotos compartidas en el grupo de facebook "Aprendiendo entre Todos" por Gladys Sardella (Buenos Aires, Argentina) y Fabiana Sacnún (Rosario, Argentina). Comenta Gladys Sardella: "Les comparto esta muestrita con la receta correspondiente. Dan Turnidge cono 5 (1180º) Carbonato de Litio 5%, Frita 3110 (yo usé FK10 de Kelper Omar Dominguez) 50%, Cuarzo 22,5, Oxido de Cinc 22,5%, más 3 de bióxido de manganeso. Fue en oxidación en horno eléctrico a 1180º, 3º por min hasta los 400º con meseta de 10min y 4º por minuto hasta los 1180º con meseta de 20 minutos. Si con esta curva dio cristalitos habría que probarlo con una mejor curva." Comenta Fabiana Sacnún: "Para continuar con el hilo de la base Dan Turnidge, que hace mucho circuló por aquí. Estas dos muestritas son producto de un seminario que acabo de dar. La base original que había compartido Gladys Sardella era: Dan Turnidge cono 5(1180º) Carbonato de Litio 5% Frita 3110, 50% Cuarzo 22,5 Oxido de Cinc 22,5% A falta de la frita 3110 y sus sustitutos, en el seminario se trabajó con la 804 de Crecer en igual proporción. Los resultados idénticos! Quema, cono 5, bajada lenta hasta los 900 aproximadamente." ☆Source/Alternate names: Dan Turnidge. also known as MFE crystalline Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 900C hold 1 hour Notes: Alisa Clausen: Gloss, transparent glaze with stark white streaking. White crystals developed around edges of test tile, which is an extruded square tube. Runny. Glaze is crazed. With added 2 nickel: gloss, transparent glaze with softer white and pink streaking. Bright blue crystals along edges of test tile and bottom dipping line. Runny. Glaze is not crazed. Notes: John Sankey: I use this glaze with Fusion 75 frit plus 3 manganese dioxide and 1 cobalt oxide as colorants; it does not craze but it is runny as virtually all crystalline glazes are.

recipes.name: Darby's Base
recipes.description: I use both of these with a 10% addition of Mason 6600 black. Rosie's turns a satin grey, while Darby's is a satin black. Here are a couple of simple glazes you might try. Both are semi-gloss until you add stains, then they become more of a satin matt. The trick to getting a good matt glaze at cone 04 is to soak the kiln at the end of the firing, and then cool a bit slower than usual (fire down). A matt glaze becomes that way because micro-crystals grow out of the glass. It takes time for that to happen, and the typical electric kiln simply cools too quickly. Both of these came out of student triaxial blends at the Kansas City Art Institute. submitted by: Pete Pinnell source for original recipe: Kansas City Art Institute

With 10 zirconia, glossy, white glaze, crazed on white midrange stoneware, oxides did not move under base. With 2 cobalt carbonate, glossy, dark blue glaze, no visible crazing. With 1 cobalt carbonate plus 2 chrome oxide, semigloss, dark green glaze, no visible crazing. With 1 copper carbonate, very glossy, transparent glaze, light green, crazed. With 10 ochre, slightly less glossy, ochre brown glaze, slight crazing. With 10 red iron oxide, slightly less glossy, dark brown glaze, no visible crazing. Notes: Steve Slatin: some of the Cushing glazes are formulated for the far edge of what works. My favourite, Rusty Bronze done as green runs at cone 6, and if you have a cool at all slow it gets very matte, but if you turn off your kiln at cone 5Â½ and do a fast cool, you get a fabulous mix of glossy where thick and microcrystalline with a nice texture shift where thin. And one percent of bentonite in the glaze bucket just changes it entirely.

recipes.name: Dark Iron Red
recipes.description: A nice dark red glaze at cone 6. Some areas turn a bit metallic and have a reflective silver tint when facing some directions of light. You might be able to explore using less than 4% bone ash white still maintaining the red. Application thickness didn't seem to make much of a difference. I was able to apply a fairly thin coat on the mugs and had good results. Doesn't seem to run much especially when applied thin. I added a very small amount of epsom salt to help suspend the glaze. As for the potash feldspar I used custer feldspar (forgot to change it). I slow cool nearly everything so I'm not sure if this would work with a faster firing schedule or not.

recipes.name: Dave's Rutile - high viscosity
recipes.description: Goal here is to adjust the classic rutile blue to a higher viscosity at maturation temperature so as to prevent it from running onto the shelf. This is an adjustment of "Ray's Rutile" from Britt's "High Fire Glazes". I used Britt's "Rutile Blue 1" and "Rutile Blue 2" as guides as well. Britt's 1 has no magnesium, and Britt's 2 does and uses dolomite. I used talc for the magnesium The specific gravity was 1.39 with a single dip of 3 seconds. Add 8% rutile to this base glaze. Tends to pinhole, but I think that's the trade-off for fixing the viscosity. I use a liner glaze and only use colored glazes on the outside of pots.

recipes.name: David Beatie's Blue Celadon
recipes.description: Here's a recipe I got from a fellow ceramic artist and glaze guru. I'm putting it on my account to make sure I don't loose it because it works GREAT for a celadon blue. As with any celadon blue, I get nice saturated colors by mixing it thick (sp gr = 160) and applying several layers (2-4).

recipes.name: David Beatie's Clear Base
recipes.description: I obtained this recipe from a friend and fellow glazy user. I mainly use this glaze on my sculptures for coloring irises in eyes. I haven't tested it with many colorants yet, but it creates possibly the best golden yellow-ochre celadon (with 6% umber) that I've ever tested/made. If need creates it, I will certainly test out other pigments in this base. Usage notes: The test tile I used crazes because it was fired on bisqued cone 10 stoneware. If you use terra cotta or some other earthenware, it should fit perfectly. Since I am a sculptor, the crazing doesn't bother me, I may even stain it with ink if the situation warrants it. I intend to use it on Cone 10 or Cone 6 stoneware that has first been fired to Cone 3, then re-fired with this glaze and a few others to Cone 04.

recipes.name: David Tsabar's Red - Rojo
recipes.description: David Tsabar recalculation using frit 3134 of a popular Chrome/Tin Red glaze with many names: Scott's Red, June Perry Red, McDonald's Red, Ron Roy Red Burgundy, Purple Red, Raspberry.... Frit 3134 gives pink/purple color and local (Argentina ) frit 804 a nice red. %analysis frit 804: https://glazy.org/materials/826. "Maybe" Ferro Frit 3110 can be used for the red color. See pictures with frits 3134 and 804 with different amounts of chrome and tin. Better results over white body, thick, cone 6 tip touching the shelf. At cone 5 the color is less bright. Attention: if you get a glaze with almost no color, check your whiting. Some whitings do have a lot of magnesia in it, causing the loose of red color. Recálculo hecho por David Tsabar usando frita 3134 de Ferro (muy parecida a la 174 de Crecer-Argentina) de un esmalte rojo de cromo/estaño muy popular con muchos nombres: Scott's Red, June Perry Red, McDonald's Red, Ron Roy Red Burgundy, Purple Red, Raspberry.... Hice pruebas con Caolín Patagónico y Tinkar Z en vez del caolín. La muestra con Caolín Patagónico parece ofrecer una mejor calidad de esmalte. También usando la frita 804 de Crecer (Argentina), que parece brindar el mejor rojo. Ver los diferentes resultados con las dos fritas y diferentes cantidades de cromo/estaño. Mejor resultado sobre pasta blanca, capa más bien gruesa de esmalte y a cono 6. A cono 5 el color es más apagado. Atención: si se obtiene un esmalte casi sin color, controlar la calidad del carbonato de calcio. Algunos carbonatos de calcio contienen demasiado magnesio, causando la pérdida del color.

recipes.name: David's Base Slip for Low-Fire Bisque

When covered with Amaco LG-10, there is no crazing or shivering or flaking off and even with tapping vigorously on the surface, it does not chip off; quite durable. I ran a number of test of slips of various COE and this one is in the middle of the COE range for the acceptable results for crazing/shivering/flaking/durability. (COE = 5.9)

recipes.name: Dax Clear a02
recipes.description: Working on a base glaze that can do the most. I want reds, greens, blues, purple, browns, black, white, tan. I also want translucent, opaque, variegated. Finally, I want it cheap and made with readily available, consistent materials.

recipes.name: Dax Satin Base
recipes.description: This is a very nice feeling satin magnesium glaze. I am still testing for durability, but so far so good. It does take cutlery marks, but they wash off. So probably not the best for interiors of a bowl or plate. Firing cycle is Cone 5, Skutt Medium speed cycle with a 39 min hold. It's the same cycle I use for all my glazes and I did not want a satin that needed a special cycle to come out well. This on fulfills that. Another consideration was material consistency and availability it. I did not want to use any exotic or expensive materials. This recipe costs roughly $0.50 per pint.

recipes.name: DaxClear_A16
recipes.description: When calculating this glaze I set the following goals, in order of importance: - Food Safe. I will be putting the glaze through a number of tortue tests to make sure it is safe to use. This includes acid tests, alkali tests, scratch, thermal shock, and much more. - Theoretically and practically standardized. So far, it passes theoretical formula limits for a safe glaze. For most Mole values, the glaze is near the center of the range for limits. - Very clear and glossy. I want a “crystal clear” to start with that I can use over under glaze, or on a nice bare clay body. - Consistent results. I don’t want a temperamental glaze. This means it fires well over a few different cones, from 4-7 at least. It behaves the same whether it is a bit on the thin or thick side. It does not run, craze, shiver, or crawl. - Consistent materials. I prefer to use as many manufactured blends as possible as they are the most steady in availability, formula, and price. I also prefer to use materials that I use when making a clay body. Fewer materials to buy and store is a good thing. - Cheap. Why not? If I can find equivalent materials that are cheap, then I would prefer them. After all, cutting costs is a major reason to make your own glazes. At my calculated current price, I can make a pint of this glaze for $0.55. As a comparison, my local supplier sells clear for $10.00 a pint. - Plays well with colorant oxides. While I can make up a variety of glaze bases, it would be even better if I can use a single base to do a large variety of child-glazes. - Does not fingerprint. I noticed that Hansen 5x20 has a bad habit of picking up fingerprints when many other glazes don’t. I would like to make one that does not. This is attempt #16 that I have run through the kiln and the best I have come up with yet. I will do more test with oxides, stains, and washes with it next and publish any good ones.

recipes.description: From Steve Davis Website: http://kazegamas.com/ Shinos 2: http://kazegamas.com/shinos2.htm There are 72 shinos shown on 4 web pages. They are organized from left to right with 3 tiles of the same glaze shown on 3 different clay bodies. They are Aardvark Clay's Nara Porcelain, Long Beach, and Black Mountain. Every shino was glazed with a doulble dip, waxed with a simple "S" pattern, and left to dry for 2 weeks to grow sulfates on the surface. The "S" pattern has no sulfate build up. A medium reduction was started at cone 012 through cone 2. From there the kiln was fired in neutral to cone 10.

I was fortunate enough to acquire black cobalt oxide from china, which is actually one of the best cobalt pigments I've ever worked with. Dolomite and sodium were both used in order to push blue towards a brighter, purple-blue color. Calcium and a small amount of strontium serve as additional color enhancers.

If not, I pedestal my piece and use only shredded paper to avoid scarring. recipes.description: From Charlie Cummings Sometimes shiny, sometimes matte. Put it over a cloth texture, and you have invented ceramic denim. It reacts to the slip color under it. It also breaks light brown over lines, brush strokes, or throwing rings. This glaze uses dolomite. All of the books say it isn't active at this range, but my students didn't know that. I would have told them it wouldn't work, but I like to let them make their own mistakes...or show me I'm so so wrong. Now I just need to convince them to try other colorants. This glaze likes a big kiln and a slow firing. The results from the small kiln were cool too, but incredibly different.

recipes.name: Derek's Kaki Biaxial D4 (Custer Substitution)
recipes.description: This is a Custer substitution I did because I did not have mahavir at the time. Now I do, but I figure this would be good for everyone to see and compare. Here's my firing profile and then the stuff copied over from Derek's recipe info. Reduction started at 014, damper is inserted until temperature stalls for an hour and then the kiln is ramped at 120/hr until peak temperature. Damper was then inserted and kiln turned off ---DEREKS INFORMATION AND SCHEDULE--- Adjusted glaze using original Kaki D4 from a Kaki-type glaze biaxial. Firing profile adjusted from various schedules posted on http://carol.knighten.org/ 150°F/hr to 250°F 375°F/hr to 2050°F 120°F/hr to 2250°F 60°F/hr to 2290°F 40°F/hr to 2315°F Hold of 15 minutes at 2315°F 400°F to 1700°F (Down fire) Hold 1 hour at 1700°F Original firing schedule was 2 hour hold. One hour seems just as good. Perfect cone 10 firing. Adjusted firing schedule for medium Bailey electric kiln with Bartlett controller: 150°F/hr to 250°F hold 1 hour 350°F/hr to 2050°F 120°F/hr to 2250°F 60°F/hr to 2290°F 40°F/hr to 2315°F Hold of 15 minutes at 2315°F 999°F to 1700°F (Down fire) Hold 1.5 hours at 1700°F

recipes.name: Derek's Kaki Biaxial D4 (Custer Substitution)
recipes.description: This is a Custer substitution I did because I did not have mahavir at the time. Now I do, but I figure this would be good for everyone to see and compare. Here's my firing profile and then the stuff copied over from Derek's recipe info. Reduction started at 014, damper is inserted until temperature stalls for an hour and then the kiln is ramped at 120/hr until peak temperature. Damper was then inserted and kiln turned off ---DEREKS INFORMATION AND SCHEDULE--- Adjusted glaze using original Kaki D4 from a Kaki-type glaze biaxial. Firing profile adjusted from various schedules posted on http://carol.knighten.org/ 150°F/hr to 250°F 375°F/hr to 2050°F 120°F/hr to 2250°F 60°F/hr to 2290°F 40°F/hr to 2315°F Hold of 15 minutes at 2315°F 400°F to 1700°F (Down fire) Hold 1 hour at 1700°F Original firing schedule was 2 hour hold. One hour seems just as good. Perfect cone 10 firing. Adjusted firing schedule for medium Bailey electric kiln with Bartlett controller: 150°F/hr to 250°F hold 1 hour 350°F/hr to 2050°F 120°F/hr to 2250°F 60°F/hr to 2290°F 40°F/hr to 2315°F Hold of 15 minutes at 2315°F 999°F to 1700°F (Down fire) Hold 1.5 hours at 1700°F

recipes.name: Derek's Manganese Red
recipes.description: I named this glaze after Derek Au, I got it out of a glaze book written by Murfitt. It's super glossy and really hard to photograph. It forms some manganese patches so you may want to dial down the manganese. It has a nice muddy brown color where it breaks and it's slightly purply where red.

recipes.name: Deslizamento Simples (1)
recipes.description: Esmaltes de gama média, John Britt, pág. 169. Argila tabaco. Já craquelou ao passar, além de ter passado muito grosso. Vou trabalhar a sobrefoculação com silicato de sódio, além do que realmente necessitava um pouco mais de água.

recipes.name: Deslizamento Simples (2)
recipes.description: Baseado em Esmaltes de gama média, John Britt, pág. 169.

recipes.name: Deslizamento Simples (3)
recipes.description: Esmaltes de gama média, John Britt, pág. 169, alterado baixando sílica e alumínio proporcionalmente, porque achei exagerado. Vou recalcular com Albita (feldspato sódico) para obter mais sódio e menos potássio. Já craquelou ao passar. Vou trabalhar a defloculação com silicato de sódio. Aderiu muito bem ao biscoito. Vou testar no ponto de couro como engobe. Gostei muito da opacidade e do branqueamento. Talvez baixe mais um pouco a sílica e o alumínio, visto que os engobes estão bem mais abaixo no Stull. Vou pensar... Talvez eu aumente a São Simão e diminua o caulim... Eu coloquei 100% de água e ficou ralo. Depois coloquei CMC para deslizar. Penso em colocar 80% de água e 20% de CMC e também silicato de sódio. Ainda não sei bem sobre a consistência e deslizamento que pretendo e penso que deverá variar conforme a ocasião ou até que eu tenha alguma certeza para usar em estado de couro ou no biscoito. Acredito que pegará bem as cores.

recipes.name: Destello Chocolate con caolin brasilero (Aventurine)
recipes.description: Receta de Destello Chocolate usando caolín Imerys de Brasil. Buen efecto venturina sin escurrimiento excesivo. Demostró buen resultado frente al test ácido. Sparkling Chocolate using Imerys Kaolin (very similar to EPK). Nice aventurine effect, no running. Passed 4 days vinegar test without apparent changes.

recipes.name: DEV 004
recipes.description: This development has a story. I was impressed by a simple glaze using 80 Albany slip and 20 Frit 3134. However, I wanted a less dark glaze showing the same surface. Therefore I took the analysis of Albany slip and omit the Iron - and recalculate to a recipe. I obtained an interesting glaze with some movement. There were some bubbles, but I think it was due to a too fast firing. Other coloring oxides to try.

recipes.name: Devon frost
recipes.description: Frosty matte with UK materials. Not matte at all for me at cone 7. Lovely little snowflake crystals in a milky base.

recipes.name: Devon slate
recipes.description: This recipe attempts to keep the RO:R20 ratio at the same level as HSCM. Some of the calcium is replaced with Magnesium sourced from the GB. There are versions with 12.5, 6.25 and 0% cornish stone. This is because the amount of flux and alumina in Kaolins can vary significantly - your millage will vary it's best to test all three. Variation 2 is a 5050 blend of the other versions, so is easy to add to your tests. Devon china clay a lot of potassium compared to american Kaolins, so this might work well for you. It works really well for me! This is part of a set of glazes. Your milage will vary: Cornish slate has 12.5 cornish stone: https://glazy.org/recipes/9415 Devon slate has no cornish stone: https://glazy.org/recipes/9468 Westcountry slate is a blend of devon and cornish slate with 6.25% cornish stone: https://glazy.org/recipes/9469

recipes.name: Dianetics Celadon
recipes.description: Continuing the naming tradition after holy books, this is the Bible Celadon recipe with twice as much EPK and set back to 100%. It's fairly glossy, transparent, and is more green from the Alumina and titanium contaminants, but it's not crazing on our studio's stoneware, but has some on black mountain. I might be testing sme rare Earth's in this base as the Bible Celadon quickly becomes foggy from the inclusion of high percentages of colorants.

recipes.name: Dick White's Turquoise
recipes.description: This is a re-formulation of Val's Turquoise by Dick White to improve the Alumina content. The original Val's Turquoise recipe leaches copper due to the change in formulation of Gerstley Borate from the old days. Lemon/Vinegar test shows discoloration using the original recipe. This new formulation makes the glaze more stable.

recipes.name: Dickman's Sinter
recipes.description: From Steve Davis Website: http://kazegamas.com/ Shinos 2: http://kazegamas.com/shinos2.htm There are 72 shinos shown on 4 web pages. They are organized from left to right with 3 tiles of the same glaze shown on 3 different clay bodies. They are Aardvark Clay's Nara Porcelain, Long Beach, and Black Mountain. Every shino was glazed with a doulble dip, waxed with a simple "S" pattern, and left to dry for 2 weeks to grow sulfates on the surface. The "S" pattern has no sulfate build up. A medium reduction was started at cone 012 through cone 2. From there the kiln was fired in neutral to cone 10.

recipes.name: DJ's Perfect Purple
recipes.description: "I have introduced a cooling cycle to the firing. The cycle is as follows and the firing is accompanied by a Cone 6 witness cone. After 12 consecutive firings, the witness cones are identical from firing to firing." The firing cycle: Rate Temp Hold Time rA1= 360 F1 = 900 0 rA2= 300 F2 = 1800 0 rA3 =200 F3 = 2016 0 rA4 = 108 F4 = 2197 0.3 rA5 = Full F5 =1800 0 rA6 =150 F6 = 1300 0 rA7 = 0000 To summarize, I fire at a rate of 360/hr to 900 degrees F, then at 300 degrees/ hr to 1800 degrees F, 200 degrees/hr until 2016 degrees F is reached, then 108 degrees/hour to 2197 at which time I hold it at that temperature for 30 minutes. The kiln is shut off until a temperature of 1800 degrees F is reached and then turned on to slow the rate of cooling to 150 degrees/hr until 1300 degrees F is reached. At this point the kiln is turned off and cools naturally. Western Pennsylvania Potters Community http://wpapotters.blogspot.com/2012/04/links-to-cone-6-oxidation-glaze-tests.html http://www.wpapotters.blogspot.com/2011/10/cone-6-oxidation-results-group-8.html

With 3 cobalt carbonate, translucent, gloss, dark blue, running. With 1 cobalt carbonate and 2 rutile, translucent, gloss dark blue with dark to black pooled areas. With 1 cobalt carbonate and 4.5 rutile, translucent, olive green ground with blue rivulets and streaks. With 1 cobalt carbonate and 6 rutile, gloss, overall and covering medium green, breaking brown with slight bluish streaking. With 1 cobalt carbonate and 2 chrome oxide, gloss, covering medium to dark green. With 2 cobalt carbonate and 2 chrome, gloss, covering dark greenish teal. With 2 cobalt carbonate and 2 copper carbonate and 2 tin dioxide, gloss, covering dark green, slightly lighter than above. With 2 cobalt carbonate and 2 copper carbonate and 10 tin dioxide, gloss, covering teal green. With 2 cobalt carbonate and 2 copper carbonate and 3 titanium dioxide and 2 rutile, semigloss, covering, grey blue ground with greenish brown cast. With 1 cobalt carbonate and 1 red iron oxide, gloss, cover, very dark blue. With 1 cobalt carbonate and 3 red iron oxide, gloss, dark blue with almost black pooling. Very fluid and high edges but did not run, crazed. With 1 cobalt carbonate and 5 ochre, gloss, very dark blue, fluid edges. With 2 cobalt carbonate and 1 tin dioxide, gloss, very dark blue, fluid and ran off tile. With 3 rutile, translucent, gloss, pale yellow, crazed. With 6 rutile, translucent ground, pale yellow, heavily streaked with opalescence. Very fluid but did not run off tile, crazed. With 6 rutile and 6 red iron oxide, semimat, covering medium brown baizes. Appears to have and overall sparkle made up of tiny crystals. With 3 copper carbonate, translucent, gloss, pale green. With 6 copper carbonate, translucent, gloss, medium green with dark green streaking. Very fluid, but did not run, crazed. With 3 copper carbonate and 3 rutile, translucent, gloss, medium green streaking and shell over light brown ground, crazing. With 3 copper carbonate and 6 rutile and 1.5 cobalt carbonate, gloss, covering, very fluid with several streaking colours over a medium green grown, streaking is turquoise, brown and blue, very fluid and ran off tile in one area, breaking brown. With 4 copper carbonate and 6 rutile, almost translucent gloss, very fluid, exaggeration of above, ran off the tile. With 1 cobalt carbonate and 4 rutile and 2 red iron oxide, gloss, covering multi coloured glaze, brown ground and breaking, with streaking blue, green and beige, a lot of movement without running, a good runner up for Floating Blue. With 1 cobalt carbonate and 5 rutile and 0.5 red iron oxide, semigloss, covering and variegated green, dark green ground with lighter green speckling. With 5 red iron oxide, translucent, gloss, medium brown. With 10 red iron oxide, translucent, gloss, dark brown. With 5 tin dioxide, gloss, covering, soft white, slight yellowish cast. With 10 tin dioxide, gloss, covering, white. With 5 zirconia, translucent, cream, badly crazed. With 10 zirconia, gloss, covering, stark white. With 5 titanium dioxide, translucent, pale umber, slight opalescence where pooled. With 10 titanium dioxide, translucent, gloss, light yellow ground, with thick streaking white crystals and blue opalescence, ran off tile. With 5 titanium dioxide and 5 red iron oxide, gloss, covering medium brown with dark blue streaking, red in one of the streaks, a lot of movement, high edge, but did not run. With 1.5 titanium dioxide and 15 red iron oxide, gloss, medium brown ground with a lot of movement streaking, blue and black, ran off tile. With 1 rutile and 12.5 red iron oxide, semigloss, brown and black streaking, darkest where pooled. With 4 manganese dioxide and 6 rutile, gloss, overall beige with blueish pooling. With 4 manganese dioxide and 0.4 cobalt carbonate and 6 rutile, gloss, overall beige with very fluid grey blue streaking and pinkish casts, ran off tile.

recipes.name: Donte's Lumos
recipes.description: This is my oxidation glaze Lumos. Some time ago when i first started testing glazes by trial and error i found a glaze called "Fake Shino" I have no idea where it was from but it looks like someone made a melty base glaze and added R.I.O to it in order to simulate a cone 10 Shino. I Disliked the glaze but loved the base and ended up mixing it with every glaze that wasn't white. The Glaze is a white iridescent opaque glaze that alone makes an ok white but when combined with most other glazes makes a great additive.

recipes.name: Donte's Majin Buu
recipes.description: A translucent base I have been working with in order to get a clear-ish melt. Instead of mixing zinc and tin, I instead found a new pigment called erbium oxide. instead of mixing oxides to get the light pink I enjoy, this chemical just makes pink. I love it. I never thought it would be as simple as taking a base I have been working on and adding one new oxide at 10%. I tested it in my tester kiln twice. soon i will be testing it in a slow cool kiln and post results. These tests were all fired in my tester kiln. I am curious to see what it will look like in the lager kiln that holds much more heat for a longer time. when i can i will update with a better picture. these are just testiles.

recipes.name: Donte's Pur Pur Rain
recipes.description: A revision / continuation of Donte's translucent base with 4% rutile and 6% manganese dioxide. I have been looking for a type of melty rutile base for a very long time but cant quite get it right. along the way I made this glaze. It either needs a higher gravity or it needs a double dip. you can probably see in the test tiles but the good purple needs a thick layer. The top test tile is double dipped while the bottoms are a single dip.

recipes.name: Donte's Translucent base recipe (in search of hyasinth)
recipes.description: I have been using this base recipe because its just clear enough. the goal was to make a melt blue on a rutile base glaze. im getting pretty close. i think this time I will have to put either 4-5 % manganese dioxide or lessen the amount of rutile. Maybe put in about .25 or .5% cobalt carbonate to really get that blue in there instead of using manganese.

recipes.name: Dontes Base
recipes.description: This is a base. I am working on a translucent base that is a little more stable than i am used to working with. Seems fine to me although it dose not seem to like red clay bodies. It has great texture melt when you add color to it. Although this picture is on a bmix with grog tile i bet it would look great on porcelain.

recipes.name: Dontes' Blue Bomber Crystal Glaze ^6 ox
recipes.description: This is a crystalline glaze Bass by Gerry zucca which I added .3 Cobalt carbonate to with a hold between 1600-1500 down 50/hr. The instruction in the book says not to use it the way i have buuuuuut..... no advancement was ever made that way ;) I do love this base although you do not need alot of the glaze to make it work. 1-2 coats or a very fast dip ( if you do dip) for about 1.5 seconds. if you are painting make sure you layer down by having most of the glaze be at the top of the pot.

recipes.name: Dontes' Dune Glow
recipes.description: This is a crystalline glaze Bass by Gerry zucca which I added 0.5 R.I.O and 1 Manganese carb with a hold between 1600-1500 down 50/hr. The instructions in the book says not to use it the way i have buuuuuut..... no advancement was ever made by following that. I do love this base although you do not need a lot of the glaze to make it work. 1-2 coats or a very fast dip ( if you do dip) for about 1.5 seconds. if you are painting make sure you layer down by having most of the glaze be at the top of the pot. if you put too much of the glaze it will craze a little bit. these glazes work without a hold as well but they make crystals when you put a hold on them. of course it is NOT FOOD SAFE as it, it must be heavily leached before eating off the heavy zinc crystals.

recipes.description: Tole painters and living room curtains from the 80s will remember this one! I had a batch of MC6 Raspberry base with 5 tin and 0.15 chrome but then I decided I didn't really care for it so I added EPK to increase Al and Si and added Ultrox (Zircopax) to lighten. One could formulate a simpler recipe without the EPK. Big thanks to Derek for his tests on CrSn pinks which were really helpful figuring out what to do.

recipes.name: Dusty watermelon
recipes.description: This glaze is the result of me ‘improving’ on one of the glazes I had previously tested. I recently reread “Mastering Cone 6 Glazes” about making stable and functional glazes. After rereading how to make a stable glaze I finally understood that all the numbers they were referring to in the book was talking about the UMF and wanted to go back on some glazes that I believed could be improved from some tweaking in the chemistry. That glaze in question was Charle’s Titanium with copper carbonate (3%) and rutile (2%). I noticed some flaws with that test. It crazes, there wasn’t enough silica and alumina which made it way too fluid, and the R2O:RO flux ratio didn’t meet an ideal ratio of 3:7. After going through the recipe I readjusted the ingredients. I met the minimum amount of silica and alumina that is required for a “stable glaze” in Ron Roy and John Hesselberth’s book ,MC6, while also lowering the thermal expansion at the same time which makes the glaze less likely to craze. Then finally I took in account for the colorants which also influence the flux ratio in the extended UMF, so I added 2% zinc which helped me meet the ideal ratio for a stable glaze. I strongly recommend the book to those interested in making durable and functional cone 6 glazes. Substitution for wollastonite by using whiting. https://glazy.org/recipes/101138

recipes.description: From Steve Davis Website: http://kazegamas.com/ Shinos 2: http://kazegamas.com/shinos2.htm There are 72 shinos shown on 4 web pages. They are organized from left to right with 3 tiles of the same glaze shown on 3 different clay bodies. They are Aardvark Clay's Nara Porcelain, Long Beach, and Black Mountain. Every shino was glazed with a doulble dip, waxed with a simple "S" pattern, and left to dry for 2 weeks to grow sulfates on the surface. The "S" pattern has no sulfate build up. A medium reduction was started at cone 012 through cone 2. From there the kiln was fired in neutral to cone 10.

Controlled cooling in electric kiln; on Laguna C.6 porcelain. Photo is somewhat shadowed. Oxide stripes: Cu Carb., Co Ox., R.I.O., Amamo Velvet Black, under glaze. Texture to right of first oxide stripe, Copper. Some crazing.

recipes.name: Emerald
recipes.description: Started with Old Forge Strontium recipe and swapped SrO with Barium. Tweaked R2O:RO levels, boron levels, Al:Si levels - pretty much a new recipe. R2O is low which helped eliminate popped/unhealed bubbles when using CuCo - which raises the R2O. I haven't tested this with other colorants yet. It was the emerald color I was going for. Only issue now is that it crazes like crazy. I'm working on trying to sub the Barium for a Barium frit - which are hard to find. The one I want only comes in large pallets and I only need a few pounds for testing. There's a few with lower barium levels that are available in smaller quantities. The barium gives it this green color. When I add Whiting or other AEs, the color goes more olive.

We covered the bisqued pot with the black englobe, (brushed on) and then dipped the pot in the lichen glaze. Then colored commercial underglazes were sprayed on the glaze. Wonderful effects. The black engobe gives better contrast with the lichen glaze. I also tried the lichen glaze both over and under my regualr cone six glazes, some very interesting, very nice effects. try it. submitted by: Kathy Darby source for original recipe: Randy Brodnax

Thin: craze Thick: nice scales Too thick: beads Needs testing to find the right application system. May crawl, so.... 1. Clara's method: Reglaze the scars and refire. Result: nice, scars can only been seen if immersed under water. 2. Chinese method: Thin glaze layer/ bisquefire, Thin glaze layer/ bisquefire, Thin glaze layer/ bisquefire... until having it thick enough. Then.... fire at cone 5/6. Result: perfection success!!! 😊
