recipes.description: A stiffer formula for a slip based black, using less cobalt than Satin Black. My test tiles used 2% cobalt. The results have a slightly silvery surface, so I'm going to try to reduce the cobalt to 1.5%. The formula with Custer feldspar was the most appealing. St. Johns black (using nepheline syenite) also came out well, flashed, and the petalite test had bumps on the surface. The crawling glaze applied over the top is "Sperry Crusty": 70% custer 30% magnesium carbonate.

recipes.name: ethos iceberg
recipes.description: A nice white glaze that shows hints of blue and purple ( on white stoneware ) where applied thinner. The name is very appropriate because this glaze really resembles natural ice. I developed this one after some failure with Lynette's Opal. I really wanted the subtle blue but with the original recipe there was none of that. I also found the original recipe overly complex. With those things in mind I recreated this glaze from scratch and did some testing for further optimization. There's still a bit too much boron in the current recipe so it gets runny at around cone 6. I'll adjust for that in the future. I start by adding 90% water then gradually add more water to get to 1.45 SG. At this SG it will still be too thick and prone to shivering so make sure to deflocculate to appropriate viscosity. I usually use tri-soda dissolved in some water and add it with a syringe to adjust to appropriate viscosity, but any deflocculant should do. I'm sharing all of my production glazes. If you like this one please show some ❤️ over at my instagram. When posting content of your work covered with this glaze please tag @ethosceramics and use #ethosglaze as hashtag. !ethos ceramics

recipes.name: ethos patina

It tends to be a bit too muddy so usually I'll add a bit of tri-soda ( you can use whatever deflocculant you prefer ). I'm sharing all of my production glazes. If you like this one please show some ❤️ over at my instagram. When posting content of your work covered with this glaze please tag @ethosceramics and use #ethosglaze as hashtag. !ethos ceramics

recipes.name: Fake ash - Martell
recipes.description: Here's one that I formulated and have used for a number of years. It is best applied by spraying but can be dipped, poured, etc. You have to work with the thickness to got the desired result. A light application will orange peel like a salt glaze while heavier applications will run. Too much thickness and you will get blistering. This glaze works well with most oxides. It also works best on porcelain or with white slips but don't be afraid to try anything...you never know. You can get this glaze to work at cone 8 and 9 by substituting Ball Clay for Kaolin. You might want to do a sub at cone 10 as well to observe the difference. Regards, Craig Martell-Oregon

recipes.name: Floating Blue 2
recipes.description: This glaze is brown or pond scum green when applied thinly so needs to be fairly thick. Will be a nice bright blue when the glaze thickness is correct and darker Blue on iron rick bodies. Also don't fire too hot, the included firing scheduled should get you to ^5.5 also works best with Specific Gravity of about 148. Setting viscosity with a Ford cup will save you countless hours of testing and this method will help you get the right thickness on the pot. Viscosity should be about 20-22 seconds using the Ford cup. This glaze works much better if dipped rather than poured. This is because a consistent thickness is a key to repeatable results along with not firing too hot. Start with a single dip of 5-7 seconds followed by a second dip on the top 1/4 to 1/3 of the form. Use cookies and test first because it may run onto shelves until you get it dialed in. Tony Hansen has a great article on using a Ford cup on his Digitalfire site. Here's the link https://digitalfire.com/glossary/viscosity Best to fire to cone 5 or 5.5 with a 15 min hold then drop 100 degrees for 45 minutes. See the firing schedule below. How to mix: Add about 78% water. This should bring you to a Specific Gravity of about 148.5 Check Specific Gravity - should be 148.5 or thereabouts. Glaze works best for me at 148 - 150. Check and Set Viscosity with a #4 Ford cup to about 20-22 seconds. Chances are you'll need to flocculate or deflocculate the glaze to get it to 20-22 seconds. This link will take you to an article by Pete Pinnell that does a great job of explaining how to get a glaze to a properly flocculated state. Give is a quick read, I'm sure you'll find it worthwhile. http://www.claytimes.com/articles/glazeadjusting.html You'll know you've got the right thickness when a 5-second dip gives you about 1mm or just less than the thickness of a dime. I got my Ford cup on Amazon, here is the link: https://www.amazon.com/TCP-Thickness-Viscosity-Measuring-Viscosimeter/dp/B00IL7DVNW/ref=sr11?dchild=1&keywords=Ford+%234+Cup&qid=1587238297&s=automotive&sr=1-1

recipes.name: Fools Gold
recipes.description: 7mls. of dissolved solution (below) = 1.50 grams (less stable)Silver nitrate is poison and corrosive. In solution, if spilled, it stains the surface a revolting liver colour forever. If splashed on hands or skin...liver again for many weeks. Rehearsal for age spots. Crystals are the way to go. Silver nitrate crystals are weighed by grams and added to distilled water. The ratio is one gram to 10 mls of water. So 5 grams go into 50 mls. etc. Store the dissolved solution in a coloured bottle and keep it out of light. When measuring the solution to be added to your glaze WEAR RUBBER GLOVES,CLOTHING YOU HATE and open the windows wide. This stuff doesn't smell at all but it's powerful . Add the needed amount to the MIXED and SIEVED glaze and stir carefully. It will make the texture of the glaze peculiar at first, sort of curdled but keep on stirring and it will smooth out. Wash the stirring implement thoroughly especially if it's metal. This glaze is best painted on in three smooth coats. Use a special brush for this glaze as it will be perm. stained black. recipes.name: G1916Q
recipes.description: From Digitalfire.com: https://digitalfire.com/recipe/g1916q Modified: 2020-09-16 09:32:23 An expansion-adjustable cone 04-02 transparent glaze made using three common Ferro frits (low and high expansion), it produces an easy-to-use slurry. ##Notes This recipe can produce a super-transparent surface of high quality. It has good application properties (if mixed properly, see below) and melts to a clear at cone 04-02. All of the frits are commonly available. Remember that cone 06 firing produces a poor glaze:body bond, we recommend firing cone 04 or 03 if possible (ware strength also increases greatly). This glaze can be made to fit pretty well any clay body (by adjustment in frit proportions). We recommend drop-and-hold firing, for example the 04DSDH schedule. There are three frits: -Frit 3195 is almost a complete glaze on its own, it just needs a little kaolin. It fires slightly silky rather than completely glossy but with the addition of one of the frits below a high gloss is achieved. But it is somewhat above middle-of-the-road for thermal expansion (the 85:15 frit:clay variation, G1916J, will craze on most of our clay bodies). -Frit 3110 is super high expansion and high gloss. Blend it with Frit 3195 it to deal with shivering. -Frit 3249 is super low expansion and high gloss. Blend it with Frit 3195 to deal with crazing. In one variation we employ 30% of this and For example, to fit Plainsman Buffstone at cone 04 we find that a 55:30:15 3195:3249:Ball Clay mix works well. This frit-juggling strategy affords a wide range of adjustment for tuning the glaze fit to a body, a very important matter at low temperatures where crazing and shivering can occur with even slight thermal expansion misfit. In some situations using only Frit 3195 and ball clay might be ok. However we recommend to 65:10:10 frit mix because the 3249 and 3110 cancel out each other's thermal expansion influence and increase the gloss of the otherwise silky 3195. The presence of 3249 also reduces boron blue issues. Stress-test the fit by subjecting a piece of thin-walled ware to boiling-water-into-ice-water (and vice versa) immersion. This will reveal misfit that will happen with time. There can be issues with clouding. Thinner application and higher firing (e.g. cone 04, 03) both help. If the glaze goes on too thick using normal techniques consider bisquing higher to reduce its porosity. This recipe employs #5 ball clay, a material known to produce better glaze slurries. No. 1 Glaze ball clay is another. However if you do not have either, then other ball clays should OK. EPK is also ok. To achieve even coverage it is a good idea to employ a thixotropic slurry (one that gels slightly). The 15% clay is plenty to suspend the slurry (adding bentonite is not needed).

recipes.name: Gartside 28 (+2 Cobalt)
recipes.description: This is Brian Gartsides famous clear parts recipe. I broke it down in to weight because I work better that way. I calculated it by simple division: 4 into 100, 2 into 25 and 2 into 12.5, then rounded up on Glaze Master. I left it at totaling 98 because I did not want 4 decimal places. Original in parts 4 Frit 3134 4 EPK 2 G-200 Feldspar 2 Silica 1 Talc 1 Whiting 16 Water Now in weight Amount Ingredient 28.6 Frit--Ferro 3124 4 parts 28.6 Kaolin--EPK 14.3 Feldspar--G-200 2 parts 14.3 Silica 7.1 Talc 1 part 7.1 Whiting 100 Total Unity Oxide .138 Na2O .074 K2O .204 MgO .584 CaO 1.000 Total .6 Al2O3 .212 B2O3 .006 Fe2O3 3.562 SiO2 .004 TiO2 .001 P2O5 5.9 Ratio 6.5 Exp Results Gloss to semi gloss transluscent glaze See color variations at website, Glaze tests, more tests www.alisapots.dk My parts base tests crazed on my stoneware. However the weight variation did not. I think it because my parts measuring by spoon full was much too variable. Best regards from Alisa in Denmark

recipes.name: Gartside 28 Base,3 Rutile, 3 Copper Carb. ^6 Ox.
Gartside Base
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Brian Gartside, converted to weights by John Sankey Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 900C hold 1 hour Notes: Alisa Clausen: the original was 4 parts by volume frit, 4 parts EPK, 2 parts silica, 2 parts feldspar, 1 part calcium carbonate, 1 part talc. Transparent gloss, colours very well. I think the sheer spectrum of colours that resulted from this base, gives a good incentive for those who seek not to have many, many glazes in their studios, but rather a couple of bases they can colour. Personally, I think that is an excellent idea, as I too, have two to three bases that I use regularly, and colour as I need them. I usually have a few kilos dry glaze of each base, so that I can mix smaller amounts with colouring oxides. recipes.name: Gay Barium Blue
recipes.description: I've always been a big fan of Barium Blues. Here's a recipe I modified from "Silverman Blue" This one is a lovely translucent blue matte color, with a more vitrified feel than Lana's Purple Matte. Try swapping the barium for strontium (1:1) to get a more green color as well. Try different colorants in it as well, it should make a pretty yellow glaze with iron. I found this glaze turned opaque and yielded a deep blue color in thick areas if slow cooled in this manner: Ramp 1 - 200f/hr, 2100f, hold 0s Ramp 2- 108f/hr, 2232f (cone 6), hold 0s Ramp 3- 9999f/hr, 1700f, hold 0s Ramp 4- 50/hr, 1500f, hold 0s (this is a variation of Steven Hill's c6 electric firing cycle)

recipes.name: GBCG1 - Glassa cristallina base generica Frit 3110
recipes.description: È possibile modificare il rapporto di questi ingredienti in base alle proprie esigenze e gusti individuali, entro determinati parametri. Più fritta usi (rispetto agli altri ingredienti), più basso sarà il punto di maturazione della glassa. Più silice usi (come accennato in precedenza), meno lo smalto può tendere a impazzire , ma meno cristalli produrrai. Puoi vedere dalla composizione del silicato di zinco, Zn2SiO 4, che per ogni due atomi di ossido di zinco, abbiamo bisogno di uno di silice per ottenere una molecola di cristallo. A parte la silice necessaria per i cristalli, è necessaria ulteriore silice per lo smalto stesso; quindi bisogna assicurarsi di averne abbastanza. L'aumento e la riduzione della quantità di ossido di zinco in uno smalto influenzerà direttamente il numero di cristalli che lo smalto sarà in grado di crescere. L'aggiunta di ossidi / carbonati aggiuntivi come quelli di titanio, calcio, stagno e così via influenzerà l' opacità , le dimensioni e la forma dei cristalli, lo sviluppo ausiliario e il colore.

recipes.name: George Washington Uni.
recipes.description: From Steve Davis Website: http://kazegamas.com/ Shinos 2: http://kazegamas.com/shinos2.htm Spalls from excess Lithium There are 72 shinos shown on 4 web pages. They are organized from left to right with 3 tiles of the same glaze shown on 3 different clay bodies. They are Aardvark Clay's Nara Porcelain, Long Beach, and Black Mountain. Every shino was glazed with a doulble dip, waxed with a simple "S" pattern, and left to dry for 2 weeks to grow sulfates on the surface. The "S" pattern has no sulfate build up. A medium reduction was started at cone 012 through cone 2. From there the kiln was fired in neutral to cone 10.

recipes.name: Ginger Mint
recipes.description: This is an updated version of the Ben Fiess HFG0020B spearmint recipe.. we had a group discussion about its functionality on another thread, and I made this copy to tweak the fluxes. - https://glazy.org/recipes/17833 I balanced the fluxes to make it more functional, though it would need a bit more silica to be food safe in my book - I took out 4 wollastonite and this made the Ca reading drop - if you are going by extended UMF you may want to keep the extra Ca in to balance out the Cu addition to the flux ratio. If you want it to run less, you can try 3 lithium instead of 5...... otherwise make sure it's 5 1/2 or a cool 6. Original test tile on Ben Fiess's website is a STUNNING Deep grass green with golden undertones. My test came out more deep olive and Not so gorgeous in cone 6 natural cool, so I tried it in a slow cool cycle and ended up with this gorgeous silky satin matte glaze. Needs a liner glaze for functional work.

recipes.name: Ginger's Crystal Factory (base)
recipes.description: This glaze at an SG of 145 - 148, two dips, does not run at cone 10. It also gets results at 6. It likes to be in a crowded kiln/on a tight shelf. Slow cool not needed or necessary and doesn't change much (fewer crystals just a bit bigger). If you try it, please keep my name on the recipe. I'm ecstatic about this and happy to share, but I want the credit!! :) Don't forget to dissolve the soda ash in hot water before you put it into the recipe ;) No clay means this one settles out. Use the epsom Luke! It seems to be best fresh, probably something to do with the soda ash being soluable. I recommend making small batches and using quickly.

recipes.name: Ginger's Crystal Factory (spodumene variation) (dont do this)
recipes.description: this glaze was originally developed by Ginger Lukas, the original is here- https://glazy.org/recipes/34635 my notes -- just putting this up for reference so nobody repeats my mistake wondered if I could get similar results without lithium carbonate, because lithium is expensive, so I reformulated it to source from spodumene - unfortunately, this resulted in zero crystal growth and a fairly standard / boring clear white I dont know a ton about cone six so if this could be redone in another way drop me a line and I will try this was fired cone 6, and I didnt write down any notes - but I think it was a standard cone 6 in a kiln using an old style kiln-sitter, so shut off when cone 6 bends, no cooling holds or anything like that -- --------------- original notes from ginger lukas------- This glaze at an SG of 145 - 148, two dips, does not run at cone 10. It also gets results at 6. It likes to be in a crowded kiln/on a tight shelf. Slow cool not needed or necessary and doesn't change much (fewer crystals just a bit bigger). If you try it, please keep my name on the recipe. I'm ecstatic about this and happy to share, but I want the credit!! :) Don't forget to dissolve the soda ash in hot water before you put it into the recipe ;) No clay means this one settles out. Use the epsom Luke! It seems to be best fresh, probably something to do with the soda ash being soluable. I recommend making small batches and using quickly.

recipes.name: Ginger's Crystal Factory + 2 Cobalt
recipes.description: This glaze does have flaws - I basically threw everything I knew to make crystals in a bucket and fired it - bam, first try we get this recipe. That's my studio practice regarding glazes, haha. It seems to be best fresh, probably something to do with the soda ash being soluble. I recommend making small batches and using quickly. I will admit that I made the heart test tile in advance because I wanted this blue to work out. These colors do not run. Stable!! Double dip, didn't move an inch. (Have not tried this against a long hold). I can't be held accountable for SG over 150 ;) The more you put on the more crystal action you get. This glaze at an SG of 145 - 148, two dips, does not run at cone 10. It also gets results at 6. It likes to be in a crowded kiln/on a tight shelf. Slow cool not needed or necessary and doesn't change much (fewer crystals just a bit bigger). If you try it, please keep my name on the recipe. I'm ecstatic about this and happy to share, but I want the credit!! :) Don't forget to dissolve the soda ash in hot water before you put it into the recipe :) Also, there's no clay in this recipe, so the epsom salts/bentonite are essential unless you want it to bottom out real quick. I prefer epsom - I added a pinch to my big batch and it stirs perfectly.

This biaxial test has a fixed R2O:RO ratio of about 0.27:0.73 and B2O3 fixed at 0.3. Tests were prepared by adding 40% water by weight, blending at high speed, then drying into a paste on plaster. The test samples were then rolled into balls and placed on top of test tiles. These tests are all grouped in this collection: Gloop Biaxials B2O3 0.5 & B2O3 0.3, oxidation cone 6 A similar biaxial with B2O3 fixed at 0.5 yielded rougher results: Gloop Biaxial with B2O3 0.5, test E2, "good gloop"

recipes.name: Gloss clear base- Brisbane
recipes.description: This cone 10 glaze will produce a glossy and transparent surface . Here is a breakdown of the materials and their contribution to the glaze. This has proven to be a stable base glaze using ingredients sourced from Milton in Brisbane and Picasso’s at the Tweed. A milky consistency provides a good ability to dip or spray Potash Feldspar : This is the main fluxing agent in the glaze. It helps to melt and vitrify the glaze during firing, resulting in a smooth and glassy surface. Silica : This material provides structure to the glaze and promotes a strong bond between the glaze and the clay body. Whiting : This is a source of calcium and acts as a secondary flux in the glaze. It helps to adjust the thermal expansion of the glaze and promote a more even firing. Kaolin : This material is a source of alumina and acts as a stabilizer in the glaze. It also helps to promote good adhesion between the glaze and the clay body. Zinc Oxide : This material can help to promote a bright and clear appearance in the glaze, as well as improve the fit between the glaze and the clay body. Bentonite : This is a clay material that helps to suspend the other materials in the glaze and prevent settling.

recipes.name: Glossy Ba crystalline base
recipes.description: Shout out to Ceramic Materials Workshop. https://www.ceramicmaterialsworkshop.com/ Can be applied thin enough to avoid runs. Will run if thick. All the test tiles I uploaded were 75:100 water to dry ingredients. The bowls were 1:1 water to dry ingredients. The increased water content helps obtain a thinner application. I don't track specific gravity. Pretty standard crystalline base. Uses Ba instead of Ca. Does not need a crystal firing schedule. All my test photos are from slow cool firings. My schedule is (all temps in F): ramp to 2232 hold15 minutes 9999->2050 no hold 50->1400 off I haven't tested this in reduction. I have no reason to believe that it would misbehave in reduction. I have not tested this with any post firing treatments that some use with their crystalline glazes. Important note on this glaze - it WILL degrade over time. F644 is soluble and over time the glaze chemistry will change just sitting in the bucket. If you find an older batch of this glaze is not producing the results you expect, mix a new batch.

recipes.name: Glossy Deep Blue Green
recipes.description: Deep teal over stoneware deep blue with slip. Satin to almost gloss glaze Well I finally got around to typing this thing up...^9-10 Blues Thank you one and all for all the donated recipes. I only tested 31 out of almost 100 I received. I'll continue testing and reporting as the winter DRAGS on. All the glazes were tested on #900 Miller clay which is a toasty ^10 stoneware. One side of the test tile was brushed with a thick coating of Cynthia Bringle's wet/dry white slip. Each glaze was dipped in three thicknesses on a heavily textured tile. All tiles were fired to a (hard)^9 (10 tipping)reduction firing. 1 hr. Body reduction at ^08 and 1 hr. glaze reduction at ^9 then a quick reox. before shutdown. Any time potash or Custer spar is called for, I used G-200. All ball clay is OM-4 . Many glazes I substituted 75% of the amount of Barium with Strontium. All kaolin is EPK. Remember... glazes don't travel well. Your results will probably be TOTALLY different. Please test before use. Tracy Wilson Saltbox Pottery

recipes.name: Golden Shino
recipes.description: This recipe can create a gorgeous golden shine where the correct thickness, and a deep red/saffron where thin. Best when fired under heavy reduction. Feel free to play with the soda ash concentration. More soda may result in more carbon black, less soda may result in a dryer, saffron-red glaze instead. Feel free to try out different kaolins. Grolleg, for example, may flash a brighter orange, and a dirtier kaolin may result in better metallic colors. I have not tested this in a wood firing, but I would recommend it only for an inside liner, as its not a hi-alumina type. Alternatively, you could try leaving out all the soda ash and seeing what that would do.

recipes.name: Gota de Aceite/Caolín
recipes.description: Usando caolín patagónico las manchas son mayores pero la superficie es menos tersa que usando Tinkar Z (arcilla de bola local). - Precisa buena carga para desarrollar las manchas. Cuidado, puede escurrir! - Curiosamente, las primeras muestras desarrollaron manchas negras sobre fondo marrón rojizo metálico, pero las piezas mostraron manchas marrón rojizo metálico sobre fondo negro (ver todas las fotos). - Basado en la siguiente receta, decimales ajustados y colorante afuera: https://glazy.org/recipes/36081 With Caolín Patagónico (local Kaolin/Argentina) the spots are bigger, but the surface have some pinholes. Using Tinkar (local ball clay), no pinholes, but littler spots. - Needs to be on the thick side for the spots. Attention, it can run. - Interestingly, the first test samples developed black spots on a reddish brown metallic background, but the pieces showed reddish brown metallic spots on a black background (see all pictures). - I used local Crecer frit 804, but original recipe called for Ff 3195 (not the same, but it worked nicely) - Based on the following recipe, adjusted decimals and coloring oxides outside: https://glazy.org/recipes/36081 Original notes from recipe 36081: A cone 6 Oilspot based off of CeramicMaterialsWorkshop.com (A.K.A Matt and Rose Katz... go take the classes!) Cone 10 Oilspot formulations and a bunch of cone 10 Oilspot tests by TC Staton. I just added boron to their cone 10 Oilspot formula and then shifted it around on stulls map until it worked out the best for me at cone 6. Glaze application thickness is important... do some application thickness tests when first trying this glaze out. It needs to be thick enough that the glaze will produce the Oilspot bubbles... but also thin enough that all the bubbles will heal over by the end of the firing.

recipes.name: GPT-2 Rising Sun Chang
recipes.description: This glaze recipe did not exist. It was generated by GPT-2, a machine learning language model. Released early last year, GPT-2 is a large language model with 1.5 billion parameters trained on a dataset of 8 million web pages. The model can be "fine-tuned" with custom data sets, for example collections of poetry or cooking recipes. After training, these custom-tuned models can generate "fake" texts, e.g. poetry or recipes. I fine-tuned the GPT-2 355M model using over 10,000 public Glazy recipes as training data. Although the loss was still going down after 6,000 steps, I stopped training at that point as I noticed more duplicates being generated and I was afraid of overfitting my relatively small dataset. I then generated a couple thousand "fake" recipes using two different "temperature" settings, which controls the "creativity" of the output. The results for both sets were surprisingly good: At first glance the recipes seemed "real" with proportional mixes of feldspars, clays, silica, fluxes and colorants/opacifiers. Even the total ingredient amounts added up to a reasonable number, usually in the range of 90-110%. The duplication rate was about 5% for t=0.7 and 4.5% for t=0.9. After removing duplicates, I imported these fake recipes into Glazy in order to see their resulting analyses and visualize them on the Stull Chart. I was surprised to find that, as with "real" glaze recipes, most of these generated recipes fell comfortably within the major Stull regions of Bright, Matte, and Semi-Matte. The set with temperature setting of 0.9 seemed to generate more variation. This recipe, "Rising Sun Chang", is one of the recipes GPT-2 created (including the name). Other GPT-2 generated recipes are here: GPT-2 Three's Company GPT-2 Yellow Textured For more information about this and other ceramics-related machine learning projects, please visit: https://thisvesseldoesnotexist.com/#/about Direct links to fake recipes: Temperature 0.7 Generated Recipes Temperature 0.9 Generated Recipes Related Post: https://glazy.org/posts/145568

recipes.name: Green Sana's (revised for C10R)
recipes.description: I have a revised glaze for you. But first let me tell you a bit about your current recipe. As you gave it, this glaze is a high alkaline earth glaze, a bit low in alumina, but otherwise smack in the midfire range c4-c7. It's unusual in the fact that it has 5.2% Titanium oxide and this will cause problems, pinholing being one of them. The glaze is prone to pinholing because there's too much carbonate in the raw materials. The COE at 7.2 is a bit high but it could well fit a stoneware of 6.+ COE. Ok. Here's the new version. This version closely matches the Unity Formula of your original. I have switched to Wollastonite and Talc to reduce the carbonate level. You could also use copper oxide black 40 units, or copper oxide red, 35 units and reduce the carbonate a bit more but the copper oxides are very hard to disperse and you may get speckling if you do not thoroughly screen the mix. The gerstley borate is higher than I'd wish but if I use Ferro frit 3134 (or 3195) in its place the alumina goes up almost 50% and the KNaO content goes up too, increasing the COE to 7.7 or higher; the glaze could craze markedly. The best course would be to try this mix first and see if it gives you the blue-green you want without pinholes. If out-gassing is still a problem, then perhaps one could use half Gerstley B and half 3195. I suggest, if this sits ok with you, that you go this route and see what happens and only make a further revision if needed. Tom Buck Sana's Green is actually a C10R recipe that I posted here a while back because I was having pinhole problems with it. Here's the C10R version that Tom put together for me. Richard Los Angeles from richard gralnik

recipes.name: Greenland Ice (Custer/3124)
recipes.description: Kim Ulrick: "This is the same as Icy Blue. It just has more colourant added. Somewhere between 1 and 2 Copper Carbonate it changes from a delicate blue to this darker grey/blue/green." Icy Blue: https://glazy.org/recipes/38238 Used Target and Solve function to sub Custer Feldspar and Frit 3134 to suit Canadian materials. Mixed to an SG of 1.5, and added epsom salts solution to flocculate. Dipped 2 coats, with a third coat on the right corner. Tiles were bisqued to ^04. Though original recipe is fired to ^8, this version does well at ^6 using Digitalfire's recommended Drop and Soak + Slow Cool firing schedule to suit the darker Plainsman clays. It produces a beautiful buttery satin surface with great visual depth. A new favourite!

recipes.name: Greymon
recipes.description: From my base glaze tests I found a beautiful glaze. Multifaceted blue, yellow, red, with texture provided by the titanium diox. make sure to mix well before application as the titanium is heavy. This glaze will do best with 1.2 - 1.3 Specific gravity and has great reactions on a textured surface. Without the hold (on the way down aka slow cool) it will usually turn a type of textured blue / grey. Note: this glaze works best with texture, notice how in many of the pictures the blue comes out where there is an edge or level of depth.

recipes.name: H14 - NR Ghost White
recipes.description: H14 ist eine glänzende, deckende, weiße Glasur. Auf der stehenden Glasurprobe fließt sie nicht und eignet sich so gut für Tassen und Schüsseln. Auf der liegenden Glasurprobe ist H14 sehr deckend und füllt Unebenheiten aus. Auf Witgert Ton Steinzeug weiß Nr. 11 Ton bleibt die Glasur glänzend weiß, sowohl stehend als auch liegend. Auf WMS 2502, creme mit Spots Ton kommen die einzelnen Spots je nach Dicke der Glasur durch. Damit erzielt sie ein sehr ähnliches Bild wie Pyritweiß. Auf der liegenden WMS 2502 Glasurprobe ist die Glasur stark deckend, sodass die Spots nur sehr marginal durchkommen.

recipes.name: H17 - Toubes Blue-Green Matt

recipes.name: H18 - Malmö
recipes.description: H18 ist eine matte, deckende, blau-graue Glasur. Auf der stehenden Glasurprobe fließt sie nicht und eignet sich so gut für Tassen und Schüsseln. Auf der liegenden Glasurprobe ist H18 deckend. Sie füllt Unebenheiten nicht wirklich aus, daher sollte sie auf sehr gut gearbeiteten Werkstücken benutzt werden. Auf Witgert Ton Steinzeug weiß Nr. 11 Ton ist die Glasur matt blau-grau, sowohl stehend als auch liegend. Zwei Lagen Glasur reichen für eine deckende Glasur aus. Auf WMS 2502, creme mit Spots Ton kommen die einzelnen Spots nicht wirklich durch zwei Lagen Glasur durch. Sehr dünn aufgetragen, kommen die Spots in hellbraun durch. Auf der liegenden WMS 2502 Glasurprobe ist die Glasur deckend, sodass die Spots nur sehr marginal durchkommen.

recipes.name: Hamish's basalt tenmoku
recipes.description: This glaze varies a lot depending how it is applied and fired. A thin application in gas reduction will be browner, whereas a thicker application will be black. It can break nicely on areas where the glaze becomes thinner such as the rims of pots. If you hold the kiln at top temp and the glaze is thickly applied then it will run. It is stable in a normal firing schedule. In soda it can be very jazzy and tends to want to run more. Yellows and mustard colors can result as well as crystal growth. There is a lot of potential for layering slips under this and also glazes over and under this, as is shown in my pictures. Any questions don't hesitate to reach out to me. I love talking about glazes! You can email me through my website: https://www.hamishjacksonpottery.com/ Or send me a message on instagram: @hamish.jackson.pottery

recipes.name: Hamish's granite celadon
recipes.description: This celadon is made with 80% of a granite I collect and process. DP = Devil's Playground where I collect this granite in Western Utah. I have run lots of experiments with this granite. I tried many different celadons, adding lime, wood ash and other fluxes to it. In the end, wollastonite at about 20% seems to produce the brightest, bluest celadon. I do also like it with wood ash. If you want a greener celadon then you can use whiting (about 15% whiting to 85% granite). A main influence on this glaze is atmosphere. In oxidation it can be anywhere from amber to green. Reduction brings out the bluer tones. It is alway translucent unless you do a seriously prolonged slow cooling. Thickness plays a significant role in the results too. The thicker the glaze, the richer the color. You can see this in some of the areas where the glaze is allowed to pool in the pictures here.

recipes.name: Hamish's granite tenmoku
recipes.description: This is a nice iron rich glaze that varies a lot depending how it is applied and fired. A thin application in gas reduction will be browner, whereas a thicker application will be black. It can break nicely on areas where the glaze becomes thinner such as the rims of pots. If you hold the kiln at top temp and the glaze is thickly applied then it will run. It is stable in a normal firing schedule. In soda it seems to maintain its tenmoku nature and does not get so much variation and yellowing as DP 776. There is a lot of potential for layering slips under this and also glazes over and under this, as is shown in my pictures. Any questions don't hesitate to reach out to me. I love talking about glazes! You can email me through my website: https://www.hamishjacksonpottery.com/ Or send me a message on instagram: @hamish.jackson.pottery

recipes.name: Hamish's Hyrum Dam liner glaze
recipes.description: This glaze has been very reliable for me. I ran lots of experiments with this Hyrum Dam material and found that I liked it best mixed 50:50 with nepheline syenite. I also like how simple it is to mix up. The sediment itself is very fine so all I have to do is weigh it out with the neph sye, add it to water and sieve it. Usually there are a few twigs and roots but the material itself is very clean and fine already. Happy days! I have used this glaze mostly as a liner in soda firings but also in wood kilns and gas reduction too. It varies nicely when hit with soda or wood ash, and can be glossy or matte depending on how you fire. Recently I have been slow cooling it and getting some lovely satin finishes.

recipes.name: Hamish's Yellow
recipes.description: This glaze has a lovely silky satiny feel. It is a solid reliable yellow glaze that does not run unless very thick. It requires salt or soda to go yellow although does not need much. I have fired this glaze in the middle of the kiln where very little soda hit it to good effect. When it gets a lot of soda those areas go a typical white/grey/blueish tone. You can clearly see this one one of the side handles teapots in the pictures here. You can substitute any other granite of feldspar or neph sye for the Devil's Playground Granite I use from Western Utah. The bone ash is not strictly necessary but terns the flecks in the glaze redder as opposed to brown (makes the glaze warmer). I have also had good results with only using 5% bone ash. You can also use 10% zircopax rather than 15% if you like (I find the zircopax helps make the glaze solid and not run). Very similar results in terms of color. When this glaze is thin it goes more towards reddish brown: see the underside of one of the teapot lids pictured here. This yellow glaze will be warmer buttery color if you reduce the kiln and a paler more canary like yellow if you oxidise it. Excess of soda also makes the color a bit brighter/paler/whiter. You can also adapt the color of this glaze by adding iron and/or rutile. I have some examples of test tiles doing this on my blog here: https://www.hamishjacksonpottery.com/blog/2022/10/18/devils-playground-granite-glaze-tests-round-4-pictures-and-notes Slow cooling the kiln will make this glaze even more silky, satiny and buttery feeling. Any questions don't hesitate to reach out to me. I love talking about glazes! You can email me through my website: https://www.hamishjacksonpottery.com/ Or send me a message on instagram: @hamish.jackson.pottery

recipes.name: Hannah's Golden Fake Ash
recipes.description: This is a slightly different version, so I thought I'd post it. The version of "Hannah Fake Ash" that survived into Glazy is https://glazy.org/materials/52 and https://glazy.org/materials/7005 Found on the Clayart mailing list in a message by Bob Johnson. Bob writes: > A while back Bill Schran and Jackie Miller asked me to share the recipes for Hannah's fake ash and Andie's fake ash. Sorry for the delay, but I am happy to do so: I believe that these glazes are available on the internet, so I believe I am not violating any confidences. Hannah's Golden Fake Ash (cone 6 oxidation or reduction) Strontium Carbonate 9.90 Whiting 28.43 RedArt 56.96 Ferro 3195 4.71 Add: Bentonite 1.00 Red Iron Oxide 3.24 Yellow Iron Oxide 2.75 > Note: Various versions of this can be found on the internet. This one, I believe, was originally a cone 10 recipe that may have been modified by Steven Hill for cone 6 electric. It was originally developed by Hannah Brehmer of Ashland, Oregon. Hannah's Blue Ash is essentially the same recipe, but with 1.27% cobalt oxide instead of the iron oxides. (If using cobalt carbonate instead of the oxide, you must make the conversion.) Steven Hill also has a fake ash, made with copper carb, that gives a greenish hue. You can find it also on the internet at http://www.carolclarksonpottery.com/blog/2016/05/25/Copper-Ash-Glaze-Recipe-Steven-Hill.aspx > Andie's Golden Fake Ash (cone 6 oxidation or reduction) Strontium Carb 12 Lithium Carb 2 Gerstley Borate 10 Bone Ash 5 Dolomite 24 RedArt 27 Kentucky Old Mine #4 20 > Note: This is very well-behaved, for an ash-type glaze. I like to use it in combination with Val Cushing's G4 ash glaze, with 3% RIO + 2% Yellow iron oxide + 5% rutile. Put the Val Cushing near the top of the pot, because it will run. You can see this combination on a covered jar shown on my Flickr page at https://www.flickr.com/photos/psychoceramics/ > The Val Cushing G4 ash glaze recipe is in the ClayArt archives. See: https://lists.clayartworld.com/pipermail/clayart/2014-November/003974.html > Anyone else have a favorite ash (or fake ash) glaze you are willing to share? > Bob Johnson in Wilbur, Oregon

recipes.name: Hansen Clear GA12 Darker Green
recipes.description: "I have introduced a cooling cycle to the firing. The cycle is as follows and the firing is accompanied by a Cone 6 witness cone. After 12 consecutive firings, the witness cones are identical from firing to firing." The firing cycle: Rate Temp Hold Time rA1= 360 F1 = 900 0 rA2= 300 F2 = 1800 0 rA3 =200 F3 = 2016 0 rA4 = 108 F4 = 2197 0.3 rA5 = Full F5 =1800 0 rA6 =150 F6 = 1300 0 rA7 = 0000 To summarize, I fire at a rate of 360/hr to 900 degrees F, then at 300 degrees/ hr to 1800 degrees F, 200 degrees/hr until 2016 degrees F is reached, then 108 degrees/hour to 2197 at which time I hold it at that temperature for 30 minutes. The kiln is shut off until a temperature of 1800 degrees F is reached and then turned on to slow the rate of cooling to 150 degrees/hr until 1300 degrees F is reached. At this point the kiln is turned off and cools naturally. Western Pennsylvania Potters Community http://wpapotters.blogspot.com/2012/04/links-to-cone-6-oxidation-glaze-tests.html http://www.wpapotters.blogspot.com/2011/10/cone-6-oxidation-results-group-7.html

recipes.name: Hardwick Pumice/PV Ash
recipes.atmosphere: Oxidation, Neutral, Reduction, Wood, Salt & Soda
recipes.description: Crazes on my body and has small to medium bubbles at cone 10 wood with early reduction and neutral to oxidation through maturing temperature. At cone 7-9 this last batch went cloudy mint green. obviously not mature as the pieces on the bag wall were cone 12 and went clear dark green. Still beautiful, but very different look to glaze. It is possible that late reduction from cone 7 until completion or the rapid cooling due to 200 degree crash cool and possible damper left open effected glaze color and surface.

recipes.name: Heath A2V
recipes.description: Kat Rose In the picture shown, blue is 4% Cu and 0.5% Co, the purple is 4% Mn and 0.5% Co. The right side is thick application and that is shows the blooms. These tiles were fired flat so next test is to fire vertically and see what happens. I have been using the Persian Blue with 4% Cu and the blooms appear where the glaze is thick. I love it. My new favorite glaze. The surface is luscious - somewhere between semi gloss and gloss. buttery Base Clear A2V Ivory 8% Rutile Heath Blue Frost 6% Cobalt Carbonate 2% Rutile Heath Persian Blue 4% Copper Carbonate Heath Pen Argyl Green 8% Copper Carbonate 2% Rutile Heath Blue Mist 0.25% Cobalt Carbonate 4% Titanium Dioxide (for warmer blue use rutile) Heath Elephant Ear 7.5% Spanish RIO 0.4% Chrome Oxide 0.6% Nickle Oxide

recipes.name: Heath A2V Base /frit

recipes.name: Heath A2V gray

recipes.name: Heath A2V Ivory /frit

recipes.name: Heath A2V Pen Argyl Green
recipes.description: Comments from Walter: We have used this glaze on functional pots for years....it has tied up the copper quite well...no deterioration of surface or color after years of use in our own home Pen Argyl is the borough we live in Pennsylvania (USA)....the high school is "the Green Knights" If any of these glazes have "A2" or "A2V" in the name, I developed the base glazes about 35 years ago, the individual colorants in each glaze have evolved out of my wife, other potters, and myself doing variations....several others have come from my working with my students doing glaze research....two exceptions areVal 's Turquoise (Val Cushing) and JP Purple (variations on a June Perry Red/Purple base)

recipes.name: Heath Brain Crawl?
recipes.description: This is a version of Walter Ivan Heath's recipe and I added 8 percent Zircopax and then ran a color blend. I like it better because it was stiffer and retained some of the beads better with the Zircopax. You could also had more . notice the tiles #3 with 4% rutile, #8 with 8% more zircopax, etc. Colorants are: 1. 0.5% red iron 2. 2% red iron oxide 4% titanium dioxide, 3. 4% Rutile. 4. 3% manganese dioxide, 5. 7.5% tin oxide 0.2% Chrome oxide. 6. 3.5% copper carbonate 7. 0.5% Chrome oxide 8. 0.5% Cobalt carbonate 9. 8% tin oxide 10. 8% any stain (in this case 4254 inclusion purple)

recipes.name: Hennessy Blue Celadon
recipes.description: Note from Derek: This glaze is listed in John Britt's High Fire Glazes as "Hennesy Celadon". This is a fairly old recipe listed in a few glaze databases, for instance https://www.cmich.edu/colleges/CCFA/CCFADepartmentofArtandDesign/Documents/CeramicsHandbook4.pdf These lists all have Red Iron Oxide at 5% additional. This glaze is meant to be a "blue" celadon, so there's no way the original recipe calls for 5% Red Iron Oxide. I assume the original poster intended ".5%" iron oxide rather than "5%". However, John Britt lists Red Iron Oxide at 2% in his book. You could try anywhere from .5% to 2% iron oxide (red, black or yellow). This is a similar glaze listed as Hennessy Celadon SUNY NP as: https://newpaltzceramics.files.wordpress.com/2013/09/high-fire-glazes.pdf G-200 Potash feldspar 41 Grolleg kaolin 13 Silica 19 Dolomite 5 Wollastonite 22 Veegum T 2 Red iron Oxide: .25 Notes from import: This glaze was revised by VC. The theory here is that wollastonite is closer to the Ca source that the Chinese used (calcined chells for CaO plus high K2O) - no carbonates in wollastonite.

recipes.name: High-Boron Clear
recipes.description: This is a relatively high-boron clear to be used thin (around 145 s.g.) over stains and light or dark clay bodies. Too thick and slight bubbling or blue streaks may result. There are some other "super clear" high-boron glazes in Glazy, for example Laura Speirs Clear, WCAC Clear, and Clear Glaze, but they often also have higher R2O:RO flux ratios that can lead to crazing. They also often use large amounts of Gerstley (or Gillespie) Borate. My recipe has lower expansion to reduce the possibility of crazing, and uses more consistent frits, and it results in a cleaner clear without a dirty yellowish cast. This recipe is meant for cone 5, I can create a slightly different cone 6 version if someone is interested. Revised version of this recipe here: https://glazy.org/recipes/113617

Pools into blue on the interior of vessels and flatter horizontal surfaces. The interesting rivulets and variegations come out best on a vertical surface. recipes.name: Honey Oatmeal
recipes.description: Recipe in English: Neph sye 34 Silica 32 Ulexite 14 Wollastonite 11 Kaolin 5 Dolomite 4 ————— Zirconium Dioxide 8 (or 10 for better coverage and brighter colour) Tin Oxide 4 Titanium Dioxide 3 Iron oxide 1 Manganese may be omitted. It doesn't add much to the surface or colour. Opaque warm glaze Love the specks and the feel of it Should try on a highly textured piece to see how it breaks 🤔 I use gum solution 15% gum + 75% water, then add dry ingredients to it and after mixing add water to get specific gravity right (usually 1.40-1.45 for my glazes). That is how I mix all my glazes to avoid crawling. It just sometimes makes glazes too thick to pour (but I just use a deflocculant then).

recipes.name: Hopper Reticulated Glaze (base)
recipes.description: First published in Ceramics Monthly in 2013. Robin Hopper reticulated (crawling) glaze recipe. The glaze fuses greatly at the higher temperature (Cone 9), giving smooth surfaces, whereas, at the lower temperatures (Cone 6), the glaze will be either beaded or dry and crispy like dried mud. The glaze may be colored with any colorants and stains. Hopper recommends that the glaze be applied over a simple black slip in order to intensify the color of the covering glaze. Any black slip would be suitable to use. Other colored background slips greatly extend the possibilities of palette. Note: This glaze should not be used on surfaces that come into contact with food.

recipes.name: Horsley Variation
recipes.description: From Steve Davis Website & Blog: http://kazegama.com/ Website: http://kazegamas.com/ Shinos 3: http://kazegamas.com/shinos3.htm Alumina is A-12 Calcined Alumina There are 72 shinos shown on 4 web pages. They are organized from left to right with 3 tiles of the same glaze shown on 3 different clay bodies. They are Aardvark Clay's Nara Porcelain, Long Beach, and Black Mountain. Every shino was glazed with a doulble dip, waxed with a simple "S" pattern, and left to dry for 2 weeks to grow sulfates on the surface. The "S" pattern has no sulfate build up. A medium reduction was started at cone 012 through cone 2. From there the kiln was fired in neutral to cone 10.

recipes.name: Horsley's Satin Matte White

recipes.name: HOS 1 ekwc
recipes.description: Hoogbak Satijn Opaak glazuur vanuit het boek van het EKWC: Satin Gloss Base glaze. A typical lime-alkali glaze recipe: the main fluxes are nepheline syenite and whiting. Due to its high viscosity this glaze shows many very fine bubbles resulting in a subtle gloss and semi-transparency. It reacts well to ceramic pigments. An interesting silvery matt surface can be obtained by adding 27% manganese oxide and 3% copper oxide. A combination of 4-5% manganese, 5% copper and 9% cobalt carbonate will yield a shiny, slivery metallic result.

recipes.name: HTB1V

A bronze coloured glaze can be obtained by adding 5% copper oxide and 25 manganese oxide. Reducing the quartz tot 8% and increasing the whiting up to 17% can give a more matt surface.

recipes.name: Hunter Green
recipes.description: Opaque earthy Chrome Green. Has not been tested in reduction atmosphere. Highest temperature test sample I've done with this glaze is Cone 8. Lowest temperature I've fired this to is Cone 5. Very consistent glaze. Very Stable. Has occasional black speckles when used on clay bodies with traces of iron. Turns dark brown on darker clay bodies such as Cone 10 Black Mountain. The hotter the glaze fires, the darker brown it turns. Stay bellow a cone 7 and it will be green.

recipes.name: Ian Currie T.S.1
recipes.description: Frank Martin Art Deparment/Ceranics 92nd street YM-YWHA 1395 Lexington Ave NY, NY. 10128 Frank Martin on fri 1 aug 97 Steve there seems to be a question as to what defines a Tessha Glaze. It's definitely a Iron Saturated glaze type, whether or not any of these glazes below fit your idea of what one is let me know. I tend to feel that this glaze type will work best in the middle or the lower half of the kiln for a good medium reduction. The thickness of the glaze I feel is also important. Don't apply to thinly. When testing small amounts of glazes I like to start out with equal milliliters of water as grams of glaze. Later if it is a winner, there's no guessing how much water to add. Here are some glazes to try, good luck. BOUBARIC TESSHA SATURATE IRON Ian Currie T.S.1 CONE 10 REDUCTION Potash Feldspar 39.5 Talc 6.15 Whiting 11.8 Kaolin 9.2 Silica 33.4 Red Iron Oxide 12.0

recipes.name: Imperial Snapdragon Yellow Glaze
recipes.description: From "My Work, My Way: Fifty Years in the Studio" by Harlan House, 2019. https://www.harlanhouse.com/ https://www.harlanhouse.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/2019%20HHBK-FINAL.pdf I liked the yellows I was getting with wood ash, but I wanted something less fluid, and softer in tone. It took just a little over 12 years to get it right. ISY is a glaze that is open to kiln fuming, so if any copper reds, or other volatile glazes are in the area near ISY, it will affect the yellow. This can be wonderful, and of course it can go south in a heartbeat. I used Jun blue and peach black temmoku in combination with this glaze a lot, especially on wall platters. It is a soft glaze and therefore an open glaze so food will stain it…eye candy only.

recipes.name: Intense Blue
recipes.description: Richard Baxter glaze published in Ceramics Review Jan/Feb 2019 issue #295. He sieves with mesh 80 then 120. He says cobalt may vary from 2-3%. Test with more or less oxide or carbonate. Less cobalt gives a brighter tone with a quality like Illuminated glass, while more cobalt creates a darker and denser finish. Barium gives the glaze its fat, smooth quality and lithium boosts the color. On porcelain he applies a thin layer of white glaze as a mask before dipping in the blue glaze to avoid staining the clay body. Don't use for functional liner. Baxter ramps temp at 55C per hour to 528C, then fast rate to cone 6. He soaks for 20 minutes at top.

recipes.name: Intense Blue
recipes.description: I supplied the base recipe, but use two different colorants. 1) Cobalt Oxide - 2 2) Copper Carbonate 5 Please refer to the pictures in order to see the different results. You don't have to fire it in a microcrystalline kiln cycle, but I do, and that's why I included the firing cycle. Please feel free to post photos of this glaze without the cooling ramp too. This glaze doesn't run that much, unless Strontium Crystal Magic is applied on top.

recipes.name: Israeli Blue #1
recipes.description: from Naama Satin deep blue going to tan where thick. Feels wonderful and buttery Well I finally got around to typing this thing up...^9-10 Blues Thank you one and all for all the donated recipes. I only tested 31 out of almost 100 I received. I'll continue testing and reporting as the winter DRAGS on. All the glazes were tested on #900 Miller clay which is a toasty ^10 stoneware. One side of the test tile was brushed with a thick coating of Cynthia Bringle's wet/dry white slip. Each glaze was dipped in three thicknesses on a heavily textured tile. All tiles were fired to a (hard)^9 (10 tipping)reduction firing. 1 hr. Body reduction at ^08 and 1 hr. glaze reduction at ^9 then a quick reox. before shutdown. Any time potash or Custer spar is called for, I used G-200. All ball clay is OM-4 . Many glazes I substituted 75% of the amount of Barium with Strontium. All kaolin is EPK. Remember... glazes don't travel well. Your results will probably be TOTALLY different. Please test before use. Tracy Wilson Saltbox Pottery

recipes.name: Janice Hill's Teal from Chrome and Cobalt
recipes.description: With 13% Gerstley borate and a sufficient alumina level, this recipe is versatile enough to go from cone 5-9. It looks fabulous at cone 7. The chrome and cobalt combine make a strong teal blue-green, and the titanium keeps it from looking like a flat commercial glaze. The silica level gives it a pretty gloss that feels good on the mouth and keeps the glaze well encased in the silica matrix. The formula is "robust" as defined by glazy.org's database of articles. The boron level is enough to melt the glaze at cone 5 but not too much to melt it off the sides in a high firing. I have fired it in an electric kiln and in a wood-fired kiln with an atmosphere that shifted between, oxidation, neutral and light-reduction. I haven't fired it to cone 10. One drawback of this version is that it is unforgiving because of the chrome. If you don't wipe the glaze off the wax resist really well, you may find little bits of color in places where you don't want it. Also, if you like a crisp line of wax, you'd better make it really crisp because that line will show. I'm working on a second version with ingredients that flow more. On the other hand, there is no trick to getting the color. I've fired it with both a slow-cool (1800-1400) and crash cool (2230 and off). They are both great, but I like the crash cool best because it reflects light so beautifully--it practically sparkles.

recipes.name: Jen's Juicy Fruit Variation (Red Matte)
recipes.description: "I have introduced a cooling cycle to the firing. The cycle is as follows and the firing is accompanied by a Cone 6 witness cone. After 12 consecutive firings, the witness cones are identical from firing to firing." The firing cycle: Rate Temp Hold Time rA1= 360 F1 = 900 0 rA2= 300 F2 = 1800 0 rA3 =200 F3 = 2016 0 rA4 = 108 F4 = 2197 0.3 rA5 = Full F5 =1800 0 rA6 =150 F6 = 1300 0 rA7 = 0000 To summarize, I fire at a rate of 360/hr to 900 degrees F, then at 300 degrees/ hr to 1800 degrees F, 200 degrees/hr until 2016 degrees F is reached, then 108 degrees/hour to 2197 at which time I hold it at that temperature for 30 minutes. The kiln is shut off until a temperature of 1800 degrees F is reached and then turned on to slow the rate of cooling to 150 degrees/hr until 1300 degrees F is reached. At this point the kiln is turned off and cools naturally. Western Pennsylvania Potters Community http://wpapotters.blogspot.com/2012/04/links-to-cone-6-oxidation-glaze-tests.html http://www.wpapotters.blogspot.com/2011/10/cone-6-oxidation-results-group-5.html

Number 13 on the grid was used. I ran a line blend from 0-20% with natural red iron oxide. In this line blend each glaze also had 2% light rutile added. The tile that had 10% red iron came out a nice pumpkin orange due to the added rutile. Glazes with 6-8-10-12% iron oxide all yielded interesting orangish glazes. 10% was the most orange. recipes.name: John Post's Black
recipes.description: This glaze is a very nice satin black in reduction between cones 9 and 10. The small amount of crystals are most likely due to the titanium dioxide. I like this variegation in the glaze as I do not care for glazes which have an overall flat matte appearance.

recipes.name: John Post's Calcium Matte 7

This is the base matte glaze I use with my students in the classroom. It applies like a dream because of the high clay content. It also stays suspended well and does not hard pan if left unused for a while. These glazes only work if you slow cool them. recipes.description: Fired to Cone 10 on Laguna's Rod's Bod clay body. The dark iron specks come from the clay. After I fire to cone 10 in light reduction I let the kiln drop to 1900 degrees F. Then I slow cool this glaze between 1900-1700 for two hours.

recipes.name: John Post's Mystic Purple
recipes.description: This glaze base is a variation of Black Mountain Turquoise. I used glaze calculation to replace the Kona F-4 feldspar in that glaze with Nepheline Syenite. I am using cobalt carbonate as the only colorant in this glaze. Tile is Laguna's Rod's Bod clay body. Because this glaze is high in magnesium it grows purple-lavender crystals while it is cooling. I hold my kiln between 1900-1500 for a few hours on the way down to promote the crystal growth.

recipes.name: John Post's Soft Fat White 335
recipes.description: This glaze comes from an Ian Currie grid I created which was fired to cone 6 in light reduction in a gas kiln. The clay body is Laguna's Speckled Buff. The goal of the grid was to explore a UMF where the fluxes were set at .3 KNaO, .35 CaO .35 MgO. Sue McLeod has been exploring cone 6 glazes using Stull's chart from 1912. The magic flux ratio to create durable glazes using Stull's chart sets the R2O fluxes at .3 and the RO fluxes at .7. This glaze was #24 on an Ian Currie grid. The original input for the Currie Grid was 4 Gerstley Borate 7 Frit 3134 22 Dolomite 6 Talc 61 Nepheline Syenite 2 Bentonite

recipes.name: John Post's Tomato Red
recipes.description: From John Post @ http://www.johnpost.us/ http://www.macomb.k12.mi.us/utica/burr/art/JohnPost-2014/main-pages/iron-reds.html This is glaze number 13 from the first Currie grid that I ran of Pete's Tomato Red # 3 from Clay Times. I also ran a line blend of this glaze using natural red iron oxide in increments from 0-20%. This glaze has the most red color with 10% red iron. It is a mottled greenish-red with 8% red iron and a darker red with 12% red iron. Older Notes (from database import): 8% less red. 12% is a more broken-looking orange. 14% goes to a duller brown. Variation: +2% lithium carb + 10-12% RIO, bright iron rust spangles. Variation: add 2% rutile to the red version to get pumpkin orange. See more info at http://www.johnpost.us/. Must have adequately thick application and slow cooling for iron crystals to form. From article by Pete Pinnell in Clay Times. May/Jn 2009, p.21.Less shiny than Tomato Red Pete's #3. Calls for Spanish RIO, but Pete says it doesn't much matter.

recipes.description: CORRECTION Should have 1% cobalt carb. And 4% RUTILE. I am discontinuing this glaze in favor for a similar version without lithium. It improves the UMF, lowers the COE, ups the silica and saves some costs. I have used this glaze a lot but maybe due to nepheline syenite or whiting changes, the last two batches I mixed fired badly. The revision, although not an exact color copy, has been behaving with the usual glazes I use it with. Revision https://glazy.org/recipes/246832

recipes.name: John's Goldstone

The right one Rio % seems to be around 20/25%. Sample by Bel Reinhardt (Brasil) uses Ff 3110 and 20% RIO Venturina con diferentes % de ox de Fe. El % correcto parece estar en torno al 20%. Usé la frita FK10, de Omar Dominguez, teóricamente igual a la 3110. La muestra de Bel Reinhardt (Brasil) usa la 3110 original de Ferro y 20% de ox de hierro.

recipes.name: John's Nikkel Yellow 2 (John Britt Mid-Range Glazes p147)
John's Nuka
recipes.description: ☆Receta compartida por Ricardo Luza y Clara Giorello en el grupo de Facebook Aprendiendo entre todos. ☆Notas de Ricardo Luza: Usé mezcla de cenizas de madera, principalmente álamo y un sustituto para la Piedra de Cornwall (receta más abajo en las notas). Esmalte muy bonito, con pintas, tiende a burbujear un poco, sobre todo en zonas de mayor carga. ☆Notas de Clara Giorello: Usé cenizas de leña de monte, mayormente espinillo, y el mismo sustituto que Ricardo para la piedra de Cornwall. Esmalte blanco muy bonito, con pintitas. Aparecen algunos pinchados (pinholing), y, definitivamente, precisa más temperatura que cono 5. Indudablemente cono 6, y quizá 7, dependiendo de las cenizas usadas. Cuando es superpuesto sobre otros esmaltes, fluye hermosamente, ya a partir del cono 4, sobretodo sobre tenmokus. ☆Sustituto de la Piedra de Cornwall (por volumen): Feldespato potásico 8 partes + Cuarzo 2 partes + Caolín 1 parte ☆ Origen de la receta: Mid-Range Glazes, John Britt ☆Cornwall Stone substitute (volume): Potash Feldspar 8 + Silica 2 + Kaolin 1

recipes.name: John's Oil Spot #3
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Temmoku (Oilspot) From John Britt http://www.ceramicstoday.com/articles/oilspot.htm Article on oil-spot glazes. John's web site: http://www.johnbrittpottery.com/ (Works nicely in electric kilns) Must be applied thickly. Fired in oxidation. Reduction between cone 9-11 will smooth out bubbles and help flux the iron. You can re-fire any pieces w/craters.

recipes.name: John's Red

recipes.name: John's Red
recipes.description: Receta del libro de John Britt (Esmaltes de Medias Temperaturas). Rojo de cobre punteado de azul flambé. Agregando entre 0.4% y 0.6% de Carburo de Silicio se acentúa el rojo, sobre todo sobre pasta con hierro. Ver las muestras con y sin Carburo de Silicio. Frita 3134 = Frita 174 de Crecer (Argentina) John Britt's recipe (Mid-Range Glazes). Nice Copper Red flambé. Adding 0.4/0.6% Silicon Carbide makes it redder, especially on Iron clay body. See pictures with and without SiC.

recipes.name: John's Red

recipes.name: Jun glaze
recipes.description: Recipe used in "Effects of microstructure on the sky-green color in imitating ancient Jun glazes" Jianfeng ZHU,3 Pei SHI,33 Fen WANG, Longlong DONG and Ting ZHAO School of Materials Science and Engineering, Shaanxi University of Science & Technology, Xi’an 710021, China > The sky-green glaze of ancient Jun ware was successfully imitated with the addition of 4 wt % calcium phosphate for introducing the phosphorus (P) to the composition. Effects of the calcium phosphate contents on the chromaticity, precipitated phase and microstructure of sky-green glaze were investigated. Based on the analysis of colorimeter, XRD, FT-IR, XPS and SEM, a possible coloring mechanism was proposed to explain the variation of glaze colors with the increasing of calcium phosphate content. The results indicated that the addition of calcium phosphate contributed to increasing the content of calcium iron phosphate [Ca19Fe2(PO4)14] and the size of phase separation droplets in glazes. The formation of Ca19Fe2(PO4)14 decreased the ratio of Fe2+ to Fe3+ and the increased size of phase separation droplets weakened the structural color, which increased the L and b value of glazes. Therefore, the color of sky-green glaze got more green and white gradually.

recipes.name: KAREN'S TOUCH GLAZE
recipes.description: Color: on porcelain in OX THIN = warm rusty beige breaking to copper rust on rim & ridges THICK = warm beige w/ copper rusty rim Both thin & thick show very fine rusty flecks On porcelain in REDTN THICK = almost sea foam greenish w/ orangey copper rust w/ flecks where thin I consider this to be a glaze which in OX looks like REDTN - for those of you who pine for that. As I previously mentioned, in OX put it over PORCELAIN SHINO & you get a funky rough surface in solid copper w/ fine rusty flecks - this is thin. Thick edges are unattractive (?) white. If firing in REDTN, slow cool for max. orange. This is a variant of the famous Mamo glaze. If you want to try other colorants, drop out the tin (it's incl. to promote ornage) from the base as well as dropping the RIO & bone ash. But BE CAREFUL - this glaze pulls apart if too thick in big fatal crawls. I abandoned it as a white for this reason & I swear it once pulled so badly it broke (?) the pot it was on. This was not the above version however. Good luck & enjoy. Karen Gringhuis

recipes.name: Kemp Base 5
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: similar oxides to Kemp Soft Green Notes: Martha Muzychka: not nice at all, very pale with brown streaks. With 1.5 copper carbonate and 0.25 cobalt oxide, breaks to an icky greyish brown where thick. Notes: Alisa Clausen: With 3 copper carbonate, shiny green overall with dark (not esp. pink) speckles in bottom of test bowl. I like this green very much, very bright and clear like the green on a Macintosh apple or a darkish celedon, and there is no G.B. I think this glaze would complement a speckled iron clay body nicely for some real play in the surface.

recipes.name: Kemp Lichen
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Clay Times Nov/Dec 2001 Brian Kemp Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 800C hold 1 hour Significant Flaw: crawls Notes: Alisa Clausen: The glaze pulled, separated and crawled from the underlying glaze of contrasting colour (I used Nutmeg) making a high and textured lichen effect. The glaze is slightly dry and although the effect is very textured, it separated into islands with sharper borders than the rounder, ball like islands I was aiming for. With the fine help of Bacia, I was able to get this glaze to work this far, because she told me that it must be applied very thickly, until it crackles a bit when dried, but to much so that it will fall off the pot as you lift it into the kiln. There is a lot to experiment with this glaze. It can also be coloured with stains and oxides. Notes: A few years ago I participated in a workshop with Randy Brodnax who works with lichen glazes, among other techniques. His recipes follow. We covered the bisqued pot with the black englobe, (brushed on) and then dipped the pot in the lichen glaze. Then colored commercial underglazes were sprayed on the glaze. Wonderful effects. The black engobe gives better contrast with the lichen glaze. I also tried the lichen glaze both over and under my regualr cone six glazes, some very interesting, very nice effects. try it. submitted by: Kathy Darby source for original recipe: Randy Brodnax

Every shino was glazed with a doulble dip, waxed with a simple "S" pattern, and left to dry for 2 weeks to grow sulfates on the surface. The "S" pattern has no sulfate build up. recipes.name: Kiln Brick Patching Compound
recipes.description: A recipe similar to my cement/mortar recipe (https://glazy.org/recipes/160891) with the addition of grog - I wanted to post the recipes separate as their mixing consistencies are different and didn’t want any confusion. This kiln brick patching compound can be made with either grog OR powdered kiln brick. You may sub EPK for New Zealand Halloysite - Clay materials should be calcined. You can mix this with 37.5 grams of water for a paste like consistency but can add more water if you wish to pour it into a hole. Even out areas with a putty knife after a short drying period. Curing and drying times may vary dramatically - efflorescence may occur during cure, any crystalline debris should be vacuumed off before firing.

recipes.name: Kiln Soft Brick Cement/Mortar
recipes.description: My recipe for cement/mortar to join soft brick. This cement will set naturally from the sodium silicate and also becomes stronger when fired. This recipe will withstand up to cone 10 oxidation from my testing but may go further. Ideally, the Hawthorne bond and New Zealand Halloysite will be calcined but regular can be used as long as the bricks are going to be compressed (either by band or by gravity). EPK may be used in place of New Zealand Halloysite. Before applying cement, dip the soft brick in water until the joining surface is wet. Enough cement should be used that it oozes out of the bricks being joined, let dry slightly and scrape off excess with a putty knife. As little amount of cement between bricks as possible is best. Use the scrapings to mold and fill any sections that are not even. Curing and drying times may vary dramatically - efflorescence may occur during cure, any crystalline debris should be vacuumed off before firing.

recipes.name: Kirkland Copper Red
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Daniel Kirkland Notes: Daniel Kirkland: fire either in oxidation or in neutral, reduce when the kiln is cooling. From cone 10, close the damper, let the kiln cool to a very dull red colour (cone 018 to 016), then turn the gas back on and reduce heavily for anywhere between 20 minutes and 1 hour. Consistently comes out as a very rich deep red. Notes: Karin Givon: I start the reduction at cone 011, reduce it for about half an hour or so, then keep the kiln in light reduction for the rest of the fire, tried many recipes and they all work pretty well with this schedule. Notes: Wyndham Dennison: My reduction starts at 015 where I have the six venturi burners paps open to one turn open and the damper closed to give a wisp of smoke out the bottom peek of my downdraft. The top reaches reduction first then the bottom 30 min later. I balance the damper to keep the back pressure where a lick of flame is coming out the bottom peek. After about 3 hr I open the PAPS another half turn then as the kiln heats up to cone 6 I open the PAPS another half turn and open the damper so as to have the mim back pressure but still some. As my kiln heats it creates its own fire storm and the draft starts running hard at about 2000F so I have to watch and maybe push in the damper to control the ox/reduc ratio. If I reduce too heavily then I get a muddy liver colored red, but in this kiln, good bright reds come from a lt to neutral from cone 6 to cone 10 in about 9-10 hr for a about a 45 cu ft stack.

recipes.name: Kohiki Crackle Slip
recipes.atmosphere: Oxidation, Neutral, Wood, Raku, Salt & Soda
recipes.description: Mix to a yogurt consistency, very thick. Allow it to sit overnight. The nepheline syenite will diffloculate the slip. Apply this to a thick, wet slab. Use a heat gun to partially dry. When tacky, brush with a course brush to create patterns. Heat dry the slip until it becomes matte. You can test the slip by flexing the slab to see if anything splits. Gently stretch the slab out by casting it repeatedly against a table. This takes some practice, but if it's gentle enough, the slip will split and crack with the brushwork. You can immediately form the soft slab into a form, or allow it to dry and cut it into smaller pieces for assembly. The colorants are optional, and can be exchanged for others. I was trying to develop something that would look nice over terra cotta. Derived from the Akira Satake Kohiki Slip for c10.

recipes.name: Lake-effect Snow
recipes.description: Approximate re-formulation of MC6G High Calcium Semimatte 2 + 5 TiO2 using only EPK, Wollastonite, Frit 3134, Silica. Fired in a manual electric kiln (vintage Duncan) with slow cool. This has a lot of clay; calcining some of it would probably help as it tends to crack on drying, though it doesn't usually crawl. Or re-formulating with 3124 and reducing clay, which I might do someday. I keep the specific gravity high (1.5 or more) to try to minimize cracking. (Less water hopefully leading to less shrinkage on drying.) I found it makes little "flocs" of something - like little soft lumps - on standing. If I don't stick blend before applying it seems to crack way more and may crawl. Again I think if I calcine some of the EPK this may not happen. Can be made whiter by adding more zircopax; 8% is pretty much copy paper white.

recipes.name: Lamont Caramel Apple
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Chris Schafale Notes: Alisa Clausen: used local ball clay for OM-4. Covering iron red brown semi gloss glaze. The underlying darker colour of a brown to black is muted by a variegated shell surface with a greenish cast. Where the glaze is thickest, the colour becomes a warmer toffee brown. Where thinnest, the glaze is more even in colour, which is a dark tenmoku-like brown, with black edges. This glaze will could give a good play of colour with two different applications on the same work. Without RIO, a fat, semi-gloss white glaze. Milky where thinner, opaque and white where thicker. Surface is smooth with some very small crystals. Pooled around edge where thickest but did not drip.

recipes.name: Lana Wilson's Purple - Aqua
recipes.description: A very not-food safe glaze. Do not use on ANYTHING meant to touch food. Best on sculptures and planters. This has been one of my all-time favorite glazes since my years as an undergraduate. Cone range actually is from cone 06- cone 6. Its not really a glass so much as sintered oxides. I made everyone's lives much easier, and just calculated a scenario where the frit was in the "additives" section, so the body recipe is just 50/50, plus additive. This should make calculating a batch extremely easy. Fritt 3110 works, as well as any frit supplying barium. I think this works much better at c6 than at c04/06. The aqua part just doesn't come out very well at lower temperatures. I've got a more low-fire specific version here: https://glazy.org/recipes/342544

Then I generously apply a even thinner mixture and re-fire to cone 04. If I don’t get a rich enough purple (o.k. some people call it deep blue) then I apply more very thin watery glaze and lots of it and re-fire. Note: thin for purple and thick for aqua.

recipes.name: Laura Speirs Clear
recipes.description: From Laura Speirs December 31st, 1996 http://www.potters.org/subject00146.htm A fabulous clear glaze! I tested about 15 clears last year and only came up with 2 that I would consider using. This glaze is incredibly forgiving - doesn't show drips, overdips, differences in thickness, is glassy clear w/o yellow, and doesn't craze. I am absolutely thrilled with this glaze. It only has 4 ingredients, too. I use this over slips and underglazes and it's fine. I also use lusters over it with great results. What can I say? This is THE PERFECT clear glaze. Have fun. Laura in Oregon Recommended by Léïa-Fahé Villeneuve: This is my absolute fave: F-4 spar 40.00 Gerstley borate 30.00 Ball clay 20.00 Silica 10.00 It is super clear and shiny. Has never gone milky in my use. I tried a lot of recipes as i also use mainly coloured slips and underglazes. it does not show drips if the application is uneven, it is very shiny. it does not cloud. I apply it very thin and it is amazing! the studio where I studied has now made it the studio clear. We all call it "Perfect Clear" I found it here: http://lindaarbuckle.com/arbucklehandouts.html

recipes.description: From Steve Davis Website & Blog: http://kazegama.com/ Website: http://kazegamas.com/ Shinos 3: http://kazegamas.com/shinos3.htm There are 72 shinos shown on 4 web pages. They are organized from left to right with 3 tiles of the same glaze shown on 3 different clay bodies. They are Aardvark Clay's Nara Porcelain, Long Beach, and Black Mountain. Every shino was glazed with a doulble dip, waxed with a simple "S" pattern, and left to dry for 2 weeks to grow sulfates on the surface. The "S" pattern has no sulfate build up. recipes.name: Leach 4321 + 10%frit
recipes.description: ☆Receta compartida por Sonja Vitulić (Rawson - Argentina) en el grupo de Facebook "Aprendiendo entre todos" ☆Notas de Sonja: "Hola a todos! Comparto un pequeño ensayo que hice, con una base de esmalte clásica de Leach: 4-3-2-1; esto es: 40 Feldespato; 30 Cuarzo; 20 Carbonato de Calcio y 10 de Caolín. Pero a esto le agregué 10% de flux BS-804 de Crecer (el que tenía). MI criterio es el siguiente: elegí desde hace un tiempo trabajar a 1190-1200°C. Las horneadas me resultan más prácticas (aunque mi horno llegue bien a 1260°C) y no reniego más con la debilidad en todo sentido de los benditos 1040°C. No sé hacer cálculo de Seguer, y seguramente Horacio sabrá una mejor forma de bajar la temperatura a la base original... jajajaaa!!! Yo le mandé flux... Por otro lado, le subo la temperatura (1190-1200) a los esmaltes comerciales que ya tengo agregándole 15 ó 20% de cuarzo y/o caolín, o mezcla de ambos". Nota de Clara: integré la frita a la base, por eso los números son diferentes de los de Sonja ☆Origen de la receta: Bernard Leach, Receta para cono 10 (4321)

recipes.name: Leach 442 mit ungewaschener Asche
recipes.description: Erster Versuch einer Asche-Seladon-Glasur mit ungewascherner Asche aus dem Hausofen sowie Feldspat und Kaolin von Keramik Kraft. Einmal auf Wittgert 11 Steinzeugton, gebrannt auf 1280°C mit 60min Haltezeit (geschätzt Ortonkegel 10-11), einmal auf rotem Steinzeugton "MRH" von Argilières Hins in Belgien, gebrannt auf 1250°C mit 30min Haltezeit (geschätzt Ortonkegel 9). Varianten mit etwas Tenmoku-Wynnum (für RIO), 0,2 % CuO und 0,1% Co3O4, letzte beiden auch gemischt bzw. halb/halb. Kegel 10/11 zu viel; Glasur fast abgelaufen. Kegel 9 ok aber Glasur beginnt unmittelbar zu defloculieren und ist nach einigen Tagen fest. Weitere Versuche mit gewaschener Asche durchführen.

recipes.name: Leach Blue
recipes.description: handed over by Bob Santerre Glossy medium blue where thick and glossy slate blue where thin. Well I finally got around to typing this thing up...^9-10 Blues Thank you one and all for all the donated recipes. I only tested 31 out of almost 100 I received. I'll continue testing and reporting as the winter DRAGS on. All the glazes were tested on #900 Miller clay which is a toasty ^10 stoneware. One side of the test tile was brushed with a thick coating of Cynthia Bringle's wet/dry white slip. Each glaze was dipped in three thicknesses on a heavily textured tile. All tiles were fired to a (hard)^9 (10 tipping)reduction firing. 1 hr. Body reduction at ^08 and 1 hr. glaze reduction at ^9 then a quick reox. before shutdown. Any time potash or Custer spar is called for, I used G-200. All ball clay is OM-4 . Many glazes I substituted 75% of the amount of Barium with Strontium. All kaolin is EPK. Remember... glazes don't travel well. Your results will probably be TOTALLY different. Please test before use. Tracy Wilson Saltbox Pottery

recipes.description: This Glaze book was given to me about a year ago with many many crystal glazes; i read the book and chose a base with work with but almost every one of them said to hold the glazes at the top of cone 6 for about 1-3 hours. i didn't want to mess up my other glazes so i chose instead to do a slow cool cycle from 1600-1500F down 50F/hr so it would not mess up my other glazes, it worked great. recipes.name: Lewing Zn Base
recipes.description: From Clayart: http://www.potters.org/subject30033.htm Paul Lewing on tue 23 may 00 Recently I have been fooling with a zinc base glaze and was reading up on Bristol glazes. They were developed as a substitute for lead, presumably for low-fire glazes, although one of my books mentions them being used at midrange temperatures. This is the base I've come up with: Lewing Zn Base Zinc Oxide 11.35 Gerstley Borate 10.79 Custer Feldspar 48.44 Whiting 4.05 Silica 20.45 EPK Kaolin 4.91 This is a recipe that was published in the current issue of Clay Times, and I'm quite proud of it. It's the first glaze I've designed by just making up an empirical formula using Insight, and it was ready to put into my production line after only two 100g tests. If anyone out there has used it, I'd like some feedback. Anyway, my question is, is this a Bristol glaze? Is it only the fact that it's a Zn base that makes a glaze a Bristol glaze, or is there some further criterion? I can't find any in any of my books. Thanks, Paul Lewing, Seattle
