recipes.name: Li Floating Blue
recipes.description: I liked the looks of Joe Thompson's (@oldforgecreations) "OldForge Floating Blue" (https://glazy.org/recipes/77013). It reminds me of Amaco Potter's Choice Sapphire Float, which is a commercial glaze I like. I'm just a hobby potter with a full-time job as a chemist, elsewhere; so when I had some time this weekend for some glaze trials, I wanted to try OldForge Floating Blue. I didn't have any SrCO3 (nor any SrO). I also don't have any whiting, but I ususally substitute wollastonite and adjust that quantity and the SiO2 quantity accordingly. I was not motivated enough to go to the local Clayworks supply store to purchase some SrCO3, either. However, I had some Li2CO3. I substituted one third the quantity of Old Forge's SrCO3 with LiCO3. I only had one afternoon for this, thus I did not set up an experimental design and mix differing quantities of Li2CO3 to evaluate effects of varying Li2CO3 content. So, I made an educated guess at one third the SrCO3 quantity as a SWAG trial, substituting Li2CO3. Procedure: I was a bit concerned about the partial solubility of the Li2CO3. Given I'm using 1% by mass of Li2CO3, a potentially significant amount of this strong flux would be in solution - the first dip of the tile would mean less percentage of that flux in the visible glaze matrix. To compensate for that concern, I glazed tiles with four, three, and two dips of glaze to compare. I glazed a fourth tile with two dips, then held the tile horizontally and poured the third layer of glaze over that tile to see what effect, if any, would result. I did not sieve this test batch. I added one milliliter of water (municipal tap water) for each gram of total dry solids. I did not measure the specific gravity. I blended with an immersion blender. The mix was a bit on the thick side; but given my concern about the partial solubility of Li2CO3, I did not want to use more water than necessary. Firing schedule: I fired with a slowed-down rate - 100°F/hr - of heating on both the upside and downside of the firing schedule between 1050°F and 1150°F to mitigate quartz inversion expansion/contraction. I fired to 2100°F, then slowed down to a rate of 108°F/hr up to cone 6 (2232°F) with no hold, dropped 100°F and held for 10 minutes. Conclusions: Based on the results (please see posted pictures), I do not see a significant difference between three and four dips other than the expected muted texture of the tile. The tiles with three and four dips demonstrate an attractive phase separation effect. One can also observe the lack of sieving but to me, it's an interesting look. Two dips was satisfactory. I do not notice as obvious a phase separation effect, without magnification, as I see with more dips, but the glaze flowed nicely, pooling at texture. Upon magnification, one can observe the phase separation in the tile with two dips; thus my concern about the partial solubility of Li2CO3 was not an issue with this formulation. The tile with two dips and an orthogonal pour over the two dips suggests one can affect the the look of the 'float' by varying application direction. I will be using this glaze again. I tried some layering, but I only observed a sliver of the base glaze because I dipped a bit deep for this top layer. Next time I try layering this glaze on top, I'll not dip it so deeply. I did not post pictures of the tiles with layering as I am not pleased with the trials of the base glazes I used. But, the Li Floating Blue layer was pleasing. Changed status back to testing - doing acid and base tests because of possible durability issues

recipes.name: Light Tsaber's Celadon
recipes.description: This is the second recipe I've made up that tried to make Tsaber's Crackle Celadon fuse in one ^10 firing. While it is a success and is much more fused, it has less crackle and doesn't have the same unctuous, thick quality. It seems nice an stable though with a very mild sky blue hue and great transparency. While this test was fired to a soft 11 it will probably handle ^9 and 10 very well. I will fire these tiles a second time to see if they develop more crazing and intense hues.

recipes.name: Light turquise cone 6
recipes.description: The usual cone 10 base (45 petalite, 30 strontium, 25 spodumene) is a bit dry at cone 6 on its own and with smaller amounts of copper - I guess the reason the blue and turquoise melt is that they contain cobalt and copper which are fluxes. So for smaller amounts of copper or just the base itself, I fluxed it some more. I'm not sure what happened with the chrome. It's a tiny amount but it still seems a bit bumpy. The problem may be unrelated and may have more to do with not applying a thick enough layer of the chrome containing glaze. But the main effect, of a matte light copper blue, worked. As the tiles show, it really does benefit from the full 5% tin. I haven't tried it with zircopax instead - it may also work. The base on its own is very nice on white stoneware - frosty, satin and crazed.

recipes.name: Linda's Pink Shino
recipes.description: From Steve Davis Website & Blog: http://kazegama.com/ Website: http://kazegamas.com/ Shinos 3: http://kazegamas.com/shinos3.htm There are 72 shinos shown on 4 web pages. They are organized from left to right with 3 tiles of the same glaze shown on 3 different clay bodies. They are Aardvark Clay's Nara Porcelain, Long Beach, and Black Mountain. Every shino was glazed with a doulble dip, waxed with a simple "S" pattern, and left to dry for 2 weeks to grow sulfates on the surface. The "S" pattern has no sulfate build up. A medium reduction was started at cone 012 through cone 2. From there the kiln was fired in neutral to cone 10.

recipes.name: Lori's Suprise Purple
recipes.description: Some one on the list recently asked for a purple raku glaze. What I thought I had here when I was mixing it was a copper matt untill I lifted it out from under the reduction can. At first it was almost black but inside of 15 mins it is the deepest prettiest purple I have ever seen and I have no idea who gave the receipe to me. They sure do deserve credit. I sprayed this on JM5, a buff colored ^5 stoneware I had bisqued to ^08. I fired it in a small old electric I sometimes use for raku to 1830. After pulling it we went right to a pile of sand with 8' x8' piece of slick newspaper on the botton and as we covered it we threw in another the same size on top of the pot, covered it with the can sealing the edges, waited about an hour untill it was cool enough to touch and got the purple surprise. If someone uses this glaze I would really like to hear about their results. submitted by: Lori Wilkinson e-mail:

recipes.description: I've not seen this specific variation on here. The classic floating blue, but simpler than others. Excellent over virtually anything. Specific Gravity: 168 For 1kg batch, used 700g water Dark Rutile

recipes.name: Love Child
recipes.description: From Mark Burleson's The Ceramic Glaze Handbook p. 104. May be very fluid if applied too thickly. Crystalline matte, works well w/most colors. Excellent sprayed.

recipes.name: Love Child
recipes.description: From "The Ceramic Glaze Handbook" by Mark Burleson, Lark Ceramics A crystalline matte glaze for earthenware. No special cooling required. Displays color very well. Layers in cool ways on top of other glazes.

recipes.name: Love Child Strontium Lithium
recipes.description: Matte blue/green glaze, taken from ceramic arts daily

recipes.name: Low Chappell Floating Blue
recipes.description: Receta, muestra de esmalte y fotografía compartida en el grupo de Facebook "Aprendiendo entre Todos" por Sílvia Cabezudo (Tandil- Argentina. Adaptación del esmalte de cono 6 "Chappell Floating Blue" ( https://glazy.org/recipes/2492 ) calculada por Horacio E. González (Las Golondrinas/Argentina) para baja temperatura (cono 05). Notas de Sílvia Cabezudo: "FLOATING BLUE CHAPPELL para 1020/40°C que recalculó Horacio Ernesto González, usando frita 174 de Crecer (3134 de Ferro). Usé la frita FC 104 de Ceramikería/Argentina, que era la única disponible en ese momento. A cono 05 quedó infracocido, por lo tanto lo llevé a 1160°C, sin mantenimiento final. Feldespato 10 + Dolomita 5 + Carbonato de Calcio 3 + Caolín 8 + FritAalcalina ( de Ceramiquería) 63 + Cuarzo 11 // Rutilo 4 + Hierro 2 + Cobalto 1" Nota : el recálculo de Horacio para cono 05 tenía en cuenta el uso de la frita 174 de Crecer (3134 de Ferro). Usando la frita de Ceramikería (de la cual no hay análisis conocido, a cono 05 quedó infracocido. Sería interesante ver el resultado a cono 05 usando la frita 174 de Crecer (3134 de Ferro)

recipes.name: Low COE Magnisum Satin Matte Base
recipes.description: This is a magnesium based matte glaze base. It is well suited for adding in mason stains for color. It is a low expansion / LOI glaze and should fit many bodies of clay well without having crazing issues. This is a modification of Tony Hanson's G1215U. It Has been tested with 8% Zircopax Plus.

recipes.name: Low Down Blue
recipes.description: I tested this glaze for some planters. This is the blue that I developed. The base recipe was adapted by Kari Radasch from a Woody Hughes recipe published in Ceramics Monthly.

recipes.name: Low Expansion Clear
recipes.description: I added Ultrox to make it matte. It did not work with Nebula, it dunts John's Britt pg. 77

recipes.name: Low expansion Selsor Oribe
recipes.description: A tweak of John Britt’s really low expansion selsor https://glazy.org/recipes/119900 that fits my Standard 553 clay. I reduced talc for brighter color, and increased silica. The surface is perfectly smooth with 325 mesh silica

recipes.name: Low fire blue/white
recipes.description: I fire this anywhere from 04-1. If applied thin on a red body, it picks up colorant from the iron and turns blue. If thick, it turns a white but shows a lot of depth in the glaze matrix between the surface and the clay underneath. It can blister in volatile atmospheres with the added flux. But that's a "can". If you can manage to not kill the glaze with the added flux, the fluctuation in atmospheres can allow for localized oxidation/reduction around the pinholes, which is gorgeous if you ask me.

recipes.name: Low Fire Shino
recipes.description: Semi dry, metallic sheen, somewhat runny. Can bubble at cone 3.

recipes.name: Low Fire Shino
recipes.description: Modified from Heather Banas' recipe https://glazy.org/recipes/128570. Runny.

recipes.name: Low Fire Shino Flesh Revised
recipes.description: From WORKSHOP ELECTRIC KILN GLAZES, Lana Wilson, 2004 https://img-cache.oppcdn.com/fixed/14340/resume.pdf Originally from Alfred and too shiny so I cut the Lithium carbonate from 29% down to 9%. First I use John Conrad Black Engobe wiped off and fired to cone 6, then I apply Low Fire Shino Flesh, watery thin consistency, no wiping off and re- fire to cone 04.

recipes.name: Low Fire True Matte
recipes.description: Relatively clear when applied thinly. Looks even more clear over a light slip. Works great with Zircopax and Mason Stain to make a matte black and matte white. Will crawl where thickly applied in soda atmosphere.

recipes.name: Low Tide
recipes.description: Licorice variation developed by Nancy Gallagher. Normal E1 firing, natural cooling.

recipes.name: Low-Expansion Glaze for Flameware
recipes.description: Calls for 200 mesh silica and white talc. From a Ceramics Mo article on Flameware May 2011.

recipes.name: Low-fire Shino
recipes.description: Receta publicada en el libro "Mid Range Glazes" de John Britt

recipes.name: Lowfire Body #2 (60/40 pink slip)
recipes.description: Grog omitted (now I am not sure if grog was actually omitted or not, ugh!); Bentonite (Volclay) omitted; added a 2 oz bottle of Duncan low fire under glaze CC-186 (Tomato Red); original batch size = 930 grams (without grog) or 1000 grams (with grog); very light pink/coral color; subsequently added another 2 oz bottle of CC-186 to make darker. Experimenting with as a slip.

recipes.description: Calcium boraat shiny semi transparant base glaze: on our white clay it crazes.

recipes.name: LTtra generic transparent EU
recipes.description: All purpose transparent glaze without frittes. Fires well at 1205-1230C. Clear liner glaze

recipes.name: Lubbock Black
recipes.description: Significant Flaw: spitting Notes: Alisa Clausen: Gloss black with some blue pooling in center of test bowl. Spit a halo on to shelf around test bowl.

recipes.name: Lubbock Blue Green
recipes.description: Significant Flaw: spitting Notes: Alisa Clausen: Dark blue to almost black, gloss. It spit all over like crazy, jumped over to a pot next to the test and left a huge halo of blue on the shelf and on the adjacent wall. Turns out the recipe called for 0.5 cobalt, not 5!

recipes.name: Lubbock Honey Brown
recipes.description: Significant Flaw: running Notes: Alisa Clausen: two tests of this glaze both produced a fluid to runny, light yellow to honey brown glaze. Pooled in the center of test bowl to a glistening light yellowish glaze with a ring of darker browns. No signs of purple or opalescence as claimed in either test.

recipes.name: Lubbock White
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: similar oxides to Robin Egg Blue Notes: Alisa Clausen: Stable, gloss white. No discernable difference where double dipped.

recipes.name: Lucas Mottled Iron
recipes.description: Glaze Type: High-fire Nice wet and dry glaze. Runs. From Peter Beasecker. Great in salt and soda.

recipes.name: Lucido
recipes.description: Smalto liscio, lucido. Coprente con 5% rutile e 1% carbonato di cobalto; dato più spesso crea effetto colatura, screziato. Trasparente con 2% di rutile ventilato e 1% ossido di rame nero; tendenza a cavillo quando dato più spesso.

recipes.name: Lucie Rie #15 Dolomite
recipes.description: Notes from Vinod Chettur: Unmodified glaze is smooth but dry matte. For less matte variation try addition of 10% ulexite. This glaze is suitable for non-functional ware. Lucie Rie's greatness is not necessarily in a specific glaze recipe but in the way she used them with multiple colorants and underlying slips. You can find her recipes in the book - Lucie Rie and Hans Coper: Potters in Parallel (Art Reference) https://www.amazon.com/Lucie-Rie-Hans-Coper-Re…/…/0713646977 or in Ceramic Review #150.

recipes.name: Lucky 11
recipes.description: I don't remember where I got this one, but it's a super nice Boron Chun Red. Apply thick like any chun, we start our reduction at 014 and stall for an hour. I wouldnt take this glaze to cone 12 as it will probably run when thick the chance effect seems to be halted by dirtier stonewares

recipes.name: M19 - Crawly White
recipes.description: An opaque white glaze that crawls in a controllable way. The thicker the application, the bigger the crawl effects. I used to use it over coloured engobes. At cone 8 the crawling is defined, but it starts to melt back over as cone 9 is approached. At cone 9, most of the crawling is lost, but it becomes a lovely satin smooth surface at the higher temps. Actually magnesium carbonate light was used, but this material wasn't in the database (?)

recipes.name: MA490 - Orange Red (Kaki)
recipes.description: Glossy, opaque, speckled. Varies from firing to firing. Like most iron glazes, turns into a dull brown where too thin. From the Wolf Matthes book "Emaux et Glaçures Céramiques".

recipes.name: MA639 - Flat Satin-Matt Purple
recipes.description: Very flat and unvariegated surface. Color is intense. Calculated from formula 639 of Wolf E. Matthes "Emaux et Glaçures Céramiques".

recipes.name: MA96 - Glossy, translucent, crazing
recipes.description: Email tiré du livre de Wolf Matthes Emaux et glaçures céramiques. Brillant, translucide, craquelé. Nuances de vert par ajout de cuivre (0,5% – 1% sur la photo des tuiles). CoE : 75

recipes.description: This is a glaze from Warren Mackenzie who called it a cone 3-4 glaze. I have fired this glaze to a hot cone 6 with success. The glaze is a wonderful transparent gloss glaze at cone 4 without the oxides. I use it at cone 4 over stains and Amaco velvet underglaze.

recipes.name: Mackenzie Grey
recipes.description: From Phillip Schmidt http://phillipschmidtpottery.com/my-favorite-glaze-recipes/ This is Warren Mackenzie’s famous matte grey glaze. An excellent, simple, and beautiful recipe that I formulated my Matte Yellow glaze from. Notes: Cone 10 reduction glaze What I love about it: The grey is variable from thick to thin, going from brown to red to greenish to grey and sometimes even a wonderful sea blue; it’s a beautiful matte glaze that feels wonderful too; great for pouring over large pieces. What I don’t like about it: Not very durable–metal marks from silverware, acidic drinks left inside overnight will etch the glaze; crazes

recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Clay Times, March/April, 2005 Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 1100C hold 1 hour Significant Flaw: crazing Notes: Alisa Clausen: Apply thinly, runs and pinholes if thick. Very marked black edges on test tile.

recipes.name: Macrocrystalline jm2 (mkh 39)
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Crystalline From Charlie Cummings Yep, it grows crystals. Nice ones if you give it time. I stopped playing with it because every time I put it in the kiln my CCCS color base (from my last post) would have problems. Specifically, the chrome and the iron versions would blister. I think it may have something to do with the large amount of zinc in the glaze...or I may be superstitious.

recipes.name: Madden Blue
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Sharry Madden Notes: Sharry Madden: very shiny, clear, stable, no cracks to the naked eye. The test tile was frozen for 24 hours, then put into a tub of boiling water, to test for cracks. This was done 3 times in a row, with no cracks.

recipes.name: Magnesium Mat-Carleton Ball
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Magnesium matt Morning all...I've been talking to June about some glazes and it turns out we both are aware of an old Carleton Ball glaze. She from remembered association; me from checking an old copy I have of the typescript of his syllabus. What we were both looking at is the above glaze My text immedaitely following reads: Bright transparent glazes allow colors to show well but in general....etc This appears on pg 47. of my typescript. Unfortunately, pg. 46 is missing of my copy as well as pp. 40-44. I inherited the typescript from a teacher and am delighted I've got it (it even includes class responsibilities and where to keep tools take care of glazes etc.) but I sure would like the missing pages. If anybody has them, I'd be thrilled to send a self-addressed stamped envelope for a copy and the xeroxing costs. At this point, I haven't any info on the colorants to add to the glazes? TIA Emily in Astoria where my head is clogged, I can't breathe, those lousy flowers are everwhere and the sun it still don't shine. How DO they GROW?

recipes.name: Mahavir Celadon
recipes.description: Back in the US I've struggled to find a porcelain clay body and glaze that I was satisfied with, but after hundreds of tests and failed attempts I finally have something that comes close to the quality of what I had become accustomed to in China. Having just moved back to the US and unsatisfied with results using Custer feldspar, I was delighted to find Mahavir Potash feldspar being imported from India. Being higher in high-expansion R2O fluxes, Mahavir-based glazes are slightly more likely to craze when replacing Custer 1-to-1. This glaze is quite similar to other "blue celadon" glazes although with a slightly lower R2O level. Preparation Lacking a good ball mill, I've used this glaze after sieving it through a 100-mesh sieve. If I had a ball mill, I'd first try 2 hours. Application I bisque my ware at cone 08. This is a high enough temperature to get the ware to a less fragile state with all carbon/organics/etc. burned off. But at this temperature the ware is still porous enough to accept a thick layer of glaze. I've found cone 04 bisque ware to be too "tight" and difficult to apply the thick layer of glaze needed for some celadons and other glazes. I pour my glazes with a watering can (http://www.derekau.net/2017/03/12/pouring-glaze-with-a-watering-can/). Done properly this technique gives a very even application without the trouble and waste of spraying. See also Derek's Porcelain: https://glazy.org/recipes/25288

recipes.name: Mahavir Celadon (Calcined NZK)
recipes.description: This is a version of Mahavir Celadon (https://glazy.org/recipes/22821) that replaces some of the New Zealand Halloysite with calcined Halloysite, which makes this glaze less prone to drying issues that can lead to crawling. Calcined kaolin can be made by firing the kaolin in your regular bisque kiln. Ideally the kaolin will be spread evenly and not too thick, perhaps 1" or 3cm deep. Using calcined kaolin, the glaze will not shrink as much during drying, leading to less drying cracks.

recipes.name: Mahavir Clear +10 Holmium
recipes.description: From Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holmium): Holmium oxide has some fairly dramatic color changes depending on the lighting conditions. In daylight, it has a tannish yellow color. Under trichromatic light, it is fiery orange-red, almost indistinguishable from the appearance of erbium oxide under the same lighting conditions. The perceived color change is related to the sharp absorption bands of holmium interacting with a subset of the sharp emission bands of the trivalent ions of europium and terbium, acting as phosphors.

recipes.name: Majolica (Arbuckle)
recipes.description: 1⁄2 - 3+ tbsp. Epsom salts. to 5 gallons of glaze (flocculates the glaze for less settling and better application). Smooth, white, opaque. Colorants w/flux usually applied in a thin wash to raw glaze surface. Does not move in firing. May crawl if thick in corners or pinhole over rough-trimmed surfaces. Fire w/small 03 cone in the sitter to give a small 04 tipped to about 2 o'clock in front of the peep hole. Use of chrome in decoration may cause sufficient fuming to make the background blush pink in high tin glazes (above 5%). If this is a problem, drop the tin a bit, and add that amount x 1.5 of additional zirconium opacifier.

recipes.name: Majolica Arbuckle
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Majolica Very white opaque viscous glaze. Make sure all trimmed areas are ribbed smooth, or pinholing may result. Glaze thickness is an issue. Too thick an application may produce white dotting thru colored surface decoration, and/or pinholing. Suggested colorants: Frit 3124 1 + 1/2 bentonite + copper, cobalt, or iron 1 by volume. Refractory colorants 2-3 frit 3124 + 1/2 bentonite + 1 rutile, or chrome. Most stains 2-3 frit + 1/2 bentonite + 1 stain. Do not use body stains like Mason 6020 pink, Ti yellow, or Lavender as they are too refractory and will pig-skin.

recipes.name: Majolica Midrange 2
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Ca B Majolica Variation of Mid-range Majolica that replaces Gerstley borate with a frit to eliminate surface blemishes of the overglaze majolica colorants. Ferro Frit 3134 can be substituted for Pemco Frit P-54. Good as a majolica-like opaque white glaze with oxides and stains brushed over it. Very stable - does not run, applies well with a brush or by other methods. Doesn't craze on cone 10 porcelain fired to cone 6 - test on cone 6 body. Tested on Aardvark stoneware clays: (listed best to worst for smooth surface) Porcelain, Hopkins White 60, Joe Soldate 60, Rio Red (the last two may have a fairly gritty surface, even at cone 6). Possible Glaze Flaws: This glaze is fairly powdery without any binder. It will crawl slightly if applied too thickly followed by a wash of color on the raw glaze. YOU MUST add CMC to glaze batch to harden the raw surface of this glaze. Use about one tablespoon of CMC powder (soaked in a pint of hot water overnight) per 3000 gram batch. Colors: Use mason stains mixed 50/50 with Pemco frit P-25 or Ferro Frit 3124, or use 70 stain/30 gerstley borate in a watery mix for colors over glaze or some combination of gerstley borate and frit. Using too much gerstley borate may make the stain change color or become pastel. Purple stains may need to have more flux added up to 3 parts flux to 1 part stain. If you use all frit, add liquid starch or CMC to colors for easier brushing and to minimize smearing before they're fired. A small amount of bentonite may also help to keep the all-frit mixture from settling out. These binders are not as necessary with the gerstley borate. Use these Duncan EZ-stroke transparent underglazes as overglaze wash for color: EZ003, EZ004, EZ007, EZ012, EZ014, EZ019, EZ020, EZ021, EZ024, EZ025, EZ027, EZ028, EZ030, EZ032, EZ161. Almost all the other EZstrokes will work, especially if thinned slightly. The dark blue and the orange EZstrokes will wrinkle and get rough if applied too thickly. Cover coat CC 154 should work as well. Most other Cover Coat colors will work when thinly applied, but may be dry if thick. Try adding a teaspoonful of frit or gerstley borate to a jar of CC underglaze for glossier color. Other color possibilities include washes of the common colorants (mix chrome and rutile 50/50 with gerstley borate or frit). A thin red iron or red earthenware slip or possibly a red terra sigillata on the foot or other exposed clay areas makes a nice contrast if used on a white clay body. Richard Burkett 1991. Other color possibilities: A nice dark blue green with: 2% cobalt carb + 3% chrome oxide + 2% black iron oxide added to the glaze. SDSU 1992

recipes.name: Majolica Midrange 96
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Majolica From Linda Litteral - SDSU Glaze class 1996. She called it 'A-7 Chinese.' Tested for new Midrange majolica for class use. Almost boron free - good for stain colors that are subject to dissolving in boron glazes. Very stable, does not move during firing unless quite thick. Will crawl slightly if very thick. Applies well either by dipping or brushing. Works well with almost all Duncan EZ-Stroke underglaze colors as majolica washes, as do Amaco velvet red versions of the zirconium encapsulted red stains. Probably most stains would work well also. Color possibities: Use mason stains mixed 50/50 with Pemco frit P-25 or Ferro Frit 3124, or use 70 stain/30 gerstley borate in a watery mix for colors over glaze or some combination of gerstley borate and frit. Using too much gerstley borate may make the stain change color or become pastel. Purple stains may need to have more flux added up to 3 parts flux to 1 part stain. If you use all frit, add liquid starch or CMC to colors for easier brushing and to minimize smearing before they're fired. Use these Duncan EZ-stroke transparent underglazes as overglaze wash for color: EZ003, EZ004, EZ007, EZ012, EZ014, EZ019, EZ020, EZ021, EZ024, EZ025, EZ027, EZ028, EZ030, EZ032, EZ161. Almost all the other EZstrokes will work, especially if thinned slightly. The darker blues EZstrokes will wrinkle and get rough if applied too thickly. CoverCoat CC 154 should work as well. Most other CoverCoat colors will work when thinly applied, but may be dry if thick. Try adding a teaspoonful of frit or gerstley borate to a jar of CC underglaze for glossier color. Other color possibilities include washes of the common colorants (mix chrome and rutile 50/50 with gerstley borate or frit). A thin red iron or red earthenware slip or possibly a red terra sigillata on the foot or other exposed clay areas makes a nice contrast if used on a white clay body. Variations: Other color possibilities: A nice dark blue green with: 2% cobalt carb + 3% chrome oxide + 2% black iron oxide added to the glaze. Or almost any commercial stain added to the glaze in 5-12% amounts. How long have you been using this glaze? About a year. Where is it used? San Diego State University Where did this recipe come from? From Linda Litteral - SDSU Glaze class 1996. She called it 'A-7 Chinese.' What do you like most about this glaze? very stable, good support for most stain colors Is this glaze reliable? very, but like many majolica glazes it may crawl if applied too thickly. Does this glaze tend to craze/crawl/pinhole/etc.? like many majolica glazes it may crawl if applied too thickly. How do different firing temperatures/atmospheres affect the glaze? should work in oxidation or reduction firings, but not with all stain colors. How does the glaze behave on different clay bodies? best on finer textured clays or smooth, well-ribbed surfaces if used on more heavily grogged clay bodies. How thickly should the glaze be applied to the pot? medium (average) application for best opacity. may crawl if too thick. How does this glaze interact with other glazes? should work with most other glazes like any typical white gloss glaze, due to the low boron content What is your kiln type and size? Alpine Globar, approx 8 cu. ft. How do you typically fire? 6-8 hour heating, 24-36 hour cooling, no soak. Do you experience problems with the raw glaze? may settle badly without the bentonite/epsom salt addition. Adding a small amount of CMC gum solution may also help a bit and harden the raw glaze surface. GlazeBase Glaze Submitted by: Richard Burkett Ice Cream Flavor: Ben and Jerry's Pistachio -------------------------------------------------------------------- ----

recipes.name: Majolica Tile 1
recipes.description: I've been working with earthenware the last few months, after not having done so for many years. Right now I am firing to cone 02 and doing two types of decoration: one with metallic slips for a burnt earth look and one with glazes. My interest here is only the glazed ware. In the cases where I brush on the glaze, there is absolutely no pin holing, whether I apply the glaze very thickly, thickly or thinly. It's not so much the pin holing itself which interests me ( I will work to eliminate that) but rather that it does not occur when I brush on the glaze (whether I apply it thickly or thinly and even on several occasions I have brushed in on raw, fired it and had no pinholes). Any ideas why? bob kavanagh (60 km west of montreal)

recipes.name: Malcom Davis Carbon Trap
recipes.description: From Steve Davis Website: http://kazegamas.com/ Shinos 1: http://kazegamas.com/shinos1.htm NC-4 substituted for F-4 There are 72 shinos shown on 4 web pages. They are organized from left to right with 3 tiles of the same glaze shown on 3 different clay bodies. They are Aardvark Clay's Nara Porcelain, Long Beach, and Black Mountain. Every shino was glazed with a doulble dip, waxed with a simple "S" pattern, and left to dry for 2 weeks to grow sulfates on the surface. The "S" pattern has no sulfate build up. A medium reduction was started at cone 012 through cone 2. From there the kiln was fired in neutral to cone 10.

recipes.name: Marc's Clear
recipes.description: A high gloss clear glaze with a smooth surface and very few bubbles. It was designed to be used with ceramic stains on cone six porcelain slip-casting bodies. It is at its best when applied thin to medium and fired to a full cone 6. It has a fairly low CTE so tends not to craze on most clays. This glaze is fairly high in alumina and silica and gets its fluxing power through diversifying both the R2O and RO fluxes. Replace the talc with zinc for tan/brown stains based on chrome-iron-zinc system. It will cloud a little on iron stoneware clays. For better clarity drop the silica down to 16 -18%. The CTE will still be ok and likely not craze on most stoneware bodies even with the lower silica. For optimum results sieve through 100 mesh or 80 at least twice. Tends to settle in the bucket at low SG so maybe add 1-2 % bentonite.

recipes.name: March Crackle
recipes.description: From "My Work, My Way: Fifty Years in the Studio" by Harlan House, 2019. https://www.harlanhouse.com/ https://www.harlanhouse.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/2019%20HHBK-FINAL.pdf Named because of its color, a warm grey that mimic’s what happens to our landscape in March. This is another accident. I mixed two glazes up, and loved what happened. Trouble is, I only knew what one of them was. I spent a huge amount of time trying combinations and finally hit gold. It turns out to be about half white crackle, and half RGM, which both look the same in the wet state… I use good India ink to emphasise the crazing. The surface must be dry, so wear rubber gloves as even your sweaty hand will keep the ink from entering the craze. Use a small sponge, and cover the glaze with ink. As it starts to dry, use a larger damp sponge to get most of the ink off the surface. Finally, use a clean sponge to get the last smear of ink off the glaze. Let that dry for a day or so, and sponge it again. You will find out that it is not a good idea to get the ink on the exposed clay body. You will, and you will curse. You will likely re-fire, which is how I found Naples Yellow. This is a messy job, so wear things you don’t want to wear again…and gloves, rubber gloves. Nepheline Syenite 56.9 Whiting 3.44 Grolleg Kaolin 17.24 Dolomite 2.58 Silica 15.51 Bentonite 3.44 Iron oxide 0.86 Timing… If you want very large crackle patterns ink should be applied very soon after the piece is out of the kiln. If you want smaller cracked ice type of pattern, wait for a month and ink then. Of course, you can do both. You can also use good artist’s drawing inks, and they come in good colors. Play. Black first early, and red or blue later is a nice combination.

recipes.name: Mason Color Works White Underglaze Base
recipes.description: For years I relied on the internet to find information about ceramics. One of the most useful and reliable sources both then and now is Vince Pitelka's website. There he shares his knowledge on all aspects of the studio, from making your own tools to loading & firing kilns. (Although I have yet to try his Fabulous Top-Secret Extra-Special Spicy Cheesy Black Bean Dip recipe!) For all of Vince Pitelka's Handouts, please visit: https://www.vincepitelka.com/handoutsinformation/ One very useful recipe on his website is for Mason Underglaze, which actually includes three recipes: CMC solution (great on its own as a glaze additive to slow drying and improve brushability), Underglaze Liquid (which can be used with any underglaze to greatly improve brushability), and finally the Mason Underglaze recipe itself. If you do any underglaze decoration, even just to sign your name, I hope you'll try out these recipes! One note: You should be able to purchase "food grade", non-toxic propylene glycol via the internet, DO NOT just buy automobile anti-freeze which may contain other additives. ## Mason Underglaze Recipe https://www.vincepitelka.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/Mason-Underglaze-Recipe.pdf This recipe for an opaque white underglaze base comes from the Mason Color Works of Liverpool, Ohio, manufacturers of Mason ceramic stains. It’s been in use for decades, and seems to give good results for underglaze brushwork. Like most commercial underglazes, it is not appropriate for trailing or other thick-application techniques. #### Dry Materials F-4 Soda Spar -------------- 20 Kaolin ----------------------- 10 Ball Clay --------------------- 5 3124 Frit ---------------------10 Zircopax --------------------- 5 (or any other zircon opacifier) Total Dry Materials ------- 50 Add Underglaze Liquid -- 75 For colors other than white, add: Ceramic stain -------------- 40 Add the stain after everything else is combined, including the underglaze liquid. Vary the amount of stain for a darker or lighter color, and of course if you add a significant amount of stain you will need to add additional water to adjust the consistency of the final mix. To make the underglaze liquid, combine: Non-toxic antifreeze ------ 2 parts Water ----------------------- 2 parts CMC Liquid --------------- 1 parts To make CMC liquid, stir 30 grams of dry CMC in 1 qt. hot water and let it sit for 2 days. Be sure to use non-toxic antifreeze! Normal antifreeze is ethylene-glycol and is toxic. Instead, use non-toxic propylene-glycol antifreeze. It’s available in auto-supply stores and is safe for people and pets. The CMC gum and propylene glycol in this mixture make it thicker and smoother than a slip containing only water, giving a smoother brushing consistency especially when applying underglaze to dry greenware or bisqueware. When making this recipe: Dry-mix all the dry ingredients, add about 3/4 of the underglaze liquid and blend thoroughly, and then blend in more underglaze liquid a little at a time as needed until you achieve the desired brushing consistency. You may not need the full amount of underglaze liquid. Clarification This recipe can be a bit confusing. When a recipe just provides numbers without specifying the weighing increments, the increments can be whatever you wish – grams, ounces, pounds, etc. For the sake of accuracy when mixing glazes or slips, we generally use grams. With any recipe, there is always the question of what factor to multiply the base recipe by in order to get a certain amount of final product. For example, glaze recipes are almost always given in a form where the dry raw materials for the glaze base add up to 100, plus the modifiers, colorants, etc. In a recipe that contains only dry materials, we know from experience that a batch of 12,000 grams of dry material will fill a five-gallon bucket to the rim once combined with water. But this recipe includes underglaze liquid added by weight, and that does confuse matters Since the instructions tell us to make a quart of CMC liquid, a logical starting point is to figure out the whole recipe based on using that full quart of CMC liquid in the underglaze liquid, adjusting all the other amounts proportionally. As explained below, by doing this we end up needing a little over 3000 grams of dry materials, and the recipe produces about a gallon and a half of underglaze base. Here’s how we figured that. Combining one quart of CMC liquid with two quarts of water and two quarts of non-toxic antifreeze as per the recipe gives five quarts of underglaze liquid. A quart of water weighs 946 grams. Multiply that times five (five quarts) to get 4730 grams of underglaze liquid. The recipe specifies 75 measuring units of underglaze liquid, and if we divide 4730 by 75 we get 63.07, rounded off to 63. Thus if we use the whole five quarts of underglaze liquid, in order to get the correct proportional amounts of dry materials we multiply each amount by 63, which gives a total dry materials weight of 3150 grams. Based on these calculations, our recipe is: F-4 spar ----------------- 20x63 = 1260 grams Kaolin -------------------- 10x63 = 630 grams Ball Clay ------------------- 5x63 = 315 grams 3124 frit ------------------ 10x63 = 630 grams Zircopax ------------------- 5x63 = 315 grams Total weight of dry materials -- 3150 grams Underglaze liquid ------ 75x63 = 4725 grams Total weight of batch ------------ 7875 grams Since 12,000 grams of dry glaze materials yields a full five-gallon bucket of glaze, we can extrapolate and estimate that since the dry materials weigh 3180 grams (including the CMC gum), this recipe should make about six quarts, which is a lot of underglaze base. If you want more or less underglaze base, just proportionally adjust the number of grams of everything, and adjust the quantity of CMC liquid and underglaze liquid that you prepare.

recipes.name: Mason Colorworks Underglaze Recipe
recipes.description: This has worked well for me in cone 04 firing and cone 6. The top temperature is dictated by the stain used, refer to manufacturer info. Liquid - for a 500g batch 300 g non toxic antifreeze 150 g CMC liquid Up to 300 g water To make CMC liquid, stir 30 grams of dry CMC in 1 qt. hot water and let it sit for 2 days. To calculate the amount of liquid for a different batch size, multiply the batch size (before stain is added) by 150%, to get total liquid. Divide that number by 5. Multiply that number by 2 for the antifreeze and water, and use it as is for the CMC liquid. Always add the antifreeze and CMC liquid first and then water to set the desired consistency. Screen printing underglaze recipe To 500 g batch of dry ingredients (plus stain) - add 300 g of non toxic antifreeze, mix, add just enough water to get a pudding consistency. Weigh 350 g of prepared mixture and add 25g snot, mix thoroughly with immersion blender, scrape sides frequently. I don't sieve underglaze for screen printing, the screen is 110 mesh or finer. How to make snot - to one cup of boiling hot water in blender, add 3 heaping teaspoons of CMC powder, blend for 2-3 minutes. Store unused snot in tightly closed container. Discard after about a year or when it starts to stink. This can be safely added to any ceramic glaze, underglaze, or stain to improve brushability or dry strength. This is the information I used to make this recipe. I found it a bit confusing so I configured it how it makes sense to me and it seems to work fine. Appalachian Center for Crafts - Clay Studio Vince Pitelka, 2015 Mason Color Works White Underglaze Base This recipe for an opaque white underglaze base comes from the Mason Color Works of Liverpool, Ohio, manufacturers of Mason ceramic stains. It’s been in use for decades, and seems to give good results for underglaze brushwork. Like most commercial underglazes, it is not appropriate for trailing or other thick-application techniques. Dry Materials F-4 Soda Spar -------------- 20 Kaolin ----------------------- 10 Ball Clay --------------------- 5 3124 Frit ---------------------10 Zircopax --------------------- 5 (or any other zircon opacifier) Total Dry Materials ------- 50 Add Underglaze Liquid -- 75 For colors other than white, add: Ceramic stain -------------- 40 Add the stain after everything else is combined, including the underglaze liquid. Vary the amount of stain for a darker or lighter color, and of course if you add a significant amount of stain you will need to add additional water to adjust the consistency of the final mix. To make the underglaze liquid, combine: Non-toxic antifreeze ------ 2 parts Water ----------------------- 2 parts CMC Liquid --------------- 1 parts To make CMC liquid, stir 30 grams of dry CMC in 1 qt. hot water and let it sit for 2 days. Be sure to use non-toxic antifreeze! Normal antifreeze is ethylene-glycol and is toxic. Instead, use non-toxic propylene-glycol antifreeze. It’s available in auto-supply stores and is safe for people and pets. The CMC gum and propylene glycol in this mixture make it thicker and smoother than a slip containing only water, giving a smoother brushing consistency especially when applying underglaze to dry greenware or bisqueware. When making this recipe: Dry-mix all the dry ingredients, add about 3/4 of the underglaze liquid and blend thoroughly, and then blend in more underglaze liquid a little at a time as needed until you achieve the desired brushing consistency. You may not need the full amount of underglaze liquid. Clarification This recipe can be a bit confusing. When a recipe just provides numbers without specifying the weighing increments, the increments can be whatever you wish – grams, ounces, pounds, etc. For the sake of accuracy when mixing glazes or slips, we generally use grams. With any recipe, there is always the question of what factor to multiply the base recipe by in order to get a certain amount of final product. For example, glaze recipes are almost always given in a form where the dry raw materials for the glaze base add up to 100, plus the modifiers, colorants, etc. In a recipe that contains only dry materials, we know from experience that a batch of 12,000 grams of dry material will fill a five-gallon bucket to the rim once combined with water. But this recipe includes underglaze liquid added by weight, and that does confuse matters Since the instructions tell us to make a quart of CMC liquid, a logical starting point is to figure out the whole recipe based on using that full quart of CMC liquid in the underglaze liquid, adjusting all the other amounts proportionally. As explained below, by doing this we end up needing a little over 3000 grams of dry materials, and the recipe produces about a gallon and a half of underglaze base. Here’s how we figured that. Combining one quart of CMC liquid with two quarts of water and two quarts of non-toxic antifreeze as per the recipe gives five quarts of underglaze liquid. A quart of water weighs 946 grams. Multiply that times five (five quarts) to get 4730 grams of underglaze liquid. The recipe specifies 75 measuring units of underglaze liquid, and if we divide 4730 by 75 we get 63.07, rounded off to 63. Thus if we use the whole five quarts of underglaze liquid, in order to get the correct proportional amounts of dry materials we multiply each amount by 63, which gives a total dry materials weight of 3150 grams. Based on these calculations, our recipe is: F-4 spar ----------------- 20x63 = 1260 grams Kaolin -------------------- 10x63 = 630 grams Ball Clay ------------------- 5x63 = 315 grams 3124 frit ------------------ 10x63 = 630 grams Zircopax ------------------- 5x63 = 315 grams Total weight of dry materials -- 3150 grams Underglaze liquid ------ 75x63 = 4725 grams Total weight of batch ------------ 7875 grams Since 12,000 grams of dry glaze materials yields a full five-gallon bucket of glaze, we can extrapolate and estimate that since the dry materials weigh 3180 grams (including the CMC gum), this recipe should make about six quarts, which is a lot of underglaze base. If you want more or less underglaze base, just proportionally adjust the number of grams of everything, and adjust the quantity of CMC liquid and underglaze liquid that you prepare.

It is not temperature sensitive and produces good results at cone 5, 6 and 7 (medium blue surface breaking an olive type green where thin). Be sure to use a smallest particle sized alumina you can find (it is available in very fine grades, much finer that the average ceramic material). recipes.name: Mayan Blue
recipes.description: from Clayart about a year ago Deep teal over white slip. other wise dark blue/black where thick. Brown where thin. Crawled slightly over the slip. Well I finally got around to typing this thing up...^9-10 Blues Thank you one and all for all the donated recipes. I only tested 31 out of almost 100 I received. I'll continue testing and reporting as the winter DRAGS on. All the glazes were tested on #900 Miller clay which is a toasty ^10 stoneware. One side of the test tile was brushed with a thick coating of Cynthia Bringle's wet/dry white slip. Each glaze was dipped in three thicknesses on a heavily textured tile. All tiles were fired to a (hard)^9 (10 tipping)reduction firing. 1 hr. Body reduction at ^08 and 1 hr. glaze reduction at ^9 then a quick reox. before shutdown. Any time potash or Custer spar is called for, I used G-200. All ball clay is OM-4 . Many glazes I substituted 75% of the amount of Barium with Strontium. All kaolin is EPK. Remember... glazes don't travel well. Your results will probably be TOTALLY different. Please test before use. Tracy Wilson Saltbox Pottery

recipes.name: Midnight Cobalt Blue

I only tested 31 out of almost 100 I received. I'll continue testing and reporting as the winter DRAGS on. All the glazes were tested on #900 Miller clay which is a toasty ^10 stoneware. One side of the test tile was brushed with a thick coating of Cynthia Bringle's wet/dry white slip. Each glaze was dipped in three thicknesses on a heavily textured tile. All tiles were fired to a (hard)^9 (10 tipping)reduction firing. 1 hr. Body reduction at ^08 and 1 hr. glaze reduction at ^9 then a quick reox. before shutdown. Any time potash or Custer spar is called for, I used G-200. All ball clay is OM-4 . Many glazes I substituted 75% of the amount of Barium with Strontium. All kaolin is EPK. Remember... glazes don't travel well. Your results will probably be TOTALLY different. Please test before use. Tracy Wilson Saltbox Pottery 4 Shaw Rd. recipes.name: Midrange Majolica 2
recipes.description: This recipe was imported from Louis Katz's Hyperglaze database available on his website: http://falcon.tamucc.edu/lkatz/allglazes.txt More information about Louis Katz can be found on his website, http://www.louiskatz.net/ Louis Katz Notes: I am not a safety expert and any information contained in this file about safety should be ignored in favor of advice from experts. All of the materials in all glazes are potentially hazardous. All of these glaze recipes are given without any representation of accuracy or safety. They may work, they may not. They may be safe when fired or they may not. All of the materials used in them have hazards associated with them. You must be have sufficient training in the hazards before you use the the materials. You will have to determine the suitability and safety for your use. Do not assume that a lack of a warning about a material means that it is safe. Cone: 5 - 6 Color: Very Opaque White Testing: Tested Surface texture: Semi-Gloss Firing: Oxidation Glaze type: Ca B Majolica Recipe: Percent Batch Pemco Frit P-54 27.30 2184 Nepheline Syenite 4.10 328 Calcined Kaolin 8.64 691 EPK 10.13 810 Whiting 19.72 1578 Flint 30.11 2409 Totals: 100.00 % 8000 Gm Also add: Zircopax 25.00 2000 Add CMC gum to harden surface Comments: Variation of Mid-range Majolica that replaces Gerstley borate with a frit to eliminate surface blemishes of the overglaze majolica colorants. Ferro Frit 3134 can be substituted for Pemco Frit P-54. Good as a majolica-like opaque white glaze with oxides and stains brushed over it. Very stable - does not run, applies well with a brush or by other methods. Doesn't craze on cone 10 porcelain fired to cone 6 - test on cone 6 body. Tested on Aardvark stoneware clays: (listed best to worst for smooth surface) Porcelain, Hopkins White 60, Joe Soldate 60, Rio Red (the last two may have a fairly gritty surface, even at cone 6). Possible Glaze Flaws: This glaze is fairly powdery without any binder. It will crawl slightly if applied too thickly followed by a wash of color on the raw glaze. YOU MUST add CMC to glaze batch to harden the raw surface of this glaze. Use about one tablespoon of CMC powder (soaked in a pint of hot water overnight) per 3000 gram batch. Colors: Use mason stains mixed 50/50 with Pemco frit P-25 or Ferro Frit 3124, or use 70 stain/30 gerstley borate in a watery mix for colors over glaze or some combination of gerstley borate and frit. Using too much gerstley borate may make the stain change color or become pastel. Purple stains may need to have more flux added up to 3 parts flux to 1 part stain. If you use all frit, add liquid starch or CMC to colors for easier brushing and to minimize smearing before they're fired. A small amount of bentonite may also help to keep the all-frit mixture from settling out. These binders are not as necessary with the gerstley borate. Use these Duncan EZ-stroke transparent underglazes as overglaze wash for color: EZ003, EZ004, EZ007, EZ012, EZ014, EZ019, EZ020, EZ021, EZ024, EZ025, EZ027, EZ028, EZ030, EZ032, EZ161. Almost all the other EZstrokes will work, especially if thinned slightly. The dark blue and the orange EZstrokes will wrinkle and get rough if applied too thickly. Cover coat CC 154 should work as well. Most other Cover Coat colors will work when thinly applied, but may be dry if thick. Try adding a teaspoonful of frit or gerstley borate to a jar of CC underglaze for glossier color. Other color possibilities include washes of the common colorants (mix chrome and rutile 50/50 with gerstley borate or frit). A thin red iron or red earthenware slip or possibly a red terra sigillata on the foot or other exposed clay areas makes a nice contrast if used on a white clay body. Richard Burkett 1991. Other color possibilities: A nice dark blue green with: 2% cobalt carb + 3% chrome oxide + 2% black iron oxide added to the glaze. SDSU 1992

recipes.name: Mn-Cu crystalline 1.1
recipes.description: This is a Mn based crystalline glaze. It is dichroic for me. It does not run at cone 6 with a thin application. It will run with a thick application. My understanding of dichroic effects is that they occur when there are two or more states of a single material in the glass. This is only possible in oxidation firings with self reducing materials; Fe, Cu and Mn. This glaze has plenty of both Cu and Mn. I was aiming to catch either the Cu or the Mn in the act of changing states. I fire using the E-4 schedule in John Britt's mid-range book. That schedule completes at 1,400 F. I cooled quickly from 1,400 F. So once the firing cycle was complete I immediately pulled the peep hole plugs. After about 2 hours the kiln was at 1,000 F. I then used a piece of soft brick to prop the kiln lid open about 2.5 inches. I waited a couple of hours until the kiln hit 500 F then I opened the lid. I pulled the tiles out of the kiln. About 30 minutes later they were cool enough to handle. So from 1,400 F to room temp in about 5 hours. Important to note that I have not yet tried this glaze with a "normal" cool down. I was trying to capture this specific effect and it worked. However, others here on glazy have posted that this effect may be due to crystals rather than multiple states. I am not claiming authority here and I am open to being wrong. This glaze produces a surface completely covered in crystals. So it is possible the crystals are responsible for the dichroic effect. A test with a "normal" cooling cycle would clarify and I will do that at some point. But right now I am going to use it on some work and I know the quick cooling works. :)

recipes.name: Moon-White Glaze
recipes.description: Recipe used in "Preparation of the moon-white glaze by carbothermic reduction of Fe2O3 and SiC", Jianfeng Zhu, Pei Shi∗, Fen Wang, Ting Zhao, School of Materials Science and Engineering, Shaanxi University of Science & Technology, Xi’an 710021, PR China > Conclusions: The moon-white glaze was successfully reproduced with the addition of 0.02wt% SiC under an oxidizing environment. With increasing of the SiC content, C was formed so that Fe2O3 reduced while the rations of Fe2+ to Fe3+ in glazes increased. The SEM microstructure showed that the discrete droplet phase separation structures were developed in glazes and their sizes were less than 100 nm, so the structural color was formed owing to the Rayleigh scattering. A dual coloring changing mechanism with the increasing of the SiC content was in effect for the moon-white glaze, covering the carbothermic reduction and the varying size of phase separa- tion droplets. Note that I didn't go through the trouble of adding the exact materials used in the study. I am uploading those material analyses as an image to this recipe. Note: Not sure about what final cone this glaze test reached. Fired to 1250C and then soaked for 40minutes. I just guessed cone 8.

Pour and/or trail under and over either of the Shinos to produce a variety of colours and effects. When used under Murrow Shino, black shows in the crawl lines. When used under Murrow Smooth Shino, a curdly blue-black colour results.

recipes.name: Murrow Shino
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Hank Murrow Significant Flaw: crawling Notes: Hank Murrow: white where thick; red where thin. Best with early reduction firing with a long concluding period of oxidation, or a soak in oxidation during cooling. Yields a very soft and fat surface with crawling. Crawls more strongly if fired soon after glazing. Note the low (3.3:1) silica to alumina ratio. Cryolite seems to deepen the colour. Perhaps while outgassing, the fluorine content carries iron from the clay to the glaze surface. Low-melt spodumene contributes phosphorus, which (as in Shaner Red) also helps the fire colour. McNamee kaolin is a Georgia clay having a lovely blush of colour in the wood fire, probably because of its iron/titanium content, which is also beneficial in Shinos; Helmer kaolin can be substituted. Notes: Tony Clennell: Shino glazes must be made at least 24 hours before use. Screen them each day before using, this helps get the thickness more even. Thickness has a huge impact on the look of CT glazes. We glaze everything that day, load and candle overnight. Reduction begins at 012 just beginning to tip, then reduction with a climb in temperature ( the oxyprobe is just over 6) a higher reading than 7 is creating smoke but I think is interfering with reduction. We climb to Cone 9 in medium reduction again at around oxyprobe 6- 6.5 and slow the kiln down at cone 9 for an hour soak till 10 is down.

recipes.name: Nati Folk
recipes.description: Receta compartida por Nati Prefumo en el grupo de facebook Aprendiendo entre todos. "Comparto una formula de un esmalte de baja (1040) que realicé. Aqui va en porcentajes. 55 esmalte alcalino (mfa-002 dp colors) 10 cuarzo 10 caolin 10 carbonato de calcio 10 carbonato magnesio 5 feldespato Eso da un 100 + 13 silicato circonio + 2 dioxido titanio + 2 oxido hierro + 2 oxido estaño Es bastante cubritivo, medio cremita con pintitas marrones. La receta la basé en un esmalte que me gustó de clara giorello publicado en glazy. Mas especificamente es el numero 7379 de glazy (Folk Art Guild White, cono 5/6). Lo reformule para baja y segun los materiales de los que yo disponia." ☆Recipe and picture shared by Nati Prefumo in Facebook group "Aprendiendo entre todos". "I share this Low-fire recipe glaze (1040°C): Low fire glaze MFA 002 (Dp Colors/Colorobbia Brasil) 55; quartz 10; kaolin 10, whiting 20, Magnesium Carbonate 10, potash feldspar. +13 zirconium silicate + 2 Titanium dioxide + 2 RIO + 2 Tin. I was trying to replicate a cone 5 glaze published in Glazy by Clara Giorello (Folk Art Guild White, n°7379".

recipes.name: No Run (?) Bronze/gold - v.2
recipes.description: This is based on a glaze by Ruth Gillett This version goes completely off the Stull chart and is clearly overfired in these samples, especially on the porcelain where application may have been too thick. Obviously in this quantity the Mn is an Alkaline Earth flux (RO). See notes from the original by Ruth Gillett (#4576) below. Works well when not applied too thickly. The runs on the original tiles seem to be the result of too thick application more than over firing, but it is very sensitive to the amount of heatwork. Obviously this glaze is only to be used on non-food work. ORIGINAL NOTES FROM RUTH GILLETT RECEIPE NUMBER 4576 I am aiming for a thin glaze that doesn't drip, semi matt and gold / bronze in colour. My theory is that if Manganese really is a weak flux, and in a fake bronze glaze we add 50% or more as a colorant, then we should really consider it one of the ingredients, and make sure the remaining 40-60% combine to an utterly stable base glaze with room for that much additional flux without running off the pot. don't know why the bottom of the bowl is black, is it the alumina? was the glaze too thin there? is this really a cone 9 glaze? is this too much copper at too high a temperature? I am retesting to find out Glazy is including the Manganese as a Alkali metal. if this is calculated as an alkali earth then this has a .22 / .78 Al M to Alk Eth ratio

recipes.name: NR Cone 6 Cobalt Crystalline (CMW variant)
recipes.description: I have a few posts of this glaze on my Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/ebhpottery/?hl=en This is my cone 6 version of the CMW cone 10 cobalt crystalline - This was achieved through a simple boron increase and the rest of the chemistry remains virtually identical. This particular formulation is the mix of frits that I found to behave the most consistently between schedules and bodies. The glaze result is quite application dependent and prefers a thicker application (3 second dip) but can change personalities drastically with minor changes. When testing, I used CMC as a gumming agent though it would be advisable to do some material subbing to get some bentonite in there.

recipes.name: NR Crystal Base - Blank Slate
recipes.description: This is a basic reformulation of one of my cone 6 glazes with some contextualization on how to reduce or virtually eliminate running. Colorant additions are your own choosing, reference pictures will be titled with their respective colorants and amounts (keep in mind colorants impact chemistry and therefore impact melt). There are multiple methods to reduce running in crystalline glazes, this glaze focuses primarily around dialed in application. By adding CMC gum (or any gumming agent) to a glaze, we are able to control the rate at which it is absorbed into the clay body (also the rate it dries). What is important to note here is the glaze stays fluid for quite a while, in dipping applications we are able to use this to a unique advantage. After dipping our pieces, we can dry them upside down from how they are fired - This will allow the glaze to flow down the piece as it dries and create a gradient of application where the greatest loading of glaze remains at the top and the least at the bottom. As the glaze melts, it will flow slightly down the piece but in a controlled manner thanks to the gradient created. Best practices to use/test this glaze: - Use the same firing approach to achieve your target cone every time - Test your clay body at different glaze thicknesses (for dipping: 1,2,3,4,5 second holds) to gauge your absorption - Gumming agents can be annoying to get into solution, use a hand blender to mix the glaze - Organic gumming agents can be targets for bacteria growth in the glaze, use a splash of isopropyl alcohol in your glaze to keep it more shelf stable - As a “just in case” it is beneficial to create your pieces with foot that may collect glaze, it is not necessary but you really need to dial in your application before you can be entirely sure you won’t experience running. https://www.instagram.com/ebhpottery/

recipes.name: NR Crystal Base - Lavender Opal
recipes.description: Back again with another crystalline variant of my base, it is a slight lavender color under some light but is color changing to blue depending on lighting source (neodymium’s dichroic property). Some other results of this glaze and more can be found on my Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/ebhpottery/ UPDATE: If applied thick, the glaze will have a beautiful matte white and gray crystal. UPDATE #2: When applied to a cone 6 porcelain (such as STD 213) the lavender quality of the neodymium will come through much stronger in the background. Additionally the crazing becomes minimal compared to stoneware.

Application can range from thin to thick and will still be a forgiving glaze. As I post more to my Instagram I will showcase this glaze used as a liner interacting with different crystalline glazes here: https://www.instagram.com/ebhpottery/ NOTE: If you do not have access to New Zealand Halloysite, you can directly sub in EPK. recipes.name: OF Strontium sub G200
recipes.description: THIS Glaze was originally developed by JOE THOMPSON. I have included his notes at the bottom of this so that he gets proper credit. You can search for him or OldForge in Glazy. Dude makes some phenomenal oxidation glazes. https://glazy.org/u/2625 ## Here are MY notes I was initially excited about this glaze. But, because Thompson is in the UK there are some differences in materials. I tried his original version with custer, but was really disappointed with the glaze looking kind of anemic and too matte for my taste. So, I tried it with two different base fluxes, imerys g200 and neph sye. Overall I think the neph sye version looks best. But some the g200 version looks better. Probably a mistake but I used grolleg for the g200 base and NZ Kaolin for the neph sye base, and I think that may have affected the runniness of the glaze as well. Photos: Since I did this all in one firing, and basically did two separate batches of glaze with some modifications to balance them out, I shot all the photos together for comparison. It's interesting. So the G200 version is on the LEFT and the Neph Sye version is on the RIGHT. Application & Firing: I did a thick application of glaze on each tile. Each tile is made of Coleman, a high grolleg porcelain that is usually cone 10 but, for testing its fine. Its what I had. I bisque to cone 012, not cone 04 like many do here in USA. I tested colorants, mason stains, and an encapsulation stain I had just cuz I was curious. :/ I suspect application and firing cycle would also affect drippiness as well. Since these were fired in a test kiln, firing in a larger electric with a hold / cool would probably make some of them run like hell. As always, test before. These were fast fired in a tiny test kiln, oxidation, in Minneapolis at Northern Clay Center in September 2019. Please contact me here or on IG @redneckpaycheck any time with questions. ## Here are JOES notes Glaze developed on the Ceramic Materials Workshop Understanding Glazes course - https://www.ceramicmaterialsworkshop.com/about-glaze-calculation-online.html Before taking the course I'd only encountered Strontium in matte glazes that behaved oddly, so I thought there was something about Strontium that caused the matteness and weirdness. During the course I learnt that wasn't true, and during the Labs I developed this gloss base with Strontium as the AE flux. Without the Rutile it's a fairly boring clear gloss. With the rutile and most other colourants it becomes something far more interesting. All tests shown include the rutile along with the named colourants. Glaze edited on 22nd June to swap the generic Potash for Custer. The potash formula on here is different enough to change the calculation, and my potash is closer to custer than the potash on here.

Probably a mistake but I used grolleg for the g200 base and NZ Kaolin for the neph sye base, and I think that may have affected the runniness of the glaze as well. Photos: Since I did this all in one firing, and basically did two separate batches of glaze with some modifications to balance them out, I shot all the photos together for comparison. It's interesting. So the G200 version is on the LEFT and the Neph Sye version is on the RIGHT. Application & Firing: I did a thick application of glaze on each tile. Each tile is made of Coleman, a high grolleg porcelain that is usually cone 10 but, for testing its fine. Its what I had. I bisque to cone 012, not cone 04 like many do here in USA. I tested colorants, mason stains, and an encapsulation stain I had just cuz I was curious. :/ I suspect application and firing cycle would also affect drippiness as well. Since these were fired in a test kiln, firing in a larger electric with a hold / cool would probably make some of them run like hell. As always, test before. These were fast fired in a tiny test kiln, oxidation, in Minneapolis at Northern Clay Center in September 2019. Please contact me here or on IG @redneckpaycheck any time with questions. Here are JOES notes Glaze developed on the Ceramic Materials Workshop Understanding Glazes course - https://www.ceramicmaterialsworkshop.com/about-glaze-calculation-online.html Before taking the course I'd only encountered Strontium in matte glazes that behaved oddly, so I thought there was something about Strontium that caused the matteness and weirdness. During the course I learnt that wasn't true, and during the Labs I developed this gloss base with Strontium as the AE flux. Without the Rutile it's a fairly boring clear gloss. With the rutile and most other colourants it becomes something far more interesting. All tests shown include the rutile along with the named colourants. Glaze edited on 22nd June to swap the generic Potash for Custer. The potash formula on here is different enough to change the calculation, and my potash is closer to custer than the potash on here.

recipes.description: Glaze developed on the Ceramic Materials Workshop Understanding Glazes course - https://www.ceramicmaterialsworkshop.com/about-glaze-calculation-online.html Before taking the course I'd only encountered Strontium in matte glazes that behaved oddly, so I thought there was something about Strontium that caused the matteness and weirdness. During the course I learnt that wasn't true, and during the Labs I developed this gloss base with Strontium as the AE flux. Without the Rutile it's a fairly boring clear gloss. With the rutile and most other colourants it becomes something far more interesting. All tests shown include the rutile along with the named colourants. Glaze edited on 22nd June to swap the generic Potash for Custer. The potash formula on here is different enough to change the calculation, and my potash is closer to custer than the potash on here.

recipes.description: Glaze Type: High-fire Gray green = + 1% copper oxide Date: Wed, 9 Aug 2000 From: Sheron Roberts Subject: Re: opalescence The following is a glaze I tried from the Tony Birk book, The Complete Potter's Companion, revised edition. Fired to cone 10, oxidation it produced an interesting opal like surface. On the inside of the bowls, where the glaze was thickest, the color was like mother of pearl, very pretty. I would suggest testing first though. "Clear" Feldspathic 2280F/ 1250C "This glaze is translucent rather than transparent, with the characteristic "milk and water" look of a feldspathic glaze. When it is thick, it has fine bubbles trapped in the glaze which give give sparkle, and it combines well with copper oxide (1%) to make gray green - a celedon without reduction." The above is straight from the book, I have not tried the copper oxide addition, yet. Sheron in NC

recipes.name: Orange Red
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Iron saturate rio 11-17% source: Michael Bailey, Glazes Cone 6 This is a "kaki" (plum) saturated iron red. It can be a brilliant red-orange with just the right amount of iron. It does better if you do a controlled cooling as it is a crystalline glaze and needs the slow cool for the crystals to grow (fast cool will yield a chocolate brown gloss).You have to do a line blend on this one to get it right as iron oxides are never the same. I use Spanish red iron oxide. Generally increments of 1% RIO will be fine. But, you really need to do the line blend to get the best red and to fully appreciate the range of colors in that small range of RIO additions. From Bill Buckner

recipes.name: Orange Red
recipes.description: Mismo análisis que Aventurine C6 OR1, Van Gilder' Red, Bailey Red... A cono 6, ox y retención en bajada a 960°C, sólido rojo naranjoso flotando sobre marrón opaco oscuro. Formación de cristales, más notorio sobre pasta blanca. A cono 5, en reducción, con mis materiales, forma cristales claros flotando sobre fondo oscuro. No hay naranja, ni rojo, ni aventurina. Ciertamente faltó temperatura, pero es muy bonito igual Same chemistry as Aventurine C6 OR1, Van Gilder' Red, Bailey Red... At cone 6, ox, controlled cooling cycle with a hold at 960°C, and the right thickness, orange/red crystals over a dark brown background. Better crystals on white clay. At cone 5, reduction, with my raw materials, I got light crystals floating on a shiny dark, almost black, background. No orange, red or aventurine. Needs more temperature, but really nice anyway. Nota que acompaña el esmalte original Original notes in Glazy: Glaze Type: Iron saturate rio 11-17% source: Michael Bailey, Glazes Cone 6 This is a "kaki" (plum) saturated iron red. It does better if you do a controlled cooling as it is a crystalline glaze and needs the slow cool for the crystals to grow (fast cool will yield a chocolate brown gloss).You have to do a line blend on this one to get it right as iron oxides are never the same. I use Spanish red iron oxide. Generally increments of 1% RIO will be fine. recipes.name: Oribe Green Sugar Maples
recipes.description: "I have introduced a cooling cycle to the firing. The cycle is as follows and the firing is accompanied by a Cone 6 witness cone. After 12 consecutive firings, the witness cones are identical from firing to firing." The firing cycle: Rate Temp Hold Time rA1= 360 F1 = 900 0 rA2= 300 F2 = 1800 0 rA3 =200 F3 = 2016 0 rA4 = 108 F4 = 2197 0.3 rA5 = Full F5 =1800 0 rA6 =150 F6 = 1300 0 rA7 = 0000 To summarize, I fire at a rate of 360/hr to 900 degrees F, then at 300 degrees/ hr to 1800 degrees F, 200 degrees/hr until 2016 degrees F is reached, then 108 degrees/hour to 2197 at which time I hold it at that temperature for 30 minutes. The kiln is shut off until a temperature of 1800 degrees F is reached and then turned on to slow the rate of cooling to 150 degrees/hr until 1300 degrees F is reached. At this point the kiln is turned off and cools naturally. Western Pennsylvania Potters Community http://wpapotters.blogspot.com/2012/04/links-to-cone-6-oxidation-glaze-tests.html http://www.wpapotters.blogspot.com/2011/10/cone-6-oxidation-results-group-7.html

recipes.name: Oribe v3
recipes.description: I love Oribes. They are by far my favorite glaze. This is the third iteration of my Oribe. This one is done after completing Ceramic Materials Workshop's Advancing Glazes course. It is an improvement over the other two versions. This glaze is right on the edge of running but doesn't. It does have plenty of crystals. I recently found out that this does NOT produce crystals unless slow cooled. Firing schedule: 250->1950 F 108->2232 F hold 20 minutes 9999->2050 F 50->1400 F Application is important. I have found that the crystals only happen with a fairly thick application. If the application is too thin, no crystals. Too thick and it will run. So you have may need to play with the application to get it right. I bisque to cone 08. I mix with 75:100 water to dry ingredients. So 100 gram batch gets 75 grams of water. I dip everything. The test tile pictured is a 3 second dip.

recipes.name: Overberg Oilspot
recipes.description: A work in progress. Spots are matte grey on a shiny dark red-brown backround that can appear black, although there are small areas where the background goes clear. Not sure what causes the spots. Very sensitive to balance of MgO and CaO. Replacing CaO with MgO results in a matte, blistered surface with faint spots, while replacing MgO with CaO causes the spots to disappear. Fired in an electric kiln to 1132C, with progressively slower rate of temperture rise, then cooled at 4C / min. Original version had SRE instead of Overberg EW. Tried RIO additions of 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14%

The size of the spots depends on the thickness, and with this much clay, crawling can be a problem if the glaze coat is thick. A reformulation with less clay and a different Talc can be found here.

recipes.name: Overberg Oilspot 2 (reformulation 3, -MgO, +CaO)

recipes.name: Pablo Red
recipes.description: Notes: Rod Wuetherick: Copper red glazes are by nature finicky. The nicest copper reds have very low amounts of copper in them, usually less than 1% added to the batch. Tin will help stabilize the copper a bit, but this is not a silver bullet by any means. If you start going over 1% the copper reds are livery in appearance and not personally my favourite but some like it. Copper reds are really all about the firing process, moderate reduction not heavy; 5.5 - 6.0 on the oxy-probe. I have found the zinc to be useless and think it is an old school glaze addition in reduction firings. According to most sources it just volatizes, and how much it takes part in the melt is of constant debate. I can tell you from my experience that I have never noticed a difference in high fire reduction glazes if you leave out the zinc. Fire almost as fast as you can, extended firings tend to show your copper where the stack is and it finds its way up there without further encouragement.

recipes.name: PB Celadon (ZC)
recipes.description: This test used SiO-2 PRAI white grogged stoneware clay, raw glazed and fired once in oxidation Δ8. The glaze was mixed fairly thick using several drops of Darvan 7 to improve flow, and leather hard and bone dry test cylinders were dipped for 3 seconds. The published recipe calls for China Clay, but to achieve adhesion on leather hard greenware, EPK was substituted. Greenware can be glazed either leather hard or bone dry, and raw glazing benefits from using less water in the glaze. If the glaze does not shrink as much as leather hard greenware, it can peel off during drying, which can be remedied using/substituting plasticizers such as Bentonite, VeeGum, Ball Clay, etc. Bone dry greenware raw glazes with good adhesion, and clay bodies containing plastic clays can usually handle the water from the glaze. Each clay body & glaze combination should be tested in the intended size of the work. More resources are listed in Posts—Education—Resources for Raw Glazing and Single Firing.

recipes.name: PD393.2
recipes.description: I've been exploring Mn glazes. This one is based on phase diagram of Mn-Al-Si. In the center of the phase diagram are a couple of unique crystals. Phase diagrams use weight not molecular weight. So that translation from phase diagram to glaze recipe is a bit of guess work, at least for me. As there are three unique crystals possible I will continue to tweak this base to see if I can coax out all three. I really like this glaze. It is completely melted at cone 6 but does not run. It checks all the boxes for a durable glaze; 3:7 flux ratio, good boron level (extended UMF because of the presence of large amount of Mn), glossy Si:Al ratio, 8.76 and it is glossy. I use equal parts water to dry glaze by weight. So 100 gram batch gets 100 grams of water. I bisque fire to cone 08. All my test tiles are single dip. Shout out to Matt Katz and Ceramic Materials Workshop. Not only did I learn how to formulate this glaze in the CMW courses but Matt recommended the text book that has the all the phase diagrams; Phase Diagrams for Ceramists by Levin McMurdie and Hall.

recipes.name: Pegamento para pastas de gres
recipes.description: El vinagre común se usa como aditivo en pastas cerámicas para reparar roturas de piezas crudas a baja temperatura. Se elabora mezclando arcilla seca de la misma pieza con vinagre, una mezcla que sirve como adhesivo e incluso como relleno de piezas rotas o con grietas. Siempre me llamó la atención el hecho de que el vinagre no surtiera el mismo efecto en las pastas de gres. Hasta que me di cuenta de que en estas últimas, falta un elemento presente en las pastas de baja: el carbonato de calcio. Al entrar en contacto con el ácido del vinagre, este burbujea y se descompone, desprende CO2, y queda presente la cal (CaO). Este es el elemento que actúa como "liga" al unir las pastas de baja, de manera similar a como lo hace en un revoque fino de albañilería. En contacto con el aire la cal se "carbonata" nuevamente, endureciendo el revoque. Basándome en esto, preparé una mezcla similar a la de la pasta de gres que usamos en el taller, pero sustituyendo el cuarzo y la dolomita por carbonato de calcio, como se ve en la receta. La cabrita de la foto tenía quebrado un cuerno en tres partes, para pegarla preparé un poco de la barbotina mezclada y vinagre, que apliqué con un pincel a las partes a pegar y ¡voilá! el invento funcionó. Soportó bien el secado y posterior cocción de la pieza. No se puede guardar la barbotina húmeda porque el calcio se volvería a "carbonatar", perdiendo la capacidad de adherir las partes. No creo que sirva para reparar grietas grandes ni partes de piezas, solo como un pegamento. Esta receta solo sirve para la pasta que estoy usando (gres de media, cono 4). Para pastas más claras o de otra temperatura, seria necesario probar incluyendo el carbonato de calcio como hice en este caso.
