recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Peter Pinnell Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 800C hold 1 hour Notes: Alisa Clausen: used Johnson Matthey J frit instead of 3134, kaolin instead of china clay. Applied thick. A mat glaze that is well melted and very smooth surface. The colour is a strong aqua green. The glaze is well covering and has a slight sheen, although mat. Where it is thicker, has more sheen than where thinner, but green in both areas. Has a lush and thick look overall. Tested same glaze with ball clay instead of kaolin. Resulted in a very similar glaze, but is slightly darker in overall colour. It is not as uniform in colour or as bright as the recipe with kaolin. It has an appearance that the aqua colour is higher surface, over a darker ground. With kaolin the glaze has an even colour, with ball clay, there is more colour play on the surface. Variation on Pete Pinnell's Weathered Bronze w/o lithium. See Clay Times article p.19 Mar/Apr. 2004. More of a satin-matt. Breaks white/light green. A better-behaved raw glaze w/o lithium.

recipes.name: Pink Powder Box
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Mid-fire (Mimi Obstler's Out of the Earth Into the Fire p147) Here's the recipe, fired to about cone 5.4 or 6.2 (depending on which cone you want to read). Or fired to 1200C at 50C/hr. I added 1% TiO2 which gives a nice blush of crystalline effects, without the yellowish orange you get from rutile. Where this glaze is thicker though and right together with the crystals/bubbles, there's a foamy texture inside the glaze. I can tell because I fire on stilts and when the stilts come off, a little circular crust of glass stays on the stilt pin and the interior of the glaze where the stilt pulled off the surface looks like froth. Foam. (P.S. is this behavior an indicator of a fit problem?) So the glaze goes onto greenware and gets put in the kiln on stilts. Fired. Tons of what I thought were crystals but maybe they really are bubbles, as revealed by the froth. The presence of some sharp-edged pinholes argues that my crystals are bubbles maybe. Conventional wisdom I: soak more or cool more slowly. Done that I: Goes up to temp at 60C/hr, soaks 25 minutes, cools at 150C/hr to 900, then at 60C/hr to 700. If it gets any slower than that, won't I be a laughing stock? Conventional wisdom II: try refiring to convince yourself that it needs to soak some more. Done that II: Refired a set of pieces. Foam is still there. Some of the sharp edged pinholes have closed up. I have used this same recipe with 8% rutile (lovely effect by the way if your rutile is finely enough ground). It doesn't exhibit the same problem as far as I can see. A few pinholes where quite thick but nothing like this. So. Is this because titanium actually makes a glaze more refractory? I'm kinda puzzled about calculating how to make something melt more smoothly. Especially since it already seems totally loaded up with melter, all that boron. Thanks for any pointers to enlightenment Jan Walker Cambridge MA USA

recipes.name: Pinnel Celadon
recipes.description: Pinnel Celadon, a blue celadon taken from John Britt's cone 10 glaze book, page 68. Glossy and wonderfully stiff. I'm including a "failed" test to make a lime-colored celadon using this recipe as a base, and I'm including the colorants I used in the description of the photograph. One thing I've experienced about blue glazes is that the amount of iron in the recipe always seems a little too low. I ran this test with 0.25% more iron and got better results than my friend who tested the same glaze out, but followed the directions verbatim. Perhaps iron oxide here is a little weaker? This recipe starts with 0.5% yellow iron oxide. I increased it to 0.75%. I'm sure one could conceivably increase it all the way to 1%, and still get a nice swimming pool blue-green, but with much more intensity than a more pure light blue.

recipes.name: Pinnell Blue Celadon (NZK & Wollastonite)
recipes.description: This is an adjustment of Pete Pinnell's Blue Celadon glaze as found in John Britt's The Complete Guide to High-Fire Glazes. I have replaced Grolleg Kaolin with New Zealand Halloysite and Whiting with Wollastonite, trying to stay as close to the original recipe's UMF as possible. This Wollastonite version has a much finer matrix of small bubbles than the Whiting version. Furthermore, although the two recipes have approximately the same amount of silica, the Wollastonite version has better color, perhaps because part of the silica is supplied by Wollastonite.

recipes.name: Pinnell Green Black
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Clay Times Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 800C hold 1 hour Notes: Alisa Clausen: used Johnson Matthey J frit instead of 3134, local kaolin instead of Grolleg. Applied thick. A semi mat with movement in the surface. The glaze looks similar to the original Weathered Bronze where thinnest, but with a better melt and therefore slightly more gloss. However, where thickest, this is the brightest of greens of all of the Pinnell new formulations of Weathered Bronze. It is a strong aqua to grass green, with movement in the surface, showing some minute whitish streaking. It is black and green where thinnest. John Hesselberth has tested this glaze for copper leaching and recommends this glaze for decorative use only. 3% copper + 5 % Ti = more green 5% copper + 5% Ti = more black Variation on Pete Pinnell's Weathered Bronze. Black crystals, breaks black over edges and texture. A bit more matte. See Clay Times Mar/Apr. 2004 for article p.19.

recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Clay Times, March/April, 2004 Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 800C hold 1 hour Notes: Alisa Clausen: used Johnson Matthey J frit instead of 3134, local kaolin instead of Grolleg. Applied thick. With 3% copper carbonate: a mat glaze with a dry but well melted surface. Colour is green to grey where thickest brown where thinner. Resembles the original Weathered Bronze, but greyer overall. There are green flecks that break through the surface of the glaze. 4% copper: Much greener overall with many green flecks joining over a grayish ground surface colour. Small crystals are more obvious on surface and has a slightly lichen effect in some areas where thicker. 5% copper: The green specs are brighter. Therefore there is a stronger contrast between them and the grey ground. The ground is browner where thinner, but the green is as strong.

recipes.name: PMSP 4 Base
recipes.description: Chemical Analysis Na2O 0.18 Al2O3 0.35 SiO2 3.26 K2O 0.01 B2O3 0.27 MgO 0.02 CaO 0.79 Alumina:Silica ratio is 1.00 : 9.41 Neutral:Acid ratio is 1.00 : 5.30 Alkali:Neutral:Acid ratio is 1.00 : 0.62 : 3.26 Expansion coefficient: 68.0 x 10e-7 per degree C Oxides causing abnormal expansion effects: B2O3 The question that I have for Ron is about the expansion of the glazes listed below. A while back you told me that the expansion for the PMSP-4 glaze was a little low. You sent me a revised version which had a slightly higher expansion. I then looked at Tony Hansen's 5-20 glaze and found it to be pretty close to my PMSP-4. What range do you think the expansion should be in for a cone 6 oxidation glaze? PMSP-4 Expansion coefficient: 68.0 x 10e-7 per degree C Ron Roy's version of PMSP-4 Expansion coefficient: 71.1 x 10e-7 per degree C Tony Hansen's 5-20's glaze Expansion coefficient: 69.2 x 10e-7 per degree C In terms of my experience firing these glazes, I have found the PMSP to be water clear. Your revision to be mostly clear with bubbles only in areas of relief where the glaze has pooled. The 5-20's glaze for me was cloudy. I'm wondering if Ron Wright is getting more bubbles because he is trying to get a THICK clear? My clear gets a 4 second dip and I can't find any bubbles in it under a 1.5x magnifying glass. For anyone following this thread, all of the above glazes are given below. All are cone 6 oxidation. My firing takes about 8-9 hours to bend a large cone 6 and then I soak the kiln for another half hour to hour until cone 7 is at 2 o'clock. I then turn all of the switches to medium for 3 hours before shutting it off. The correct formula for Post's PMSP-4 is this one. The one posted on the database is incorrect. John Post Sterling Heights, Michigan

recipes.name: Purple Emily's
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Magnesium matt This is a very reliable glaze. The surface is very smooth to the touch. It would be a good glaze for color variations. We have done a small amount of testing with mason stain additions and it seems to respond well to most colors, particularly the yellow. How long have you been using this glaze? In a college studio setting for about a year. Where is it used? Anne Arundel Community College Where did this recipe come from? I have two versions of this glaze. This is the best and I am not sure if it came from the Penland Pottery book or not. I don't know the source of the other one. What do you like most about this glaze? The reliability and the feel. Is this glaze reliable? Yes, very. Does this glaze tend to craze/crawl/pinhole/etc.? We have had some crawling when it is applied thickly or overlapped heavily with other glazes. Controlling the thickness is essential. How do different firing temperatures/atmospheres affect the glaze? It seems to stand up well to temperature variations. When it is hotter it will tend to go more translucent. How does the glaze behave on different clay bodies? The color is pretty powerful. Over a stoneware body in reduction it will go a bit darker, and it will be brighter and bluer over a white body. What consistency should the glaze be for pouring/dipping? A cream consistency, so that you can see the cutile of your fingers when a hand is dipped in the glaze. How thickly should the glaze be applied to the pot? Medium, a full 3 second dip is adequate. How does this glaze interact with other glazes? It breaks up nicely and goes to a navy blue when used with our clear glaze. What is your kiln type and size? Most of our work with it has been in an Alpine 20 natural gas kiln. We have also used it in a 23" dia. L&L econo kiln. The colors in oxidation are a bit lighter, and the surface is not as smooth. How do you typically fire? The gas schedule is just 7.5 to 8 hours to reach cone 6. We fire between cone 6 and 7. Reduction starts at cone 010, and continues to cone 6, with the dampers being opened gradually as the firing gets closer to completion, but we maintain reduction to the end. No soak. We close the dampers but don't close the burner ports. We open the kiln 36 hours later. It is usually still pretty warm a the top. What is your water pH? very close to 7 GlazeBase Glaze Submitted by: Rick Malmgren Ice Cream Flavor: Bryer's Mint Chocolate Chip -------------------------------------------------------------------- ----

recipes.name: PV #7 satin clear 2
recipes.description: Dec 2022 revised 218310 recipe since 3134 Frit and Whiting were not locally available for production size batch. This change plus using Tony Hanson’s PLC6DS glaze firing schedule with a 20 min. hold produced a better SATIN finish. It also eliminated minute pinholes. White, green and light blue also were better. (1/7/23 test tiles vs. 8/18/22 tiles.) Satin cone 6 glaze derived from Bill Carty's glaze workshop at Peter's Valley in 2021. Based successful work by another group in the class, I chose test tile #7 from 5x5 initial matrix of 0.3 Boron glazes. Follow up testing at home on current clay bodies (Standard's 181, 182 w grog and 306, and Laguna's BMix 5) proved it the most versatile when compared to H++ and Rob's clear (Glazy #35497). Both H++ and Rob's clear crazed on 182 w grog and were GLOSSY clear glazes.

Glaze was silky smooth SATIN. See for new formulation & pics Glazy 291711. /21/22: worked well on white clay bodies; however was a bit too glossy. On Std 308 it had pinholes. Will bisque to ^04 and glaze fire with Hansen's PLC6DS. Clear satin cone 6 glaze derived from Bill Carty's glaze workshop at Peter's Valley in 2021. After assessing classes 4 days of testing, I chose test tile #7 from 5x5 initial matrix of 0.3 Boron glazes. Follow up testing at home on current clay bodies (Standard's 181, 182 w grog and 308, and Laguna's BMix 5) proved it the most versatile when compared to H++ and Rob's clear (Glazy #35497). recipes.description: Dec 2022 revised 218310 recipe since 3134 Frit and Whiting were not locally available for production size batch. This change plus using Tony Hanson’s PLC6DS glaze firing schedule with a 20 min. hold produced a better SATIN finish. It also eliminated minute pinholes. White, green and light blue also were better. (1/7/23 test tiles vs. 8/18/22 tiles.) Satin cone 6 glaze derived from Bill Carty's glaze workshop at Peter's Valley in 2021. Based successful work by another group in the class, I chose test tile #7 from 5x5 initial matrix of 0.3 Boron glazes. Follow up testing at home on current clay bodies (Standard's 181, 182 w grog and 306, and Laguna's BMix 5) proved it the most versatile when compared to H++ and Rob's clear (Glazy #35497). Both H++ and Rob's clear crazed on 182 w grog and were GLOSSY clear glazes.

recipes.name: R3517 Shino
recipes.description: From Steve Davis Website & Blog: http://kazegama.com/ Website: http://kazegamas.com/ Shinos 3: http://kazegamas.com/shinos3.htm Alumina is A12 Calcined Alumina Ferro 3110 sub for F-493 There are 72 shinos shown on 4 web pages. They are organized from left to right with 3 tiles of the same glaze shown on 3 different clay bodies. They are Aardvark Clay's Nara Porcelain, Long Beach, and Black Mountain. Every shino was glazed with a doulble dip, waxed with a simple "S" pattern, and left to dry for 2 weeks to grow sulfates on the surface. The "S" pattern has no sulfate build up. A medium reduction was started at cone 012 through cone 2. From there the kiln was fired in neutral to cone 10.

recipes.name: Raku - Adjusted Copper 80/20 #3 - Tom Buck-Digitalfire
recipes.description: -Tom Buck: Fresh-mix the glaze before use. As revised, is easy to use since it has an adequately broad melting range and doesn't run so over-firing is not a problem. Also, reduction can be heavy and lengthy and still yield a bright copper metal finish. -I found it simple to apply a thin coat. Fired and responded to reduction as expected. Great on texture!

recipes.name: Raku - Dewitt's Plate Tectonic
recipes.description: -Dewitt: "This is a super-duper awesome, yummy glaze! It is a bit crusty and then when you get the firing just hot enough (cone 04+) it begins to glassify while other bits of it float on the surface, much like oceanic plates in the magmatic (stet) melt. Sometimes I layer a coat of copper carb. on top before I fire it to give it a metallic/bronzy finish (05)." -Bowl and vase from 2 separate firings. SG: 1.63. Both to 1825 deg. F. Bowl had longer fire time and tighter reduction. Varies from a gorgeous aged, patinized bronze to multi earth-toned patches of colour. So cool!

recipes.name: Raku - Ferguson's White Crackle
recipes.description: Coastal Claymakers: "Allow to rest for 1 min after removing from kiln. When it "pings" put into reduction chamber, cover with paper and allow to flame then close cover. leave for 3 min then "burp" to allow paper to reignite. Close lid and let cool naturally." -regular smaller crackle effect, stays whiter than other tested crackle whites.

recipes.name: Raku - Gold
recipes.description: very reliable amber-gold colour. nice transparency with crackles. first firing: 1825 F. - colour improved and deepened in 2nd test by giving thicker coat and firing lower to 1725 F.

recipes.name: Raku - Hollingsworth's Hawaiian Copper Blue
recipes.description: -The first photo shows a single thin coat. A beautiful sandy texture that sparkles in the light. Also 1.8% tin oxide instead of 1.5%. Will post a test piece with the CAD formula to compare...

recipes.name: Raku - Kelly's Low-Fire Shino

Glossy with some silvery opalescent luster.

recipes.name: Raku -Crusty Rusty

recipes.name: Raku -Dewitt's Craters

recipes.name: Raku -Fatty White Crackle

recipes.name: Ravenscrag Gloop tests
recipes.description: Here is a simple starting point using a single material for anyone wanting to explore clay/glaze "gloop" effects. Ravenscrag Slip used alone at cone 6 will drip down the walls of a piece and stretch across spaces without pulling apart. Alone it is a thixotropic clay-like material (used as a major component of slip glazes at cone 6 and up). With additions of ball clay and a little epsom salts in the water to counteract its tendency to delocculation it can be shaped - coiled, pinched, rolled, etc., into various forms. The ball clay stops it from "glooping" but small additions of wollastonite bring it back (additions of frit 3124 will do the same but I think the wollastonite makes it a more viscous melt). Here are some tests using: 100g Ravenscrag Slip 20g OM#4 ball clay 5-25g Wollastonite increasing by 5g increments from left to right and a pure Ravenscrag test at the far right. All tests have 2g mazerine blue stain added. The beige button is pure Ravenscrag, no stain. Traces of an "R" scratched into the button at leatherhard remain visible. Ravenscrag is a product of Plainsman Clays, Medicine Hat, Alberta and was developed by Tony Hansen, I believe. I have no idea if this product is available outside N. America so might not be of use to everybody. Ravenscrag.com

Se usa sobre otros esmaltes, haciéndolos "correr" y muchas veces cambiando las tonalidades de color. recipes.name: Reader's Digest ^6 Red Glaze
recipes.description: https://books.google.com/books?id=WnL6RWTLOcQC&printsec=frontcover#v=onepage&q&f=false Known as Toby's/Randy's/Ketchup Red When Nytal talc was taken off the market this glaze changed dramatically. Nothing I did could get it to be anything but a flat and ugly brown. Slow cooling and or a soak works for some. It did not for me. I added 2% bone ash and that fixed the problem but changed the glaze. It became more fluid, glossy and variable in color. Dick White has reformulated the glaze to use bone ash and that may be closer to the original. I like it in the new form so have not tried the reformulated version. With a rutile wash over it, it turns a beautiful gold. As a base glaze (minus the RIO) it has been used in other glazes. These glazes probably can do without the bone ash. Mystery Blue 1% cobalt carbonate 3% rutile Periwinkle 1-3% cobalt carbonate Annie's Tan 16% RIO 6% rutile 2.5% manganese dioxide Green 1-3% copper carbonate

recipes.name: Reading Error Shino
recipes.description: A shino recipe we've had at the Dunedin School of Art for some time, though it was titled "RJ Shino". I didn't understand why it didn't match the traditional recipe for RJ Dry Shino (and why the fired results didn't look like it either). However, I discovered at some point down the line someone had accidentally written 29% soda ash instead of 2.9% soda ash! So I renamed it Reading Error Shino :) It goes a beautiful lustrous orange red and gold in reduction. Also due to its very high soda ash quantity, when a glazed pot is left to dry it will carbon trap quite easily.

recipes.description: For red/purple test A: https://glazy.org/recipes/30381 B: https://glazy.org/recipes/30379 C: https://glazy.org/recipes/30377 D: https://glazy.org/recipes/30378 Used 1000 mesh SiC.

recipes.name: Red corner B
recipes.description: For red/purple test A: https://glazy.org/recipes/30381 B: https://glazy.org/recipes/30379 C: https://glazy.org/recipes/30377 D: https://glazy.org/recipes/30378 Used 1000 mesh SiC.

recipes.name: Red corner C
recipes.description: For red/purple test A: https://glazy.org/recipes/30381 high silica B: https://glazy.org/recipes/30379 high silica and alumina C: https://glazy.org/recipes/30377 base D: https://glazy.org/recipes/30378 high alumina tiles are arranged as A B C D Some notes: SiC copper reds have a way of not coming out. Ever since I found out that they existed, I tried the few recipes that floated around (that was pre John Britt's cone 6 book). They all came out wildly different from what I had expected. This is not 'a recipe'. This is a way for you to find your own glaze. If your glaze doesn't come out, this test or one like it will probably give you a heads up as to what went wrong and how to fix it. Pay special attention to the relationship between the melt fluidity and transparency of the clear and celadon stages of this glaze (pics at the end), and the resulting effect when you add in the copper. The red forms in a small area of the biaxial. Too fluid and none forms (may be related to a wrong particle size of elemental copper in the melt ). Where the base becomes opaque from silica, none forms. Around that area, where the base is opalescent, purples form, and the glaze becomes very sensitive to the clay body it's on. The cleanest reds seem to form where the clearest clears form. In passing, some of the clear glazes ( and fewer of the iron glazes) are very nice as reduction clears/light celadons/qing bai glazes. More insight - a bit of magnesium will stiffen up the glaze a bit and can be helpful in getting the glaze to stay on vertical surfaces. Lithium and Barium will cause glazes which are otherwise opalescent not to be, so purples will be lost and turn into reds. Reds will turn dark, I suspect from carbon trapping. Refiring to bisque temperature will cause carbon trapping as will covering with a clear glaze. This is very different from atmospheric reduction because the reduction agent is inside the glaze. I use 1000 mesh SiC but 600 and up will probably work, maybe you'll have to use a bit more or a bit less. You should sieve them a lot to disperse the SiC. The glaze should be in very good suspension for the SiC to stay dispersed. If the slurry settles two seconds after you stir it, or if it keeps spinning for 15 seconds after you stop stirring, or if it looks like it's not spinning 'in one piece' when you stir it, it's not flocculated enough and will not give a red or a celadon. And may form ugly patches of carbon trapping from areas where there's too much SiC. The corner recipes are all linked but only one of them has all the pics. A related and previous test showing the effects of magnesium (stiffening) and silica (the same as here), https://glazy.org/recipes/27988, An actual recipe that I've actually mixed a kg of and actually used on actual pots: https://glazy.org/recipes/31772 Used 1000 mesh SiC.

recipes.name: Red Lustre Buck #7
recipes.description: Use Borax Decahydrate. Here, designed by me, are two copper red matt lustres. This one is for fresh mix daily, or dry mix and wet only what you can use in a day. The borax is washing machine borax. Pemco frit 830 or Hommel frit K3 will work also. Use a few drops of detergent to disperse colorant oxides. The above glaze is quite fluid at C07/06 and needs to be heavily reduced. Move from kiln to reduction medium as quickly as possible and leave 20 minutes or so. It produces brillant reds with some blue flashes. High gloss finish most of the time. There you go. I have used these glazes with good results. recipes.name: Red Oilspot
recipes.description: A cone 6 Oilspot based off of CeramicMaterialsWorkshop.com (A.K.A Matt and Rose Katz... go take the classes!) Cone 10 Oilspot formulations and a bunch of cone 10 Oilspot tests by TC Staton. I just added boron to their cone 10 Oilspot formula and then shifted it around on stulls map until it worked out the best for me at cone 6. Glaze application thickness is important... do some application thickness tests when first trying this glaze out. It needs to be thick enough that the glaze will produce the Oilspot bubbles... but also thin enough that all the bubbles will heal over by the end of the firing. I scaled out a 75g batch and mixed it with 50 mils water.

recipes.name: Red Orange
recipes.description: "I have introduced a cooling cycle to the firing. The cycle is as follows and the firing is accompanied by a Cone 6 witness cone. After 12 consecutive firings, the witness cones are identical from firing to firing." The firing cycle: Rate Temp Hold Time rA1= 360 F1 = 900 0 rA2= 300 F2 = 1800 0 rA3 =200 F3 = 2016 0 rA4 = 108 F4 = 2197 0.3 rA5 = Full F5 =1800 0 rA6 =150 F6 = 1300 0 rA7 = 0000 To summarize, I fire at a rate of 360/hr to 900 degrees F, then at 300 degrees/ hr to 1800 degrees F, 200 degrees/hr until 2016 degrees F is reached, then 108 degrees/hour to 2197 at which time I hold it at that temperature for 30 minutes. The kiln is shut off until a temperature of 1800 degrees F is reached and then turned on to slow the rate of cooling to 150 degrees/hr until 1300 degrees F is reached. At this point the kiln is turned off and cools naturally. Western Pennsylvania Potters Community http://wpapotters.blogspot.com/2012/04/links-to-cone-6-oxidation-glaze-tests.html http://www.wpapotters.blogspot.com/2011/10/cone-6-oxidation-results-group-8.html

recipes.name: Red Towy
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Iron saturate I've spent the last 3 years working on cone 5 iron red glazes, starting with Randy's Red, and I've found some things that work to make it redder. I started by taking each ingredient, cutting it down, and gradually adding it back till I had double the amount in the recipe. I found some adjustments that work. Then I researched adding other ingredients in various amounts, and found a couple that seem to help. My new recipe I call Towy Red, after my dog. He's a Welsh Springer Spaniel, and has spots this color. He's named after the River Towy in Wales (rhymes with Howie). Then I tried different irons. I tried black iron, yellow iron, and 5 different reds, including Spanish Red. I found that the redder it was before it was fired, the redder it would be after. The best I have found so far has been an iron from Pfizer that is bright red-orange raw. I'm almost out, and don't know where to get more. Any suggestions? The Spanish Red I got from a local supplier, and it's earthy red-brown. To get the red, you need a lot of calcium, and almost as much, but not more, magnesium. All of these iron reds have a very high silica/ alumina ratio, at least 20 to 1, some as high as 100 to 1. Of course they run like the Energizer Bunny, but I only use them on tile. submitted by: Paul Lewing e-mail:

recipes.name: Reitz Chamelion
recipes.description: I discovered this glaze on accident while trying to make a batch of Reitz green. Someone in my studio had mixed black iron with black cobalt oxide. This glaze has a lovely stony matte finish. If applied very thin on light stoneware it creates a gold tan color. Slightly thicker glaze application yields a black color. A heavier application creates a blue-green color. Applying this glaze extremely thick somehow creates little pimples that create a rough, not food safe texture, so mix to a specific gravity of 145-155, and dip 1-3 times for the different colors. This glaze is fairly reliable and seems to appear the same whether its very reduced, lightly reduced, or slightly oxidized.

recipes.name: Resolute 04 + 2 RIO
recipes.description: From Linda Arbuckle: Notes: Crazes, holds some bubble thick. > "I put this together for a friend of mine who was using a lowfire barium amber. I was looking at Sr ambers and olive green transparent lowfire glazes. At some point I’d like to add just a touch more lithium to the Higher Power and Amber Assault + Li and Sr tests to get rid of very mild crazing I see under magnification. Other goals were to have a lowfire glaze that had enough clay to apply well. I find the very high frit lowfire glazes have to go on so very thin that they’re a challenge to dip-glaze well. They always look too thin to me, and if they’re thick, they trap bubbled and get crater-y." Firing Notes: All tiles fired upright. 03 sitter cone to give an junior cone 04 bending visual. Average coating of glaze on the left, thicker on the right. On terracotta clay with slips (white, black, green, pink, yellow). I’d like to test bumping the lithium up just a tad on the Higher Power to get rid of the slight crazing. Doesn’t show crazing unless viewing under magnification, so it’s slight.

Use these Duncan EZ-stroke transparent underglazes as overglaze wash for color: 003, EZ004, EZ007, EZ012, EZ014, EZ019, EZ020, EZ021, EZ024, EZ025, EZ027, EZ028, EZ030, EZ032, EZ053 (lip red), EZ161. Most others will work.EZ017 is slightly dry, EZ006 is quite dry - not recommended. Cover coat CC 154 works as well. Most other Cover Coat colors will work when quite thin, but will be dry if thick. Try adding a teaspoonful of frit or gerstley borate to a jar of CC underglaze for glossier color. Other color possibilities include washes of the common colorants (mix chrome and rutile 50/50 with gerstley borate or frit).

recipes.description: Golden Magnesium Matte full of crystals (regular cooling cycle). Looks very thick and robust (which it is). Very stable. Recipe in English: Silica 34 Neph Sye 31 Ulexite 12 Whiting 10 Magnesium Carbonate 8 Kaolin 5 ——— Fe2O3 10 I use gum solution 15% gum + 75% water, then add dry ingredients to it and after mixing add water to get specific gravity right (usually 1.40-1.45 for my glazes). recipes.name: Robusto 2B (1)
recipes.description: Gama Média - Britt. Página 77. Não craquelou. Parece muito bom, principalmente porque não tem zinco como os demais transparentes. Porém eu vou recalcular com outros ingredientes porque a frita 3195 aqui é muito cara.

recipes.name: Robusto 2B (2)
recipes.description: Feito com base em Robust E - Gama média - Britt - Página 77 e add + 10% de Si porque estava em compressão. Foi recalculado com outros ingredientes tendo em vista que a Frita 3195 aqui é cara e de difícil acesso. Ficou em compressão. 70% água + 30% CMC.

recipes.name: Robusto 2B (6) - Incolor
recipes.description: Amo esmaltes transparentes com brilho !!!! Feito com base em Robust 2B - Gama média - Britt - Página 77. Realmente é um esmalte Robusto! Com muita sílica, muito alumínio, cálcio suficiente, etc ...! Está todo dentro dos limites e lindamente no meio do Stull !!! Foi recalculado com outros ingredientes tendo em vista que a Frita 3195 aqui é cara e de difícil acesso. Eu retirei 10 moléculas de cálcio para doar ao magnésio para baixar a expansão. É um transparente bem bacana porque é sem zinco. Para usar com a argila Nova Terracota ou argila muito escura deve adicionar uma pequena quantidade de ferro para que não fique leitoso. Acredito eu que 1%seja mais do que suficiente. Vou investir em mais pesquisas com ele. Para outras cores como amarelo, vermelho, laranja, etc... Aliás: Para qualquer outra cor sem cromo sugiro o https://glazy.org/recipes/115004, onde terá cores mais fortes. 70% água + 30% CMC.

recipes.name: Robusto E (8) - Incolor
recipes.description: Amo esmaltes transparentes com brilho!!!! Feito com base em Robust E - Gama média - Britt - Página 77. Realmente é um esmalte Robusto! com muita sílica, muito alumínio, cálcio suficiente, etc...! Está todo dentro dos limites e lindamente no meio do Stull!!! Foi recalculado com outros ingredientes tendo em vista que a Frita 3195 aqui é cara e de difícil acesso. 70% de água + 30% de CMC. É tão transparente, tem tanto brilho que qualquer 3% de corante dá cores fortes. Não deu bons resultados com óxido de cobre e não pode ser trabalhado com cromo porque contém zinco. Com óxido de cobalto não deu bom resultado acredito eu que por causa da granulometria. Apresentou grãos e outras partes sem nada. Não se misturou bem. Teria que moer o óxido, e como a granulometria dos corantes é em torno de 400 é melhor usar com corantes. É muito transparente e tudo aparece! Para outros corantes como os verdes alface, por exemplo teria que usar mesmo uma quantidade maior. Acredito que em torno de 8% ou até mesmo talvez anexar um Zircopax ou algo para contrastar. Devem ser feitas novas experiências. Isso é só um começo. Vou investir em um estudo maior em cima desse esmalte. Qualquer expansão acima dessa craquela. Se retirar um pouquinho de magnésio para dar para o cálcio: craquela. Craquelou com 5,6 deixando no mesmo lugar.

Não pode ser trabalhado com cromo porque contém zinco. Com óxido de cobalto não deu bom resultado acredito eu que por causa da granulometria. Apresentou grãos e outras partes sem nada. Não se misturou bem. Teria que moer o óxido, e como a granulometria dos corantes é em torno de 400 é melhor usar com corantes. É muito transparente e tudo aparece! Para outros corantes como os verdes alface, por exemplo teria que usar mesmo uma quantidade maior. Acredito que em torno de 8% ou até mesmo talvez anexar um Zircopax ou algo para contrastar. Devem ser feitas novas experiências. Isso é só um começo. Vou investir em um estudo maior em cima desse esmalte.

recipes.name: Robusto Semi-Opaco(2)
recipes.description: Feito com base em Robust E - Gama média - Britt - Página 77. Foi recalculado com outros ingredientes tendo em vista que a Frita 3195 aqui é cara e de difícil acesso. Eu adicionei o Zircopax e depois retirei o magnésio, dividindo entre sódio, lítio e cálcio e eu acertei sílica e alumínio para retornar onde estavam anteriormente, com objetivo de aumentar o derretimento e acertar a expansão. Gostei e entrou para a minha paleta de cores. Alterado para 100% já com o zircopax. No primeiro eu havia adicionado 80% água + 20% CMC e estava bom. Nesse eu add 70% água e 30% CMC, como ficou grosso passei só 2 mãos e não obtive um bom resultado. O primeiro era bem mais branco... Eu preciso acertar essa densidade.

recipes.name: Ron Roy High Calcium Semimatte Base 2
recipes.description: "I have introduced a cooling cycle to the firing. The cycle is as follows and the firing is accompanied by a Cone 6 witness cone. After 12 consecutive firings, the witness cones are identical from firing to firing." The firing cycle: Rate Temp Hold Time rA1= 360 F1 = 900 0 rA2= 300 F2 = 1800 0 rA3 =200 F3 = 2016 0 rA4 = 108 F4 = 2197 0.3 rA5 = Full F5 =1800 0 rA6 =150 F6 = 1300 0 rA7 = 0000 To summarize, I fire at a rate of 360/hr to 900 degrees F, then at 300 degrees/ hr to 1800 degrees F, 200 degrees/hr until 2016 degrees F is reached, then 108 degrees/hour to 2197 at which time I hold it at that temperature for 30 minutes. The kiln is shut off until a temperature of 1800 degrees F is reached and then turned on to slow the rate of cooling to 150 degrees/hr until 1300 degrees F is reached. At this point the kiln is turned off and cools naturally. Western Pennsylvania Potters Community http://wpapotters.blogspot.com/2012/04/links-to-cone-6-oxidation-glaze-tests.html http://www.wpapotters.blogspot.com/2011/10/cone-6-oxidation-results-group-7.html

recipes.name: Rosie's Base
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Ca Na B. Translucent satin glaze. From Pete Pinnell. For colors add up to 10% Mason stain 6600 black makes a nice satin grey. I use both of these with a 10% addition of Mason 6600 black. Rosie's turns a satin grey, while Darby's is a satin black. Here are a couple of simple glazes you might try. Both are semi-gloss until you add stains, then they become more of a satin matt. The trick to getting a good matt glaze at cone 04 is to soak the kiln at the end of the firing, and then cool a bit slower than usual (fire down). A matt glaze becomes that way because micro-crystals grow out of the glass. It takes time for that to happen, and the typical electric kiln simply cools too quickly. Both of these came out of student triaxial blends at the Kansas City Art Institute. submitted by: Pete Pinnell source for original recipe: Kansas City Art Institute

recipes.description: from Alfred U. days Tan where thin Beige where med. and mottled light blue where thick. Satin matt to gloss. Well I finally got around to typing this thing up...^9-10 Blues Thank you one and all for all the donated recipes. I only tested 31 out of almost 100 I received. I'll continue testing and reporting as the winter DRAGS on. All the glazes were tested on #900 Miller clay which is a toasty ^10 stoneware. One side of the test tile was brushed with a thick coating of Cynthia Bringle's wet/dry white slip. Each glaze was dipped in three thicknesses on a heavily textured tile. All tiles were fired to a (hard)^9 (10 tipping)reduction firing. 1 hr. Body reduction at ^08 and 1 hr. glaze reduction at ^9 then a quick reox. before shutdown. Any time potash or Custer spar is called for, I used G-200. All ball clay is OM-4 . Many glazes I substituted 75% of the amount of Barium with Strontium. All kaolin is EPK. Remember... glazes don't travel well. Your results will probably be TOTALLY different. Please test before use. Tracy Wilson Saltbox Pottery 4 Shaw Rd. Woolwich, ME 04579 phone: 207-443-5586 fax: 207-442-8922 email: web: http://www.ime.net/dwilson/

recipes.name: Salvation Glaze
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Tim Eberhardt Notes: Tim Eberhardt: I have used it as a base and as a salvation treatment for work that comes through the glaze fire with less than satisfactory results for 5 years with no problems. Take the cobalt out and you get a satiny white glaze that you can add stains and oxides to in order to get a palette of colours. The hotter you fire the less it will have the crystaly look and the bluer the glaze will become. The cooler, the more purple and pink you will see. If you use this over previously fired pieces, what is underneath will affect the outcome somewhat. I spray a couple of coats over pots I think require salvation. It always works miracles. Increase the borate to 21 for cone 6. Notes: Ron Roy: way short of alumina so it is not going to be durable - best not to use it as a liner. Because it is short of alumina it may be runny. The expansion is a bit on the low side so adding a low expansion material like zirconia could be risky. Notes: Steve Slatin: because this is magnesium rich, low in alumina and high in silica, it will react with the underlying glaze and not just provide a new layer of effects (granted, a refiring with a second coat of glaze always does this to some extent). The effects will include new colour effects because magnesium-rich glazes often have different colour effects from Na/K based glazes, and provide a more varied effect as the lower levels of the glaze surface will include mostly the original colouration and the top layer, rich in Mg, will include the other colouration, and there may be crystalline effects because of the extremely high Si:Al ratio of the salvation treatment, and there may be internal refraction because of the difference in glass characteristics between the already-established normal flux/silica-ratio glass on the pot surface vs the extra-high ratio salvation surface lying on top of it. Why doesnt it run off the pot? My guess here is that Eberhardt mixes it much as he mixes his regular glaze, and then brushes or dips a much thinner layer of the salvation onto the already glazed pot than he would use if it were a base glaze (which is easy enough -- its tough to put a thick layer over a glazed surface). This thin layer when fired is sufficient to create effects but not so thick as to run all over.

recipes.name: Sapergia Base
recipes.description: We've been having a terrible time with one of our production glazes. We've used it for several years without a problem, but after moving a year ago we started getting major blisters. Some firings are ok, then we'll have a terrible load even tho we fire the same schedule each time. We thot it might be the new water (it's softer, so we wondered if it might have more sodium), but tried the 'old' water, got the same blisters, altho not as bad (for a load or 2). We typically fire (propane) to ^10 tip touching, in about 11-12 hours) start reduction at ^012 at the coolest spot in the kiln. We take an hour from ^9 to ^10, then usually leave the damper open for an hour to quick cool before we close it. We tried closing it immediately for a slow cool, hoping to smooth out the glaze, but still had blisters and had lost all our great blues. The temp is within 1/2 cone throughout the kiln, and reduction seems fairly even. The other thing is that it isn't every pot in that glaze. On one shelf, the pots on one side might be blistered and the other side fine, and one shelf up or down the opposite side is affected. It seems worse when the glaze is thin. Sometimes a re-fire helps smooth them out. Our 2 claybodies are Plainsman H443 (brown) and H551 (white). Could it be the clay? We have some blisters in other glazes too, altho not as bad. The only common ingredient in custer spar. I hope I've given you enough info to help me. It's been a year of seconds, losing about 20%. submitted by: Barb & Ray Sapergia e-mail:

recipes.description: use OM-4 Ball clay or equal (eg, Bell Dark) use Custer feldspar (or equal, eg, G-200 f.s.) Recently, a glaze recipe for satin black was posted here with a request for revision to C6 brown in oxidation. Here is such a recipe. C6 Base Glaze, oxidation or reduction Add 2-5% iron oxide red for browns; 1-2% Cobalt carbonate for blues; 2-4% Copper carbonate for greens. Try other colourants for variation. On some bodies, the glaze may require a 30-minute soaking. The Seger formula for the revision above is: CaO 0.51; MgO 0.24; KNaO 0.25; Al2O3 0.40; SiO2 4.10 which places the glaze in the middle of the 3-7 cone range. The glaze will be glossy Ratio = 10.3 and it should fit most stoneware bodies, perhaps even some porcelaineous stonewares since the Expansion coefficient is 6.6x10-6. The original glaze as cited was relying on the high level of colourant oxides to help bring it closer to balance but it would be overfired at C9 (if the body fails to release silica to the glaze). recipes.description: A cone 10 recipe I picked up from the studio I work at as a lab tech. Absurdly simple, yet wonderfully effective. This glaze can be applied as a slip on greenware or leather hard clay and single-fired or bisqued on before using other glazes. You can carve through this on unfired clay to make great scroffito patterns. The glossy/satin finish contrasts beautifully with raw clay body, especially porcelain. You can actually make this glaze stiffer by SUBTRACTING the Albany Clay and ADDING feldspar. I find this hilarious. I've created a glaze called "Etch Black" now that tests this theory out.

recipes.name: Satin Black on Black Crystalline
recipes.description: High fire crystalline based on the late Peter Ilsley's 'Dusty Rose'. This crystalline glaze is best applied in three different thickness, starting with the bottom 3rd at 0.5mm thick, middle 3rd at 1mm thick and the top 3rd at 1.5mm thick. Like most crystallines it requires the piece be placed on a catcher with a layer of kiln wash (70% Alumina Hydrate 15% Kaolin 15% Calcined Kaolin) applied to the foot of the piece and the raised section of the catcher that the piece is to sit on then join the piece and catcher with water. Fire to maturity, then crash cool to 1080ºC (‪1976º‬F‬) to aid nucleation and raise to 1100ºc (‪2012º‬F) with in 10 minutes and hold at 1100ºc (‪2012º‬F) for 1 hour. Further holds include, 1080ºC (‪1976º‬F‬) 1 hour, 1100ºc (‪2012º‬F) for 1/2 hour, 1080ºC (‪1976º‬F‬) for 10 minutes, and 1050ºC (‪1922º‬F‬)for 1/2 hour. Then clamp up kiln and end firing! You may choose to do a Post Reduction from 815ºC (‪1499º‬F‬) to 700ºC (‪1292‬º‬F).

recipes.name: Satin Nightmare
recipes.description: Satin matt. Very similar to Shaner red. Very metallic brown going to deep red over white slip. Well I finally got around to typing this thing up...^9-10 Blues Thank you one and all for all the donated recipes. I only tested 31 out of almost 100 I received. I'll continue testing and reporting as the winter DRAGS on. All the glazes were tested on #900 Miller clay which is a toasty ^10 stoneware. One side of the test tile was brushed with a thick coating of Cynthia Bringle's wet/dry white slip. Each glaze was dipped in three thicknesses on a heavily textured tile. All tiles were fired to a (hard)^9 (10 tipping)reduction firing. 1 hr. Body reduction at ^08 and 1 hr. glaze reduction at ^9 then a quick reox. before shutdown. Any time potash or Custer spar is called for, I used G-200. All ball clay is OM-4 . Many glazes I substituted 75% of the amount of Barium with Strontium. All kaolin is EPK. Remember... glazes don't travel well. Your results will probably be TOTALLY different. Please test before use. Tracy Wilson Saltbox Pottery 4 Shaw Rd. Woolwich, ME 04579 phone: 207-443-5586 fax: 207-442-8922 email: web: http://www.ime.net/dwilson/

recipes.name: SATIN OATMEAL
recipes.description: (the club's standard oatmeal was too runny - my variation sits better and is a good base glaze. Surface waxy where thinnish, to glossy if thick. Underglaze painting shows through with softened edges. The titanium makes it reactive when over-dipped with some other glazes, and you may get areas of aventurine.) Here are a couple of standards from the Richmond Potters Club, and a few of my own formulation that have worked well in ^6 oxidation. They aren't revolutionary (my exciting ones have things like barium in them, or are less predictable for a classroom situation) but they have been reliable, and allow for some play. They all calculate out to well within the INSIGHT limit formulas for maturity at ^6. If anyone tests these and comes up with problems, new ideas, good variations etc. could they let me know? I'll look forward to a larger list being posted to clayart. Veronica Shelford

recipes.name: Scotchie Textured
recipes.description: 1260 degrees centigrade dry matt blue textured glaze. Not sieved and hand blended to stucco consistency. Apply thick and dab on with brush or sponge. Can apply more after each firing and refire to get thicker texture (not done here). Cryolite gasses damage kiln elements and give off fluorine gas which dissolves silica. Very dangerous. Should be fired in kilns outside in well ventilated area.

recipes.name: Scotchie’s Textured
recipes.description: Amazing crackling cryolite glaze. Cones 3 and 6 are pretty dry, at cone eight the surface gets a little smoother and more vitrified. It eats through shelves and bricks. It also off gases fluorine gas, so this glaze needs to be fired outside in a well ventilated area.

recipes.name: Seafoam Chun
recipes.description: This recipe is a modified version of "Coleman I", a blue chun/celadon from John Britt's Cone 10 glaze book, page 67. Chromium is a very powerful colorant. I've found that if you add a very tiny amount to a clear glaze, you get a delicate, bright key-lime green color. Since this celadon is colored with something other than iron, its not a true celadon by textbook definitions, but that doesn't diminish its beauty. Chromium and zinc don't mix, I had to eliminate the zinc from the original recipe. If you swap iron or cobalt for the chromium, you can add the zinc back in and get a floating blue effect! Custer - 40.4 Silica - 28.8 Whiting - 8.4 Grolleg - 2.6 Barium Carbonate - 4.2 (I switched with strontium 1:1) Gerstley Borate - 12.6 Frit 3110 - 0.5 Wood Ash - 2.0 (I used pecan wood ash, but any kind works) Zinc - 0.5 (Eliminate if using small amounts of chromium) Red Iron Oxide - 1.2

recipes.name: Semi Matte Red
recipes.description: White RETRY My experience with copper red is that what matters most is to begin reduction at cone 012 fairly heavy and then go into moderate reduction after cone 05 drops. Continue moderate to light reduction until cone 10 then a brief oxidation peroid of about 10 minutes. If you over reduce it will be liver brown and under reduced will be celadon. One solution to a problem (uneven, spotty reduction and under reduced)we had was to turn down the gas and air. To slow it down and reduce at the above schedule. We were firing in an Alpine updraft with blowers and just running the same schedule as the people who fired before us. (It was a community center). They were firing at 4 pounds pressure (natural gas) with the blowers at 70. Something like that. But we reduced the gas and the air and the firing was 100% better. No more spotty reduction or unreduced pots. (I kind of miss those unwanted interesting results though.) submitted by: John Britt e-mail:

recipes.name: Semi-matte OFF WHITE
recipes.description: This is a semi matte off-white recipe with Dolomite as Flux and Tin (8%) as opacifier. It should give good coverage also with only 5-6% Tin. It has been tested with oxides and gave good results with: - Nickel Carbonate 1,3% (more white/beige) - Manganese dioxide 1% (light brown) - Cobalt oxide 0,3% (Light blue) - Copper Carbonate 2% (Light green) The water content is 120%. If applied too thick it can cause pinholes, 2-3 sec dipping should be enough. Normal firing schedule at 1240 C with 20 min soaking time.

recipes.name: SG-104 Chappell's Temmoku Green Semi-Gloss
recipes.description: feldspathic, opaque, semi-gloss From "The Potter's Complete Book of Clay and Glazes" (2nd edition) by James Chappell "Fires to an opaque dark olive in oxidation, and black in reduction." The original recipe called for sieved stoneware clay, so I put in goldart. Try whatever you have on hand. At cone 8 it is a rich purplish black, if you subsequently do a strike firing at bisque temps, it becomes a nice olive green-yellow, as you can see in my picture. The test tile is cone 8 and the bowl is cone 8 followed by cone 04 (I just threw it in with my bisque to see what would happen)

recipes.name: SG-42 Clear Glaze
recipes.description: C.M.C. 1 tsp I have been off-line for several days (art fair a'comin') and upon retrieving my e-mail found several of you interested in my recipe for a cone 6 clear glaze that worked well (for me, anyway) over underglazes. (Sorry for the delay) It works over the Amaco Reward Velvet Underglazes, including reds, purples, etc. I will post the original recipe and then add my revisions. OK. The above glaze crazed on my A.R.T. #135 porcelain at cone 6. Being absolutely non-technical, I stumbled in to the following substitution: I substituted calcined kaolin (comercial name Glomax, from A.R.T.) for the EPK. I also substituted Amorphous Silica for the Flint. I don't use C.M.C. I do add Flocs...it settles out. It is glossy and very clear. My samples from two/three years ago still look good, no delayed crazing. I don't use it on anything, because I found a whole palette of glazes while I was looking for a good clear, and have lost interest in underglaze decorating. The pursuit was interesting, though ;-) I found the Pemco Frit 626 through Trinity supply in Texas. I do not know about substitutes. submitted by: Candice Roeder source for original recipe: James Chappell

recipes.name: SG-90 Chappell's Clear Gloss Base - sub custer
recipes.description: feldspathic, transparent, gloss From "The Potter's Complete Book of Clay and Glazes" (2nd edition) by James Chappell "This glaze fires to a bright, clear, gloss in reduction or oxidation. It is a good base for most colorants." The original recipe calls for Kingman feldspar, but that is no longer available. Chappell says Custer can sub, so try that. If Custer doesn't work or disappears, other options may be Mahavir Indian feldspar k, or a 3:7 blend of minspar 200 and G-200HP. Calls for 1 tsp CMC. Results: good functional glaze. Durable, no leaching, dishwasher safe, resistant to scratches. It looks spectacular with 12% iron and remains functional.

recipes.name: Shaner Shino
recipes.description: From Steve Davis Website & Blog: http://kazegama.com/ Website: http://kazegamas.com/ Shinos 4: http://kazegamas.com/shinos4.htm There are 72 shinos shown on 4 web pages. They are organized from left to right with 3 tiles of the same glaze shown on 3 different clay bodies. They are Aardvark Clay's Nara Porcelain, Long Beach, and Black Mountain. Every shino was glazed with a doulble dip, waxed with a simple "S" pattern, and left to dry for 2 weeks to grow sulfates on the surface. The "S" pattern has no sulfate build up. A medium reduction was started at cone 012 through cone 2. From there the kiln was fired in neutral to cone 10.

recipes.name: Shatz Clear
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Ceramics Monthly September 2005 Jayne Shatz Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 900C hold 1 hour Notes: Alisa Clausen: Gloss, transparent glaze. Described as a great liner glaze in article. I would choose something else, without barium and without so much Gerstley. I made this glaze with a boron frit instead of G. B. and the result looked the same, with a very good melt. I would suggest also subbing strontium for the barium. That would get rid of the barium and since there are no colour enhancing issues, (where I have found strontium not to be as good as catalyst as barium) it could be a success. 100 gr. barium carbonate equals 74.8 gr. strontium carbonate (6.5 gr. s.c. for this recipe).

recipes.name: Shino C10R Revised Shaner
recipes.description: NOTE: originally specified anhydrous Soda Ash Lowell Baker: Here are three more shino glazes for you to explore. One is probably well known, Shaner's shino, it is the one we use at Mohawk C's 'ceramics lab' stoney creek. As quoted this is a high alkali glaze (sodium and lithium) and unusually high alumina 1.6 moles (29.5% by weight). This glaze doesn't fit the pattern of C10R glazes but works if one applies it carefully. (The iron comes from the raw materials and totals 0.01 moles, 0.35%) A thin singlecoat yeilds variegated organge especially on a embossed surface. If a second coat is applied, one gets a greyed white, and if the glaze is even thicker it will crawl. From: Tom Buck

recipes.name: Shino Carbon Trap
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Shino Originally specified lithium oxide -almost certainly this should have been lithium carbonate. Works well in soda and salt kilns, too. You might try sifting some ash directly onto the work after glazing, to implement the fly ash in the kiln. I've done that with good results, in heavy reduction. Dannon Rhudy

recipes.name: Shino Carbon Trapping Orange
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Shino As per your request for a shino, here is one I developed and am particularly fond of. I do not know how low it could be fired. I fire it to ^10-11. One of the most important aspects of shinos is HOW they are fired. To get good fire color, I reduce from ^010 on until the end, then I back the burners off to low and oxidize for 1-2 hours before shutting down. For testing, apply at various thicknesses from very thin to very thick for a variety of color/texture types. submitted by: Bill Buckner

recipes.name: Shitstorm
recipes.description: Seriously do not make this glaze. This is a rough guess at the recipe of a mix of three glazes, a brown that just sucked, some clear that crazed, and a blue (Cretaceous Blue) that I never really loved. But I love this! But don't use all this junk - target and solve or import the glazechem file into https://glaze.warewolves.ca/ and make a version out of a more reasonable set of materials. Maybe just omit the talc. Honestly you could probably use MC6G Calcium Semi-Matte 2 and add these colorants. The stain is Mason 6388 Mazerine; it was cheaper than cobalt carb at the time. I sub it for cobalt carb at 1 Cobalt Carb = 0.88 Mazerine, so 0.6 Mazerine = 0.68 Cobalt Carb. Not much diff probably. I hand-blend this before using because it makes flocs (wollastonite?) and if I don't hand blend they make little blisters and/or nodules. Fired to a hard Cone 6 witness, Cone 7 bending. (Though this firing only made it to about 1188C - need new elements?) Fast drop to 1000C, then slow cool from 1000C down to 800C over 3 hours.

recipes.description: SiC chun for cone 6 electric. Pretty dramatic. Bright blue on dark clay, light opalescent blue on buff clay, and quite celadon like on white stoneware. Likes to be thick and likes to crawl a bit too. A bit of cmc gum makes the application very even but a bit thin. Two layers of that are a good thick application. recipes.name: siebert majolica + tin
recipes.description: I added 2% Tin to this glaze that is already opacified with Zircopax. It’s my usually cone 04 production glaze on Earthen Red clay from Highwater Clays. It does not run but also is stiff and is prone to crawling, especially where applied thick. No crazing on my medium-low expansion clay body. It shivers on high expansion white earthenware clay. Mix dry ingredients with 2% bentonite and mix with 80% of total weight in water. For example for a 3000g batch (with additives 3,420g) add 2,800ml water. Test SPG and add more water if needed. I usually flocculate too with Epsom salts.

recipes.name: Sigillata Blanca / White Sig
recipes.description: Castellano: Agregar a 200 gr de Tinkar Z: 1 litro de agua destilada + 1 gr de Hexametafosfato de Sodio (calgón - defloculante). Batir. Dejar descansar 24 horas. Usar la parte de arriba. Descartar el sedimento. Copia perfectamente la textura de la pieza, conservando el brillo satinado desde el cono 05 hasta cono 6 (no la he llevado más arriba). La uso también para escribir sobre gres oscuro. English: Tinkar Z = a local Ball Clay (Argentina) Add to 200 gr ball clay: 1 liter of distilled water + 1 g of Sodium Hexametaphosphate (calgon - deflocculant). Shake. Let rest 24 hours. Use the top. Discard the sediment.

recipes.name: Silver Nitrate Glaze
recipes.description: 1 gram of silver nitrate is 10 mls. of the solution below ( that's one dissolved gram) Silver nitrate is poison and corrosive. In solution, if spilled, it stains the surface a revolting liver colour forever. If splashed on hands or skin...liver again for many weeks. Rehearsal for age spots. Crystals are the way to go. Silver nitrate crystals are weighed by grams and added to distilled water. The ratio is one gram to 10 mls of water. So 5 grams go into 50 mls. etc. Store the dissolved solution in a coloured bottle and keep it out of light. When measuring the solution to be added to your glaze WEAR RUBBER GLOVES,CLOTHING YOU HATE and open the windows wide. This stuff doesn't smell at all but it's powerful . Add the needed amount to the MIXED and SIEVED glaze and stir carefully. It will make the texture of the glaze peculiar at first, sort of curdled but keep on stirring and it will smooth out. Wash the stirring implement thoroughly especially if it's metal. This glaze is best painted on in three smooth coats. Use a special brush for this glaze as it will be perm. stained black. recipes.name: Slip Avery/Fake Avery
recipes.description: I've tried a bunch, and not had much luck until recently. I've been using one for a few firings now that I like pretty well; it responds in an interesting way to different atmospheres and clay bodies. A little more inFiring: Some salting is involved in all of the wood firings I have used this slip in- generally about 1 1/2 - 3 pounds per chamber. These are not super long firings -in the 14-18 hour range, so a lot of the surface effect comes from the salt rather than from a lot of ash. I have also used it in salt/soda and it looked great-more orange than brown. I haven't used it with a real heavy load of salt but if you try it I'd like yo know how it looks. Mix just a little on the thin side and its works on bisque just as well as on geenware I've been working up some variations using Helmer kaolin, but haven't hit one I like yet. If you get a response about the Avery will you pass it along? Thanks- if you try this out let me know what you think. submitted by: John Anthony e-mail:

recipes.name: Slip Hands in Clay white
recipes.description: I have been using a slip recipe that I got form HANDS IN CLAY for quite awhile. It works wonderfully..I mix up a 5 gallon pail of it, then put smaller amounts in jars and add mason stains to different jars to get the colors i want - I really don't measure, just add enough by sight until it looks right. One of those small sample packets (1/4 ounce?) usually does great in a cottage cheese container filled with the white slip. Then I brush the slip on green pots, let it dry overnight if it's humid summer in northern Wisconsin, or cover with plastic overnight if the woodstove is on...the waiting makes the carving through the slip give a nicer line I feel. Once my drawings are done, I bisque, then cover with a clear glaze and fire to cone 7 or 8. the nice thing about this slip recipe is that it is good for cones 6-11, and it's true because I've used it in my electric kiln at 6 and my wood kiln at 12! recipes.description: Glaze Type: slip I recently made up a test batch of Jeremy Nudell Kalin's recipe for a fake Avery woodfire flashing slip. I put it on some test bowls made from Miller 510, which is a packaged cone 10 white stoneware, the makeup of which I don't know. The slip was a little thin when I mixed it , so I used a little epsom salts to thicken to what I am used to with an Avery slip going on leather hard. Fired to ^10, it flashed gorgeously, but also cracked and jumped off the pots. Any suggestions for a better fit? Bentonite? I guess I should find out more about the clay body before submitting this, and I will do that. In the meantime, any suggestions would be most welcome.TIA submitted by: John Anthony source for original recipe: Jeremy Nudell Kalin e-mail:

They are quite versatile. These recipes are from Zakin's book on Electric Kiln Ceramics. Some of the clays used in the recipe are coarse and the slip should not be strined. recipes.name: Slip Robin Hopper's
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Slip Robin Hopper cites this decorating slip: He says it is useable from C04 to C12, and if unaltered fires to a 'basic white.' (On a buff stoneware fired C10R, it gives a grey-tone white).To this slip, to get black, he would add 5% (+/-) of his black stain which has the following ingredients: 20% chromium oxide 20% cobalt (oxide or carbonate) 20% manganese (di)oxide 20% iron oxide red 8% feldspar (any) 8% kaolin (any) 4 flint He states this mixture is best after being ball-milled for a minimum of four hours to eliminate specking. He says 5% is enough for a clear glaze, more may be needed for an opaque glaze (or slip as above). If this approach isn't suitable to your friend, perhaps it will provide a simple guide towards a black slip. Salut! Tom.Buck submitted by: Tom Buck source for original recipe: Robin Hopper e-mail:

recipes.name: Snowflake TRI1
recipes.description: Precisa cono 7 (foto 1) para desarrollar correctamente, quizá 8. A cono 6 casi no se aprecian las escamas (foto 2 y 3) He probado muchas recetas de escarchados. Casi todas de buen resultado, pero presentan un problema: Nodulizado (crawling). Se puede solucionar con reesmaltado, pero queda una cicatriz a veces indistinguible, a veces notoria. También se puede evitar con múltiples esmaltados, sumando una capa de esmalte en cada bizcochado. Excelente resultado, pero muy trabajoso. Por casualidad y sin buscarlo expresamente, en un triaxial, encontré una receta que no noduliza, por más grueso que se aplique el esmalte. El problema es la aplicación de un esmalte ultra-defloculado, pero revolviendo con paciencia se soluciona. También calcinar la cuarta parte del carbonato de calcio soluciona la ultradefloculación, y lo vuelve más manejable. Se aprecian muchas pequeñas burbujas (foto 4) Thick. No crawling, but little bubbles. See all the pictures, at cone 7 and 6. Needs full cone 7, maybe 8. Picture 1: cone 7 Picture 2 and 3: cone 6 Picture 4: bubbles, cone 7

recipes.name: Soft Grey Matte
recipes.description: FORMULA & ANALYSIS ------------------ CaO........ .46 12.04% MgO........ .01 .11% K2O........ .06 2.53% Na2O....... .12 3.50% ZnO........ .36 13.49% Fe2O3...... .00 .32% TIO2....... .01 .42% AL2O3...... .37 17.61% SiO2....... 1.79 49.97% P2O5....... RATIO 4.82 EXPAN 592.94 WEIGHT 214.43 I have test results for the original simple glaze and Ron's 2 complicated versions. All 3 glazes were tested on white and red stoneware, vertical and horizontal tiles. They were all fired in the bottom half of my Skutt to cone 6 electric. The firing took approzimately 12 hours with a 1 hour soak at top temp. I added 2% rutile to all the glazes to test for color response, and used OM4 ball clay (instead of bell dark). I was somewhat surprised at how similar the glazes came out. The vertical tiles were virtually identical. All three were a soft gray opaque matt. My white stoneware has a little granular illmenite in it, and small spots bleed through. I double dipped 1/2 of each tile, and the glaze ran just a little. There was no discernable crazing. The horizontal tiles had noticable differences. These tiles were more mottled than the vertical ones, kind of like on oatmeal effect. The original glaze was a warmer gray than either of the 2 complex versions. The second complex version, where thick, was dry and sugary, and more silvery than either of the other 2. On all tiles, the red stoneware was more of a tan color than the white. recipes.name: Song Dynasty Inspired Tianmu/Tenmoku Glaze
recipes.description: This glaze was inspired by analyses of Song Dynasty dark iron glazes in Nigel Wood's "Chinese Glazes". I find this glaze superior to typical Tenmoku glazes like Leach Tenmoku due in part to the inclusion of magnesium. The minor additions of titania and manganese add to the depth. Rather than a slightly translucent dark brown typical of recipes like Leach, my glaze is an opaque, rich, and almost black. (If you wanted an even deeper black, you could add a small percentage of cobalt oxide, say 0.5%.) I've paired this glaze with Kaki Biaxial D4 (8% Bone Ash, 13% RIO) This glaze was developed with a series of line and biaxial tests, unfortunately I cannot find the original images. ALWAYS STORE YOUR IMAGES IN GLAZY DEREK! I've posted here the firing schedule i developed for iron saturate glazes, it is based on ideas from Carol Marians. This black iron glaze probably doesn't even need a hold at 1700F. I'd just try it in a normal cone 10 oxidation firing with natural cooling and see what happens. Original Firing Schedule (used by Kaki glazes): 150°F/hr to 250°F 400°F/hr to 2050°F 120°F/hr to 2250°F 60°F/hr to 2290°F 40°F/hr to 2310°F Hold of 10 minutes at 2310°F 400°F to 1700°F (Down fire) Hold 2 hours at 1700°F Adjusted Firing Schedule: 150°F/hr to 250°F 375°F/hr to 2050°F 120°F/hr to 2250°F 60°F/hr to 2290°F 40°F/hr to 2310°F Hold of 15 minutes at 2315°F 400°F to 1700°F (Down fire) Hold 1 hour at 1700°F Original firing schedule was 2 hour hold. One hour seems just as good. Perfect cone 10 firing.

recipes.name: Sonoran Crawler
recipes.description: This is a magnesium crawl glaze that contains a lot of clay. This means it can be applied on top of some other glazes and still retain its reticulations. I invented this glaze myself. My goal was to make a crawling glaze that could be applied thick and not flake off. Mix this glaze up thick- preferably in small batches and to the consistency of yogurt. Apply a thin layer of a dark glaze, high in clay such as satin black to leather-hard ware or green ware, or barnard slip, and bisque this lower layer onto the clay. Dark clays also work well. Apply a couple coats of Sonoran Crawler on top of the bisqueware with a brush and cease application once you observe cracking. The glaze will crack in the direction of your brush strokes! The more times you brush over the glaze as it dries, the better it adheres. Under heavy reduction or on top of certain iron bearing bodies it can flash. You can try adding a pinch of soda ash to the glaze in order to make it a little less thick without lowering the water content. Thinning this glaze down with water WILL cause it to peel off the piece, keep that specific gravity REALLY high. One day I may try mixing it to a thick paste and applying with a palette knife, but for now, yogurt consistency with a calligraphy bamboo brush works for me. Test this glaze on top of various glazes. I've not had great luck with it over Temmoku, the fine powdery temmoku glaze prevents it from adhering properly. Shinos on the other hand seem to work well underneath it, and the soda ash from the shinos changes the texture in interesting ways. To adjust the texture, change the ratio of Talc and Spodumene: Decreasing talc, increasing spodumene by 2% results in a smoother, more lumpy surface. Decreasing spodumene and increasing talc by 2% results in a rougher, more papery-bark-like surface. Of course, test adjustments before using. Can you tell I have a bit of an obsession? Thank you Klaes for trying out my glaze, altering it and uploading photos! I'll try it myself. I added Borax to the recipe because I believe it will help it stick to the surface better.

The example bowls were all sprayed and then had their bottoms wiped. They had less than a mm of bare clay and they did not stick or run. This is a very stable glaze. A copy of Blue Skies, except have added a specific frit that I actually have access to, had to swap out Soda Feldspar with Potash Feldspar because it's still not available to buy, and have subbed Zircosil for Tin. While I was at it, I adjusted the flux ratios, but it is at exactly the same place on the graph as Blue Skies. So not really the same glaze at all. recipes.name: Splotchy Lavender Glaze
recipes.description: GREAT BLUE/RED /DARK BLUE! My experience with copper red is that what matters most is to begin reduction at cone 012 fairly heavy and then go into moderate reduction after cone 05 drops. Continue moderate to light reduction until cone 10 then a brief oxidation peroid of about 10 minutes. If you over reduce it will be liver brown and under reduced will be celadon. One solution to a problem (uneven, spotty reduction and under reduced)we had was to turn down the gas and air. To slow it down and reduce at the above schedule. We were firing in an Alpine updraft with blowers and just running the same schedule as the people who fired before us. (It was a community center). They were firing at 4 pounds pressure (natural gas) with the blowers at 70. Something like that. But we reduced the gas and the air and the firing was 100% better. No more spotty reduction or unreduced pots. (I kind of miss those unwanted interesting results though.) submitted by: John Britt e-mail:

recipes.name: Starry Starry Night
recipes.description: Based on my standard oil spot glaze, but inspired by comments by Matt Fiske on his oil spot glazes this adds a small amount of Vanadium Pentoxide. The vanadium seems to be brought to the surface with the oil spot, and then spreads out from it, creating a slightly iridescent yellow/ochrey spot. It also seems to make the firing need a longer soak to smooth off. Adding larger amounts of Vanadium extends the size of its spots, and also makes them more orange/salmon pink. By the time you get up to 3%, it pretty much covers all of the black glaze, and the iridescence has increased. Fire: 120C/hr to 1290, soak for 90 minutes, fast cool by removing bungs and lifting the lid by say 5cm down to below 1000C. Cone values are approximate as I don't use them.

recipes.name: Steel Brown
recipes.description: Steel Brown is a great glaze. It has a look I havent seen in many other glazes. While its chemistry is really weird the iridescent shimmer and metallic color are really enticing. The only drawback of this glaze is the crusty, chunky bits that it seems to develop from a thick application on certain bodies. I can only hazard a guess that it's some lithium-iron-aluminate as this base behaves very well when not in the presence of iron. Great for sculptural use, but keep it thinner for usable ware and the like.

recipes.name: Steve Davis Carbon Trap
recipes.description: From Steve Davis Website: http://kazegamas.com/ Shinos 1: http://kazegamas.com/shinos1.htm There are 72 shinos shown on 4 web pages. They are organized from left to right with 3 tiles of the same glaze shown on 3 different clay bodies. They are Aardvark Clay's Nara Porcelain, Long Beach, and Black Mountain. Every shino was glazed with a doulble dip, waxed with a simple "S" pattern, and left to dry for 2 weeks to grow sulfates on the surface. The "S" pattern has no sulfate build up. A medium reduction was started at cone 012 through cone 2. From there the kiln was fired in neutral to cone 10.

recipes.name: Stroke & Coat Base
recipes.description: My community studio basically drinks Stroke and Coats by Mayco.. we do a lot of paint nights and kid stuff, so they're perfect. They don't move, they behave like fired on tempera paint, and they self glaze. You can use them from 05 to 6 with no color changes. S&C are billed as "wonderglaze", they're a really strange thing. Mix the recipe and then add the cmc afterwards to make it brushable (or not). Flocculate however you want. I don't really ever touch bentonite anymore unless i'm making a mud mask. Note about CMC - if you are mixing it from powder, use hot water, let it stand for a few minutes, and before you mix it up add .02 copper to it (way less than a pinch) to keep it from rotting over the long term. Note about Zircopax, from TH: Suppliers of encapsulated stains recommend a zircon addition, but are often unclear about why. Here is the reason, it is a "fining agent". If you are using this as a lowfire glaze, the zircopax isn't as big a deal. It really counts when you get to cone 6 temps, then it keeps the stain from gassing out, which you definitely have to worry about in quantities more than 8%.

recipes.name: Strontium Bible Celadon Base
recipes.description: Reformulated from Bible Celadon, using equal molar amounts of strontium. This Recipe has some crazing on Coleman Porcelain, and is a very beautiful blue-green on a toasty stoneware. It can melt and run when applied too thick and fired even slightly above ^10, but at about ^8 this glaze wont craze even though it forms a glass (still looking into this) so as always watch your kilns; as they say, "Kilns dont over fire, people over fire kilns". This glaze base has become a favorite of the people who work at the studio with me. It does have a tendency to hardpan if left too long (I believe the strontium is ever so slightly soluble) so you may want to add 1-2% bentonite/macaloid/veegum. Happy glazing and always keep testing. Colorants as tested in reduction 1% RIO = blue w/ tint of green 1% Nickel Carbonate = green gray

recipes.name: Strontium Bible Clear/Celadon Base Fritted
recipes.atmosphere: Reduction, Salt & Soda, Wood, Neutral, Oxidation
recipes.description: I received good results from Alexander Kuttel's Strontium Bible Celadon Base. This is a reformulated version that sources KNaO from a frit for a better surface and grolleg kaolin opposed to EPK for better color response. Because the frit does not source as much Al2O3, more kaolin is needed to supply adaquate levels for durability. The high kaolin could potentially cause issues with crawling. If you experience problems with this, try replacing 1/3 to 1/2 of the raw kaolin with calcined kaolin. If calcined kaolin is not available or you would like to still use grolleg for the calcined portion (to keep TiO2 down for the best color response) you can make your own fairly easily in a kiln. There are various resources online that provide the information to do this. This glaze does not craze on any clay bodies tested.

recipes.name: Synthetic ash
recipes.description: Shout out to Ceramic Materials Workshop, and Matt specifically. He kept nudging me in the right direction on this one. This glaze gives a really nice fake ash effect with all the fun of a Cr chartreuse. Due to the relatively high amount of Si and the addition of Cr this is an ash glaze that doesn't run. I don't recommend decreasing the Si. It's needed to prevent the glaze from bubbling due to the Cr. The glaze crazes like mad. Nothing to be done. The glaze has to be in this position on Stull in order to work, so that means it's going to craze. Decided to call this a synthetic ash instead of fake ash. Looks like the ash glaze from a synthetic tree. Or Nickelodeon Slime. Synthetic ash sounds better than slime. I am still experimenting with it. I love it as is, but I'd like to get an opaque version. So I will be trying various opacifiers; Ti, Sn, Zircopax. It's on my to do list but not a priority.

I like a dirty, old fashioned cobalt look that comes from using a Blue Mix instead of straight cobalt: 5 Cobalt oxide/ 4 Red Iron oxide/ 1 Manganese oxide (dry mix then use as colorant) Brush over glaze colors (thin and thick applications give vastly different results (you did say you wanted excitement out of your electric kiln firings, didn't you?)): 10% Blue Mix - 90% Tang Clear 50% Copper Carbonate - 50%Tang Clear (also try 20/80 for flatware) 50% Red Iron oxide - 50% Tang Clear (also try 20/80 for flatware) It is a softer glaze and has issues with soluble ingredients forming crystals in the bucket when stored in cool temperatures.

recipes.name: Temmoku
recipes.description: From Phillip Schmidt http://phillipschmidtpottery.com/my-favorite-glaze-recipes/ This is a Bethel University classroom glaze graciously given to me by professor Kirk Freeman. Thanks Kirk! This temmoku is shiny and true black, and breaks to a beautiful coppery brown with hints of red on edges and around handles. Notes: This is a cone 10 reduction glaze. I dip my mugs one time only but for 12-20 seconds each (depending on how thick I perceived the glaze to be mixed that time around... Being it was a studio glaze, it was mixed up by different people who have different ideas of accuracy and thickness). This ensures a nice thick coating that is not globby and gives a fantastic color. What I love: The temmoku has a beautiful black color and the copper breaks are AMAZING; it doesn’t run even when you dip for 20 seconds, and I've taken it to at least cone 10.5; it looks amazing with coffee inside a temmoku glazed mug. What I don’t like: the dried raw glaze can easily transfer from your fingertips to a white glazed pot without you noticing, and then you have red fingerprints on white pieces. But that’s about it! You can use this glaze in an oxidised atmosphere and the results are beautiful, albeit different. The glaze turns a dark color with hues of black, brown, and dark green. Great in the soda kiln for a consistent dark glaze!
