recipes.name: Temoku Oxidation
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Temmoku Closest thing to redux temmoku I can find. Works well with Penland Purple overlapped as a "chun". Must be fired to hard ^10 for colour to develop - at 9 it is boring brown. Use 1/4 to 1/2% macaloid as as suspender How long have you been using this glaze? Over 7 years Where is it used? My studio Where did this recipe come from? CM compilation of glazes. Sorry, date unknown, but older than 10 years. What do you like most about this glaze? Consistency - apply thickly and it stays put. Good for tableware. Is this glaze reliable? ABSOLUTELY Does this glaze tend to craze/crawl/pinhole/etc.? Rub any pinholes on dry glaze to avoid pinholing in final product. Wear gloves as this glaze will stain your hands - and your clothing. How do different firing temperatures/atmospheres affect the glaze? Will fire to ^9 (gets glossy) but the colour is awful! Firing to ^10 at 4 o'clock for best results. How does the glaze behave on different clay bodies? Have used on 3 different clay bodies with identical results. What consistency should the glaze be for pouring/dipping? Medium thick How thickly should the glaze be applied to the pot? Medium thick - if applied thinly, you can get some red flashes - but unless clay is extremely smooth (non-stoneware) the end product is non-functional. How does this glaze interact with other glazes? Overlapping with Penland opal gives a wonderful "chun" effect in ox. What is your kiln type and size? PSH CRT 180 - 6.5 cubic ft. How do you typically fire? I "candle" overnight. 20-24 hours depending on electricity demands. Do you experience problems with the raw glaze? Rapid settling!! I use .25 - .5% macaloid as a suspender - or it becomes a cement lump. Also, takes a long time to dry. Be patient! What is your water pH? I use R/O water GlazeBase recipe Submitted by: Sam Cuttell - alias the cat lady Ice Cream Flavor: Mowie Cowie -------------------------------------------------------------------- ----

recipes.name: Tenmoku #19a
recipes.description: Tenmoku glaze developed by Ron (Sam) Small in the 1970s for electric cone 9 firings, where it produced mainly black/brown, but occasional rust colours where thinly applied and in specific firings. Now used in cone 10 reduction, where it reliably produces rust, where thin and black/brown where thicker. Develops "tea dust" yellow pyroxene crystals in the thick black region, when cooled slowly. The tea dust effect probably relates to its relatively high MgO content.

recipes.name: Tenmoku (IV)
recipes.description: The recipe is one of four initial recipes from the book The practice of stoneware glazes by Daniel de Montmollin. In the book there is not specified the type of feldspar. I used the soda feldspar because I had it. You can try to use another type of feldspar. Glaze is glossy, doesn't run, dark brown to black, with metal-like shine. With some glazes it can create oil spot combination if used as a first glaze. My firing schedule: 120°C per hour, go to 1240°C, one hour hold at highest temperature, natural cooling. I'm using the white stoneware body - 254 and 264 clay made by Georg&Schneider (former Creaton). I'm firing in an oxidation atmosphere, in the electric kiln.

recipes.name: Tenmoku Mirror Black
recipes.description: Notes: Mel Jacobson: this glaze was found written on the side of plastic pail I bought at an auction in 1965. As with all mirror blacks the thickness of the glaze, the quality of the reduction, and the care in cooling the kiln will play a dramatic influence on the final product. Breaking to rust is the result of thin areas. If you wish to use this as iron red just apply a thin coat. As most veteran potters will verify: make 2000 pots, apply mirror black glaze, and fire the kiln 73 times, you will learn to use it.

recipes.name: Tenmoku with Rice Straw Ash
recipes.description: I acquired some rice straw ash and looked online for recipes to test out the material. This glaze is from a University of Texas online glaze database (approx 2004) at: http://general.utpb.edu/fac/stanleyc/ http://general.utpb.edu/fac/stanleyc/formulae/glaze/tenmokus.htm The note "rice straw is about 98% silica" seems to be in regards to rice hull ash, so I am not sure whether or not the original recipe called for rice straw ash or rice husk ash. Furthermore I can find no information on "Raval" feldspar, I just used my normal potash. Regardless, I think the result looks nice. At cone 11 thick applications will run a bit. Glaze should probably be further refined, but it's a good demonstration of adding a small percentage of rice straw ash to an otherwise typical Tenmoku. Temmoku: Base glaze for R Chun Raval Feldspar 65.00% Whiting 18.00 Rice straw ash 7.00 Silica 10.00 Add: 0 Iron Ox. 6.50 Any high silica ash would be a good substitute, grass ash should work well, rice straw is about 98% silica with high phosphorous content.

recipes.name: Textured Blue
recipes.description: Satin glaze. Deep purple where thick. Midnight blue where medium. soft purple with slip. Well I finally got around to typing this thing up...^9-10 Blues Thank you one and all for all the donated recipes. I only tested 31 out of almost 100 I received. I'll continue testing and reporting as the winter DRAGS on. All the glazes were tested on #900 Miller clay which is a toasty ^10 stoneware. One side of the test tile was brushed with a thick coating of Cynthia Bringle's wet/dry white slip. Each glaze was dipped in three thicknesses on a heavily textured tile. All tiles were fired to a (hard)^9 (10 tipping)reduction firing. 1 hr. Body reduction at ^08 and 1 hr. glaze reduction at ^9 then a quick reox. before shutdown. Any time potash or Custer spar is called for, I used G-200. All ball clay is OM-4 . Many glazes I substituted 75% of the amount of Barium with Strontium. All kaolin is EPK. Remember... glazes don't travel well. Your results will probably be TOTALLY different. Please test before use. Tracy Wilson Saltbox Pottery

It is a matt, dry whitish glaze that I used on many of the iris vases. They were sprayed with TOM in the green state, and once fired. An over glaze brush full of wet chrome oxide gave me green leaves. You can scratch through the chrome to make all sorts of linear marks… have fun. Cobalt water color over glaze gives a good light blue, and wet cobalt slip yields a deep blue. Add Manganese and you may get into the blue-purple range. To make Thomas, just add 10 pounds of 400m or 40 micron silica to the above formula, and use Grolleg kaolin instead of EPK. Thomas is a whiter, dryer version of TOM and a little less crackle when it is thick. These two glazes were always applied quite thin.

recipes.name: Tom Buck Celadon
recipes.description: (Also found in John Britt's High Fire Glazes, p. 68. There is a typo in the book, the recipe should be using Wollastonite. This recipe is basically Pinnell Blue Celadon using Wollastonite instead of Whiting.) From the Clayart archives: http://www.potters.org/subject95906.htm Tom Buck on fri 1 sep 06 I assume you are firing to Cone 10 and in reduction part of the time, otherwise you would not be quoting from John Britt's book, one of the few places where my original Celadon glaze is cited. I mostly do Cone 6 oxidation (+raku) these days but I did design the Celadon blue for Cone 10 with light or zero reduction. Black iron oxide (FeO) is a very stable compound in a Cone 10 firing but it will act as a "flux oxide" and if present above a minimal level it will melt alumina and silica. Which is why so little black oxide is used in a celadon; half (maybe) acts as flux, half as colourant. If you have spanish red iron oxide, be aware that it contains 83-87% by weight of Fe2O3 (iron oxide red) and so that lower Fe2O3 content has to be considered when you replace Black Iron Oxide, FeO, which is high grade probably close to 100% by weight. Also, if your yellow iron oxide is pigment grade (and not yellow ochre which contains some clayey material then it too is high grade close to 100% Fe2O3.H2O or hydrated red iron oxide. So, try my recipe and use Yellow Iron Oxide (pigment grade) in place of the 1% by weight of Black Iron Oxide (FeO). If you wish to be precise, add 1.13% yellow oxide and you will get 1% FeO when reaching higher cones. The success of this glaze depends on your claybody and how you fire the ware. If you have spanish red, 1.18% will equal 1% black oxide. Celadon colours are "solution" colours, that is, the iron oxide will actually dissolve (as opposed to dispersion or suspension) in the Liquidus (molten glaze), and when cooled, the widely located iron oxide (FeO) molecules will reflect incident white light in green or blue wavelengths. may your tests go well. peace Tom B. From another thread in Clayart, Mike Gordon lists the recipe with Wollastonite rather than Whiting: http://www.potters.org/subject115949.htm Mike Gordon on mon 28 mar 11 TOM BUCK CELADON Cone 10 Custer Feldspar 30.00 Wollastonite 25.00 Grolleg Kaolin 21.00 Silica 24.00 Black Iron Oxide 1.00 From yet another thread, Tom seems to indicate that his celadon recipe does in fact use Wollastonite. http://www.potters.org/subject35039.htm Tom Buck on sun 21 jan 01 Perhaps you do not need this now. But I was doing some writing in Nov and had to put off some things. The basic problem with the Pinnell CB is WHITING, and 20 units is a lot of CO2 coming above 1800 F/1000 C. BTW Whiting is 44% CO2 and 56% CaO. You need a good soak to heal the burst bubbles, and where the glaze is thin healing may not occur even then. The solution is to replace the Whiting with Wollastonite (CaO.SiO2) and when you do this the Silica/Flint needs changing too. here is how it comes out 30 Custer fs 25 Wollastonite 21 Grolleg 24 Flint additives as before. Molecularly, the two recipes provide the same amounts of fluxes and glass-formers. It still will be glossy and with the same expansion/contraction. til later. Peace. Tom B.

Rust brown base with streaking in darker browns and slightly green browns. Edges have a bluer nuance. Some areas under surface are honey brown. Where very thick, the glaze ran in large drips. recipes.name: Tove AA7C1LG (modified)
recipes.description: Based on https://glazy.org/recipes/51748. I updated to use ingredients I have access to. I also removed Li carb. I avoid using soluble materials. I love this glaze. Very reliable with respect to appearance. It always looks like the test tile, brushed, dipped, doesn't matter. A little thicker or thinner? Glaze still works. I fire with a slow cool cycle (E4 in John Britt's mid-range book). The glaze does not run at cone 6. It has low Si and Al (1.94, 0.19), and a Si:Al ratio of 10.31. The flux ratio is out of whack in the UMF but an acceptable 0.2:0.8 in extended UMF accounting for the Cu, Ti, and Fe. The glaze is fluxed primarily with Zn (0.48). It falls in the region of Stull that we would expect crystals and it is great at producing crystals.

I increased chrome ox from 0,02 to 0,03% only because it was a bit difficult to weigh the tiny amount for a 100 g test ;-) The original "Cone 6 glossy pink" glaze is based on a tweak of Tony Hansen's 20X5. Notice 0.03 chrome is not a mistake - it is 1/10 of the usual, already low, amount of chrome oxide in chrome tin pinks and reds.

recipes.name: Traditional Qingbai Glaze (Glaze Ash 20%)
recipes.description: Qingbai: A "two-component" Glaze --- The combination of Yaoli Glaze Stone and Er hui glaze ash is pretty much as close as you can get to the original qingbai recipes. An example of "二元配方"- "two-component" (or "two-ingredient) recipes. While the recipe of only two ingredients may be quite simple, the ingredients themselves are quite complex and require very technical processing. This glaze must be fired very carefully or carbon-trapping may occur. #### Related Glazes --- Traditional Qingbai Glaze (Glaze Ash 25%) Similar mixture of Glaze Stone and Glaze Ash but with Glaze Ash at 25%. #### Quotes --- Nigel Wood (1999). Chinese Glazes. The Porcelain Glazes of Southern China: > In virtually all yingqing glazes the iron oxide colourants were natural impurities in the raw materials used to make the glazes, while their relatively high calcium oxide content encouraged a pronounced iron-blueness to develop when the glazes were fired in strong reduction. > This simple technology - where porcelain stone was mixed with glaze ash (calcium carbonate) - proved to be extraordinarily versatile. Every mixture between about 5% glaze ash and 95% glaze stone, and 40% glaze ash and 60% glaze stone, gave Jingdezhen porcelain glazes of high quality. As less glaze ash was used in the recipes, the porcelain glazes became progressively whiter, stiffer and more opaque. Rajbanul Akhond (2019). A Brief Recipe Book for Chinese Ceramics: > Qingbai wares (also called 'Yingqing') were made at Jingdezhen and at many other southern kilns from the time of the Northern Song dynasty until they were eclipsed in the 14th century by underglaze decorated blue and white wares. Qingbai in Chinese literally means "clear blue white". The qingbai glaze is a porcelain glaze, so called because it was made using pottery stone. The qingbai glaze is clear, but contains iron in small amounts. When applied over a white porcelain body the glaze produces a greenish blue color that gives the glaze its name. Some have carved or formed decorations. > In Jingdezhen, during the late Ming and early Qing dynasties, glazes used for blue-and-white ceramics were made with glaze ash, a material mostly composed of burned limestone with a few or less percent of botanic ash, mixed in various proportions with porcelain stone – or glaze stone, a refined grade of porcelain stone –, the glaze ash content ranging typically from 10 to 20% which indicate the constant presence of variable amounts of calcium (4.3e9.1%, CaO). #### Further Reading: --- Wikipedia, Qingbai Ware. M. S. Tite, I. C. Freestone, M. Bimson (2007). A technological study of Chinese porcelain of the Yuan Dynasty. M. S. Tite, I. C. Freestone and N. Wood (2012). An investigation into the relationship between the raw materials used in the production of Chinese porcelain and stoneware bodies and the resulting microstructures.

recipes.name: Translúcido
recipes.description: Foi feito com base no G2926B do Digitalfire. - Calculado com materiais brasileiros quase nas mesmas moléculas do original e algum arredondamento. - Silica #500, caulim #400 e 3% de ultrox para evitar o craquelado e um melhor derretimento. O Ultrox também tem a função de acalmar alguns corantes para que não arrepiem, como por exemplo os vermelhos, amarelos e laranjas. - Muito bom para texturas, especialmente as de baixo relevo, em argila clara, de preferência branca, com 3% de corante. - Nesse caso o ideal para quem usa pincel é usar com uma baixissima densidade (SG1,32 - 150% de água) e 4 camadas, mas para que tudo funcione bem o ideal é empastá-lo. - Mancha muito em lisos chapados, deixando marcas, mesmo com SG de 1.32 e 4 camadas. - Com 8% de corante parece não derreter tão bem (ainda não tenho certeza), mas quando usado em pinturas com sobreposição como majolica funciona muito bem e derrete sim. - Nesse caso o ideal é uma densidade bem alta e é muito bom com gotas sobre Majolica ou também empastado para silkscreen. - Também funciona muito bem sem cor em várias argilas, não modificando em quase nada suas cores naturais, mesmo com os 3% de ultrox (que uso também para não craquelar) desde que respeitada a baixa densidade. - Em breve devo publicar outras linhas à partir desse, com algumas alterações na base para um bom derretimento em conjunto com algumas adições, que no momento estão em testes e não translucidas.

recipes.name: Tsaber's Crackle Celadon
recipes.description: This glaze needs heat. It forms a beautiful glossy ice blue when fired nice and hot (or fired twice), otherwise it won't fully form a glass and will come out a semi-matte if you only hit cone 9. If you're having trouble getting it to fuse even with higher temps, add more Whiting or Barium Carbonate to bring the glaze into a better flux ratio.

recipes.name: TT Standard Oil Spot
recipes.description: Classical oil spot glaze, original recipe developed from analysis of Chinese sherds and then tweaked. Thickness and firing are critical. Like all temmoku style glazes, if too thin it comes out brown. Otherwise, thicker application produces larger oil spots. Beware that if applied very thickly in a single application it doesn't shrink tightly on to the pot, and on the outside of pieces chunks of glaze will come off in the kiln and it won't heal over. Firing cycle is also significant. Depending on what I want, I go at 120 - 200C/hr up to 1290 or 1300, then soak for 1-2 hours (longer if thick) so it smoothes off properly. Fast cooling (i.e. bungs open and kiln lid opened 5-10cm) ensures that the spots remain in the grey epsilon form, or slow cool if you want the red/brown alpha form of red iron oxide. You can refire to create a really high gloss finish and shift the colour towards red. Cone values are approximate as I don't use them.

recipes.name: UCLA #1258 Satin Transparent
recipes.description: A few of these glazes contain lead compounds. Lead is very valuable in promoting desirable glaze properties at the temperatures we are firing; long firing range, bright color response, high index of refraction, rich surface effects, better elasticity and tensile strength than most leadless glazes, and coefficients of expansion that generally minimize crazing and shivering faults. We are using lead in fritted form; pre-melted into an insoluble silicate glass that is ground into a fine powder and used as a component of the unfired glaze. This lowers the toxicity of the materials significantly but one still must use glazes containing toxic materials with caution and care with attention to good hygienic practices. A few other materials containing toxic heavy metals are used as fluxes (barium compounds) and colorants (arsenic, antimony, cadmium and selenium). We normally use them in relatively safe insoluble forms, but you should always use caution unless you have a full technical understanding of the exact nature and toxicity of the specific material you are using. We are not using any of the “raw” forms that are known to be dangerous in any class glazes (usually oxides and soluble salts). Do Not: Smoke or drink while handling lead compounds or unfired glazes containing lead. Do Not: Use lead-bearing glazes on items intended for, or potentially usable for, food service, especially on forms that could be used for storage of highly acidic foods such as fruit juices, salad dressings, kim chee, pickles, etc.. The few lead-bearing stock glazes provided for your class are safe if properly fired, but it requires expert knowledge to verify exactly which glazes are completely safe and under what conditions of application, firing, and practical use they are acceptable for food service. Do: Wash your hands after handling lead compounds or lead bearing unfired glazes. Do: Wear an approved dust filter mask while preparing unfired glazes containing lead compounds and while spraying wet glazes containing lead and other known toxic materials. Do Use common sense!

recipes.name: Underglaze Base from Vince Pitelka
recipes.description: This is the Mason stain base from Vince Pitelka via Derek Au I use no more than 15% of stain by weight (Wet materials weight x % = dry weight of Mason stain) any more seems to cause problems and doesn’t help the color. Most seem best at 5 to 15 % Underglaze liquid; 2 parts water 2 parts Propylene Glycol - food grade 1 part CMC solution - (CMC solution is 30g CMC in 1 quart hot water - stirred and left to sit for 2 days) it is added BY WEIGHT at a ratio of 3 parts of this liquid mix per 2 parts of dry ingredients to make complete Underglaze Base When making this recipe: Dry-mix all the dry ingredients, add about 3/4 of the anticipated underglaze liquid and blend thoroughly, and then blend in more underglaze liquid a little at a time as needed until you achieve the desired brushing consistency. the finished underglaze base can be stored then add Mason stain by % weight to easily create smaller quantities of colors as needed Mixing well is very important as mason Stains will clump. For detailed use I screen through a 60 mesh sieve to avoid any clumps I find that 15 % Best Black #6600 makes a great black. I use 8% additional Zircopax to make a great white underglaze. recipes.name: V&O Light Blue
recipes.description: from Alfred/ Jim Chalkley Couldn't detect any light blue but I remember it used to be beautiful on carved porcelain. (Jim, are you out there?) All the glazes were tested on #900 Miller clay which is a toasty ^10 stoneware. One side of the test tile was brushed with a thick coating of Cynthia Bringle's wet/dry white slip. Each glaze was dipped in three thicknesses on a heavily textured tile. All tiles were fired to a (hard)^9 (10 tipping)reduction firing. 1 hr. Body reduction at ^08 and 1 hr. glaze reduction at ^9 then a quick reox. before shutdown. Any time potash or Custer spar is called for, I used G-200. All ball clay is OM-4 . tracy wilson Tracy Wilson Saltbox Pottery 4 Shaw Rd. Woolwich, ME 04579 phone: 207-443-5586 fax: 207-442-8922 email: web: http://www.ime.net/dwilson/

recipes.name: Val Cushing Base 2
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Cushing Handbook 1994 cone 4/5/6 Leadless Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 800C hold 1 hour Notes: Alisa Clausen: Transparent gloss, oxides did not move under glaze. With 1 copper carbonate, transparent gloss light blue/green glaze.

recipes.name: Val Cushing Base 3
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Cushing Handbook 1994 cone 5/6 Alkaline Mat Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 800C hold 1 hour Significant Flaw: crazing Notes: Alisa Clausen: used Johnson Matthey J frit instead of 3110. Glossy transparent base which crazed badly. Oxides became very fluid under glaze. With 1 copper carbonate, glossy transparent light green glaze, crazed and oxides became extremely fluid and runny under glaze. With 5 red iron oxide, glossy transparent light yellow glaze, crazed. With 1 manganese dioxide, glossy transparent glaze, slightly purple, crazed.

recipes.name: Val Cushing Base 4
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Cushing Handbook 1994 cone 5/6 Satin Mat Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 800C hold 1 hour Notes: Alisa Clausen: used Johnson Matthey J frit instead of 3110. Semi mat, smooth, whitish base, oxides did not move. Oxides showed through and did not move. Smooth, silky texture and a good mat surface, without being dry. All oxides tested in base resulted in a speckled surface. With 10 zirconia, semi mat, smooth white base, oxides showed through and did not move. With 2 cobalt carbonate, semi mat, smooth deep blue with lighter flecks. With 2 chrome oxide plus 1 cobalt carbonate, semi mat dark green with light blue flecks, reversed where thinner. With 1 copper carbonate, semi mat olive green/brown with light green flecks, reversed where thinner. With 10 ochre, semi mat yellow ochre. With 10 red iron oxide, semi mat deep ochre brown with lighter flecks.

recipes.name: Val Cushing Base 5
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Cushing Handbook 1994 cone 5/6 Stone mat Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 800C hold 1 hour Notes: Alisa Clausen: used Johnson Matthey J frit instead of 3110. Mat, milky base. Oxides are visible but slightly muted by covering glaze. Glazes appear slightly under fired. Can see higher areas of thicker glaze, for example, where it dripped. Not melted in. With 3 copper carbonate, mat, light green glaze with slightly darker areas where thinner. With 5 red iron oxide, mat, yellow glaze. With 3 chrome oxide, mat, dark green glaze, brown where thinner. Appears under fired.

recipes.name: Val Cushing Base 6
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Cushing Handbook 1994 cone 5/6 Barium Stone Mat Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 800C hold 1 hour Significant Flaw: underfired,potentially toxic Notes: Alisa Clausen: mat, milky glaze, oxides are visible but slightly muted. All of the tests appear under fired. With 3 copper carbonate, mat, strong turquoise in colour, smooth. Thick to thin application shows a visible difference. With 1 chrome oxide, under fired, bright yellow colour with a slight light green cast. With 0.5 manganese dioxide, mat, purplish with specks, smooth and appears melted.

recipes.name: Val Cushing Base 7
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Clay -Times, March/April 2005 Val Cushing Source/Alternate names: similar oxides to Xavier Satin Matte Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 1100C hold 1 hour Notes: Alisa Clausen: With 2 titanium dioxide plus 1.2 cobalt carbonate plus 1.2 copper carbonate, gloss, slightly variegated, medium denim blue glaze with slight green cast. Covering. Where thickest, glaze is a semi mat and greener in colour. With 1.2 cobalt carbonate, slightly less glossy, a semi gloss, smooth glaze. A purple blue, with some lilac on the thicker areas. No green. With 2 titanium dioxide plus 1.2 cobalt carbonate, gloss, medium blue glaze. Colour is the brightest blue of three tests.

Additional notes from the same glaze called Cobalt Green (from CM): Nice, rich, appealing. Unlike any green you've ever seen. Breaks white over raised decoration. Viscosity is important as glaze varies with thickness. Thick=bright green, medium=dark green, thin=grey-blue. I use Dave's porcelain from Laguna. Dean McRaine on the north shore of Kauai

recipes.name: Val Cushing Hunter/Forest Green
recipes.description: Recently, I was lucky enough to be given a great recipe for a cone 10 Albany-type clear with a nice glassy transparent surface. I believe it was one of Val Cushing's old glazes (what great glaze doesn't seem to have come from Val's extensive glaze coffers?!). Anyhow, having replaced the Albany with Alberta, I have been running color tests on this glaze for the past 6 months. Will it ever stop- I doubt it. One of the most interesting surfaces, both in color and in texture, was done with 5% Laguna Forest Green stain. I have no idea where this stain came from- unfortunately the bag looked rather old. Keep it pretty ding-dang thin, else you're likely to be chipping shelves. submitted by: Jeremy Nudell Kalin, e-mail:

recipes.name: Val Cushing Smooth Satin (+ Ochre)
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Cushing Handbook 1994 Smooth Satin/Mat Base Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 800C hold 1 hour Significant Flaw: crazing Notes: Alisa Clausen: glossy, transparent base, crazed badly on white midrange stoneware, oxides did not move under glaze. With 10 zirconia, glossy, white glaze, crazed on white midrange stoneware, oxides did not move under base. With 2 cobalt carbonate, glossy, dark blue glaze, no visible crazing. With 1 cobalt carbonate plus 2 chrome oxide, semigloss, dark green glaze, no visible crazing. With 1 copper carbonate, very glossy, transparent glaze, light green, crazed. With 10 ochre, slightly less glossy, ochre brown glaze, slight crazing. With 10 red iron oxide, slightly less glossy, dark brown glaze, no visible crazing. Notes: Steve Slatin: some of the Cushing glazes are formulated for the far edge of what works. My favourite, Rusty Bronze done as green runs at cone 6, and if you have a cool at all slow it gets very matte, but if you turn off your kiln at cone 5Â½ and do a fast cool, you get a fabulous mix of glossy where thick and microcrystalline with a nice texture shift where thin. And one percent of bentonite in the glaze bucket just changes it entirely.

recipes.name: Val Cushing's SCVC5
recipes.description: I added .2% Epsom Salts to this to improve raw glaze suspension. This glaze produced a misty affect, which I believe Eleanora Eden(?) was after some time ago. It was applied to Miller #15 Cone 6 Porcelain bisque. I fired to Cone 6 using an Orton Cone 7 centered in kiln sitter with no Guard Cones. The glaze was much as described by V.C. The semi-opacity produces a misty appearance over underglaze. The underglaze I used in the test was Duncan C154, Cobalt Navy Blue. After painting the UG onto the bisque, I re-fired to Cone 06. The glaze was applied over this in 1 & 2 coats by dipping, then fired to Cone 6. The underglaze showed through 1 or 2 coats with a better contrast under 2 coats. Lettering painted in underglaze onto the bisque showed through the glaze quite clearly. However, carving into the porcelain (also stoneware) clay surface was completely or partially obliterated under this glaze. If you carve designs onto a pot which will be covered by this glaze, you'll need to take measures not to let the carved marks be blocked back out. (Remove or prevent the glaze from covering areas where you want the carving to show.) Wax resist is harder to work with for this glaze, so I'd consider scratching or scraping off unwanted glaze. Fired to maturity, the glaze didn't run back into letters created by scratching into the raw glaze. In fact, where the scratched-in letters appeared over the dk. blue UG, they showed up very clearly, retaining a crisp edge. They stood out better against 2 coats (rather than 1) of glaze. This looks promising as a handy way to work with lettering or linear design. I got delayed crazing from this glaze over the Miller #15. None in evidence yet over Miller #55, which is a buff-white. stoneware, Cone 6-9 (this clay body doesn't perform well in microwave ovens). There also was some slight cratering of the glaze on Miller #15 where applied thickly. When 2 light coats of this glaze were poured over 2 light coats of Spinach Green, it was transmuted into an attractive semi-matt, waxy Lettuce Green (voila- a vitreous tossed salad. Come to think of it, I had one of those at Red Lobster not too long ago. There was lots of sand in it.). The base for Spinach Green, originally a Richard Behrens glaze, has been used by Peter King (see CM 12/85, p.36). It has a wide Cone range, incl. Spinach Green Gerstley Borate 50 EP Kaolin 15 Flint 35 Add: Chrome Oxide, 1-2% Testing done by Joyce Jackson

recipes.name: Van Guilder Wood Ash
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: John Britt, High Fire Glazes Significant Flaw: Ivor Lewis: unwashed wood ash glaze contains a large volume of potash-rich water. Potash is the principle melting agent in this recipe. If you apply this to bisque ware the potash rich solution will soak into the porous fired clay and make no contribution to the bulk of the glaze. Furthermore, once potash reaches its melting point it will react with silica forming potassium silicate and discharging carbon dioxide. This will cause cratering and blistering. Significant Flaw: Craig Martell: very low in both alumina and silica and will overfire and run. Notes: Ingeborg Foco: I did some tests and I liked the results. The ash was maple, Douglas fir, scrub oak and 2x4s (spruce,pine,fir), unwashed. Then I made a larger batch and had horrible results. Most of the pots ran heavily and had large craters and or blisters. Notes: Lee Love: thin test tiles pick up much less of the glaze than the thickness of your average pot.

recipes.name: VC/Easy Glossy
recipes.description: This glaze has an interesting history. A member of WCAC, Nancy Alt, had visited Val Cushing's home and purchased a vase with a lovely blue-green celadon glaze. Nancy asked Val if he could share the glaze recipe, and he not only shared it but converted it from cone 9 to cone 6 (the temperature Nancy was firing). Val's email is copied below. It shows the extremely generous nature of this amazing potter and teacher: From: Val Cushing Subject: Re: celedon glaze Date: May 12, 2009 at 12:46:57 PM EDT To: Nancy Alt Dear Nancy, This glaze is one I made for C/9 oxidation electric firing, so that it would appear to be a blue green celadon. I have revised it for you to be the same color and texture only for C/6 ox. electric . I will give you two to try , first VC Pale Emerald, C/6 , glossy , blue/green , celadon looking. as follows.......... Kona F/4 feldspar 24, Ferro Frit 3134 24, Dolomite 4, whiting 14, barium carbonate 2, zinc oxide 2, flint 24, and EPK 6. ADD TO THAT , 1/2 % COPPER CARBONATE for blue green. VC/easy glossy, C/6 ox. , electric , celadon looking , green. Cornwall Stone 46, Gerstley Borate 20, Ferro Frit 3124 26, Ball Clay 8. --- add 2% copper carb. and 1/2 % red iron oxide for celadon looking green color. Test these two Nancy and if the color is not exactly what you expected let me know and we can make a revision. We may have different "tastes" about color , but we can get what you want...My pale emerald should be quite a bit like the glaze on the jar of mine you now have. and THANK YOU . Val

Resultados : Sobre biscocho de arcilla roja genera esmalte brilloso liso blando translucido . Sobre biscocho de arcilla blanca se aprecia un color MIEL con bordes negruzcos. (Digo BLANDO porque chorrea debido a su bajo contenido de alumina). EN AMBOS CASOS SE APRECIAN ABUNDANTES VENTURINAS. sE DEBE APLICAR EN CAPA GRUESA. Talvez seja a minha queima, embora ambos façam o cone 6 a minha queima é diferente. Mas ficou bem interessante. Não a cor, mas a aparência é do "menta ou hortelã"... recipes.name: Verde Claro (Custer/EPK)
recipes.description: Used Target and Solve to sub in custer feldspar and EPK. The test batch was very runny at 1.46 specific gravity, so I added .75 ml epsom salts solution to my 100g batch. It thickened up considerably and I think the application was too thick. You can clearly see the difference between the first and second dip, and the butter yellow on the thin parts is quite nice. Pinholing likely due to thickness of application. They were also fired with other glazed pieces using the 'controlled cool" option on my kiln. Would be interesting to try it again with a regular cool. Also worth adjusting the density/viscosity and trying again.

recipes.name: Veronica's Shino Test
recipes.description: Shino glaze, this is a test, it has never been tried. The high amount of ball clay obviously makes it almost impossible to apply on the pot, even if part of the kaolin is substituted by calcined kaolin, or adding water and sodium silicate. Another approach must be pursued to reach the ideal ratio of silica and alumina Update after firing the glaze was fired in a wood kiln for approx. 12 hrs, reduction from 1000°C to 1280°C no hold, natural cooling. It was applied thicker on the crevices of the jar's lid, and cracks could be observed already when in the unfired state. When applied thin the fired glaze is dry, where thicker and fired it goes from fairly crawled to totally crawled and warped. In attempting to make it more thin i added a fair amount of sodium silicate, not measured, and unmeasured amount of tap water. The day after mixing the glaze wasn't gooey anymore and could be applied better, still the high amount of water caused the cracks. The dry result was probably due to the lack of soluble sodium/lithium travelling on the surface of the pot. Also the dry result appears only on the once fired ware, not sure if this is due to the thinner layer or the raw state of the ware.

recipes.name: Vickie's Barnard
recipes.description: kiln type: electric Cone 9 and 6, clay: Plainsman M460 and H430, electric fire, applied to bisque. ALberta slip: At cone 9 Alberta by itself it makes a rich chocolate brown. It's too refractory to work at cone 6 by itself, I was told, so I didn't test it.I added 30% Gerstley borate which was the wrong thing to do, as Alberta is very glassy to begin with, but I had intended to test at cone 6 as well so I tested for both 6 and 9. I didn't really like the result at cone 6 with the gerstley, as it was a frosty transparent olive green (at cone 9 it was a RUNNY transparent olive green. Adding Manganese or cobalt to the Alberta slip would probably give a really nice black. What I left out in making this one was Gerstley 10 (Rob uses Colemanite), but what I ended up with was a stony black with very tiny brown specks. Tends to crawl if too thick. Rob's recipe was great too, and that one SHOULD be thick, he says. His recipe also works on greenware, he said, but I haven't tried it yet. submitted by: Vickie Sproule e-mail:

recipes.name: Vintage Celadon
recipes.description: Having problems with Adam Field's Antique Celadon re oxidizing in the kiln as it fires down. This recipe aimed to make it fit more in line with Stull and so far hasn't been coming out a nasty brown. It also no longer runs. Some downsides though, the glaze isn't forming the wonderful pools of glass that the original recipe could but the color and texture are all super consistent. More testing and variations to come!

recipes.name: Viscous Purple

recipes.name: Viscous Red
recipes.description: This is a modified version of Coleman I, a chun-type blue celadon found in John Britt's Cone 10 Glaze Book. Recognizing that this recipe contained the same level of calcium and gerstley borate as an copper red, I decided to try it out as a base for a flambe-red type glaze. I was pleasantly surprised to find it made a deep crimson field, speckled with faint blue wisps, while remaining quite stiff in comparison to other reds at cone 10. The barium and zinc band together to create the flambe wisps.

If soaked in muriatic acid, the glaze will develop an oil slick like sheen that can be easily seen under bright light. I would consider this a more decorative rather than functional glaze. recipes.name: Waterfall brown
recipes.description: Are you tired of glazes that only look one way all the time anywhere any way you do them? Fret no longer. Waterfall brown, Made by John Hesselberth and Ron Roy in their book Mastering Cone 6 Glazes, has proven incredibly versitile. It can be a earthy brown/black when put on thinner or on a brown clay\ It can be a glossy swampy green with amber flashes where it breaks on a white clay I've seen yellow where it pools, ive seen brown, black, green, and yellow on the same pot Highly dependent on clay and thickness applied, my gold standard is 1.40 specific gravity. displays texture wonderfully, doesnt work as well with very fine texture . opaque on darker clay, glossier and more transparent on lighter clay See how it looks for your clay! Apply this glaze 50 times and get 50 diffrent results.

recipes.name: Waxy Matt Blue
recipes.description: from Bonnie Terry. Satin glaze. solid brown where thin to medium. Mottled breaking blues browns and gold. Well I finally got around to typing this thing up...^9-10 Blues Thank you one and all for all the donated recipes. I only tested 31 out of almost 100 I received. I'll continue testing and reporting as the winter DRAGS on. All the glazes were tested on #900 Miller clay which is a toasty ^10 stoneware. One side of the test tile was brushed with a thick coating of Cynthia Bringle's wet/dry white slip. Each glaze was dipped in three thicknesses on a heavily textured tile. All tiles were fired to a (hard)^9 (10 tipping)reduction firing. 1 hr. Body reduction at ^08 and 1 hr. glaze reduction at ^9 then a quick reox. before shutdown. Any time potash or Custer spar is called for, I used G-200. All ball clay is OM-4 . Many glazes I substituted 75% of the amount of Barium with Strontium. All kaolin is EPK. Remember... glazes don't travel well. Your results will probably be TOTALLY different. Please test before use. Tracy Wilson Saltbox Pottery 4 Shaw Rd. Woolwich, ME 04579 phone: 207-443-5586 fax: 207-442-8922 email: web: http://www.ime.net/dwilson/

recipes.name: WCAC Clear Celadon
recipes.description: Wellsville Creative Arts Center (WCAC) "Clear Celadon". This glaze has an interesting history. A member of WCAC, Nancy Alt, had visited Val Cushing's home and purchased a vase with a lovely blue-green celadon glaze. Nancy asked Val if he could share the glaze recipe, and he not only shared it but converted it from cone 9 to cone 6 (the temperature Nancy was firing). It shows the extremely generous nature of this amazing potter and teacher. For the original glaze recipe and Val's email, please see https://glazy.org/recipes/21133

recipes.name: Weathered Bronze
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Strontium matt Periwinkle: 1.5% cobalt carb. + 4% copper carb. From Pete Pinnell via Posey Bacopoulos. Soft satiny goldish green.See article Clay Times Jan/Feb 04 p.17. This is the same glaze as Strontium Matte Pete Pinnell, a cone 10 glaze. Not using colorants, or using refractory colorants can make this glaze underfired at cone 6.

recipes.name: Weathered Bronze Green
recipes.description: From Lakeside Pottery http://www.lakesidepottery.com/Pages/Glaze-recipes-at-Lakeside-Pottery.htm Need to mix really well before dipping. Weathered green when thick, breaks bronze. NOT FOOD SAFE! CAN RUN A LOT – WAX UP AT LEAST ½” or more! Make sure you stir well! This is THE MOST DIFFICULT glaze to stir. If not mixed properly the pot will come out brown.

recipes.name: Weathered Bronze Green with Fluoride
recipes.description: An adaptation of Pete Pinnell's Weathered Bronze Green, for a slow-cool at 50 F per hour between 1,800 F and 1,500 F. This was originally a Cone 10 glaze. The Lithium Fluoride and Ferro Frit 3269 helps make this glaze more reliable melting at Cone 6. Due to the 60% Nepheline Syenite with only 10% clay, this glaze badly needs a flocculant like Calcium Chloride or Ammonium Sulfate.

recipes.name: Westcountry slate
recipes.description: This is a 50/50 blend of cornish slate and devon slate. For me, this looks almost identical to devon slate. This recipe attempts to keep the RO:R20 ratio at the same level as HSCM. Some of the calcium is replaced with Magnesium sourced from the GB. There are versions with 12.5, 6.25 and 0% cornish stone. This is because the amount of flux and alumina in Kaolins can vary significantly - your millage will vary it's best to test all three. Variation 2 is a 5050 blend of the other versions, so is easy to add to your tests. This is part of a set of glazes. Your milage will vary: Cornish slate has 12.5 cornish stone: https://glazy.org/recipes/9415 Devon slate has no cornish stone: https://glazy.org/recipes/9468 Westcountry slate is a blend of devon and cornish slate with 6.25% cornish stone: https://glazy.org/recipes/9469 Also works as a base for oilspot with autumn crystal matte on top.

recipes.name: WH Star Dust
recipes.description: This is the original Randy's Red recipe without Bone ash. Due to the change in Talc and Gerstley Borate chemistry, you can't get the red color the same way as the original recipe. This produces a shiny dark brown glaze. With the addition of Vermiculite, this glaze has really nice Temmoku gold look to it without any special cooling. Vermiculite can be purchased from gardening store, Ebay, or even packaging company like Uline. I bought the coarse version and grind it down with a 100 mesh sieve. Wear a respirator when doing this.

recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Hal Whinnie Notes: Alisa Clausen: A smooth, semi matte, white glaze. Opaque where thickest, and milky where thinner. Soft white all over with an even surface. Close to a waxy surface, a little drier.

recipes.description: Daniel de Montmollin (French potter) did a lot of research on base glazes. He wrote some nice very interesting books all in French... https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/DanieldeMontmollin In his triangular scheme he distinguished 60 types of base glazes. Each time we tried to find a 'good' base glaze in the central part of his chart. (for more background https://ledouget.fr/#methodehtoc6)

I am sure the test with these opacifiers in different proportions will alter the overall surface and colour response of this glaze. With 4 rutile, white gloss with slight yellow cast. recipes.name: White Gartside 28 (+10 Tin)
recipes.description: This is Brian Gartsides famous clear parts recipe. I broke it down in to weight because I work better that way. I calculated it by simple division: 4 into 100, 2 into 25 and 2 into 12.5, then rounded up on Glaze Master. I left it at totaling 98 because I did not want 4 decimal places. Original in parts 4 Frit 3134 4 EPK 2 G-200 Feldspar 2 Silica 1 Talc 1 Whiting 16 Water Now in weight Amount Ingredient 28.6 Frit--Ferro 3124 4 parts 28.6 Kaolin--EPK 14.3 Feldspar--G-200 2 parts 14.3 Silica 7.1 Talc 1 part 7.1 Whiting 100 Total Unity Oxide .138 Na2O .074 K2O .204 MgO .584 CaO 1.000 Total .6 Al2O3 .212 B2O3 .006 Fe2O3 3.562 SiO2 .004 TiO2 .001 P2O5 5.9 Ratio 6.5 Exp Results Gloss to semi gloss transluscent glaze See color variations at website, Glaze tests, more tests www.alisapots.dk My parts base tests crazed on my stoneware. However the weight variation did not. I think it because my parts measuring by spoon full was much too variable. Best regards from Alisa in Denmark

recipes.name: White Hanlin's Gloss
recipes.description: I've tried other opacifiers, all seem to be the same chemically but I've always liked what Ultrox did on this glaze. (There's that ingredient again, I haven't tried the .75 Strontium Carb actor but don't think it would make much difference, if you try it I'd like to know the results) The following glaze meets all your specs except the one about crazing. It's a good glaze that I formulated in my Ceramics I class at University of Central Oklahoma way back there. It is very dependable, doesn't run, you can use a brush over it or under it (with a bit of understandable muting), colors stay in place, it's glossy, I use it in reduction but in oxidation it loses a bit of character due to the really white look, You can use it as a base for wax resist with glazes or oxides over. It's the only glaze I've used continually for the past 30 years and on many different bodies. I like it and like what it does. If you try it I hope that you like it too! Enjoy>>>>>>>>>>> PS...Take Rhodes 32, color it with 1% cobalt oxide and 4% red iron, apply it over this glaze and get a really neat semi-mat blue. The white sort of bubbles through the blue and it's pretty. I guess by now you maybe think I like it....OK I DO these are Bob Hanlin

recipes.name: White Pete's Charlie Ian Anderson
recipes.description: Glaze Type: Magnesium matt From Pete Pinnell, Clay Times Mar/Apr 2005 p. 21. The phosphorus contributes a number of qualifies to the glaze. It is a glass-former (like the silica), but the phosphorus and silica don't like to mix together (sort of like oil and water). This means that in the firing, the phosphorus tends to separate out and form a cloudy, slightly opalescent milkiness that I find very interesting. It also has a strong tendency to re-oxidize colorants in a glaze, which can result in unusual, vivid colors that have the richness of reduction firing, combined with the intensity of oxidation colors. A side effect of the phosphorus is that the glaze now resists going matte. It will if pushed—that is, if the cooling is slow enough, or if the piece is refired in a bisque kiln to allow enough time for the matting crystals to grow. Otherwise, it is a glossy glaze. The next step (after coming up with the base glaze) was to try out all the common glaze colorants and see what they did in this glaze. The results are fascinating, and many are beautiful. I'm currently in the process of developing more complex colors involving multiple oxides, and I'll pass those along in a future column. If you've ever mixed a tomato red glaze, you'll notice that it always includes a source of magnesium (such as talc or dolomite) and either natural or synthetic bone ash (a source of phosphorus). Together with iron and the other components, these create iron crystals, and push them into an oxidized state. As I suspected it would, Pete's CIA produces a bright tomato red with 7 or 8% red iron oxide. As the amount of iron increases to 10 or 11%, the glaze becomes quite crystalline, but just a bit more brown. The red can be made brighter by refiring it (after the glaze firing) in a bisque firing, or in any low-fire oxidation firing.2 Manganese dioxide makes a beautiful yellow (really!) in small percentages, becoming a creamy red-amber at higher percentages. Copper carbonate, which normally wants to turn a pink or red color in reduction, instead produces light blue-green to emerald green. It works from 1 to 9%. Titanium dioxide or ruffle produce very nice breaking and mottling, working best at 4 and 5%. The effect shows up best on stoneware, but also works well on porcelain with the addition of a small amount of another oxide (iron or copper, for instance) in addition to the titania. Tin oxide produces white at smaller percent-ages, which begins to break rust on edges (even on porcelain) as it nears 10%, with very pronounced cream and orange colors pro- duced on stoneware at 10% and 12%. Like the iron colors I mentioned above, it will become more orange when refired in a bisque or other low-fire oxidation firing. Frankly, I thought the results from cobalt and chrome were very boring, but that might be my taste in colors. Cobalt produced pasty, pastel blues. Chrome was nice in very tiny amounts—0.3% made a nice, very light blue-green, but larger amounts produced dull greenish browns. Please keep in mind that this is a new glaze, and I don't have extensive experience with it. I've used it (in several color variations) in a half dozen or so firings, and it is very promising, but I have yet to work out all the bugs of application and firing.

recipes.name: White/Colored Underglaze
recipes.description: Read Vince Pitelka's pdf (pic #4 and #5, see pictures) All the frits work nicely. The one with 3134 seems more melted. Works nice from low fire to mid fire. Didn't test at hight fire. Leer atentamente todas las notas y las fotos. Todas las fritas parecen funcionar perfectamente. Se adapta de baja temperatura a media temperatura (desde conos 05 a 7). Todavía no lo probé en alta temperatura (conos 8 y arriba) Origen: Pdf de Vince Pitelka, Appalachian Center for Crafts. La receta proviene de Mason Color Works de Liverpool, Ohio, fabricantes de Mason ceramic stains. Pasado a sistema métrico, las recetas quedan como sigue: Materiales Secos para base de Underglaze blanca Feldespato sódico      40 gr Caolín                            20 gr Arcilla de bola              10 gr 3124 Frita                      20 gr Silicato de Circonio     10 gr Total                             100 gr Agregar líquido para underglaze: 150 gr (en peso, no en volumen) Para Underglaze colorida, agregar a lo anterior:  Pigmento cerámico: 80 gr Procedimiento 1. Mezclar los ingredientes secos 2. Agregar 3/4 del líquido para underglaze, mezclar y colar muy bien. 3. Agregar el resto del líquido hasta encontrar el punto justo para aplicación. Quizá no sea necesario usar todo el líquido. 4. En el caso de agregar pigmento, hacerlo por último, revolviendo y tamizando muy bien. De acuerdo a la tonalidad deseada, quizá no sea necesario agregar la totalidad de los 80 gr. Quizá sea necesario agregar más líquido para underglaze. Otras recetas necesarias CMC líquido Agua caliente: 1 litro (1000 cc) CMC: 30 g Batir, mezclar, colar Líquido para underglaze , por volumen Propilenglicol       2 partes ----> 400 cc Agua                      2 partes ----> 400 cc CMC líquido          1 parte   ----> 200 cc Total                       5 partes ----> 1000 cc (1 litro)

Mat, smooth and covering glaze. Colour ranges from a deep and bright blue where thickest to a turquoise where thinner. I wanted to see if a glaze made up a glaze core, nepheline syenite and an alkaline earth flux, barium carbonate, and no boron, could fire higher and not run off the test. It succeeded. It seems that this combination could be fired even higher. At 1220C feels and looks mature.

recipes.name: Wilson Red Moss
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Ceramic Arts Buyers Guide, 2007 Lana Wilson Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 900C hold 1 hour Significant Flaw: runs Notes: Alisa Clausen: fired to cone 6. Use 3% manganese for light orange, 6% for strong orange and 10% for a dark red. Apply thickly, up to 1/4 inch to yield red, thinner yields black. As pretty much expected, at cone 6 the glaze ran off the test tile (which was only glazed 1/3 of the way down) and pooled at the bottom edge of the upright tile. I was just interested to see how much.

recipes.name: Wilson Textured Crawl
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Bacia Edelman credited to Lana Wilson Source/Alternate names: similar oxides to Dry White 1 Firing Notes: cool maximum rate to 1100C hold 1 hour Significant Flaw: crawls Notes: Alisa Clausen: Application is crucial to get this glaze to crawl. It must be applied thickly enough that there are slight cracks in the dried surface. I brushed it on. Glossy, white islands, like drops of school glue (Elmer for the Americans). The individual islands were different in overall sizes, from 1cm or less to a healthy 2 centimeters in diameter. They are varied in shape from round to oblong. The islands sit high above the clay surface and are smooth to the touch. Over a commercial 04 black, the glaze melted into the glaze, still forming distinct islands. The island edges are more geometric, like oatmeal, however still very distinct. The are not as raised as the Texture crawl by itself, but still raised about the surface of the black glaze. The black glaze pooled and formed a border around each island. Over Lili Krakowski Albany Slip substitution, the glaze is more covering and is more lichen like as opposed to raised islands. The overall surface is a labyrinth of white flattened shapes of all forms, revealing the slip only where the shapes are separated by their crevice like borders. The glaze lies almost flat, but has a very distinct lichen pattern like the pattern of our brain tissue. Lana sprays it on.

recipes.name: Wine Red
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Clay Times, March/April 2005 Richard Burkett Source/Alternate names: similar oxides to Rodgers Wine Purple, Edwards Red and Chrome Tin Red-Green Notes: Alisa Clausen: a semigloss red. I was surprised by the depth of colour. It is a deep wine red. It broke more or less clear where it is thin, making a mottled red/body-colour covering. I think this glaze will be exciting to try on a porcelain for a fake reduced red. Needs to be applied evenly for dark colour, such as dipped. Smooth surface. The Clay Times version added 0.25 cobalt carbonate.

recipes.name: Wolff Cream Gloss
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Ceramics Monthly, May 2000 Chris Wolff Notes: Alisa Clausen: used Cornwall stone for P.V. Clay. An opaque cream under very shiny clear. Interesting structure under the gloss. Nice flat surface, evenly melted. When applied over Wolff Plum, a shiny, smooth honey brown gloss, with beautiful opalescent breaking over the high areas and where it pooled, beautiful, fluid changes of colour all over the vessel. I mixed my batch a little thick to test for dripping and even with two layers of reasonably thick glazes, it pooled to a bright opalescence, but did not drip off the foots of the pots. I am really impressed with this combination as it is the type of surface I personally like very much for decorative vessels.

recipes.name: Wolff Light Blue
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Ceramics Monthly May, 2000 Notes: Alisa Clausen: CM says a speckled blue, produces a variety of blues and browns when used with Plum and Cream. A stable, gloss bluish/grey even glaze for me. Over Wolff Plum, it did its thing as described in the Ceramics Monthly, with a lot of nice streaking and opalescence like blues and pooling. The light blue on its own is a nice dove grey and it gives a very nice falling and streaking over the plum.

recipes.name: Wolff Plum
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Ceramics Monthly, May 2000 Chris Wolff Notes: Alisa Clausen: A speckled deep brown with rust and light brown specks, very shiny and smooth surface. It fired evenly from thinner to thicker, no different breaking colour.

recipes.name: Woo Blue Brown
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Robert or Marie Woo Ceramics Monthly (1975) Notes: Richard Aerni: it goes that iron/rutile blue where the application is of medium thickness, and where thinner breaks brown. I used it as a base glaze which was then wax resisted and the pot was then dipped into a glossy white, which overlay it and broke it up a bit. Notes: Barb Bihler: Apply medium to slightly thicker. This glaze goes brown if very thin, orangey-brown if thin, blue breaking to brown if medium, gets bright purplish overtones and very fat looking if thick. Runs badly if very thick. Notes: Dave Eitel: found it very temperamental

recipes.description: I took Nigel Wood's glaze and Derek Au's substitution of Grolleg and Mahavir feldspar and recalculated the chemistry with Custer feldspar. I got really got good results. This is that recipe, here's the info from Derek's entry. On page 266 of Nigel Wood's excellent book, Chinese Glazes. Glaze 9. Jun glaze 1280-1300 degrees reduction. The chemical analysis is listed as: SiO2 68.2 Al2O3 10.8 TiO2 -.- Fe2O3 1.8 CaO 10.3 MgO 1.6 K2O 5.1 Na2O 1.3 P2O5 0.9 Notes: Inge Nielsen URL: http://mypottery.blog.com/glaze-tests-and-recipes/10-jun-chun-glaze-tests/ Conclusion: This must be applied thickly – two dips. It´s a good light blue but I would like a little more glassy and less fatty surface. Correction: Actually very pretty indeed. Must be applied to the right thickness.

May 2016: This variation was to try to eliminate the crazing, which did not happen. I was disappointed by the amount of brown that comes through from my white stoneware. recipes.description: from the 11/2017 issue of ceramics monthly - using rare earths at cone 6. link here: https://ceramicartsnetwork.org/ceramics-monthly/ceramic-supplies/ceramic-glazes-and-underglazes/techno-file-rare-earths-cone-6/# add 7% neodymium oxide

recipes.name: WTF Purple
recipes.description: This was a glaze I found here: https://ceramicartsnetwork.org/daily/ceramic-glaze-recipes/mid-range-glaze-recipes/rare-earth-metals-cone-6/ My experience with it is that its a little too runny. I may tamper with the formula a little to make it stiffer and incorporate some barium or lithium in it to enhance the color, since I will be using it primarily with sculpture. It was a great introduction to dichroic glazes, and works with Holmium oxide as well. This glaze is purple under daylight and blue under fluorescent lights. (See photos 1, 2). You must use grolleg for the kaolin and apply it on a porcelain clay body. Iron will contaminate the glaze and grey the color out.

recipes.name: WTF Yellow
recipes.description: I got the base for this glaze here: https://ceramicartsnetwork.org/daily/ceramic-glaze-recipes/mid-range-glaze-recipes/rare-earth-metals-cone-6/ I used "WTF Purple" and substituted Holmium oxide for the colorant. It has a lemonade - yellow color in daylight, and a hot - pink color under fluorescent lights. Holmium oxide is MUCH more expensive than Neodymium oxide, but it is a fantastic color. I recommend testing glaze bases out with Neodymium first, then if it works, make a batch with Holmium as a substitute. Use only grolleg in this glaze body, and apply it to porcelain only. Iron will contaminate this glaze and grey it out. I found this recipe too fluxy for my purposes, so I think I'll stiffen it a bit and add different colorant enhancers to see if I can get a stronger color response.

recipes.description: Golden Yellow. From: Sankey DB/ Ron Roy Original comment: base glaze is waxy, covering, white. (a) With 3 rutile, smooth surface, slight crystals and opalescence where thickest.(b) With 8 titania, overall golden yellow (c) With 3 manganese dioxide and 3 rutile, overall yellow tan ground with pinkish white fur where thickest. With 3 manganese dioxide and 3 titania, overall tan ground with whitish fur where thickest With 3 manganese dioxide, light tan ground and pinkish where thickest I used a modification by combining (b) & (c). Not very satisfactory. Perhaps it needs to be applied very thickly. Or my raw materials are of a different composition. Difficult to call it 'Golden Yellow'. Worth to try with raw materials of another source.

recipes.name: WWW 404
recipes.description: Green with mottled yellow Source: Linda Arbuckle An interesting semi-matte (with my raw materials and firing conditions)giving a deep green where thick (pooled) lighter shades where thin, down to yellow patches. Possible crystallization. Other oxides possible: Original comment from L. Arbuckle / Debra Drencicki: With 4% manganese and 0.5% Cobalt Carbonate a brown bronzey type of gun metal underneath. With 1.5% Copper Carbonate and 0.5% Cobalt Carbonate it is a blue green. With 1% copper carbonate and 6% rutile it is a terrific green with mottled yellow. This combination has been made a studio glaze and we have named it 'sea Foam' It is especially stunning on dark red clay bodies.

recipes.name: Yellow Celadon
recipes.description: This glaze is absolutely beautiful, even though its roots are in imperfection. On page 54 of "Chinese Glazes", Nigel Wood notes that "accidentally oxidised wares were sold at a discount.... the native dealers sell them under the name of huang diao". (This account may come from the Southern Song ceramic historian Jiang Qi, writing in the Tao ji 《陶记》) This is my version of an oxidized celadon, or "黄掉" (huang diao) glaze. The color is from iron. In reduction this glaze would be a qingbai-type blue celadon. This glaze is also reminiscent of Creamware, perhaps a bit less Red Iron Oxide would be better for that effect. This recipe is originally based on the old Faux Celadon 2, which I used for a biaxial testing the effect of Zinc and Silicon Carbide on oxidation locally-reduced celadons. Happily I found that just adding a bit of iron to the base glaze produced this lovely celadon. I used this glaze with my cone 6 porcelain body.

recipes.name: Yellow Celadon (Modified)

It produced a color very similar to Turner's celadon, but it tends to bread lighter and more subtle on the high points, and really dark in the low points. Its a good one for showing off relief and texture! It is a little runny though.

recipes.name: Yellow Seto Leach
recipes.description: comments: Seems to be better on porcelain. Some- times bright yellow, sometimes browner depends on mineral content of the ash which varies from wood to wood. Darker and more opaque where thin goes to almost black. Yellow where thicker. Keep glaze thin or you will be scraping shelves. Becomes transparent yellowish brown and very fluid when thickly applied. The mid way thin/thick of application is mottled like a salt fired piece and is satin matte. But I got great reds, yellows, browns, blacks on pieces where it's thinner. To make tiny rivers of ash I make the same glaze substituting Red Art for the Ochre and trail it on with a slip trail bulb. Caution: use rubber gloves with unwashed ash glazes or face the possibility of contact dermatitis. It will mildly burn the skin. I keep Cornhuskers lotion and Hydrocortisone cream around the house anyway. I layer it with a glossy, glassy glaze that by itself has its own problems like keeping me up at night to the sound of loudly cooling and crazing pings I use a glaze with wood ash. I don't wash the ash, but I do screen it. The woodash has to be soft, white, fluffy. Not from a wood kiln! That kind is sintered and won't get the best results. You can tell it will feel crispy at first. I'm not taking responsibility for anyone using these glazes, etc. Something is probably toxic. They are examples of my research and they work out in formulation. Which is what they are examples of. So go formulate your own non-toxic glazes, if that is possible. It's probably bad for the environment too. Email me with questions as to household performance, as that may be indicative of other problems. The badly crazed surfaces are not considered to be a continous-non porous sanitary surfaces. Eric Hansen, Lawrence, Kansas

recipes.name: Zirconia 50/50 Slip
recipes.description: Source/Alternate names: Stephanie Significant Flaw: splitting Notes: Alisa Clausen: a soft looking, but hard as stone rough, textured but smooth to touch surface. This slip is very interesting, because you can paint it on and then, if you choose to brush some off or scratch into it, the slip holds your markings. It can be applied very thickly and I got some splitting in the surface, but is very well attached to pot. Looks rocky and porous where thickest and whiter and more translucent where thinnest. I cannot describe all the variables and nuances of this slip. It is very exciting and gives a subtle but screaming gorgeous surface over my orange clay body. It colours well and it is possible to colour with stains and paints after the firings. It is porous in some areas where really thick and I am sure very receptive to that sort of after firing handling. Where it came in contact with ToDo white matt, it fused well to give yet another surface, a matt, smooth hard surface. Excellent with colorants that are fluxes. Cobalt gave it a slightly more melted surface, with a grey and blue colour, good feel, handsome, understated blue. Stains fire more or less to the same colour they are in the slurry, but dry as the original surface.

recipes.description: В тонком слое медовая. В среднем слое серо-синяя (иногда до фиолетового) дымка. В толстом слое оливковая (иногда до голубого) дымка. Толще слой! 2 окунания по 5 секунд с перерывом в 5 минут. Да, потечёт, но потечёт красиво. Медленное остывание даст на этой глазури интересные эффекты.

recipes.name: 🏝 Kujukuri Turquoise 2

ingredients.material: 無鉛フリット Lead-free Frit (Tougei shop)
朝鮮カオリン Korean Kaolin
炭酸ストロンチウム Strontium carbonate

recipes.description: It is very glossy, has a lower thermal expansion than before and has a good fluidity. The extended UMF R2O:RO is 40:60 instead of 42:58 so it is slightly too green for me but I will soon publish Kujukuri turquoise 3. I made a huge series of of the same glaze named Kujukuri turquoise. Each one has a different R2O:RO ratio to get different turquoise hues. This one is 0.4:0.6. My first revision: https://glazy.org/recipes/243877 The original from Barbara Nowak: https://glazy.org/materials/211865 This is my unfinished quest to get more blue hues and more shine from my previous Simple Oribe experiment 🧪. I want an intense blue turquoise with a good fluidity! To increase the blue, I added zinc and shifted the RO:R2O ratio towards the alkali side. Zinc will increase the fluidity significantly. The strontium carbonate, in moderate amounts should intensify the color and the shine.
